title: What is this about?
text: Think about the heater in your room. You turn a knob to say what you want ("I want it warm"), something happens inside the heater, and the room temperature changes. Three things are involved: what you ask for , the device that acts, and what you get . Control engineering is the study of how to make what you get match what you asked for, reliably, even when the world interferes (somebody opens a window, the heater ages, the outside temperature drops). This first lecture sets up the vocabulary and the single most important idea of the whole course: feedback . You will see that: - every control system can be drawn as blocks connected by signals (input → system → output); - systems are classified by their signals (continuous or discrete), by how many inputs and outputs they have (SISO or MIMO), and by whether they use feedback (open loop or closed loop); - a closed-loop system measures its own output, compares it with the desired value, and acts on the difference (the error); - for the standard negative-feedback loop, a few lines of algebra give the key result $T=\dfrac{C}{R}=\dfrac{G}{1+GH}$; - the same algebra shows why feedback makes a system accurate and why it reduces the effect of disturbances (noise) by the factor $1+G aG bH$. Before any terminology, keep this picture in mind: a closed-loop system is like driving a car while looking at the road . An open-loop system is like driving with your eyes closed after having planned the steering in advance. If nothing unexpected happens, both might work; as soon as something changes, only the first one corrects itself. After this module you can: - explain what a control system does and give physical examples from the notes; - classify a system as continuous/discrete, SISO/MIMO, open/closed loop; - draw and label the open-loop and closed-loop block diagrams with the Turkish names used in the notes; - compare open-loop and closed-loop systems (the table on p. 6); - derive $C/R=G/(1+GH)$ step by step and use it with numbers; - derive the disturbance transfer functions $C/N=G b$ (open loop) and $C/N=G b/(1+G aG bH)$ (closed loop) and explain physically why feedback suppresses disturbances; - combine reference and disturbance effects by superposition. In this module the blocks $G$, $H$, $G a$, $G b$ can be treated as constant gains (plain numbers). The algebra is exactly the same when they are transfer functions $G(s)$, $H(s)$ — that is what the $(s)$ on pages 8–9 hints at. Transfer functions are introduced in [Module 02]( /m/02), the Laplace transform in [Module 03]( /m/03), and the reduction of bigger block diagrams in [Module 04]( /m/04).

title: What is a control system?
text: The notes start with the simplest possible picture: A system whose job is to produce the desired output function in response to the applied input function . The input (and output) can be of any physical nature: an electrical voltage ( elektriksel gerilim ), a mechanical force ( mekanik kuvvet ), an optical light source ( optik ışık kaynağı )… The words and will appear on every page of the course. (Note that "Giriş" is also the title of this lecture — "Introduction". Same word, two meanings: entrance / input .) Some concrete readings of the block: Input (giriş) Control system Output (çıkış) --- --- --- Voltage applied to a motor Motor + drive electronics Shaft speed Force on the brake pedal Braking system Deceleration of the car Brightness setting (light) Lamp + dimmer Light intensity in the room Thermostat setting Heater / cooler Room temperature A block is a cause → effect machine. The arrow into it is the cause (what we apply), the arrow out of it is the effect (what we observe). Everything later in the course — transfer functions, stability, responses — is about describing precisely how a block turns its input into its output. The notes then say that control systems can be classified according to different parameters ( Kontrol sistemlerini farklı parametrelere göre sınıflandırabiliriz ).

title: Classifying control systems
text: The notes give three classifications.

title: Continuous-time / discrete-time control systems
tr: Sürekli zamanlı / Ayrık zamanlı kontrol sistemleri

title: Continuous-time vs discrete-time
text: This distinction is made according to the type of signal being considered ( ele alınan sinyalin türüne göre ). - Continuous-time : signals have a value at every instant $t$ — e.g. the voltage across a capacitor, the temperature of a room, the speed of a car. Mathematically $x(t)$ with $t$ real. - Discrete-time : signals exist only at separate instants, usually every $T s$ seconds — e.g. a temperature that a microcontroller reads 10 times per second. Mathematically $x[k]=x(kT s)$. The course title, Sayısal Denetim (digital control), tells you discrete time will matter later; but the notes are explicit about where we start (see below).

title: SISO / MIMO control systems
tr: Tek girişli tek çıkışlı / Çok girişli çok çıkışlı

title: SISO vs MIMO
text: A classification according to the number of input–output ports of the system ( giriş-çıkış port sayısına göre ). SISO = Single Input Single Output; MIMO = Multi Input Multi Output. - SISO example: a room heater with one setting (input) and one temperature (output). - MIMO example: a climate-control unit that controls temperature and humidity using a heater and a humidifier — two inputs, two outputs, and each input affects both outputs.

title: Open-loop / closed-loop control systems
tr: Açık çevrim / Kapalı çevrim kontrol sistemleri

title: Open-loop vs closed-loop
text: A classification according to whether feedback is used in the system or not ( geri-besleme kullanılıp kullanılmaması durumuna göre ). This is the classification the rest of the lecture is about. " Öncelikli olarak sürekli zamanlı, tek giriş tek çıkışlı sistemler ele alınacaktır. " — First, continuous-time, single-input single-output systems will be studied. So unless told otherwise, assume continuous time and SISO.

title: Open-loop systems
text: A control system in which feedback is not used ( geri-besleme kullanılmayan kontrol sistemi ). Its general structure ( genel yapısı ): - : takes the input (the command) and produces the signal that drives the plant. - : the signal the controller applies to the system — e.g. the voltage sent to a motor, the valve opening, the heater power. - : the physical thing being controlled. What happens: the input is applied, and the system output forms. It is not possible to make any change at the output, such as improvement or measurement — nothing looks at the output. Adjustment can only be made by human control ( insan kontrolü ile düzenleme yapılabilir ). Examples from the notes : washing machine ( çamaşır makinesi ), fan cooler ( fan soğutucu ), the automobile power-transmission/drivetrain system ( otomobil hareket aktarma sistemi ), electric cutter ( elektrikli kesici ). A washing machine runs its programme for a fixed time — it does not measure how clean the clothes are. If the clothes are still dirty, you notice and run it again: that is the "human control" the notes mention. The human closes the loop; the machine does not. Similarly a simple fan blows at the chosen speed no matter what the room temperature is; you change the speed by hand if you feel hot. As the notes say, the open-loop scheme is widely used in systems operated under human supervision.

title: Why autonomous systems need feedback
text: In an autonomous system ( otonom sistem ) — one without a human or other external supervisor — the system itself must measure the output signal and interpret it to obtain the desired output. In a cooling system ( soğutucu sistem ), the ambient temperature ( ortam sıcaklığı ) is measured continuously and reported to the system input. Because the controller now knows both the desired output (the set temperature) and the current state (the measured temperature), it can form a control actuating signal proportional to the difference between them ( fark ile orantılı bir kontrol uygulama işareti ). Desired temperature $22^{\circ}\text{C}$, measured $26^{\circ}\text{C}$ → difference $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ → strong cooling. Measured $23^{\circ}\text{C}$ → difference $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ → gentle cooling. Measured $22^{\circ}\text{C}$ → difference 0 → no extra cooling needed. Measuring the output and feeding it back lets the system act on the error (desired − actual) by itself, without a human.

title: The closed-loop block diagram
text: The general structure of a closed-loop system ( kapalı çevrim bir sistemin genel yapısı ): Every label, as in the notes: Turkish label English Role --- --- --- Giriş Input (reference) Represents the desired output level ( istenilen çıkış düzeyi ) Hata kontrolü (Σ) Error detector / comparator Subtracts the fed-back signal from the input ($+$ input, $-$ feedback) Hata sinyali Error signal Desired − measured Kontrolcü Controller Turns the error into a drive signal Uygulama sinyali Actuating signal The signal that drives the system Sistem System (plant) The physical process Çıkış Output What we control Geri-besleme elemanları Feedback elements Sensor + instrumentation circuit The sensor–instrumentation circuit that converts the value formed at the output into the type of the input signal and scales it ( çıkışta oluşan değeri, giriş sinyali türüne çevirip ölçekleyen sensör-enstrümentasyon devresi ). Why must the feedback elements convert and scale ? Because you can only subtract like from like. If the input is a voltage that represents "22 °C", the output (a real temperature) must be turned into a voltage on the same scale before the comparator can subtract them. A temperature sensor giving 10 mV per °C plus an amplifier is exactly such a "feedback element". In the algebra later this block becomes $H$.

title: When the error becomes zero
text: The notes describe the loop's behaviour in words: 1. When the output reaches the same level as the input — the desired value is reached — the error signal becomes zero , and the input of the system becomes zero too: the system goes quiet (it is idle). 2. If a deviation ( sapma ) occurs at the output, the error signal appears again; as a result the actuating signal driving the system also takes a value again and sets the system in motion . So the loop is a self-correcting cycle: measure → compare → act → measure… The notes write " sistem susturdur ". This is most likely a slip for "susturulur / susar" — "the system is silenced / goes quiet". The meaning is clear: nothing is being driven when the error is zero. "Error zero ⇒ system input zero" is exactly true for a controller whose output depends only on the present error (on/off or pure gain). A controller with an integral part (mentioned on p. 5) can keep a non-zero actuating signal even when the error is zero, because it remembers past error. And with a pure gain controller the error actually settles at a small non-zero value rather than exactly zero — we will see this with the formula $E/R=1/(1+GH)$ in the section The error signal in the loop below. The notes' sentence describes the idea (the loop acts on error and calms down as the error vanishes), not an exact law.

title: On/off and linear controllers
text: The notes distinguish two families of controllers: The controller driving the system works in on/off mode — as in a refrigerator or an air-conditioning system ( buzdolabı, klima ). Controllers that handle the error signal more linearly ( daha doğrusal ) and generate the control signal by carrying out gain, derivative and integral operations on it. How to read this plot: the horizontal axis is the error $e$ (desired − actual), the vertical axis is the actuating signal $u$ the controller produces. - On/off : the compressor is either fully ON or OFF. A small error and a big error give the same full action. The fridge temperature therefore swings slightly around the set value as the compressor clicks on and off. - Gain ( kazanç ): $u=K\,e$ — the action is proportional to the error. Small error → gentle action, large error → strong action. This is the "signal proportional to the difference" of the cooling example on p. 4. - Derivative ( türev ): reacts to how fast the error is changing, $\dfrac{de}{dt}$ — it acts early when the error grows quickly. - Integral ( integral ): reacts to the accumulated error, $\int e\,dt$ — a small error that persists keeps building up action. (These three are often combined and called a PID controller; the notes do not use that name, and they do not go further into these controllers in this lecture.)

title: Open-loop vs closed-loop comparison
text: The notes summarise the basic differences in a two-column table: Açık çevrim sistem (open loop) Kapalı çevrim sistem (closed loop) --- --- Control independent of the desired output ( istenen çıkıştan bağımsız kontrol ) Control dependent on the desired output ( istenen çıkışa bağımlı kontrol ) No feedback loop → called non-feedback control systems ( geribeslemesiz ) Has a feedback loop → called feedback control systems ( geribeslemeli ) Design is easy ( tasarımı kolaydır ) Design is difficult ( tasarımı zordur ) Economical ( ekonomiktir ) Expensive ( pahalıdır ) Low accuracy ( düşük hassasiyetlidir ) High accuracy ( yüksek hassasiyetlidir ) Why each row is true: - Independent / dependent : in open loop the controller never sees the output, so it cannot know whether the desired output was achieved. In closed loop the action is computed from the difference between desired and actual. - Easy / difficult design : closing a loop creates a cycle of cause and effect (the output influences its own cause). A badly designed loop can over-react and oscillate or even run away (instability — the topic of [Module 02]( /m/02)). Open loop has no such risk from the loop itself. - Cheap / expensive : feedback needs sensors, instrumentation, a comparator and a more elaborate controller. - Low / high accuracy ( hassasiyet ): open loop relies on every block having exactly the expected value; any change (ageing, load, temperature, a disturbance) appears directly at the output. Closed loop corrects such changes. We prove this quantitatively in the sections Why feedback makes T insensitive to G and Why feedback suppresses disturbances below. A classic short-answer question: "Compare open-loop and closed-loop control systems." Reproduce the five rows (preferably with the Turkish words), add one example of each (washing machine / cooling system with temperature sensor), and draw both block diagrams.

title: Negative feedback
text: The notes now replace the descriptive blocks with symbols: - $R$ — - $E$ — the error signal (output of the comparator) - $G$ — the forward block (controller and system together) - $H$ — the feedback block (the feedback elements) - $C$ — the output The minus sign at the comparator is what makes this negative feedback ( negatif geribesleme ): the measured output is subtracted from the reference.

title: Deriving the closed-loop transfer function
text: This is the central derivation of the lecture. We want the ratio output/input, $C/R$, for the whole loop. A block multiplies its input by its gain. The input of $G$ is $E$, its output is $C$: $$ C=E\cdot G $$ The comparator gets $R$ with $+$ and the output of $H$ with $-$. The input of $H$ is $C$, so its output is $CH$: $$ E=R-CH $$ Substitute the second equation into the first and expand: $$ C=(R-CH)\,G=RG-CHG $$ Add $CHG$ to both sides: $$ C+CHG=RG $$ $$ C\,(1+HG)=RG $$ Divide both sides by $R(1+HG)$; since $HG=GH$ for scalar gains (and for transfer functions of a SISO loop): $$ \frac{C}{R}=\frac{G}{1+GH} $$ $$ \boxed{\;\frac{C}{R}=T=\frac{G}{1+GH}\;} $$ Output/input ( Çıkış/Giriş ) is the system transfer function ( sistem transfer fonksiyonu ), $T$. Sanity checks. (i) If $H=0$ (no feedback), $T=G$: we get the open-loop chain back. (ii) $1+GH\ge 1$ for positive gains, so negative feedback always reduces the gain from $G$ to $T$. (iii) Units: $GH$ is dimensionless (it goes around the loop and is compared with $R$), so $T$ has the units of $G$. $$ T=\frac{C}{R}=\frac{G}{1+GH} $$ How to remember it: "forward over one plus loop" — numerator is the path from $R$ to $C$, denominator is $1+$ the product of all gains around the loop.

title: The names in the notes
text: The notes define the symbols as follows: Symbol Turkish (notes) English --- --- --- $R$ Referans giriş Reference input $T$ Genel transfer fonksiyonu Overall (closed-loop) transfer function $G$ Açık çevrim kazancı "Open-loop gain" $H$ Geri-besleme kazancı Feedback gain The notes call $G$ the open-loop gain . The reasoning: if you remove the feedback ($H=0$), the system becomes open loop and its gain from $R$ to $C$ is exactly $G$. Many textbooks instead call $G$ the forward-path gain and use "open-loop (loop) gain / open-loop transfer function" for the product $GH$ (the gain met when going once around the loop). Both are fine as long as you know which one is meant. In this course's exams, "açık çevrim kazancı" = $G$ , as the professor defines it. On this site we write "forward gain $G$" and "loop gain $GH$" when the distinction matters. The notes also write $C(1+HG)$ in one line and $1+GH$ in the box: for scalar gains (and SISO transfer functions) $HG=GH$, so these are the same.

title: The error signal in the loop
The error signal in the loop
text: The same two equations also tell us how big the error is. From $E=R-CH$ and $C=EG$: $$ E=R-(EG)H \;\Rightarrow\; E+EGH=R \;\Rightarrow\; E(1+GH)=R $$ $$ \frac{E}{R}=\frac{1}{1+GH} $$ So the error is the reference divided by $1+GH$. With a large loop gain $GH$ the error is small — this is the quantitative meaning of "the error goes to (nearly) zero when the output reaches the desired value" on p. 5. With constant gains it never becomes exactly zero; it becomes small.

title: Why feedback makes T insensitive to G
Why feedback makes T insensitive to G
text: Divide numerator and denominator of $T$ by $GH$: $$ T=\frac{G}{1+GH}=\frac{1}{H}\cdot\frac{GH}{1+GH}=\frac{1}{H}\cdot\frac{1}{1+\dfrac{1}{GH}} $$ When $GH\gg 1$, the fraction $\dfrac{1}{GH}$ is tiny, so $$ T\approx\frac{1}{H}\qquad(GH\gg1) $$ Physical meaning. The output becomes (almost) independent of $G$ — the controller and the plant — and depends only on $H$, the sensor. If the sensor is accurate, the output is accurate, even if the motor, heater or amplifier is imprecise, ages or changes with temperature. That is the "high accuracy" ( yüksek hassasiyet ) of the comparison table, now as a formula. A sensor is usually much easier to make precise and stable than a powerful actuator. How far are we from the ideal $1/H$? Relative gap: $$ \frac{\tfrac1H-T}{\tfrac1H}=1-\frac{GH}{1+GH}=\frac{1}{1+GH} $$ How a change of G affects T. Suppose $G$ changes to $G'$ (ageing, load…). The ratio of new to old output is $$ \frac{T'}{T}=\frac{G'/(1+G'H)}{G/(1+GH)}=\frac{G'}{G}\cdot\frac{1+GH}{1+G'H} $$ For a small change, the relative change of $T$ is approximately the relative change of $G$ divided by $1+GH$: $$ \frac{\Delta T}{T}\approx\frac{1}{1+GH}\cdot\frac{\Delta G}{G} $$ (Where this comes from: by the quotient rule $\dfrac{d}{dG}\dfrac{G}{1+GH}=\dfrac{(1+GH)\cdot1-G\cdot H}{(1+GH)^2}=\dfrac{1}{(1+GH)^2}$; multiplying by $\dfrac{G}{T}=1+GH$ gives $\dfrac{dT/T}{dG/G}=\dfrac{1}{1+GH}$.) In open loop, $C=GR$, so a 10 % change in $G$ is a 10 % change in the output. In closed loop with $GH=99$ it becomes only about $0.1\,\%$. Things to try in the explorer: - Put $H=1$, $G=1$: $GH=1$, $T=0.5$ — far from $1/H$, and a $-20\,\%$ change of $G$ gives a $-11.1\,\%$ change of $T$. Feedback helps only a little. - Raise $G$ to 100: $T=0.990$, and the same $-20\,\%$ change of $G$ changes $T$ by only $-0.25\,\%$. The closed-loop curve in the second plot becomes almost flat. - Lower $H$: the ceiling $1/H$ rises — the sensor sets the closed-loop gain. Negative feedback decreases the overall gain ($T\le G$ for positive gains). What it buys is accuracy and insensitivity, not amplification. To get a large $T$ you choose a small $H$ (since $T\approx1/H$).

title: Positive feedback: where the sign changes
Positive feedback for comparison
text: If the feedback entered the comparator with a $+$ sign (positive feedback), the same steps give a different denominator. This case is not in the notes; it is shown so you see exactly which step the sign comes from. $C=EG$ and now $E=R+CH$. $$ C=(R+CH)G=RG+CHG\;\Rightarrow\;C-CHG=RG\;\Rightarrow\;C(1-GH)=RG $$ $$ \frac{C}{R}=\frac{G}{1-GH} $$ $G=2$, $H=0.25$: $GH=0.5$, $T=\dfrac{2}{1-0.5}=4$ — larger than $G$. If $GH=1$ the denominator is 0: the output would grow without bound for any input. This is why control loops use negative feedback. Positive feedback: $T=\dfrac{G}{1-GH}$. The only change in the derivation is the sign in $E=R\pm CH$, which carries through to $1\mp GH$.

title: Closed-loop gain with G = 10 and H = 1
Feedback against a 50 percent drop of G
Common mistake: forgetting H in the comparator
Design: choose H for a required closed-loop gain
Worked examples: negative feedback
text: Given: $G=10$, $H=1$. Asked: $T$, and $C$ for $R=2$. $GH=10\cdot1=10$, so $1+GH=11$. $$ T=\frac{G}{1+GH}=\frac{10}{11}=0.9091 $$ $C=TR=0.9091\cdot2=1.818$. $T=10/11\approx0.909$, $C\approx1.818$ for $R=2$. Interpretation: the ideal output would be $R/H=2$; we are $1/(1+GH)=1/11\approx9.1\,\%$ below it. Check: $E=R-CH=2-1.818=0.182$ and $EG=1.82\approx C$ ✓. $GH=100\cdot0.1=10$. $$ T=\frac{100}{1+10}=\frac{100}{11}=9.091,\qquad \frac1H=10 $$ $T\approx9.09$, close to $1/H=10$ (gap $1/11\approx9.1\,\%$). Interpretation: the forward gain is 100, yet the closed loop amplifies only about 9 — set essentially by $H$. To get closer to 10 we would need a bigger $GH$. Given: $H=1$. The forward gain drops from $G=100$ to $G'=50$ (for example an amplifier loses half its gain). Asked: output change in open loop and in closed loop for $R=1$. $C=GR$: from $100$ to $50$ — a $-50\,\%$ change. $$ T=\frac{100}{1+100}=\frac{100}{101}=0.99010 $$ $$ T'=\frac{50}{1+50}=\frac{50}{51}=0.98039 $$ $$ \frac{T'}{T}-1=\frac{0.98039}{0.99010}-1=-0.0098=-0.98\,\% $$ Open loop: $-50\,\%$. Closed loop: $-0.98\,\%$ — about 50 times less. Check with the formula: $\dfrac{T'}{T}=\dfrac{G'}{G}\cdot\dfrac{1+GH}{1+G'H}=0.5\cdot\dfrac{101}{51}=0.9902$ ✓. (The small-change rule $-50\,\%/101\approx-0.5\,\%$ underestimates here because a 50 % change is not small; use the exact ratio for big changes.) Given: $G=5$, $H=2$, $R=3$. Asked: $C$ and $E$. $1+GH=1+10=11$, $T=\dfrac{5}{11}=0.4545$, $C=3\cdot0.4545=1.364$. $E=R-CH=3-1.364\cdot2=3-2.727=0.273$. Equivalently $E=\dfrac{R}{1+GH}=\dfrac{3}{11}=0.273$ ✓. Writing $E=R-C$ (as if $H=1$) gives $T=\dfrac{5}{1+5}=0.833$ and $C=2.5$ — wrong. The comparator subtracts the output of H , i.e. $CH$, not $C$. $C=15/11\approx1.364$, $E=3/11\approx0.273$. Check: $C=EG=0.273\cdot5=1.364$ ✓. Given: $G=100$. Asked: $H$ so that $T=4$; then $T$ if $G$ falls to 80. $$ 4=\frac{100}{1+100H}\;\Rightarrow\;1+100H=\frac{100}{4}=25\;\Rightarrow\;H=\frac{24}{100}=0.24 $$ $GH=24$, so we expect insensitivity of about $1/25$. $$ T'=\frac{80}{1+80\cdot0.24}=\frac{80}{20.2}=3.960 $$ $H=0.24$. A $-20\,\%$ change in $G$ changes $T$ from 4 to 3.960, i.e. $-0.99\,\%$. Check: $\dfrac{1}{1+GH}\cdot(-20\,\%)=-0.8\,\%$ (small-change estimate) — the same order as the exact $-0.99\,\%$ ✓. Also $1/H=4.17$, slightly above $T=4$, as it must be.

title: Disturbance input (noise)
text: Environmental signal sources, other than the input signal and the output , that affect the system performance positively or negatively ( olumlu/olumsuz ) are defined as noise. Example from the notes: in a heating/cooling system, open doors or windows affect the output of the heater/cooler — the ambient temperature. Depending on the form and magnitude of the disturbance, the system can sometimes go completely out of control ( become unstable , kararsızlaşır ), or it keeps working with a limited deviation ( sınırlı bir sapma ). The disturbance is an input we did not choose and usually cannot measure directly. In the room-heating case the heater pushes heat in ($G a$ = what the controller/heater produces from the command), and the open window pulls heat out ($N$). Both act on the same physical quantity — the heat entering the room — which then determines the temperature ($G b$ = how the room converts net heat flow into temperature). That is exactly why $N$ enters at a summing point between $G a$ and $G b$ in the diagrams.

title: Noise transfer function of the open-loop system
Disturbance in an open-loop system
text: The summing junction adds the output of $G a$ and the noise: its output is $G aR+N$. Then $G b$ multiplies it: $$ C=G b\,(G aR+N)=G aG bR+G bN $$ "Transfer function valid for the noise signal only" ( sadece gürültü sinyali için geçerli ): set $R=0$: $$ C=G bN $$ $$ \frac{C(s)}{N(s)}=G b $$ Meaning: in open loop the disturbance reaches the output in full , multiplied by whatever lies after it. Nobody notices the open window, so nothing compensates.

title: Noise transfer function of the closed-loop system
Disturbance in a closed-loop system
text: With $R=0$ the first comparator outputs $0-HC=-HC$. After $G a$: $-G aHC$. The second summing junction adds $N$: $N-G aHC$. After $G b$: $$ C=G b\,(N-G aHC)=G bN-G aG bHC $$ $$ C+G aG bHC=G bN\;\Rightarrow\;C\,(1+G aG bH)=G bN $$ $$ \frac{C(s)}{N(s)}=\frac{G b}{1+G aG bH} $$ Check with the memory rule: forward path from $N$ to $C$ is $G b$; the loop is $G aG bH$; "forward over one plus loop" gives the same result ✓. With $H=0$ we recover the open-loop $C/N=G b$ ✓. On p. 9 the professor writes no signs at the second Σ. As on p. 8, both inputs are taken as $+$ (the disturbance adds to the signal). If a disturbance were drawn with a $-$ sign, only the sign of $C N$ would flip; the factor $1+G aG bH$ stays the same.

title: Why feedback suppresses disturbances
text: Compare the two results: $$ \underbrace{\frac{C}{N}=G b} {\text{open loop}}\qquad\text{vs}\qquad\underbrace{\frac{C}{N}=\frac{G b}{1+G aG bH}} {\text{closed loop}} $$ The closed loop divides the effect of the disturbance by $1+G aG bH$. With a loop gain of 99, the open window changes the room temperature 100 times less. Physically: the window lets heat out → the temperature starts to fall → the sensor ($H$) sees it → the error grows → the controller ($G a$) increases the heating → most of the lost heat is replaced. The loop does not need to know why the temperature fell; it only reacts to the deviation. That is the great strength of feedback: it corrects disturbances it was never told about. In open loop the heater keeps producing the same heat, so the full effect of the window remains. The notes also say a disturbance can drive the system "completely out of control (unstable)". Feedback reduces the size of the deviation, but a closed loop must itself be stable for this to work — stability is the subject of [Module 02]( /m/02). In the explorer, the dashed line is what the open window does to an open-loop system ($G bN$), the solid line what it does to the closed loop. Increase $G a$ (the controller gain): the closed-loop deviation shrinks, while the open-loop deviation does not change at all — it does not even depend on $G a$.

title: Reference and disturbance together
text: With constant gains (and later with transfer functions) the systems are linear , so the output for $R$ and $N$ acting together is the sum of the outputs for each acting alone ( superposition ). The reference-only part of the closed loop on p. 9 is the p. 7 result with $G=G aG b$ (set $N=0$: the two blocks are in series): $$ \frac{C}{R}\bigg {N=0}=\frac{G aG b}{1+G aG bH} $$ Adding the two contributions: $$ C=\frac{G aG b}{1+G aG bH}\,R+\frac{G b}{1+G aG bH}\,N $$ Check by direct algebra (both inputs on): $C=G b\,[N+G a(R-HC)]=G aG bR+G bN-G aG bHC$, so $C(1+G aG bH)=G aG bR+G bN$ — the same ✓. $$ C=\frac{G aG b\,R+G b\,N}{1+G aG bH} $$ For the open loop of p. 8: $C=G aG bR+G bN$.

title: Superposition: a fair open-loop vs closed-loop comparison
Worked examples: disturbances
text: Given: $G a=10$, $G b=2$, $H=1$, a disturbance $N=1$. Asked: output deviation caused by $N$ in open and closed loop. $C N=G bN=2\cdot1=2$. $G aG bH=10\cdot2\cdot1=20$, so $1+G aG bH=21$. $$ C N=\frac{G b}{1+G aG bH}N=\frac{2}{21}=0.0952 $$ Open loop: $2$. Closed loop: $0.0952$ — 21 times smaller. Check: ratio $2/0.0952=21=1+G aG bH$ ✓. Situation: we want output $C=5$. A disturbance $N=1$ appears. - Open-loop design: $G b=2$, and $G a=0.5$ chosen so that $G aG b=1$ (then $C=R$ when there is no disturbance); command $R=5$. - Closed-loop design: $G a=10$, $G b=2$, $H=1$, command $R=5$ (desired output $R/H=5$). $$ C=G aG bR+G bN=1\cdot5+2\cdot1=7 $$ Error relative to the desired 5: $(7-5)/5=40\,\%$. $$ C R=\frac{20}{21}\cdot5=\frac{100}{21}=4.762 $$ $$ C N=\frac{2}{21}\cdot1=0.0952 $$ $$ C=C R+C N=\frac{100+2}{21}=\frac{102}{21}=4.857 $$ Error relative to 5: $(5-4.857)/5=2.86\,\%$. Open loop: $C=7$ (40 % off). Closed loop: $C\approx4.857$ (2.9 % off). Interpretation: the closed loop is not perfect (the $1/(1+G aG bH)$ gap and the attenuated disturbance remain) but it is an order of magnitude more accurate — the "high accuracy" row of the table, in numbers. Check: formula $C=(G aG bR+G bN)/(1+G aG bH)=(100+2)/21$ ✓.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. Name every signal: the comparator output ($E$), each block's output (block gain × block input), and the output $C$. 2. Write one equation per block and per summing junction, with the signs from the drawing . 3. Set to zero every input you are not asking about (for $C/N$ put $R=0$; for $C/R$ put $N=0$). 4. Eliminate the intermediate signals so that only $C$ and the input remain. 5. Put all $C$ terms on one side, factor $C$, divide. 6. Check with the rule "forward path over $1+$ loop gain" (negative feedback) and with the limit $H=0$ (must give the open-loop result). 1. Compute the loop gain first ($GH$ or $G aG bH$). 2. $T=G/(1+GH)$, $C=TR$, $E=R/(1+GH)$. 3. For a change of $G$: compute $T$ before and after, then the ratio; compare with open loop (where output changes as much as $G$). 4. For disturbances: open loop $C N=G bN$; closed loop divides by $1+G aG bH$; total output by superposition. 5. Sanity: $T$ must be below $G$ and below $1/H$ (positive gains, negative feedback); attenuation ratio must equal $1+G aG bH$. - Writing $E=R-C$ when $H\neq1$ — the comparator subtracts $CH$. - Sign slip: $1-GH$ belongs to positive feedback; the notes' loop is negative, $1+GH$. - For $C/N$ in closed loop, putting $G a$ in the numerator — the forward path from $N$ to $C$ passes only through $G b$. $G a$ appears only in the loop. - Forgetting to set $R=0$ when asked for the noise-only transfer function. - Mixing up the names: in this course "açık çevrim kazancı" is $G$ (p. 7). Definitions (control system, open/closed loop, feedback elements, noise) · classify given examples · draw the open/closed-loop block diagrams with labels · the comparison table · derive $C/R=G/(1+GH)$ · derive $C/N$ for p. 8 and p. 9 · explain why feedback reduces disturbances · short numerical evaluation with given gains.

text: A room heater has a thermostat: a sensor measures the room temperature, and the heater is switched on whenever the temperature is below the set value. Classify it with all three classifications of p. 2, and say what type of controller it has (p. 5). - Continuous-time : the temperature and the sensor signal exist at every instant. - SISO : one input (set temperature), one output (room temperature). - Closed loop : the output is measured and compared with the desired value (feedback is used). - Controller: on/off ( aç/kapa ), like the refrigerator and air conditioner in the notes. Verification: the deciding question for open/closed loop is "is the output measured and fed back?" — yes. For each, say open loop or closed loop and why: (a) washing machine with a fixed programme; (b) fan cooler at a chosen speed; (c) cooling system that continuously measures ambient temperature; (d) electric cutter. (a) Open — runs its programme without measuring cleanliness. (b) Open — the speed does not depend on the room temperature. (c) Closed — the measured temperature is fed back and the action depends on the difference (p. 4). (d) Open — nothing measures the output. Examples (a), (b), (d) are the notes' own open-loop examples (p. 3). Draw the closed-loop block diagram of p. 4 and name every block and signal in Turkish and English. Which block converts the output into the form of the input signal? Giriş (input) → Σ "Hata kontrolü" (comparator, $+$ input, $-$ feedback) → Hata sinyali (error signal) → Kontrolcü (controller) → Uygulama sinyali (actuating signal) → Sistem (plant) → Çıkış (output); from the output a branch goes through Geri-besleme elemanları (feedback elements) back to the $-$ input of Σ. The feedback elements (sensor–instrumentation circuit) convert the output into the input-signal type and scale it. Give the physical reason for each of these rows of the p. 6 table: (a) closed loop is more expensive; (b) closed loop is harder to design; (c) closed loop has higher accuracy. (a) It needs sensors, instrumentation, a comparator and a more complex controller. (b) The output influences its own cause through the loop; a bad design can over-react, oscillate or become unstable, so the loop must be designed carefully. (c) It measures the actual output and corrects deviations caused by parameter changes and disturbances; mathematically $T\approx1/H$ for $GH\gg1$ (insensitive to $G$) and disturbances are divided by $1+G aG bH$. Compute $T=C/R$ for $G=20$, $H=0.5$, and the ideal value $1/H$. $GH=10$, $1+GH=11$, $T=\dfrac{20}{11}=1.818$. Ideal $1/H=2$. Gap: $1/11=9.1\,\%$, and indeed $2\cdot(1-1/11)=1.818$ ✓. For $G=4$, $H=1$, $R=2$, find $C$ and $E$, and verify $C=EG$. $T=\dfrac{4}{1+4}=0.8$, $C=0.8\cdot2=1.6$. $E=R-CH=2-1.6=0.4$ (also $E=R/(1+GH)=2/5=0.4$). Check: $EG=0.4\cdot4=1.6=C$ ✓. $G=1000$, $H=0.01$. Find $T$, $1/H$ and the relative gap. What would you change to reduce the gap? $GH=10$; $T=\dfrac{1000}{11}=90.91$; $1/H=100$; gap $=\dfrac{1}{1+GH}=\dfrac{1}{11}=9.09\,\%$ (check: $100\cdot(1-0.0909)=90.91$ ✓). To reduce the gap increase the loop gain $GH$; keeping the desired $1/H=100$, that means increasing $G$ (e.g. $G=10^4$ gives $GH=100$, gap $\approx1\,\%$). $G=50$, $H=0.2$. The forward gain drops by $30\,\%$. Find the exact relative change of $T$ and compare with open loop. Compute $T$ with $G=50$ and with $G'=35$. $GH=10$: $T=\dfrac{50}{11}=4.5455$. $G'=35$: $G'H=7$, $T'=\dfrac{35}{8}=4.375$. Ratio $\dfrac{4.375}{4.5455}=0.9625$, i.e. $-3.75\,\%$. Open loop: $-30\,\%$. Check with the exact formula: $\dfrac{G'}{G}\cdot\dfrac{1+GH}{1+G'H}=0.7\cdot\dfrac{11}{8}=0.9625$ ✓. (Small-change estimate $-30\,\%/11=-2.7\,\%$ — same order; the exact value is larger because the change is not small.) The forward gain is $G=500$. Find $H$ so that the closed-loop gain is $T=10$. What is the loop gain? $10=\dfrac{500}{1+500H}\Rightarrow1+500H=50\Rightarrow H=\dfrac{49}{500}=0.098$. Loop gain $GH=49$. Check: $\dfrac{500}{1+49}=10$ ✓. Note $1/H=10.2$, slightly above $T$, as expected. With $H=0.5$ the ideal output gain is $1/H=2$. How large must $G$ be so that $T=1.9$ (5 % below ideal)? From $T=\dfrac{G}{1+GH}$: $T+TGH=G\Rightarrow T=G(1-TH)\Rightarrow G=\dfrac{T}{1-TH}=\dfrac{1.9}{1-0.95}=38$. Check: $GH=19$, $T=38/20=1.9$ ✓, gap $1/20=5\,\%$ ✓. For the p. 7 loop, derive $E/R$ using only $C=EG$ and $E=R-CH$. Substitute $C=EG$ into $E=R-CH$: $E=R-EGH$. Collect: $E+EGH=R\Rightarrow E(1+GH)=R\Rightarrow\dfrac{E}{R}=\dfrac{1}{1+GH}$. Check: $C=EG=\dfrac{G}{1+GH}R$, which is the boxed p. 7 result ✓. For the closed-loop system of p. 9, derive $C/R$ with $N=0$. With $N=0$ the second Σ just passes the signal, so $G a$ and $G b$ are in series: $C=G aG b(R-HC)$. Then $C+G aG bHC=G aG bR$, $C(1+G aG bH)=G aG bR$, $\dfrac{C}{R}=\dfrac{G aG b}{1+G aG bH}$. This is the p. 7 formula with $G=G aG b$ ✓. $G a=5$, $G b=4$, $H=0.5$, disturbance $N=0.2$. Find the output deviation caused by $N$ in open loop (p. 8) and closed loop (p. 9). Open: $C N=G bN=4\cdot0.2=0.8$. Closed: $G aG bH=10$, $C N=\dfrac{4}{11}\cdot0.2=0.0727$. Ratio $0.8/0.0727=11=1+G aG bH$ ✓. Closed loop of p. 9 with $G a=20$, $G b=1$, $H=1$, $R=2$, $N=0.5$. Find $C$ by superposition and check by direct algebra. How far is it from the desired $R/H$? $1+G aG bH=21$. Reference part: $\dfrac{20}{21}\cdot2=\dfrac{40}{21}=1.9048$. Disturbance part: $\dfrac{1}{21}\cdot0.5=0.0238$. Total $C=\dfrac{40.5}{21}=1.9286$. Direct: $C(1+G aG bH)=G aG bR+G bN=40+0.5=40.5$ ⇒ $C=40.5/21$ ✓. Desired $R/H=2$: deviation $-0.071$, i.e. $-3.6\,\%$. (In open loop with the same $G aG b=20$ the disturbance alone would add $G bN=0.5$.) Using $T=G/(1+GH)$: (a) what is $T$ when $H=0$, and what does it mean? (b) what does $T$ approach when $G$ becomes very large? (c) what happens to $C/N$ of p. 9 when $H=0$? (a) $T=G/(1+0)=G$: no feedback — the open-loop chain. (b) $T=\dfrac{1/H}{1+1/(GH)}\to\dfrac1H$: determined by the feedback element only. (c) $C/N=G b/(1+0)=G b$: the open-loop result of p. 8 — without feedback the disturbance is not attenuated. Suppose the feedback in the p. 7 loop is added instead of subtracted. With $G=4$: compute $T$ for $H=0.2$ and say what happens at $H=0.25$. Positive feedback: $E=R+CH\Rightarrow C(1-GH)=RG\Rightarrow T=\dfrac{G}{1-GH}$. $H=0.2$: $GH=0.8$, $T=\dfrac{4}{0.2}=20$. $H=0.25$: $GH=1$, the denominator is $0$ — the formula gives no finite gain; the output would grow without bound. This is why the notes' control loop uses negative feedback. Modify the p. 9 diagram: the disturbance $N$ is added after $G b$ (directly to the output), i.e. $C=G b\cdot(\text{output of }G a)+N$. Derive $C/N$ and evaluate it for $G a=10$, $G b=2$, $H=1$. Set $R=0$: the first comparator gives $-HC$, after $G a$: $-G aHC$, after $G b$: $-G aG bHC$, then $+N$: $C=N-G aG bHC$. So $C(1+G aG bH)=N$ and $\dfrac{C}{N}=\dfrac{1}{1+G aG bH}$. Numbers: $\dfrac{1}{21}=0.0476$. Check with "forward over one plus loop": forward path from $N$ to $C$ is 1, loop $G aG bH$ ✓. Open loop would pass it fully ($C/N=1$). Using the heating example of p. 8 (open window), explain step by step why the closed-loop system's temperature changes much less than the open-loop system's, and identify which factor in the formula expresses this. Window opens → heat leaves → temperature starts to drop. Open loop: the heater gets the same command, produces the same heat; the full loss shows up ($C/N=G b$). Closed loop: the sensor measures the drop → error appears → controller increases the actuating signal → heater produces more heat → most of the loss is compensated. The remaining effect is divided by $1+G aG bH$; the larger the loop gain, the smaller the deviation. Give the English meaning: (a) Uygulama sinyali (b) Hata sinyali (c) Geri-besleme elemanları (d) Bozucu giriş (e) Genel transfer fonksiyonu (f) Açık çevrim kazancı (in the notes). (a) actuating signal; (b) error signal; (c) feedback elements (sensor–instrumentation circuit); (d) disturbance input (noise); (e) overall transfer function $T$; (f) the forward gain $G$ (the notes call $G$ the open-loop gain).

title: What is this about?
text: Imagine you have just built a room heater controller. You switch it on and want to know: Is it any good? You cannot test it with every possible situation the room will ever face (doors opening, sun coming in, people entering). Engineers do something smarter. They hit the system with a few standard test signals and watch what comes out. From those few experiments they judge three things: 1. Does it stay under control? If you ask for 22 °C, does the temperature settle somewhere, or does it run away or swing wildly forever? This is stability . 2. How good is the response? How fast does it get there, how far does it overshoot, how long until it calms down, and how close to 22 °C does it finally end up? These are the performance criteria . 3. What is the input→output rule of the system? If we can write that rule down mathematically (the transfer function ), we can predict the output for any input without building anything. This module (the professor's lecture " ") gives you the vocabulary and the first tools for all three. It ends by introducing the Laplace transform , the tool that turns the differential equations describing real systems into simple algebra. Think of a car's cruise control. "Set speed = 100 km/h" is a step input (the desired speed jumps from 90 to 100). A kick from a pothole is like an impulse (a short hard hit). "Accelerate steadily" is a ramp . A well-designed cruise control reaches 100 km/h quickly, overshoots only a little, settles, and ends up very close to 100. A badly designed one might oscillate between 95 and 105 forever, or worse, keep accelerating: unstable . After this module you can: - write, sketch and combine the three basic test inputs (step, ramp, impulse) and explain why $\delta=\dfrac{du}{dt}$ and $u=\dfrac{dr}{dt}$; - decide whether a given response is bounded (BIBO stable behaviour) or not; - read $t r$, $t p$, $m$, $t s$, $y {ss}$ and $e {ss}$ off a unit-step response and explain each one; - explain what a transfer function is and how it can be found (analytically or by system identification); - model a series RC circuit with a differential equation; - explain why we move to the Laplace transform, what $e^{st}$ and the s-plane mean, and derive $\L\{u\}=\frac1s$, $\L\{r\}=\frac1{s^2}$, $\L\{\delta\}=1$ from the definition.

title: The three basic test inputs
text: The professor opens with a strong claim : Bir kontrol sisteminde üç temel giriş fonksiyonu vardır: birim basamak, rampa ve impulse fonksiyonu. — A control system has three basic input functions: the unit step, the ramp and the impulse. Every input a system may meet can be expressed through these three, as their components or as sums of their components. Why these three? Because each one asks the system a different, very clear question: Input Turkish Everyday picture Question it asks the system --- --- --- --- Step $A\,u(t)$ basamak flip a switch; change the set-point "Can you move to a new constant value, and how well?" Ramp $A\,t$ rampa a target moving at constant speed "Can you follow something that keeps changing?" Impulse $\delta(t)$ impulse a hammer blow, a sudden kick "How do you react to a short shock, and do you calm down afterwards?" And the claim "everything else is built from these" is very practical: a pulse is a step up followed by a step down; a "rise then hold" signal is a ramp minus a delayed ramp, and so on. We will build such signals below.

title: Step function
text: A signal that is 0 before $t=0$ and jumps instantly to a constant value $A$ at $t=0$ : $$ x(t)=\begin{cases}A, & t 0\\ 0, & t<0\end{cases} $$ If $A=1$ it is the unit step ( ), written $u(t)$. Any step can then be written $x(t)=A\cdot u(t)$. Reading the graph. The horizontal axis is time $t$, the vertical axis is the signal $x(t)$. For negative time the signal sits at 0; at $t=0$ it jumps vertically to $A$ and stays there forever. The professor's sketch has exactly this shape, with the level labelled "A". Symbols. $A$ is the size of the jump (volts, °C, km/h… whatever the input physically is). $u(t)$ is the dimensionless "switch-on" function. Multiplying by $A$ just stretches it vertically. Why it exists. A step is the simplest possible change: "from now on, be at a new value". Almost every set-point change in practice (thermostat, cruise control, a motor told to go to a new angle) is a step. The value exactly at $t=0$. The notes leave $u(0)$ undefined (they write $t 0$ and $t<0$). It does not matter: a single instant has zero duration and never changes an integral or a physical response. Shifting. A step that switches on at $t=t 0$ instead of $0$ is $A\,u(t-t 0)$: the expression $t-t 0$ becomes positive only after $t 0$. Draw the axes, mark the level $A$ on the vertical axis, draw a horizontal line at 0 up to $t=0$ (or $t 0$), a vertical jump, then a horizontal line at $A$. Label it $A\,u(t)$. Nothing more is needed.

title: Impulse function
text: A signal that is zero everywhere except at $t=0$, where it is "infinitely tall" : $$ x(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t\neq 0\\ \infty, & t=0\end{cases} $$ The unit impulse $\delta(t)$ ( ) is defined as the derivative of the unit step, and its total area is 1: $$ \delta(t)=\frac{du(t)}{dt},\qquad \int {-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)\,dt=1 $$ Reading the graph. The impulse is drawn as a vertical arrow at $t=0$. The arrow is a convention: its height does not show a value (the value is "infinite"), it shows the area (also called the strength or weight ) of the impulse. A unit impulse has area 1; $5\,\delta(t)$ is drawn as an arrow labelled 5. Physical picture. Hit a bell with a hammer. The force is huge but lasts only a millisecond. What matters for the bell is not the peak force (which is hard even to measure) but the total push = force × time = area under the force curve. The impulse is the idealisation "all of that push delivered in zero time". Its area is what counts. Why "∞ at one point" needs care. A normal function that is nonzero at just one point has integral 0 (one point has no width). So $\delta$ is not an ordinary function; think of it as the limit of ever-narrower, ever-taller pulses whose area stays exactly 1 . The explorer in the next section shows this limit happening.

title: Ramp function
text: A signal that is 0 before $t=0$ and then grows linearly with slope $A$ : $$ x(t)=\begin{cases}At, & t\ge 0\\ 0, & t<0\end{cases} $$ If $A=1$ it is the unit ramp ( ). On p. 2 the notes write it $R(t)$, on p. 10 $r(t)$. It is the integral of the unit step, so $u(t)=\dfrac{dR(t)}{dt}$. Reading the graph. Zero for negative time; from the origin a straight line rises. The professor marks $t=1$ on the time axis and draws dashed guides to the value $A$: at $t=1$ the ramp equals $A\cdot 1=A$. That is the quickest way to show the slope on a sketch: slope = rise/run = $A/1=A$. Physical picture. A radar antenna tracking an aircraft flying past at constant angular speed must follow a ramp-shaped angle. Can the antenna keep up, or does it lag behind by a constant amount? That is what the ramp test reveals. The notes use three overlapping symbols: - p. 2: the unit ramp is called $R(t)$ (capital R); - p. 10: the unit ramp is called $r(t)$ (lower case); - p. 4: $r(t)=1$ is the reference (desired output), which for a step test is the unit step itself. The mathematics is not affected, but read each formula in context. In this module we write the unit ramp as $r(t)$ in the Laplace part (as on p. 10), and $r$ means "desired value" in the performance criteria section. Later modules use $r(t)$ / $R(s)$ for the reference input of a control loop. 0, ramp uses t ≥ 0" On p. 1 the step is defined for $t 0$, on p. 2 the ramp for $t\ge 0$. This is harmless: the ramp is continuous ($0\cdot A=0$ at $t=0$ either way), and the step's value at the single instant $t=0$ never matters.

title: How the three inputs are related
How the three inputs are related
text: The professor writes two relations : $$ \delta(t)=\frac{du(t)}{dt}\qquad\qquad u(t)=\frac{dR(t)}{dt} $$ So the three inputs form a chain : differentiate a ramp and you get a step; differentiate a step and you get an impulse. Read backwards: integrate an impulse and you get a step; integrate a step and you get a ramp. $$ r(t)\ \xrightarrow{\ d/dt\ }\ u(t)\ \xrightarrow{\ d/dt\ }\ \delta(t) \qquad\qquad \delta(t)\ \xrightarrow{\ \int\ }\ u(t)\ \xrightarrow{\ \int\ }\ r(t) $$ Ramp → step (easy part). The slope of the unit ramp is 0 for $t<0$ (flat line) and 1 for $t 0$ (line of slope 1). "Slope 0 then slope 1" is exactly the unit step. With the integral: for $t 0$, $$ \int {0}^{t}u(\tau)\,d\tau=\int 0^t 1\,d\tau=t=r(t), $$ and for $t<0$ the integrand is 0, so the integral is 0. ✔ Step → impulse (the subtle part). The step is flat everywhere except at $t=0$, so its slope is 0 everywhere except at $t=0$. At $t=0$ it climbs a height of 1 in zero time : the slope there is "infinite". Infinite at one point, zero elsewhere: that is exactly the impulse picture of p. 2. And the total climb is 1, which is why the impulse has area 1 : $$ \int {-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau=u(t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int {-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau=u(\infty)-u(-\infty)=1-0=1. $$ To see this as a limit, replace the ideal step by a "nearly-step" $u \varepsilon(t)$ that climbs from 0 to 1 linearly in $\varepsilon$ seconds. Its derivative is a rectangular pulse of width $\varepsilon$ and height $1/\varepsilon$, so its area is $\varepsilon\cdot\frac1\varepsilon=1$ no matter how small $\varepsilon$ is . As $\varepsilon\to0$, $u \varepsilon\to u$ and the pulse becomes taller and thinner but keeps area 1: it becomes $\delta(t)$. Area of the impulse = total change of the step. Slope of the ramp = height of the step. Remember these two sentences and you can rebuild both relations in an exam.

title: Building other inputs from the three
text: The professor's claim that every input is a combination of these three is something you will use constantly. Two rules make it work: - scaling : $A\,u(t)$, $A\,r(t)$, $A\,\delta(t)$ change the height / slope / area to $A$; - shifting : replacing $t$ by $t-t 0$ delays the signal so that it starts at $t 0$. A heater's power is 0 until $t=2$ s and then 3 kW forever. Write it with the basic functions, and find its derivative. A constant level switched on at one instant is a step. Height $A=3$, switch-on time $t 0=2$. $$ x(t)=3\,u(t-2)=\begin{cases}3, & t 2\\ 0, & t<2\end{cases} $$ Check: at $t=1$, $t-2=-1<0$ so $u=0$, $x=0$ ✔; at $t=5$, $t-2=3 0$, $x=3$ ✔. Using $\frac{du}{dt}=\delta$ and the chain rule (the inner derivative $\frac{d}{dt}(t-2)=1$): $$ \frac{dx}{dt}=3\,\delta(t-2) $$ an impulse of area 3 at $t=2$: the jump of height 3 happens in zero time. $x(t)=3\,u(t-2)$, and $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3\,\delta(t-2)$. A motor's angle reference starts at 0 and increases by 5° every second from $t=0$. Write it, give its value at $t=4$ s and its derivative. Constant rate of increase means a ramp with slope $A=5$ °/s: $$ \theta {ref}(t)=5\,t\ \ (t\ge0),\qquad \theta {ref}(t)=5\,r(t). $$ $\theta {ref}(4)=5\cdot4=20°$. $\dfrac{d}{dt}\,5\,r(t)=5\,u(t)$: the angular speed is a step of 5 °/s. This is $u=\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ scaled by 5. $\theta {ref}(t)=5\,r(t)$, $\theta {ref}(4)=20°$, $\dot\theta {ref}(t)=5\,u(t)$. (a) A rectangular pulse of height 2 between $t=1$ and $t=3$. (b) A signal that rises as $t$ from $t=0$ to $t=2$ and then stays at 2. Express both with the basic functions. Switch on 2 at $t=1$: $2u(t-1)$. Switch it off at $t=3$ by adding a step of $-2$: $-2u(t-3)$. $$ p(t)=2u(t-1)-2u(t-3) $$ Check three regions: $t<1$: $0-0=0$ ✔; $1 3$: $2-2=0$ ✔. Start a unit ramp at 0: $r(t)$. At $t=2$ we want the slope to drop from 1 to 0, so we subtract a unit ramp starting at $t=2$, namely $r(t-2)=(t-2)u(t-2)$: $$ x(t)=r(t)-r(t-2) $$ Check: $0 2$: $t-(t-2)=2$ ✔. $p'(t)=2\delta(t-1)-2\delta(t-3)$ (an up-kick and a down-kick). $x'(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$: a unit pulse from 0 to 2, which is exactly the slope of the ramp-and-hold signal ✔. $p(t)=2u(t-1)-2u(t-3)$, $\quad x(t)=r(t)-r(t-2)$.

title: Stability (BIBO)
text: A system is stable if its output shows bounded deviations in response to bounded input changes ; equivalently, it shows bounded output for bounded input : . "Bounded" ( sınırlı ) simply means "never larger than some finite number". Written as mathematics: $$ \text{if } \lvert u(t)\rvert\le M u \text{ for all } t,\ \text{ then } \lvert y(t)\rvert\le M y \text{ for all } t, $$ where $M u$ and $M y$ are finite numbers, and this must hold for every bounded input. A step of height 1, a sine wave, a pulse: all bounded. A ramp is not bounded (it grows forever), so the ramp is never used to test BIBO stability. Why we care. An unstable system is useless and often dangerous: the heater whose temperature keeps rising, the motor that spins faster and faster, the amplifier that screams (feedback howl), the aircraft whose oscillation grows. Stability is the first thing checked, before any performance criterion makes sense.

title: An integrator is not BIBO stable
Stable and unstable responses
text: The professor sketches two pictures, each with the input level shown as a dashed line labelled "giriş" (input) . Below they are redrawn with real functions chosen to have the same shape . The exact formulas are illustrative only; they are not in the notes. Kararlı sistem (stable system). Both outputs start at 0 and end up at the input level. - Blue: rises fast, overshoots to about 1.5 times the input, swings below, then above, with each swing smaller, and settles. Illustrative function: $y=1-e^{-0.45t}\left(\cos 2.2t+\frac{0.45}{2.2}\sin 2.2t\right)$. The factor $e^{-0.45t}$ shrinks the oscillation, which is why it dies out. - Pink: rises smoothly without ever overshooting and creeps up to the input level. Illustrative function: $y=1-e^{-0.9t}$. Both are bounded (they never exceed about 1.53), so they satisfy BIBO for this input. Unstable system. In the professor's right-hand sketch both curves start at the input level, and both escape. - Blue: slowly at first, then ever faster, it grows without limit. Illustrative: $y=1+0.08\,(e^{0.35t}-1)$. The exponent $+0.35t$ is positive, so $e^{0.35t}\to\infty$. - Pink: oscillates around the input, but every swing is bigger than the last. Illustrative: $y=1+0.05\,e^{0.3t}\sin 2.5t$. The envelope $0.05\,e^{0.3t}$ grows, so the oscillation is unbounded even though it keeps returning to the input line. The difference between "stable oscillation" (blue, left) and "unstable oscillation" (pink, right) is only the sign of the exponent in the envelope : $e^{-0.45t}$ shrinks, $e^{+0.3t}$ grows. That is exactly the "sönüm–yükselme" (decay–growth) idea on p. 8 and the reason the s-plane is split into a left (stable) and right (unstable) half. See [The exponential building block]( /m/02/the-exponential-building-block). A system receives the bounded input $u(t)=$ unit step. Five different systems give the outputs below. Which outputs are bounded, and what can we conclude? (a) $y=1-e^{-2t}$ (b) $y=t$ (c) $y=e^{-t}\sin 5t$ (d) $y=e^{0.1t}\cos t$ (e) $y=3+2e^{-t}$ Check whether $\lvert y(t)\rvert$ stays below a fixed number for all $t\ge0$. Exponentials with a negative exponent die out; any positive exponent or any unchecked growth (like $t$) is unbounded. Use $\lvert\sin\rvert\le1$, $\lvert\cos\rvert\le1$. (a) $0\le e^{-2t}\le1$, so $0\le y\le1$: bounded . (b) $y=t\to\infty$: unbounded . (c) $\lvert y\rvert\le e^{-t}\cdot1\le1$: bounded (and it decays to 0). (d) $\lvert y\rvert$ reaches $e^{0.1t}$ whenever $\cos t=\pm1$, e.g. $t=2\pi k$, and $e^{0.1t}\to\infty$: unbounded (growing oscillation). (e) $3\le y\le 5$: bounded . Systems (b) and (d) are not BIBO stable : we found a bounded input (the step) that produces an unbounded output. One counter-example is enough to prove instability. For (a), (c), (e) the step test is consistent with stability, but strictly BIBO asks for every bounded input; a single test cannot prove stability. (Later modules give a test based on the system's poles that does prove it.) Bounded: (a), (c), (e). Unbounded → system unstable: (b), (d). A water tank fed by a pump: the water level is the integral of the inflow, $y(t)=\int 0^t u(\tau)\,d\tau$. Is this BIBO stable? Let the pump run at constant rate 1: $u(t)=u(t)$ (unit step, bounded by 1). Using the relation $r(t)=\int 0^t u\,d\tau$ from p. 2: $$ y(t)=\int 0^t 1\,d\tau=t=r(t). $$ The output is a ramp, which grows without bound (the tank overflows). Bounded input, unbounded output: not BIBO stable . The integrator is not BIBO stable: a unit step in gives a unit ramp out. Oscillation alone says nothing. The blue curve on the left of p. 3 oscillates and is stable; the pink curve on the right oscillates and is unstable. Look at the envelope : shrinking → stable, growing → unstable. A response such as $y=1-\cos 3t$ oscillates forever with constant amplitude. It is bounded for the step input, yet it never settles, and such a system can be driven to unbounded output by a sine input at the same frequency. Do not call it "stable" in an exam without qualification; the notes' stable sketches always settle . This borderline case is treated properly once poles are introduced.

title: Step response performance criteria
text: Sistem Çıkışı ve Kontrol Kriterleri (System Output and Control Criteria). To measure a system's performance we take certain measurements on its output. The professor's advice: the best way to understand these measurements is to look at an example unit step response ( ). Why the step? Because it is the most common real command (a new set-point), it is easy to generate in a lab (flip a switch), and every quality of interest (speed, overshoot, oscillation, accuracy) shows up clearly in it.

title: The annotated unit step response
text: Here is the professor's figure, redrawn from a real underdamped response (a curve that overshoots and oscillates while settling). The values ($y {ss}=0.9$ etc.) are chosen to match the shape of the sketch; the notes give no numbers. What the figure shows, piece by piece (match each item with the sketch on p. 4): - $r(t)=1$ (upper dashed line): the desired output. The input is a unit step, so we want the output to become 1. - $y {ss}$ (lower dashed line): where the output actually ends up. In the sketch it is a little below 1. - $t r$ : the first moment the curve reaches the $y {ss}$ line. - $t p$ : the moment of the highest peak. - $m$ : the blue double arrow from the peak down to $y {ss}$ (not down to 1!). - $t s$ : the moment after which the curve stays close to $y {ss}$. - $e {ss}$ : the gap between the two dashed lines at the right end (the light-blue arrows). - Geçici Durum / Kalıcı Durum : the part of the response before settling is the ; afterwards the . Play with the knobs: the "damping knob" $\xi$ controls how oscillatory the curve is (small $\xi$ → big overshoot, many swings), and the "speed knob" $\omega n$ stretches or compresses the time axis. Notice: - $e {ss}$ depends only on $y {ss}$, not on how the curve gets there; - $m$ (as a percentage of $y {ss}$) depends only on $\xi$; doubling $\omega n$ halves $t r$, $t p$, $t s$ but leaves $m\%$ unchanged; - a tighter tolerance (2% instead of 5%) gives a later $t s$. The formulas behind these observations (for this particular kind of curve) are derived in [Module 08]( /m/08). In this module we only need the definitions and the ability to read values off a curve.

title: Definitions of the parameters
text: The professor defines five quantities. The time from the start ($t=0$) until the system output reaches its steady-state value $y {ss}$ for the first time. Why it matters: it measures how fast the system reacts. A cruise control with $t r=2$ s feels lively, one with $t r=20$ s feels sluggish. The professor uses the "0 → 100% of $y {ss}$" definition (and underlines ilk , first ). Many textbooks instead use 10% → 90% of $y {ss}$, mainly because a response that never overshoots (like $1-e^{-t}$) reaches 100% only at $t=\infty$. With the professor's definition such a response has $t r=\infty$; see the [first-order example]( /m/02/ex-a-response-with-no-overshoot). In this course, use the professor's definition unless a question says otherwise. The final value the output goes to as $t\to\infty$, once all changes in the output have died out: $$ y {ss}=\lim {t\to\infty}y(t). $$ The largest deviation of the response above the steady-state value: $$ m=y {max}-y {ss}=y(t p)-y {ss}. $$ Why it matters: overshoot means the system goes past the target. For a robot arm it may hit something; for a heater it means discomfort; for a voltage regulator it may damage electronics. It is often quoted as a percentage of the final value: $\%m=100\,\dfrac{m}{y {ss}}$. The overshoot symbol in the notes (p. 4 and p. 5) looks like a lower-case $m$; it could be meant as $M$. We use $m$ as written. The peak time $t p$ appears on the figure but has no separate definition in the text: it is the time at which the maximum $y {max}$ (and hence $m$) occurs. The time at which the deviation of the response from its steady-state value enters the desired tolerance band (and stays inside it from then on). Why it matters: it tells you when the system has "calmed down" and can be treated as finished. The tolerance is chosen by the designer; typical values are $\pm2\%$ or $\pm5\%$ of $y {ss}$. The notes do not fix a percentage, so an exam question must state it. The notes say $t s$ is "the first instant at which the deviation enters the tolerance band". Taken literally that would be wrong for an oscillating response: the curve first passes through the band on its way up (near $t r$!) and then leaves it again at the overshoot. The intended meaning, and the one shown in the professor's own figure (where $t s$ is marked at the end of the oscillations), is: the instant after which the response remains inside the band for good . The explorer above shows both numbers: "first entry into band" is close to $t r$, while the true $t s$ is much later. The difference between the desired output value (1 in our example) and the system's steady-state value $y {ss}$: $$ e {ss}=r-y {ss}=1-y {ss}\qquad(\text{unit step input}). $$ Why it matters: it measures accuracy . If you set the thermostat to 22 °C and the room settles at 21.5 °C, the steady-state error is 0.5 °C, forever. In the definition on p. 5 the notes write "Sistem kalıcı durum değeri (ess) ile istenilen çıkış değeri arasındaki farktır". The parenthesis should read $(y {ss})$: the steady-state value is $y {ss}$, and $e {ss}$ is the difference $1-y {ss}$, as the figure on p. 4 shows (arrows between the $r(t)=1$ line and the $y {ss}$ line). Sign of $e {ss}$. With $e {ss}=1-y {ss}$, a system that ends below the target has positive error, one that ends above it has negative error. Some books quote $\lvert e {ss}\rvert$; state which you use. Transient and steady state. Everything that happens before the response settles (the rise, the overshoot, the swings) is the transient ( geçici durum ): it is temporary and dies out in a stable system. What is left forever is the steady state ( kalıcı durum ). $t r$, $t p$, $m$, $t s$ describe the transient; $y {ss}$ and $e {ss}$ describe the steady state. $t s$ is the border between them. 1. Draw axes; mark $r=1$ and (if different) $y {ss}$ as two dashed horizontal lines. 2. Start the curve at the origin, rise steeply, cross $y {ss}$ (drop a dashed line: $t r$), cross 1, reach one clear peak (dashed line: $t p$), come back down below $y {ss}$, a smaller bump, and flatten onto $y {ss}$ (arrow: $t s$). 3. Add the double arrow peak → $y {ss}$ labelled $m$, the gap 1 − $y {ss}$ labelled $e {ss}$, and the words Geçici Durum ← → Kalıcı Durum above $t s$. Each swing should be visibly smaller than the previous one; otherwise you have drawn an unstable or borderline system.
