title: Transform of a damped t sin 4t plus a delayed impulse
Initial and final values from F(s)
Professor's examples (p6–p7)
text: $$ \frac{dy}{dt}+3y+\int 0^t y\,dt=u(t),\qquad y(0)=1,\qquad Y(s)=\,? $$ The equation contains a derivative and an integral of the unknown (an integro-differential equation ). In time that is awkward; in $s$ both become simple factors. Use the derivative property for $\frac{dy}{dt}$, linearity for $3y$, the integral property for $\int 0^t y\,dt$, and the step transform for $u(t)$: $$ sY(s)-y(0)+3Y(s)+\frac{Y(s)}{s}=\frac{1}{s}. $$ With $y(0)=1$, move it to the right: $sY+3Y+\frac{Y}{s}=\frac1s+1$. Write the left side over the common denominator $s$: $$ \frac{s^2Y(s)+3sY(s)+Y(s)}{s}=\frac{1}{s}+1=\frac{1+s}{s}. $$ Multiply both sides by $s$: $Y(s)\,(s^2+3s+1)=s+1$. $$ Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{s^2+3s+1} $$ Sanity check with the IVT: $\lim {s\to\infty}sY(s)=\lim\frac{s^2+s}{s^2+3s+1}=1=y(0)$ ✓ — the transform "remembers" the initial value we put in. (The time-domain solution is [Exercise "Time response of the p6 example"]( /m/03/practice-exercises).) $$ f(t)=e^{-2t}\,t\,\sin(4t)+5\delta(t-2),\qquad F(s)=\,? $$ By linearity, treat the two terms separately. The first is a product of three factors — exactly the situation the properties are for: start from the innermost known transform ($\sin4t$), then apply "multiplication by $t$", then "multiplication by $e^{-2t}$". $$ \L\{\sin4t\}=\frac{4}{s^2+16}\qquad(\omega=4). $$ $$ \L\{t\sin4t\}=(-1)^1\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{4}{s^2+16}\right). $$ Derivative by the chain rule: $\frac{d}{ds}\,4(s^2+16)^{-1}=4\cdot(-1)(s^2+16)^{-2}\cdot2s=\frac{-2s\cdot4}{(s^2+16)^2}$. So $$ \L\{t\sin4t\}=(-1)\frac{-2s\cdot4}{(s^2+16)^2}=\frac{8s}{(s^2+16)^2}. $$ $$ \L\{e^{-2t}\,t\sin4t\}=\frac{8(s+2)}{\left[(s+2)^2+16\right]^2}. $$ Every $s$ is replaced — the one in the numerator too. $\L\{5\delta(t)\}=5$ (linearity), and a delay of $t 0=2$ multiplies by $e^{-2s}$: $\L\{5\delta(t-2)\}=e^{-2s}\cdot5$. $$ F(s)=\frac{8(s+2)}{\left[(s+2)^2+16\right]^2}+5e^{-2s} $$ Order matters in this kind of problem: apply $t$ first, then $e^{-2t}$. (Doing the shift first and then differentiating also works — $-\frac{d}{ds}\frac{4}{(s+2)^2+16}$ gives the same result — but mixing them up, e.g. differentiating and forgetting to shift the numerator $s$, is the typical error.) Numerical check: at $s=1$ the formula gives $\frac{24}{625}=0.0384$, and integrating $e^{-2t}t\sin4t\,e^{-t}$ numerically gives $0.0384$ ✓. $$ F(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s^2+2s+4)}\quad\text{ise}\quad f(0)=\,?\;;\;f(\infty)=\,? $$ ("ise" = "if/then".) We are not asked for $f(t)$ — only its start and end — so the IVT and FVT are the right tools. $$ f(0)=\lim {s\to\infty}sF(s)=\lim {s\to\infty}\cancel{s}\,\frac{s+2}{\cancel{s}(s^2+2s+4)}=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{s+2}{s^2+2s+4}=0 . $$ The denominator is one degree higher, so the ratio goes to 0. Poles of $sF(s)=\frac{s+2}{s^2+2s+4}$: $s=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}=-1\pm j\sqrt3$. Both have real part $-1$ — left half-plane ✓. (The notes skip this check; it is good practice to write it.) $$ f(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sF(s)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+2}{s^2+2s+4}=\frac{2}{4}=0.5 . $$ (The notes write $0{,}5$ with a decimal comma.) $$ f(0)=0,\qquad f(\infty)=0.5 $$ Check by inverting (techniques from later in this module): $F(s)=\frac{0.5}{s}-\frac{0.5s}{s^2+2s+4}$ gives $f(t)=0.5-0.5e^{-t}\left(\cos\sqrt3t-\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\sin\sqrt3t\right)$, so $f(0)=0.5-0.5=0$ and $f(\infty)=0.5$ ✓.

title: Linearity: a sum of basic signals
Sign trap in the s-shift: a growing exponential
t squared times e^-t two ways
Delayed step, delayed ramp and a rectangular pulse
More forward-transform examples
text: $f(t)=3-2e^{-4t}+5\cos2t$ (for $t\ge0$). Find $F(s)$. $3=3u(t)\to\frac3s$; $\;-2e^{-4t}\to-\frac{2}{s+4}$ ($a=4$); $\;5\cos2t\to5\frac{s}{s^2+4}$ ($\omega=2$, so $\omega^2=4$). $$ F(s)=\frac{3}{s}-\frac{2}{s+4}+\frac{5s}{s^2+4} $$ Check with the IVT: $\lim {s\to\infty}sF=3-2+5=6=f(0)=3-2+5$ ✓. $f(t)=e^{-3t}\sin2t$. Find $F(s)$. $\L\{\sin2t\}=\frac{2}{s^2+4}$. Multiplication by $e^{-3t}$ (lower sign, $a=3$) replaces $s$ by $s+3$: $$ F(s)=\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+4}=\frac{2}{s^2+6s+13}. $$ $$ \L\{e^{-3t}\sin2t\}=\frac{2}{(s+3)^2+4} $$ Interpretation: poles $-3\pm j2$ — decay rate 3 (real part), oscillation frequency 2 (imaginary part). Reading poles like this becomes second nature in later modules. $f(t)=e^{2t}\cos t$. Find $F(s)$. "Exponential with a 2, so $s+2$": $\frac{s+2}{(s+2)^2+1}$. Wrong. That is the transform of $e^{-2t}\cos t$. $e^{+at}f 1\to F 1(s-a)$: the sign flips . With $a=2$, replace $s$ by $s-2$ in $\frac{s}{s^2+1}$: $$ F(s)=\frac{s-2}{(s-2)^2+1}. $$ $$ \L\{e^{2t}\cos t\}=\frac{s-2}{(s-2)^2+1} $$ Sanity check by pole location: $f$ grows, so the poles must be in the right half-plane — they are at $2\pm j$ ✓. The wrong answer would have poles at $-2\pm j$ (decaying), which contradicts the signal. $f(t)=t\cos3t$. Find $F(s)$. $\L\{\cos3t\}=\frac{s}{s^2+9}$. Quotient rule $\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$ with $u=s$, $v=s^2+9$: $$ \frac{d}{ds}\frac{s}{s^2+9}=\frac{1\cdot(s^2+9)-s\cdot2s}{(s^2+9)^2}=\frac{9-s^2}{(s^2+9)^2}. $$ Multiply by $(-1)^1$: $$ \L\{t\cos3t\}=\frac{s^2-9}{(s^2+9)^2} $$ Check at $s=1$: formula gives $\frac{-8}{100}=-0.08$; numerical integration of $t\cos3t\,e^{-t}$ gives $-0.08$ ✓. Note the double poles at $\pm j3$ — the signature of an oscillation whose amplitude grows like $t$. $\L\{e^{-t}\}=(s+1)^{-1}$. Then $\frac{d}{ds}(s+1)^{-1}=-(s+1)^{-2}$ and $\frac{d^2}{ds^2}(s+1)^{-1}=2(s+1)^{-3}$. With $(-1)^2=1$: $\L\{t^2e^{-t}\}=\frac{2}{(s+1)^3}$. $\L\{t^2\}=\frac{2!}{s^3}=\frac{2}{s^3}$; multiply by $e^{-t}$ → replace $s$ by $s+1$: $\frac{2}{(s+1)^3}$. $$ \L\{t^2e^{-t}\}=\frac{2}{(s+1)^3} $$ Both routes agree, as they must. This pair reappears in the professor's repeated-root example on p12. $u(t-3)$: $F=\frac1s$, $t 0=3$ → $\frac{e^{-3s}}{s}$. $(t-2)u(t-2)$ is the ramp shifted by 2 → $\frac{e^{-2s}}{s^2}$. The pulse is "on at 0, off at 1": $p(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$. Linearity and time shift: $\frac1s-\frac{e^{-s}}{s}$. $$ u(t-3)\to\frac{e^{-3s}}{s},\qquad (t-2)u(t-2)\to\frac{e^{-2s}}{s^2},\qquad u(t)-u(t-1)\to\frac{1-e^{-s}}{s} $$ This is how a switch-on/switch-off input (e.g. a heater run for one hour) is described in the $s$-domain.

title: IVT and FVT with a check by inversion
IVT and FVT on the professor's ODE result
More IVT and FVT examples
text: $F(s)=\frac{10(s+2)}{s(s+5)}$. Find $f(0^+)$ and $f(\infty)$. $sF(s)=\frac{10(s+2)}{s+5}$; as $s\to\infty$ this tends to $10$. Poles of $sF(s)$: only $s=-5$ (LHP) ✓. Then $\lim {s\to0}\frac{10(s+2)}{s+5}=\frac{20}{5}=4$. $$ f(0^+)=10,\qquad f(\infty)=4 $$ Check by inversion: $\frac{10(s+2)}{s(s+5)}=\frac{4}{s}+\frac{6}{s+5}$ (coefficients by the cover-up rule below), so $f(t)=4+6e^{-5t}$: $f(0)=10$ ✓, $f(\infty)=4$ ✓. $F(s)=\frac{5}{s(s-1)}$. A student writes $f(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sF(s)=\frac{5}{-1}=-5$. $sF(s)=\frac{5}{s-1}$ has a pole at $s=+1$ — right half-plane . The FVT is not allowed. $\frac{5}{s(s-1)}=\frac{-5}{s}+\frac{5}{s-1}$, so $f(t)=-5+5e^{t}\to+\infty$. $f(\infty)$ does not exist ($f$ grows without bound). The "$-5$" is meaningless — it even has the wrong sign. The p6 result $Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{s^2+3s+1}$ with $y(0)=1$. $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{s(s+1)}{s^2+3s+1}=1$ ✓ (matches the given $y(0)=1$). Roots of $s^2+3s+1$: $s=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{9-4}}{2}=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}\approx-0.382,\;-2.618$, both negative ✓. Then $\lim {s\to0}\frac{s(s+1)}{s^2+3s+1}=\frac{0}{1}=0$. $$ y(0^+)=1,\qquad y(\infty)=0 $$ Interpretation: although a step input $u(t)$ is applied, the output returns to 0 — the integral term $\int y\,dt$ in the equation keeps pushing it back. Theorems like these let you predict such behaviour without solving the equation.

title: Inverse Laplace transform
text: : given $F(s)$, find $f(t)=\Li\{F(s)\}$. The notes say: to find the time-domain expression of a Laplace function, look at the Laplace properties and the transform table; in this way the time-domain expression can be written directly. In practice: make each term of $F(s)$ look exactly like a table entry — by pulling out constants, creating the right numerator ($\omega$, $n!$, $s+a$) and completing the square — then read off $f(t)$. $$ F(s)=\frac{2}{s}-\frac{1}{s^3}-\frac{3}{(s+4)^2}+\frac{5}{s^2+4}+\frac{s+1}{s^2+2s+4} $$ By linearity, invert term by term. $\frac{2}{s}=2\cdot\frac{1}{s}\;\Rightarrow\;2u(t)$. The table has $\frac{n!}{s^{n+1}}\leftrightarrow t^n$; here $n+1=3$, $n=2$, so the numerator must be $2!=2$: $$ -\frac{1}{s^3}=\frac{-1}{2!}\cdot\frac{2!}{s^3}\;\Rightarrow\;-\frac12t^2 . $$ $\frac{1}{(s+a)^2}\leftrightarrow t\,e^{-at}$ with $a=4$: $\;-3\frac{1}{(s+4)^2}\Rightarrow-3e^{-4t}\,t$. $s^2+2s+4=(s^2+2s+1)+3=(s+1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2$. The numerator is already $s+1$, so this is the damped cosine with $a=1$, $\omega=\sqrt3$: $$ \frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2}\;\Rightarrow\;e^{-t}\cos(\sqrt3t). $$ $\omega^2=4$, $\omega=2$, but the numerator is 5, not 2: $\frac{5}{s^2+4}=\frac{2.5\cdot2}{s^2+(2)^2}\Rightarrow2.5\sin(2t)$. (Written $2{,}5$ in the notes.) $$ f(t)=2u(t)-\frac{t^2}{2}-3e^{-4t}\,t+2.5\sin(2t)+e^{-t}\cos(\sqrt3t) $$ Check: at $t=0$, $f=2-0-0+0+1=3$; the IVT on $F$ gives $2-0-0+0+1=3$ ✓ (only terms with numerator degree one less than the denominator contribute). Numerically at $s=1$: $F(1)=2.1657$, and the Laplace integral of the answer is also $2.1657$ ✓.

title: Partial fraction expansion
text: All terms of the p8 example were already in table form. The notes continue: in general we will not meet terms of that form; we then need to break the expression into its simple components using reduction methods. The method is : rewrite $$ F(s)=\frac{N(s)}{D(s)}\qquad(N=\text{numerator, pay};\;D=\text{denominator, payda}) $$ as a sum of small fractions, each of which is a table entry. Which small fractions appear depends on the roots of the — the poles — and there are three cases in the notes. Partial fractions as taught here require the numerator degree to be smaller than the denominator degree (a proper fraction). All examples in the notes satisfy this. If it were not the case, you would first divide the polynomials; that never happens in this module.

title: Partial fractions with three distinct real roots
Distinct roots with a pole at the origin
Distinct real roots
text: . Let $$ F(s)=\frac{N(s)}{(s+p 1)(s+p 2)\cdots(s+p n)} $$ with all $p i$ real and different. Then $$ F(s)=\frac{K 1}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 2}{s+p 2}+\dots+\frac{K n}{s+p n} $$ and, since each term is $\frac{K i}{s+p i}\leftrightarrow K ie^{-p it}$, $$ f(t)=K 1e^{-p 1t}+K 2e^{-p 2t}+\dots+K ne^{-p nt}. $$ The notes call the $p i$ "the roots" (p kökleri). Strictly, the roots of the denominator (the poles) are $s=-p 1,\,-p 2,\dots$ — the values that make a factor $s+p i$ zero. The formulas are written consistently with that: the limit is taken as $s\to-p i$. To find the coefficients : $$ K i=\lim {s\to-p i}\Big\{(s+p i)F(s)\Big\} $$ Why it works. Multiply the whole expansion by $(s+p 1)$: $$ (s+p 1)F(s)=K 1+K 2\frac{s+p 1}{s+p 2}+\dots+K n\frac{s+p 1}{s+p n}. $$ On the left, $(s+p 1)$ cancels the same factor in the denominator of $F$. Now set $s=-p 1$: every term on the right except $K 1$ contains the factor $(s+p 1)=0$ and disappears. What is left is $K 1$. In practice: cover up the factor $(s+p i)$ in the denominator of $F$ and evaluate everything else at $s=-p i$. This is called the cover-up rule ; $K i$ is called the residue at the pole $-p i$. $$ F(s)=\frac{s^2+2s+2}{(s+1)(s+2)(s-3)}=\frac{K 1}{s+1}+\frac{K 2}{s+2}+\frac{K 3}{s-3}. $$ Poles $-1,-2,+3$: real and distinct. (Note $s-3$ means $p 3=-3$, a pole at $+3$.) $$ K 1=\lim {s\to-1}(s+1)F(s)=\left.\frac{s^2+2s+2}{(s+2)(s-3)}\right {s=-1}=\frac{1-2+2}{(1)(-4)}=\frac{-1}{4}. $$ $$ K 2=\left.\frac{s^2+2s+2}{(s+1)(s-3)}\right {s=-2}=\frac{4-4+2}{(-1)(-5)}=\frac{2}{5}. $$ $$ K 3=\left.\frac{s^2+2s+2}{(s+1)(s+2)}\right {s=3}=\frac{9+6+2}{(4)(5)}=\frac{17}{20}. $$ $\frac{K}{s+a}\to Ke^{-at}$; for $s-3$, $a=-3$, giving $e^{3t}$. $$ f(t)=-\frac14e^{-t}+\frac25e^{-2t}+\frac{17}{20}e^{3t} $$ Checks: (1) recombine at $s=4$: $F(4)=\frac{26}{30}=0.8667$, and $-\frac{1}{20}+\frac{2}{30}+\frac{17}{20}=0.8667$ ✓. (2) IVT: $f(0)=-0.25+0.4+0.85=1$ and $\lim {s\to\infty}sF=1$ ✓. (3) The FVT does not apply (pole at $+3$): $f(t)$ grows like $e^{3t}$. $F(s)=\frac{2s+3}{s(s+1)(s+3)}=\frac{K 1}{s}+\frac{K 2}{s+1}+\frac{K 3}{s+3}$. $K 1=\left.\frac{2s+3}{(s+1)(s+3)}\right {s=0}=\frac{3}{3}=1$ $K 2=\left.\frac{2s+3}{s(s+3)}\right {s=-1}=\frac{1}{(-1)(2)}=-\frac12$ $K 3=\left.\frac{2s+3}{s(s+1)}\right {s=-3}=\frac{-3}{(-3)(-2)}=-\frac12$ $$ f(t)=1-\frac12e^{-t}-\frac12e^{-3t} $$ Checks: $f(0)=1-0.5-0.5=0$ and IVT $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{2s^2+3s}{s^3+\dots}=0$ ✓; FVT (poles of $sF$ at $-1,-3$) gives $\frac{3}{3}=1=f(\infty)$ ✓. Sum of coefficients $1-\frac12-\frac12=0=f(0)$ — a quick consistency test for any proper $F$ whose numerator degree is at least two less than the denominator.

title: Partial fractions with a triple root
Repeated root at s = -1 with a pole at the origin
Repeated real roots
text: . If the denominator has a root repeated $n$ times, the expansion must contain every power of that factor up to $n$: $$ F(s)=\frac{N(s)}{(s+p)^n}=\frac{K 1}{(s+p)^n}+\frac{K 2}{(s+p)^{n-1}}+\dots+\frac{K n}{s+p}. $$ Each term is inverted with table entry 7, $\frac{1}{(s+p)^k}\leftrightarrow\frac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}e^{-pt}$ (which is just $\L\{t^n\}=\frac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ plus the $s$-shift): $$ f(t)=K 1\frac{t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}e^{-pt}+K 2\frac{t^{n-2}}{(n-2)!}e^{-pt}+\dots+K ne^{-pt}. $$ $$ K i=\lim {s\to-p}\frac{1}{(i-1)!}\,\frac{d^{\,i-1}}{ds^{\,i-1}}\Big[(s+p)^nF(s)\Big],\qquad i=1,2,\dots,n $$ The notes say the root is repeated "at the point $s=p$" and write the limit as $\lim {s\to p}$. With the factor $(s+p)^n$, the root is at $s=-p$ (that is where $s+p=0$), so the limit must be $s\to-p$. The professor's own example on p12 does it correctly: for $(s+1)^3$ the limit is $s\to-1$. Why the derivatives are needed. Multiply the expansion by $(s+p)^n$ (for simplicity, $F$ has only this repeated factor): $$ (s+p)^nF(s)=K 1+K 2(s+p)+K 3(s+p)^2+\dots+K n(s+p)^{n-1}. $$ - At $s=-p$ every term except $K 1$ vanishes → $K 1=\big[(s+p)^nF\big] {s=-p}$. That is the cover-up rule again, but it only gives the first coefficient. - The cover-up trick cannot reach $K 2$: multiplying by $(s+p)^{n-1}$ instead would leave $\frac{K 1}{s+p}$, which blows up at $s=-p$. - Differentiate once: $\frac{d}{ds}\big[(s+p)^nF\big]=K 2+2K 3(s+p)+3K 4(s+p)^2+\dots$. At $s=-p$ only $K 2$ survives. - Differentiate twice: $2K 3+3\cdot2K 4(s+p)+\dots$. At $s=-p$ this is $2K 3=2!\,K 3$ — hence the factor $\frac{1}{2!}$. - In general the $(i-1)$-th derivative leaves $(i-1)!\,K i$, which explains the $\frac{1}{(i-1)!}$. So differentiation peels off one power of $(s+p)$ at a time, exactly like reading the coefficients of a Taylor series. If $F$ also has other (distinct) poles, those terms are handled with the ordinary cover-up rule; after multiplying by $(s+p)^n$ they still contain $(s+p)^n$ and vanish at $s=-p$ together with their first $n-1$ derivatives, so the formula above is unaffected. $$ F(s)=\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^3(s+2)} $$ At $s=-1$ there is a 3-fold root ( 3 tane katlı kök ), and a simple root at $s=-2$: $$ F(s)=\frac{K 1}{(s+1)^3}+\frac{K 2}{(s+1)^2}+\frac{K 3}{s+1}+\frac{A}{s+2}. $$ $$ A=\lim {s\to-2}(s+2)F(s)=\left.\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^3}\right {s=-2}=\frac{1}{(-1)^3}=-1. $$ $(s+1)^3F(s)=\frac{s+3}{s+2}$. $$ K 1=\left.\frac{s+3}{s+2}\right {s=-1}=\frac{2}{1}=2. $$ Quotient rule: $$ K 2=\lim {s\to-1}\left[\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{s+3}{s+2}\right)\right]=\left.\frac{(s+2)-(s+3)}{(s+2)^2}\right {s=-1}=\left.\frac{-1}{s^2+4s+4}\right {s=-1}=\frac{-1}{1-4+4}=-1. $$ Differentiate the result of the previous step once more, $\frac{d}{ds}\frac{-1}{s^2+4s+4}=\frac{2s+4}{(s^2+4s+4)^2}$: $$ K 3=\lim {s\to-1}\frac{1}{2!}\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{-1}{s^2+4s+4}\right)=\left.\frac12\cdot\frac{2s+4}{(s^2+4s+4)^2}\right {s=-1}=\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{1}=1. $$ $\frac{2}{(s+1)^3}\to2\cdot\frac{t^2}{2!}e^{-t}$, $\;\frac{-1}{(s+1)^2}\to-te^{-t}$, $\;\frac{1}{s+1}\to e^{-t}$, $\;\frac{-1}{s+2}\to-e^{-2t}$. $$ f(t)=2\cdot\frac{1}{2!}t^2e^{-t}-te^{-t}+e^{-t}-e^{-2t}=t^2e^{-t}-te^{-t}+e^{-t}-e^{-2t} $$ Checks: recombination at $s=1$: $F(1)=\frac{4}{8\cdot3}=0.1667$; $\frac{2}{8}-\frac14+\frac12-\frac13=0.1667$ ✓. $f(0)=0-0+1-1=0$ and IVT $\lim sF=\lim\frac{s^2}{s^4}\to0$ ✓. A shortcut check: $K 3+A=1-1=0$ — the $\frac1s$-like terms must cancel when the numerator degree is at least two below the denominator. $F(s)=\frac{s+3}{s(s+1)^2}=\frac{K 1}{(s+1)^2}+\frac{K 2}{s+1}+\frac{A}{s}$ (double root, $n=2$). $A=\left.\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^2}\right {s=0}=3$. $(s+1)^2F=\frac{s+3}{s}=1+\frac3s$. $K 1=\left.\frac{s+3}{s}\right {s=-1}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2$. $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\left(1+\frac3s\right)\right {s=-1}=\left.-\frac{3}{s^2}\right {s=-1}=-3$. $$ f(t)=3-2te^{-t}-3e^{-t} $$ Checks: $f(0)=3-0-3=0$ ✓ (IVT: $\lim\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^2}=0$). FVT: poles of $sF$ at $-1$ (LHP), $\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^2}=3=f(\infty)$ ✓. Numerically $F(1)=1$ and $3-\frac{2}{4}-\frac32=1$ ✓. For $(s+1)^3$ you need three terms $\frac{K 1}{(s+1)^3}+\frac{K 2}{(s+1)^2}+\frac{K 3}{s+1}$. Writing only $\frac{K 1}{(s+1)^3}$ (or using the cover-up rule for $K 2,K 3$) gives a wrong answer. Count: an $n$-fold root contributes exactly $n$ unknowns.

title: Complex roots
text: . A polynomial with real coefficients has complex roots only in . Write them as $s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega$. Then $$ F(s)=\frac{N(s)}{(s+\alpha+j\omega)(s+\alpha-j\omega)}=\frac{K}{s+\alpha-j\omega}+\frac{K^ }{s+\alpha+j\omega}. $$ The notes state the roots as $s {1,2}=\alpha\pm j\omega$, but the factors $(s+\alpha+j\omega)(s+\alpha-j\omega)$ vanish at $s=-\alpha\mp j\omega$. With the factors as written (and the final formula $2 K e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega t+\theta)$, which decays for $\alpha 0$), the roots are $s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega$. Everything else in the derivation is consistent with this. Why the second coefficient is $K^ $. $K$ is found with the cover-up rule at the pole $-\alpha+j\omega$. Because $N$ and $D$ have real coefficients, evaluating at the conjugate point gives the conjugate value, $F(\bar s)=\overline{F(s)}$; so the cover-up at $-\alpha-j\omega$ gives exactly $\bar K=K^ $. You only ever compute one of them. Deriving the time function (Euler). Inverting each term like an exponential ($\frac{1}{s+a}\to e^{-at}$ with complex $a$): $$ f(t)=Ke^{-(\alpha-j\omega)t}+K^ e^{-(\alpha+j\omega)t}. $$ Write $K$ in polar form: $K= K \angle\theta= K e^{j\theta}$, $K^ = K e^{-j\theta}$. Then $$ f(t)= K e^{-\alpha t}e^{+j\omega t}e^{j\theta}+ K e^{-\alpha t}e^{-j\omega t}e^{-j\theta}= K e^{-\alpha t}\underbrace{\left(e^{j(\omega t+\theta)}+e^{-j(\omega t+\theta)}\right)} {2\cos(\omega t+\theta)}. $$ The bracket is $2\cos(\omega t+\theta)$ by the same Euler identity used for the cosine transform. The imaginary parts cancel — as they must, since $f(t)$ is a real signal. $$ \frac{K}{s+\alpha-j\omega}+\frac{K^ }{s+\alpha+j\omega}\;\longleftrightarrow\;f(t)=2 K \,e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega t+\theta),\qquad K= K \angle\theta $$ Reading it: real part of the pole ($-\alpha$) → envelope $e^{-\alpha t}$; imaginary part ($\omega$) → frequency ; residue $K$ → amplitude $2 K $ and phase $\theta$. And $K$ is found "with the methods of the distinct-root case" — the cover-up rule, now with complex arithmetic. $$ F(s)=\frac{s+1}{(s+2)(s^2+2s+2)} $$ Denominator roots ( payda kökleri ): $s 1=-2$, and from $s^2+2s+2=0$: $s=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-8}}{2}=-1\pm j$. So $\alpha=1$, $\omega=1$. $$ F(s)=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{K}{s+1-j}+\frac{K^ }{s+1+j}. $$ $$ A=\lim {s\to-2}(s+2)F(s)=\left.\frac{s+1}{s^2+2s+2}\right {s=-2}=\frac{-1}{4-4+2}=\frac{-1}{2}. $$ $$ K=\lim {s\to-1+j}(s+1-j)\frac{s+1}{(s+2)(s+1-j)(s+1+j)}=\left.\frac{s+1}{(s+2)(s+1+j)}\right {s=-1+j}=\frac{-1+j+1}{(-1+j+2)(-1+j+1+j)}. $$ Simplify: numerator $j$; first factor $1+j$; second factor $2j$: $$ K=\frac{\cancel{j}}{(1+j)(2\cancel{j})}=\frac{1}{2(1+j)}. $$ $1+j$ has magnitude $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$ and angle $\arctan\frac11=45^\circ$, so $2(1+j)=2\sqrt2\angle45^\circ$. Dividing by a complex number divides magnitudes and subtracts angles: $$ K=\frac{1}{2\sqrt2\angle45^\circ}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\angle-45^\circ,\qquad K =\frac{1}{2\sqrt2},\;\theta=-45^\circ,\;\omega=1. $$ $2 K =\frac{2}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\alpha=1$: $$ 2 K e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega t+\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-t}\cos(t-45^\circ). $$ $$ f(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-t}\cos(t-45^\circ)-\frac12e^{-2t} $$ Checks: $f(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}-\frac12=0$ and IVT $\lim sF=\lim\frac{s^2}{s^3}=0$ ✓. Numerically $F(2)=\frac{3}{4\cdot10}=0.075$ and the Laplace integral of the answer at $s=2$ is $0.0750$ ✓. The notes write the final result as $f(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t-45^\circ)-\frac12e^{-2t}$ — the envelope $e^{-\alpha t}=e^{-t}$ has been dropped (and $\alpha=1$ is never written down on the page). All the coefficients ($A=-\frac12$, $ K =\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}$, $\theta=-45^\circ$, $\omega=1$) are correct; only the last line is wrong. Correct: $$ f(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-t}\cos(t-45^\circ)-\frac12e^{-2t}. $$ Three ways to see the written answer cannot be right: (1) the poles $-1\pm j$ have real part $-1$, so the oscillation must decay like $e^{-t}$; (2) all poles are in the left half-plane, so the FVT gives $f(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sF(s)=0$, but the written answer oscillates forever; (3) at $s=2$ its Laplace transform is $0.175$ instead of $F(2)=0.075$. When writing $2 K e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega t+\theta)$, read $\alpha$ off the real part of the pole and write it down explicitly before writing $f(t)$ — exactly the step that went missing on p14. Only if the poles are on the imaginary axis ($\alpha=0$) is there no envelope.

title: Completing the square
text: An alternative to complex residues: keep the quadratic factor real, rewrite it as $(s+\alpha)^2+\omega^2$, and split the numerator so that each piece matches table entries 10 and 11. Completing the square: $s^2+bs+c=\left(s+\frac b2\right)^2+\left(c-\frac{b^2}{4}\right)$, so $\alpha=\frac b2$ and $\omega=\sqrt{c-\frac{b^2}{4}}$ (real when the roots are complex). Then split any linear numerator as $$ As+B=A(s+\alpha)+(B-A\alpha)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{As+B}{(s+\alpha)^2+\omega^2}\;\leftrightarrow\;e^{-\alpha t}\left[A\cos\omega t+\frac{B-A\alpha}{\omega}\sin\omega t\right]. $$ Amplitude–phase form. A sum $a\cos x+b\sin x$ can always be written as one cosine. Expanding $R\cos(x-\varphi)=R\cos\varphi\cos x+R\sin\varphi\sin x$ and comparing: $a=R\cos\varphi$, $b=R\sin\varphi$, so $$ a\cos x+b\sin x=R\cos(x-\varphi),\qquad R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\quad\tan\varphi=\frac ba $$ (choose $\varphi$ in the quadrant of the point $(a,b)$). This links the two methods: $R=2 K $ and $\varphi=-\theta$. $$ F(s)=\frac{s+2}{s^2+2s+4} $$ Roots $-1\pm j\sqrt3$ — complex. Instead of residues, complete the square. $s^2+2s+4=(s+1)^2+3=(s+1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2$, so $\alpha=1$, $\omega=\sqrt3$. $s+2=(s+1)+1$, and $1=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\sqrt3$: $$ F(s)=\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2}+\frac{\sqrt3}{(s+1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3}. $$ As the notes say: up to here we only rewrote $F(s)$ in the formats $\frac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ and $\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ of the table (shifted by $s\to s+1$); now the transform can be read off directly. $$ f(t)=e^{-t}\cos(\sqrt3t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3t). $$ $a=1$, $b=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$: $R=\sqrt{1+\frac13}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}=1.1547\approx1.155$, $\tan\varphi=\frac{1/\sqrt3}{1}\Rightarrow\varphi=30^\circ$ (first quadrant). $$ f(t)=e^{-t}\cos(\sqrt3t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3t)=1.155\,e^{-t}\cos(\sqrt3t-30^\circ) $$ Cross-check with the residue method: $K=\left.\frac{s+2}{s+1+j\sqrt3}\right {s=-1+j\sqrt3}=\frac{1+j\sqrt3}{2j\sqrt3}=0.5-j0.2887=0.5774\angle-30^\circ$, so $2 K =1.155$ and $\theta=-30^\circ$ ✓. IVT: $f(0)=1$ and $\lim\frac{s(s+2)}{s^2+2s+4}=1$ ✓. $F(s)=\frac{10}{s(s^2+2s+5)}$. Roots: $0$ and $-1\pm j2$ ($\alpha=1$, $\omega=2$). $A=\left.\frac{10}{s^2+2s+5}\right {s=0}=2$. $K=\left.\frac{10}{s(s+1+j2)}\right {s=-1+j2}=\frac{10}{(-1+j2)(j4)}=\frac{10}{-8-j4}$. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $-8+j4$: $K=\frac{10(-8+j4)}{64+16}=\frac{-80+j40}{80}=-1+j0.5$. Polar: $ K =\sqrt{1+0.25}=1.118$; the point $(-1,\,0.5)$ is in the second quadrant, $\theta=180^\circ-\arctan0.5=180^\circ-26.57^\circ=153.43^\circ$. $f(t)=2+2(1.118)e^{-t}\cos(2t+153.43^\circ)=2+2.236e^{-t}\cos(2t+153.4^\circ)$. Write $\frac{10}{s(s^2+2s+5)}=\frac2s+\frac{Bs+C}{s^2+2s+5}$. Multiply out: $10=2(s^2+2s+5)+(Bs+C)s$. Compare powers: $s^2$: $2+B=0\Rightarrow B=-2$; $s^1$: $4+C=0\Rightarrow C=-4$; $s^0$: $10=10$ ✓. $\frac{-2s-4}{(s+1)^2+4}=\frac{-2(s+1)-2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}=-2\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}-\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}$ $\Rightarrow f(t)=2-2e^{-t}\cos2t-e^{-t}\sin2t$. $a=-2$, $b=-1$: $R=\sqrt{5}=2.236$, point $(-2,-1)$ in the third quadrant, $\varphi=-180^\circ+26.57^\circ=-153.43^\circ$, so $-2\cos x-\sin x=2.236\cos(x+153.43^\circ)$ ✓. $$ f(t)=2-2e^{-t}\cos2t-e^{-t}\sin2t=2+2.236\,e^{-t}\cos(2t+153.4^\circ) $$ Checks: $f(0)=2-2=0$ (IVT: $\lim\frac{10}{s^2+\dots}=0$) ✓; $f(\infty)=2$ (FVT: $\frac{10}{5}=2$, poles of $sF$ in LHP) ✓.

title: Partial fraction explorer
text: Pick an example: the plot shows each term of the expansion (dashed) and their sum (thick), the poles in the $s$-plane, and a numerical check that the expansion equals the original fraction. Red dashed curves show what goes wrong in the two "mistake" situations (p14 as written; initial conditions forgotten). How each pole shows up in time: a real pole at $-a$ → $e^{-at}$; a repeated real pole → extra $t$, $t^2$ factors; a complex pair $-\alpha\pm j\omega$ → oscillation of frequency $\omega$ inside $e^{-\alpha t}$; a pole at 0 → a constant; a pole in the right half-plane → growth.

title: Second-order ODE with nonzero initial conditions
Solving differential equations
text: The full method combines everything: derivative property (with initial conditions) → algebra → partial fractions → table. 1. Transform every term. Derivatives: $y'\to sY-y(0)$, $y''\to s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$. Integrals: $\int 0^ty\to Y/s$. Inputs from the table. 2. Insert the initial values; collect $Y(s)$ on the left, everything else on the right. 3. Solve for $Y(s)$ as a single fraction. 4. Factor the denominator; decide the case (distinct / repeated / complex). 5. Partial fractions; invert with the table. 6. Check: $y(0)$ (and $y'(0)$) against the given values; IVT/FVT; substitute back into the ODE if time permits. $$ y''+5y'+6y=6u(t),\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y'(0)=-1 . $$ $$ \underbrace{s^2Y-2s-(-1)} {y''}+5\underbrace{(sY-2)} {y'}+6Y=\frac6s $$ $$ s^2Y-2s+1+5sY-10+6Y=\frac6s . $$ $(s^2+5s+6)Y=\frac6s+2s+9=\frac{2s^2+9s+6}{s}$, and $s^2+5s+6=(s+2)(s+3)$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{2s^2+9s+6}{s(s+2)(s+3)} . $$ $K 0=\left.\frac{2s^2+9s+6}{(s+2)(s+3)}\right {0}=\frac66=1$ $K {-2}=\left.\frac{2s^2+9s+6}{s(s+3)}\right {-2}=\frac{8-18+6}{(-2)(1)}=\frac{-4}{-2}=2$ $K {-3}=\left.\frac{2s^2+9s+6}{s(s+2)}\right {-3}=\frac{18-27+6}{(-3)(-1)}=\frac{-3}{3}=-1$ $$ y(t)=1+2e^{-2t}-e^{-3t} $$ Checks: $y(0)=1+2-1=2$ ✓; $y'(t)=-4e^{-2t}+3e^{-3t}$, $y'(0)=-1$ ✓; substituting: $y''=8e^{-2t}-9e^{-3t}$, so $y''+5y'+6y=(8-20+12)e^{-2t}+(-9+15-6)e^{-3t}+6=6$ ✓. FVT: $\lim {s\to0}sY=\frac{6}{6}=1$ ✓. Same equation, but the student writes $y''\to s^2Y$ and $y'\to sY$: $(s^2+5s+6)Y=\frac6s$, so $Y=\frac{6}{s(s+2)(s+3)}$. Cover-up: $\frac{6}{6}=1$, $\frac{6}{(-2)(1)}=-3$, $\frac{6}{(-3)(-1)}=2$ → $y(t)=1-3e^{-2t}+2e^{-3t}$. At $t=0$: $1-3+2=0$, but the problem says $y(0)=2$ ✗. The result is the response from rest — a different problem with the same final value 1, so the FVT alone would not have caught the error. Always check $y(0)$. Correct answer: $y(t)=1+2e^{-2t}-e^{-3t}$ (previous example). The difference between the two, $5e^{-2t}-3e^{-3t}$, is precisely the part of the response produced by the initial conditions.

title: Edge cases
text: - Pole at the origin. $\frac{K}{s}\leftrightarrow K$ — a constant. A single pole at 0 is what makes a nonzero final value; the FVT is valid with it. - Double pole at the origin ($\frac{1}{s^2}$): a ramp, grows forever — FVT invalid. - Poles on the imaginary axis ($\alpha=0$): $2 K \cos(\omega t+\theta)$ — no envelope, oscillation never dies; FVT invalid. Repeated poles on the axis ($\frac{s^2-9}{(s^2+9)^2}\leftrightarrow t\cos3t$) give oscillations that grow. - Pole in the right half-plane ($s=+3$ on p10): the corresponding term grows exponentially and dominates; FVT invalid. - Complex poles with $\omega\to0$ : the pair merges into a double real pole and $e^{-\alpha t}\cos\omega t\to e^{-\alpha t}$, while the sine term $\frac{1}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t\to te^{-\alpha t}$ — the repeated-root case is the limit of the complex case. - $s-p$ instead of $s+p$ in a factor: the pole is at $+p$; the cover-up value is $s=+p$, and the term is $e^{+pt}$. - Delay factors $e^{-st 0}$ : not part of the partial fractions. Invert the rational part, then shift the result by $t 0$ (time-shift property backwards). - Numerator degree ≥ denominator degree : not proper — divide first (does not occur in the notes). - The impulse at $t=0$ : use the lower limit $0^-$; $f(0^+)$ from the IVT is the value just after the impulse.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. "Find $\L\{\dots\}$" with products like $e^{-at}t\sin\omega t$ or delays → properties (p7-type). Work from the inside out: table entry → $t^n$ rule → $s$-shift; delays last. 2. "Find $Y(s)$" from an equation with $y'$, $\int y$ → derivative/integral property (p6-type). Don't forget $y(0)$. 3. "Find $f(0)$, $f(\infty)$" → IVT/FVT (p7-type). Check the poles before the FVT. 4. "Find $f(t)$" with table-shaped terms → table (p8-type): create $n!$, $\omega$, $(s+a)$. 5. "Find $f(t)$" with a factored denominator → partial fractions (p10/p12/p14) or completing the square (p15). 1. Factor the denominator; list the poles with multiplicities. 2. Write the expansion: one term per distinct real pole; $n$ terms for an $n$-fold pole; a $K$, $K^ $ pair (or a real quadratic term) for each complex pair. 3. Distinct real: $K i=\big[(s+p i)F\big] {s=-p i}$. 4. Repeated: $K 1$ by cover-up; $K i=\frac{1}{(i-1)!}\frac{d^{i-1}}{ds^{i-1}}\big[(s+p)^nF\big] {s=-p}$. 5. Complex: $K$ at $s=-\alpha+j\omega$ → polar $ K \angle\theta$ → $2 K e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega t+\theta)$. Or complete the square. 6. Write $f(t)$; check $f(0)$ with the IVT, $f(\infty)$ with the FVT (if valid), or recombine at one value of $s$. 1. Dropping initial conditions in $\L\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$. 2. Wrong sign in the $s$-shift : $e^{-at}\to s+a$, $e^{+at}\to s-a$. 3. Not shifting the numerator after multiplication by $e^{-at}$: every $s$ becomes $s+a$. 4. Forgetting $e^{-\alpha t}$ in the complex-root answer (the p14 slip). 5. Using the FVT illegally (RHP poles, poles on the $j\omega$-axis, double pole at 0). 6. Angle of $K$ in the wrong quadrant : always locate the point $(\operatorname{Re}K,\operatorname{Im}K)$ before taking $\arctan$. - IVT check : compare $f(0)$ from your answer with $\lim {s\to\infty}sF(s)$. - Recombination check : put $s=1$ (or any convenient number that is not a pole) into both $F(s)$ and your expansion — they must be equal. - Pole check : every pole must appear in $f(t)$ as the correct exponential/envelope.

text: Explain in your own words why $\L\{f'(t)\}=sF(s)-f(0)$, and why this makes the Laplace transform useful for differential equations. Integration by parts moves the derivative from $f$ onto the kernel $e^{-st}$: $\int 0^\infty f'e^{-st}dt=[fe^{-st}] 0^\infty+s\int 0^\infty fe^{-st}dt$. Differentiating $e^{-st}$ produces the factor $-s$ (the exponential is its own derivative up to a constant), so the result is $s$ times $F(s)$, minus the boundary value $f(0)$ (the upper boundary vanishes because $e^{-st}\to0$). Consequence: every derivative in a linear ODE becomes a power of $s$ times $Y(s)$ plus known initial values, so the ODE becomes a polynomial equation in $s$ that can be solved for $Y(s)$ by algebra. Check: $f=e^{-at}$, $f'=-ae^{-at}$; $sF-f(0)=\frac{s}{s+a}-1=\frac{-a}{s+a}=\L\{f'\}$ ✓. Compute $\L\{e^{2t}\}$ directly from the definition. For which $s$ does the integral converge? $$ \int 0^\infty e^{2t}e^{-st}dt=\int 0^\infty e^{-(s-2)t}dt=\left[\frac{e^{-(s-2)t}}{-(s-2)}\right] 0^\infty=\frac{1}{s-2}, $$ valid when $\operatorname{Re}(s) 2$ (so that $e^{-(s-2)t}\to0$). This is the $e^{-at}$ formula with $a=-2$: pole at $s=+2$, right half-plane, a growing signal. Check with IVT: $\lim\frac{s}{s-2}=1=e^0$ ✓. Find $\L\{4e^{-2t}\cos3t\}$. $\L\{\cos3t\}=\frac{s}{s^2+9}$. Multiply by $e^{-2t}$: replace $s$ by $s+2$ everywhere; linearity gives the factor 4: $$ F(s)=\frac{4(s+2)}{(s+2)^2+9}. $$ Check: IVT $\lim s\cdot\frac{4(s+2)}{(s+2)^2+9}=4=f(0)$ ✓. Numerically $F(1)=\frac{12}{18}=0.667$, matching the numerical integral ✓. Find $\L\{t\sin2t\}$ with the multiplication-by-$t$ property. Same steps as the first part of the p7 example, with $\omega=2$. $\L\{\sin2t\}=\frac{2}{s^2+4}$. $\frac{d}{ds}2(s^2+4)^{-1}=-2(s^2+4)^{-2}\cdot2s=\frac{-4s}{(s^2+4)^2}$. Multiply by $(-1)$: $$ \L\{t\sin2t\}=\frac{4s}{(s^2+4)^2}. $$ General pattern: $\L\{t\sin\omega t\}=\frac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2}$ (p7 had $\omega=4$: $\frac{8s}{(s^2+16)^2}$ ✓). Numerical check at $s=1$: $\frac{4}{25}=0.16$ ✓. Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2u(t-1)+\delta(t-3)$. $\L\{2u(t)\}=\frac2s$, delay 1 → $\frac{2e^{-s}}{s}$. $\L\{\delta(t)\}=1$, delay 3 → $e^{-3s}$. $$ F(s)=\frac{2e^{-s}}{s}+e^{-3s}. $$ Interpretation: a level of 2 switched on at $t=1$ and a unit kick at $t=3$. Following the p6 example, solve $\frac{dy}{dt}+2y+5\int 0^ty\,dt=u(t)$, $y(0)=0$, for $Y(s)$ and then $y(t)$. Transform: $sY-0+2Y+\frac{5Y}{s}=\frac1s$. Multiply by $s$: $(s^2+2s+5)Y=1$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+2s+5}=\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}=\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}. $$ Table entry 10 ($a=1$, $\omega=2$): $$ y(t)=\frac12e^{-t}\sin2t. $$ Checks: $y(0)=0$ ✓; $y'(t)=\frac12e^{-t}(2\cos2t-\sin2t)$, $y'(0)=1$ — from the equation at $t=0$: $y'(0)=1-2\cdot0-0=1$ ✓. FVT (poles $-1\pm j2$): $\lim sY=0=y(\infty)$ ✓. Invert the professor's result $Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{s^2+3s+1}$ to find $y(t)$. Give exact coefficients and decimals. The roots of $s^2+3s+1$ are real and distinct but irrational: $r {1,2}=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}$. Roots $r 1=\frac{-3+\sqrt5}{2}\approx-0.382$, $r 2=\frac{-3-\sqrt5}{2}\approx-2.618$, $r 1-r 2=\sqrt5$. $Y=\frac{K 1}{s-r 1}+\frac{K 2}{s-r 2}$. $K 1=\frac{r 1+1}{r 1-r 2}=\frac{(-1+\sqrt5)/2}{\sqrt5}=\frac{5-\sqrt5}{10}\approx0.2764$ $K 2=\frac{r 2+1}{r 2-r 1}=\frac{(-1-\sqrt5)/2}{-\sqrt5}=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{10}\approx0.7236$ $$ y(t)=0.2764\,e^{-0.382t}+0.7236\,e^{-2.618t}. $$ Checks: $y(0)=K 1+K 2=1$ ✓ (given $y(0)=1$); $y(\infty)=0$ ✓ (FVT). At $s=1$: $Y(1)=\frac25=0.4$ and $\frac{0.2764}{1.382}+\frac{0.7236}{3.618}=0.2+0.2=0.4$ ✓. $F(s)=\frac{3s+2}{s(s+1)(s+4)}$. Find $f(0^+)$ and $f(\infty)$ without inverting, then verify by inverting. IVT: $sF=\frac{3s+2}{(s+1)(s+4)}\to0$ as $s\to\infty$ (degree 1 over degree 2). $f(0^+)=0$. FVT: poles of $sF$ at $-1,-4$ (LHP) ✓; $\lim {s\to0}\frac{3s+2}{(s+1)(s+4)}=\frac24=0.5$. Verification: $K 0=\frac{2}{4}=0.5$; $K {-1}=\frac{-1}{(-1)(3)}=\frac13$; $K {-4}=\frac{-10}{(-4)(-3)}=-\frac56$. $f(t)=0.5+\frac13e^{-t}-\frac56e^{-4t}$: $f(0)=0.5+0.333-0.833=0$ ✓, $f(\infty)=0.5$ ✓. For $F(s)=\frac{4}{s(s^2+4)}$, a student writes $f(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sF(s)=1$. Is that right? Find $f(t)$. $sF(s)=\frac{4}{s^2+4}$ has poles at $\pm j2$ — on the imaginary axis — so the FVT is not valid . Inverting: $\frac{4}{s(s^2+4)}=\frac{1}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{s^2+4}$; $4=s^2+4+(Bs+C)s\Rightarrow B=-1$, $C=0$. So $f(t)=1-\cos2t$, which oscillates between 0 and 2 forever; it has no final value. ("1" is only its average.) Check: $f(0)=0$ and IVT $\lim\frac{4}{s^2+4}\to0$ ✓. $F(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s-2)}$. What does $\lim {s\to0}sF(s)$ give, and what does $f(t)$ actually do? $\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+1}{s-2}=-\frac12$. But $sF$ has a pole at $s=+2$ (RHP) → FVT invalid. Cover-up: $K 0=\frac{1}{-2}=-\frac12$, $K 2=\frac{3}{2}$. $f(t)=-\frac12+\frac32e^{2t}\to+\infty$. The "final value" $-\frac12$ is meaningless. Check: $f(0)=1$, IVT $\lim\frac{s+1}{s-2}=1$ ✓. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{3}{s^2}+\frac{4}{s+2}-\frac{2s}{s^2+9}+\frac{6}{s^2+9}$. $\frac{3}{s^2}\to3t$; $\frac{4}{s+2}\to4e^{-2t}$; $-2\frac{s}{s^2+9}\to-2\cos3t$; $\frac{6}{s^2+9}=2\cdot\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}\to2\sin3t$. $$ f(t)=3t+4e^{-2t}-2\cos3t+2\sin3t. $$ Check: $f(0)=4-2=2$; IVT: $\lim sF=0+4-2+0=2$ ✓. Numerically $F(1)=4.733$ = Laplace integral of the answer ✓. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{s+5}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}$. $K 1=\frac{4}{(1)(2)}=2$ (at $s=-1$); $K 2=\frac{3}{(-1)(1)}=-3$ (at $s=-2$); $K 3=\frac{2}{(-2)(-1)}=1$ (at $s=-3$). $$ f(t)=2e^{-t}-3e^{-2t}+e^{-3t}. $$ Checks: $f(0)=2-3+1=0$, IVT $\to0$ ✓; recombination at $s=1$: $F(1)=\frac{6}{24}=0.25$, $\frac22-\frac33+\frac14=0.25$ ✓. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{1}{s^2(s+1)}$. $F=\frac{K 1}{s^2}+\frac{K 2}{s}+\frac{A}{s+1}$ (2-fold root at $s=0$, i.e. $p=0$). $A=\left.\frac{1}{s^2}\right {s=-1}=1$. $s^2F=\frac{1}{s+1}$: $K 1=\frac{1}{1}=1$; $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\frac{1}{s+1}\right 0=\left.\frac{-1}{(s+1)^2}\right 0=-1$. $$ f(t)=t-1+e^{-t}. $$ Checks: $f(0)=0$ ✓; $f'(t)=1-e^{-t}$, $f'(0)=0$ ✓ (consistent: $\frac{1}{s^2(s+1)}$ is the ramp response of $\frac{1}{s+1}$). FVT not applicable (double pole at 0): indeed $f\to\infty$. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{s^2+1}{(s+1)^3}$. $(s+1)^3F=s^2+1$, $n=3$, $p=1$. $K 1=[s^2+1] {-1}=2$; $K 2=\frac{1}{1!}[2s] {-1}=-2$; $K 3=\frac{1}{2!}[2]=1$. $$ f(t)=2\frac{t^2}{2!}e^{-t}-2te^{-t}+e^{-t}=t^2e^{-t}-2te^{-t}+e^{-t}=(t-1)^2e^{-t}. $$ Checks: $f(0)=1$; IVT $\lim\frac{s(s^2+1)}{(s+1)^3}=1$ ✓. At $s=1$: $F(1)=\frac28=0.25$; $\frac28-\frac24+\frac12=0.25$ ✓. Find $\Li\left\{\frac{6}{(s+2)^4}\right\}$. $\frac{1}{(s+a)^n}\leftrightarrow\frac{t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}e^{-at}$ with $n=4$, $a=2$: $6\cdot\frac{t^3}{3!}e^{-2t}=t^3e^{-2t}$. Check via the forward route: $\L\{t^3\}=\frac{6}{s^4}$, shift $s\to s+2$ ✓. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{2s+12}{s^2+2s+5}$, in sine–cosine form and in amplitude–phase form. $s^2+2s+5=(s+1)^2+2^2$ ($\alpha=1$, $\omega=2$). $2s+12=2(s+1)+10=2(s+1)+5\cdot2$: $$ F=2\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}+5\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}\;\Rightarrow\;f(t)=2e^{-t}\cos2t+5e^{-t}\sin2t. $$ Amplitude–phase: $R=\sqrt{4+25}=\sqrt{29}=5.385$, $\tan\varphi=\frac52$, first quadrant, $\varphi=68.2^\circ$: $f(t)=5.385e^{-t}\cos(2t-68.2^\circ)$. Residue check: $K=\left.\frac{2s+12}{s+1+j2}\right {s=-1+j2}=\frac{10+j4}{j4}=1-j2.5$, $2 K =2\sqrt{7.25}=5.385$, $\theta=-68.2^\circ$ ✓. IVT: $f(0)=2$, $\lim\frac{s(2s+12)}{s^2+\dots}=2$ ✓. Find $f(t)$ for $F(s)=\frac{5}{(s+1)(s^2+4)}$ using the $K$, $K^ $ method. Is the FVT applicable? Poles: $-1$ and $\pm j2$ ($\alpha=0$, $\omega=2$). $A=\left.\frac{5}{s^2+4}\right {s=-1}=1$. $K=\left.\frac{5}{(s+1)(s+j2)}\right {s=j2}=\frac{5}{(1+j2)(j4)}=\frac{5}{-8+j4}=\frac{5(-8-j4)}{80}=-0.5-j0.25$. $ K =\sqrt{0.25+0.0625}=0.559$; point $(-0.5,-0.25)$ in the third quadrant: $\theta=-180^\circ+26.57^\circ=-153.43^\circ$. $$ f(t)=e^{-t}+1.118\cos(2t-153.4^\circ)\qquad(=e^{-t}-\cos2t+0.5\sin2t). $$ No envelope since $\alpha=0$: the oscillation persists, so the FVT is not applicable (poles on the $j\omega$ axis). Checks: $f(0)=1+1.118\cos(153.4^\circ)=1-1=0$ ✓ (IVT gives 0). Real-form check: $5=(s^2+4)+(Bs+C)(s+1)\Rightarrow B=-1$, $C=1$ → $-\cos2t+\frac12\sin2t$ ✓. The notes give $f(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t-45^\circ)-\frac12e^{-2t}$ for $F(s)=\frac{s+1}{(s+2)(s^2+2s+2)}$. Use the FVT to show this cannot be correct, and state the correct answer. Poles: $-2$, $-1\pm j$ — all in the LHP, so the FVT is valid: $f(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s(s+1)}{(s+2)(s^2+2s+2)}=0$. The written answer contains $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t-45^\circ)$, which keeps oscillating with amplitude $0.707$ — it does not tend to 0. Contradiction. The pole real part $-1$ demands the envelope $e^{-t}$: $$ f(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-t}\cos(t-45^\circ)-\frac12e^{-2t}. $$ This tends to 0 ✓ and its transform at $s=2$ equals $F(2)=0.075$ ✓. Solve $y'+4y=8u(t)$, $y(0)=1$. $sY-1+4Y=\frac8s\Rightarrow(s+4)Y=\frac{8+s}{s}\Rightarrow Y=\frac{s+8}{s(s+4)}$. Cover-up: $K 0=\frac84=2$, $K {-4}=\frac{4}{-4}=-1$. $y(t)=2-e^{-4t}$. Checks: $y(0)=1$ ✓; $y'+4y=4e^{-4t}+8-4e^{-4t}=8$ ✓; FVT $=\frac{8}{4}=2$ ✓. Solve $y''+2y'+5y=0$, $y(0)=1$, $y'(0)=1$. Give the result in amplitude–phase form too. $s^2Y-s-1+2(sY-1)+5Y=0\Rightarrow(s^2+2s+5)Y=s+3\Rightarrow Y=\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^2+2^2}$. $s+3=(s+1)+2$: $Y=\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}+\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}$, so $$ y(t)=e^{-t}\cos2t+e^{-t}\sin2t=\sqrt2\,e^{-t}\cos(2t-45^\circ). $$ ($R=\sqrt{1+1}$, $\tan\varphi=1$, $\varphi=45^\circ$.) Checks: $y(0)=1$ ✓; $y'=e^{-t}(-\cos2t-\sin2t-2\sin2t+2\cos2t)$, $y'(0)=-1+2=1$ ✓. Without input, the response is entirely due to the initial conditions — it would be zero if they had been forgotten. Without full calculation, describe and sketch $f(t)$ for (a) $\frac{1}{s+2}$, (b) $\frac{1}{s-1}$, (c) $\frac{1}{s^2+4}$, (d) $\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+4}$. Give the pole locations. (a) Pole $-2$: $e^{-2t}$ — starts at 1, decays smoothly, down to about 2% after $t=2$. (b) Pole $+1$: $e^{t}$ — starts at 1, grows exponentially. (c) Poles $\pm j2$: $\frac12\sin2t$ — starts at 0, oscillates between $\pm\frac12$ forever with period $\pi$. (d) Poles $-1\pm j2$: $\frac12e^{-t}\sin2t$ — starts at 0, oscillates with period $\pi$ inside the envelope $\pm\frac12e^{-t}$, dies out. Sketching rule: real part → envelope (decay if negative, growth if positive, constant if zero); imaginary part → oscillation frequency. Check (d) with the IVT: $\lim\frac{s}{(s+1)^2+4}=0=f(0)$ ✓. Write $3\cos2t-4\sin2t$ as $R\cos(2t-\varphi)$. $a=3$, $b=-4$: $R=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. Point $(3,-4)$ is in the fourth quadrant: $\varphi=-\arctan\frac43=-53.13^\circ$. So $3\cos2t-4\sin2t=5\cos(2t+53.13^\circ)$. Check at $t=0$: $5\cos53.13^\circ=5(0.6)=3$ ✓. For $F(s)=\frac{N(s)}{(s+p)^2}=\frac{K 1}{(s+p)^2}+\frac{K 2}{s+p}$, explain why the cover-up rule finds $K 1$ but not $K 2$, and how differentiation solves this. Multiplying by $(s+p)^2$: $N(s)=K 1+K 2(s+p)$. At $s=-p$ the $K 2$ term vanishes, giving $K 1=N(-p)$. To isolate $K 2$ by cover-up you would multiply by only $(s+p)$, giving $\frac{K 1}{s+p}+K 2$ — infinite at $s=-p$, so no value can be read. Differentiating $N(s)=K 1+K 2(s+p)$ once removes the constant $K 1$ and leaves $N'(s)=K 2$, so $K 2=N'(-p)$. Example: $\frac{s+3}{(s+1)^2}$: $K 1=2$, $K 2=1$; check: $\frac{2}{(s+1)^2}+\frac{1}{s+1}=\frac{2+s+1}{(s+1)^2}$ ✓.

title: Introduction
text: OperationBlockFig, SumFig, PickFig, SeriesFig, ParallelFig, Loop, OneBlock, TwoLoopFig, TwoLoopMovedFig, Rule1Fig, Rule2Fig, Rule3Fig, ThreeLoopFig, ThreeLoopMovedFig, ThreeLoopStepAFig, ThreeLoopStepBFig, ThreeLoopStepCFig, ThreeLoopFinalFig, ParallelLoopFig, FeedforwardFig, FeedforwardMovedFig, ThreeLoopStepper, TwoLoopStepper } from './widgets'

title: What is this about?
text: A real control system is never a single box. Think of a room heater with a thermostat: there is a controller (the thermostat's electronics), an actuator (the heating element), the room itself (which warms up slowly), and a sensor (the thermometer) that sends the measured temperature back so it can be compared with the temperature you asked for. Each of these parts has its own transfer function. To predict how the whole system behaves — how fast the room warms up, whether it overshoots, what temperature it settles at — we need one transfer function from the set-point to the room temperature. A is the picture that shows how the parts are connected, and is the set of techniques that collapses that picture, step by step, into a single block $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} $$ which the professor calls the . Once you have $T(s)$, everything you learned about transfer functions (poles, step responses, final values…) applies to the whole system. There are two ways to get $T(s)$ from a diagram, and the notes show both: 1. Algebra — write one equation per summing junction / block, then eliminate the internal signals (p. 1–2). 2. Graphical reduction — replace pieces of the diagram with equivalent, simpler pieces until one block is left (p. 3–4). They always give the same answer; using one to check the other is a powerful exam habit. The PDF of this lecture is called “Blok Şemalar ve Akış Şemaları” (block diagrams and flow diagrams ), but the four pages of notes contain only block diagrams and block reduction. There is no signal-flow-graph material in them, so this module covers block diagrams only. After this module you can: - read a block diagram: blocks, summing junctions (with their signs) and take-off points; - write the signal equations of any diagram and solve them for $T(s)=Y(s)/R(s)$; - use the three equivalences of p. 3 (moving a summing point, moving a take-off point, collapsing a feedback loop) plus series/parallel combination; - untangle interlocking loops, as in the professor's three-loop example, and finish such a reduction; - check any reduction independently by algebra or with numbers.

title: Operation block
text: In any system, each independent unit that represents the operation between its input and its output, and which is usually written as a Laplace function, is an operation block . When operation blocks are connected to each other with lines showing the direction of the signal flow ( işlem akış yönü ), a block diagram is obtained. A block is drawn as a rectangle containing its transfer function. The arrow entering it is its input, the arrow leaving it is its output, and the rule is simply $$ Y(s)=G(s)\,R(s). $$ Why multiplication? Because $G(s)$ was defined as $Y(s)/R(s)$ for that unit (with zero initial conditions). In the time domain the unit is a differential equation; in the Laplace domain it becomes a plain multiplication. That is the whole reason block diagrams are drawn in $s$: connecting blocks then needs only addition and multiplication — no convolution, no differential equations.

title: Signals are Laplace functions
text: Every line in a block diagram carries a signal , and in this course that signal is a Laplace transform: $R(s)$, $Y(s)$, $E(s)$, $X(s)$… The professor usually drops the “$(s)$” and writes just $R$, $Y$, $X$ — that is only shorthand; they are still functions of $s$. A line is a wire carrying information, not power. Drawing a line from one place to two places (a take-off point) copies the information; it does not halve it. A block never “loads” the block before it — the diagram assumes each block's output is exactly $G$ times its input, whatever is connected after it.

title: Summing junction
tr: toplama noktası (drawn as Σ in the notes)

title: Summing junctions
text: A circle with $\Sigma$ (or a cross) inside. Its output is the sum of its inputs, each taken with the sign written beside its arrow. The signs are part of the diagram. A − at the input that comes back from the output is what makes a loop negative feedback (geri besleme): the measured output is subtracted from the reference, so the block after the junction sees the error $E=R-(\text{fed-back signal})$. If a sign is missing on a drawing, the usual convention is “+”. But in feedback diagrams the professor always writes the “−”; when one looks missing (as at the $H 1$ input of p. 4's top diagram), compare with the other drawings of the same system before deciding.

title: Take-off (pick-off) point
tr: ayrılma noktası (drawn as a dot in the notes)

title: Take-off points
text: A dot on a line from which a branch leaves. Every branch leaving it carries the same signal as the line itself.

title: Series and parallel blocks
text: The notes use these two facts silently whenever blocks are drawn next to each other (e.g. $G 3$ followed by $G 4$ becoming $1/(G 3G 4)$ on p. 4). They follow directly from $Y=GR$: Series (cascade). If $U=G 1R$ and $Y=G 2U$, then $Y=G 2G 1R$, so $$ G {\text{series}}=G 1G 2 . $$ Parallel. If the same $R$ feeds $G 1$ and $G 2$ and their outputs are added, $Y=G 1R+G 2R=(G 1+G 2)R$, so $$ G {\text{parallel}}=G 1+G 2 $$ (with a “−” sign at the junction, it becomes $G 1-G 2$).

title: The professor's two-loop example
text: To make a holistic analysis ( bütünsel analiz ) of a system, its blocks must be combined. The professor's first example is this system:

title: Reading the diagram
text: Follow the signal from left to right: - $R$ enters the first summing junction with + ; the signal $H 1X$ enters it from below with − . Its output is $E 1=R-H 1X$. - $E 1$ goes through $G 1$, giving $G 1E 1$. - The second summing junction adds $G 1E 1$ ( + ) and subtracts $H 2Y$ ( − , from above): $E 2=G 1E 1-H 2Y$. - $E 2$ goes through $G 2$; the result is called $X$. A take-off point at $X$ sends $X$ both forward to $G 3$ and backward to $H 1$. - $Y=G 3X$; a take-off point at $Y$ sends $Y$ back through $H 2$. So there are two feedback loops: an $H 1$ loop through $G 1$ and $G 2$, and an $H 2$ loop through $G 2$ and $G 3$. They share $G 2$ and the second junction, yet neither contains the other. Such loops are called interlocking , and this is exactly why Rule 3 below cannot be used directly — which is why the professor solves this one with algebra.

title: Writing the equations
text: Given: the diagram above. Asked: $T(s)=Y(s)/R(s)$. Method and why: the loops interlock, so we write the signal equations and eliminate the internal signal $X$. Only two unknowns survive ($X$, $Y$), so two equations are enough. Start from $X$ and walk backwards: $X$ is the output of $G 2$, whose input is $E 2=G 1E 1-H 2Y$, and $E 1=R-H 1X$. Substituting: $$ X=\big\{(R-H 1X)\,G 1-H 2Y\big\}\,G 2 $$ This is the professor's first equation. $$ Y=G 3X $$ Expand the braces: $$ X=G 1G 2R-G 1G 2H 1X-G 2H 2Y $$ $X$ appears on both sides. Bring all $X$ terms to the left: $$ X+G 1G 2H 1X=G 1G 2R-G 2H 2Y $$ $$ X\,(1+G 1G 2H 1)=G 1G 2R-G 2H 2Y $$ $$ X=\frac{G 1G 2R-G 2H 2Y}{1+G 1G 2H 1} $$ $$ Y=G 3\,\frac{G 1G 2R-G 2H 2Y}{1+G 1G 2H 1} $$ Multiply both sides by $(1+G 1G 2H 1)$: $$ Y\,(1+G 1G 2H 1)=G 1G 2G 3R-G 2G 3H 2Y $$ Move the $Y$ term from the right to the left: $$ Y\,(1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2)=G 1G 2G 3R $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ Interpretation. The numerator $G 1G 2G 3$ is the product of the blocks along the straight path from $R$ to $Y$ (the forward path ). Each term added in the denominator is the product of the blocks around one loop: $G 1G 2H 1$ around the $H 1$ loop, $G 2G 3H 2$ around the $H 2$ loop. Each “+” comes from a “−” at the junction (negative feedback). Sanity checks. Remove the $H 2$ loop ($H 2=0$): $T=\dfrac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1}$ — the $H 1$ loop alone, followed by $G 3$, exactly as Rule 3 below predicts. Remove both loops: $T=G 1G 2G 3$, three blocks in series. ✓ - On p. 1 the first equation is written as $X=\{(R-X,X)G 1-H 2Y\}G 2$. The term “$X,X$” is a slip of the pen: the signal subtracted at the first junction is $H 1X$ (the output of the $H 1$ block), so the correct term is $(R-H 1X)$. The next line on p. 2 confirms it, because $1+G 1G 2H 1$ only appears if the term is $H 1X$. - On p. 2, the second line is written with denominator $1+G 1G 2H$; the subscript is missing — it is $1+G 1G 2H 1$, the same denominator as the line above. - The final $T(s)$ in the notes is correct.

title: Eliminating X
text: Why eliminate $X$ rather than, say, solve for $E 1$? Any internal signal can be eliminated; the trick is to choose a signal that lets you write every loop with as few unknowns as possible. $X$ is a good choice because both feedback paths start at or after $X$: $H 1$ takes $X$ directly and $H 2$ takes $Y=G 3X$. With $X$ and $Y$ as unknowns, all loops are captured by two short equations. 1. Name the output of every summing junction and every take-off point that is not already named. 2. Write one equation for each named signal: (sum of signed inputs) or (block × input). 3. Substitute until only the output $Y$, the input $R$ and one or two internal signals remain. 4. Solve for the internal signal, substitute, collect all $Y$ terms on the left, and divide by $R$. The algebra always works, but with many loops it becomes long and error-prone. The professor continues: every problem may present a different structure; there are some techniques for complex structures, and using them when needed makes block reduction easier.

title: Reduction techniques
text: The three equivalences on p. 3 are drawn as before/after pairs joined by ⟺. “Equivalent” means: for the same inputs, both diagrams give the same output . So each rule is proven by writing the output equation of both diagrams and showing they are identical. That is also the way to rebuild a rule in the exam if you forget it.

title: Rule 1: moving a summing point before a block
Rule 1: moving a summing point before a block
text: Before. $R$ goes through $G 1$, then $X$ is added, then everything goes through $G 2$: $$ Y=G 2\,(G 1R+X) $$ After. $X$ first goes through $1/G 1$, is added to $R$, and the sum goes through $G 1$ and $G 2$: $$ Y=G 2G 1\Big(R+\frac{X}{G 1}\Big)=G 2\,(G 1R+X) $$ Both are the same, so the diagrams are equivalent. ✓ Why $1/G 1$? After the move, $X$ has to pass through $G 1$, which it did not do before. Pre-multiplying it by $1/G 1$ undoes that: $G 1\cdot\frac{1}{G 1}X=X$. Every moving rule is built on this idea: each branch must carry the same signal after the move as it did before. In the left-hand diagram of the first pair the second block is labelled “$R 2$”. It must be $G 2$: the right-hand diagram has $G 2$, and the equivalence $Y=G 2(G 1R+X)$ only holds if the same block follows the summing point in both diagrams. ($R$ is reserved for the input signal.) The reverse move works the same way: if a summing point sits before a block $G$ and you move it to after $G$, the side input must pass through $G$ (it used to be multiplied by $G$, and must still be).

title: Rule 2: moving a take-off point before a block
Rule 2: moving a take-off point before a block
text: Before. The take-off point is at $Y$ (after $G 2$), unity feedback. With $E=R-Y$: $$ Y=G 1G 2(R-Y)\;\Rightarrow\;Y(1+G 1G 2)=G 1G 2R\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{Y}{R}=\frac{G 1G 2}{1+G 1G 2} $$ After. The take-off point is between $G 1$ and $G 2$; call that signal $Z$, so $Y=G 2Z$. The feedback branch takes $Z$ and passes it through $G 2$, so the junction subtracts $G 2Z$: $$ Z=G 1(R-G 2Z)\;\Rightarrow\;Z(1+G 1G 2)=G 1R\;\Rightarrow\;Z=\frac{G 1R}{1+G 1G 2} $$ $$ Y=G 2Z=\frac{G 1G 2R}{1+G 1G 2}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{Y}{R}=\frac{G 1G 2}{1+G 1G 2} $$ Same transfer function. ✓ The quicker, local argument: before the move the branch carried $Y=G 2Z$; after the move it carries $G 2\cdot Z$ — the same signal, so nothing in the rest of the diagram can notice the difference. The opposite direction (used on p. 4): moving a take-off point forward past a block $G$ means the new point carries $G$ times the old signal, so the branch must contain $1/G$ to deliver the old signal: $$ \text{old branch signal}=Z,\qquad \text{new point}=GZ,\qquad \frac{1}{G}\cdot GZ=Z\;✓ $$

title: Rule 3: the feedback loop
text: This is the most important rule of the module; every reduction ends with it. Proof. The junction output is $E=R-HY$, and $Y=GE$: $$ Y=G\,(R-HY)=GR-GHY $$ $$ Y+GHY=GR\;\Rightarrow\;Y(1+GH)=GR $$ $$ \frac{Y}{R}=\frac{G}{1+GH} $$ Symbols: $G$ — the product of all blocks in the forward path from the junction to the take-off point; $H$ — the product of all blocks in the feedback path; $GH$ — the loop product (open-loop transfer function), the gain experienced by a signal going once around the loop. When it applies. The loop must be self-contained : nothing else leaves from or enters into the path between the summing junction and the take-off point. Extra inputs added at the junction itself are fine (a junction with three inputs can be split into two junctions in a row); a take-off point or another junction inside the loop is not. If that happens, first use Rule 1 or Rule 2 to move it out — that is exactly what the p. 4 example does. Physical meaning. Without feedback, the output would be $GR$. Feedback divides it by $1+GH$. If the loop product is large ($GH\gg1$), $T\approx\frac{G}{GH}=\frac{1}{H}$: the output is set by the feedback (sensor) path, almost independently of $G$. This is why feedback makes systems insensitive to changes in the plant.

title: Positive feedback
text: If the fed-back signal is added (sign “+” at the junction), $E=R+HY$ and $$ Y=G(R+HY)\;\Rightarrow\;Y(1-GH)=GR\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{Y}{R}=\frac{G}{1-GH}. $$ The rule to remember: the sign in the denominator is the opposite of the sign at the junction : “−” at the junction gives $1+GH$, “+” gives $1-GH$.

title: Summary of the moves
text: Move Compensating block Why --- --- --- Summing point from after $G$ to before $G$ (Rule 1, p. 3) $\frac{1}{G}$ in the side input the side input now passes through $G$ Summing point from before $G$ to after $G$ $G$ in the side input the side input no longer passes through $G$ Take-off point from after $G$ to before $G$ (Rule 2, p. 3) $G$ in the branch the branch used to carry $G\times$(new point) Take-off point from before $G$ to after $G$ (used on p. 4) $\frac{1}{G}$ in the branch the new point carries $G\times$(old signal) Self-contained loop (Rule 3, p. 3) $\frac{G}{1\pm GH}$ “−” at junction → $+$; “+” at junction → $-$ Blocks in series / parallel $G 1G 2$ / $G 1\pm G 2$ $Y=GR$ applied twice Moving a summing or take-off point never changes the loop product of any loop. After each move, multiply the blocks around every loop and compare with the original diagram. On p. 4, for example, the $H 1$ loop product is $G 1G 2H 1$ before the move and $G 1G 2G 3G 4\cdot\frac{1}{G 3G 4}H 1=G 1G 2H 1$ after it. ✓

title: The three-loop example
text: The professor's Örnek (example) has four forward blocks and three feedback loops.

title: The original diagram
text: The three loops (with A the point after $G 2$ and B the point after $G 3$): - $H 1$ loop: $\Sigma 1\to G 1\to\Sigma 2\to G 2\to A\to H 1\to\Sigma 1$; loop product $G 1G 2H 1$. - $H 2$ loop: $\Sigma 2\to G 2\to G 3\to B\to H 2\to\Sigma 2$; loop product $G 2G 3H 2$. - $H 3$ loop: $\Sigma 2\to G 2\to G 3\to G 4\to Y\to H 3\to\Sigma 2$; loop product $G 2G 3G 4H 3$. Can we collapse the $H 2$ loop with Rule 3? No: the take-off point A of the $H 1$ branch sits inside it (between $G 2$ and $G 3$). Can we collapse the $H 1$ loop? Also no: its path goes through $\Sigma 2$, which receives the $H 2$ and $H 3$ signals from outside. The loops interlock, so a point has to be moved first. In the top diagram the sign at the $H 1$ input of the first summing junction is not written. The redrawn (lower) diagram on the same page shows “−”, so the $H 1$ loop is negative feedback, and it is drawn with “−” here. (The lower diagram also leaves the input arrow unlabelled; it is $R$.)

title: Moving the H1 take-off point
text: The professor moves the take-off point of the $H 1$ branch from A forward past $G 3$ and $G 4$ to the output $Y$: Since $Y=G 3G 4\,A$, the moved branch picks up $Y$, and to keep feeding the old signal $A$ into $H 1$ it must contain the compensating block $$ \frac{1}{G 3G 4}:\qquad \frac{1}{G 3G 4}\cdot Y=\frac{1}{G 3G 4}\cdot G 3G 4A=A\;✓ $$ (The series rule turns “past $G 3$, then past $G 4$” into one move past $G 3G 4$.) Now the $G 2$–$G 3$–$H 2$ loop has nothing entering or leaving inside it: it is self-contained. Why move it all the way to $Y$ and not just past $G 3$ to B? At B the branch would sit inside the $H 3$ loop ($\Sigma 2\to\dots\to G 4\to Y$), blocking the next reduction. At $Y$ it is outside every inner loop.

title: The inner loop
text: “Let the equivalent of the $G 2$–$G 3$–$H 2$ loop be $G A$” ( $G 2-G 3-H 2$ çevriminin eşdeğeri $G A$ olsun ). With Rule 3, forward path $G 2G 3$ (series), feedback $H 2$: $$ G A=\frac{G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ The notes stop here.

title: Completing the reduction
text: Given: the p. 4 diagram. Asked: $T(s)=Y/R$. The first two steps are the professor's; steps 3–6 complete the example , which the notes leave unfinished. Branch block $\frac{1}{G 3G 4}$, as shown above. $$ G A=\frac{G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ Now $\Sigma 2\to G A\to G 4\to Y$ with $H 3$ fed back is self-contained (the $H 1$ branch leaves at $Y$, outside it). Forward path $G AG 4$, feedback $H 3$: $$ G B=\frac{G AG 4}{1+G AG 4H 3} $$ Insert $G A$: $G AG 4=\dfrac{G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 2G 3H 2}$. Multiply numerator and denominator of $G B$ by $(1+G 2G 3H 2)$: $$ G B=\frac{G 2G 3G 4}{(1+G 2G 3H 2)+G 2G 3G 4H 3}=\frac{G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3} $$ Forward path: $G 1$ and $G B$ in series, $G 1G B$. Feedback path: $\frac{1}{G 3G 4}$ and $H 1$ in series, $\frac{H 1}{G 3G 4}$. Rule 3: $$ T=\frac{G 1G B}{1+G 1G B\,\dfrac{H 1}{G 3G 4}} $$ Compute the pieces. Let $D=1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3$, so $G B=\dfrac{G 2G 3G 4}{D}$: $$ G 1G B=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{D},\qquad G 1G B\,\frac{H 1}{G 3G 4}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4H 1}{D\,G 3G 4}=\frac{G 1G 2H 1}{D} $$ ($G 3G 4$ cancels — the compensating block exactly undoes the move.) Then $$ T=\frac{\dfrac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{D}}{1+\dfrac{G 1G 2H 1}{D}}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{D+G 1G 2H 1} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3+G 1G 2H 1} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3} $$ Interpretation and check. The numerator is the forward path $G 1G 2G 3G 4$; the denominator is $1$ plus the three loop products listed in “The original diagram” — the same pattern as the two-loop example. Setting $H 1=H 3=0$ leaves $\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 2G 3H 2}=G 1\,G A\,G 4$ ✓.

title: Checking by algebra
text: The reduction can be verified independently by writing the signal equations of the original diagram, exactly like the professor did on p. 1. Call A the output of $G 2$ and B the output of $G 3$: $$ E 1=R-H 1A,\qquad E 2=G 1E 1-H 2B-H 3Y,\qquad A=G 2E 2,\qquad B=G 3A,\qquad Y=G 4B $$ So $B=G 3A$ and $Y=G 3G 4A$ — everything is expressed through $A$. Substitute into $A=G 2E 2$: $$ A=G 2\big[G 1(R-H 1A)-H 2G 3A-H 3G 3G 4A\big] $$ $$ A=G 1G 2R-G 1G 2H 1A-G 2G 3H 2A-G 2G 3G 4H 3A $$ $$ A\,(1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3)=G 1G 2R $$ $$ Y=G 3G 4A=\frac{G 1G 2G 3G 4}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3}\,R $$ Identical to the reduction result. ✓

title: Single loop with numbers: negative and positive feedback
Common mistake: forgetting the compensating block
Parallel blocks inside a feedback loop
Feed-forward path: moving a summing point
Additional worked examples
text: Given: $G(s)=\dfrac{10}{s+1}$, $H=0.5$. Asked: $T(s)$ for negative feedback and for positive feedback, and the steady-state output for a unit step in the first case. $$ T=\frac{G}{1+GH}=\frac{\dfrac{10}{s+1}}{1+\dfrac{5}{s+1}} $$ Multiply numerator and denominator by $(s+1)$: $$ T=\frac{10}{s+1+5}=\frac{10}{s+6} $$ By the final value theorem with $R=1/s$: $y {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\cdot\frac{10}{s+6}\cdot\frac1s=T(0)=\frac{10}{6}\approx1.667$. Note $1/H=2$: the loop product at $s=0$ is $GH=5$, not huge, so $T(0)$ is only near $1/H$. $$ T=\frac{G}{1-GH}=\frac{\dfrac{10}{s+1}}{1-\dfrac{5}{s+1}}=\frac{10}{s+1-5}=\frac{10}{s-4} $$ Negative: $T=\dfrac{10}{s+6}$. Positive: $T=\dfrac{10}{s-4}$. Interpretation. Negative feedback moved the pole from $s=-1$ to $s=-6$ (faster response). Positive feedback moved it to $s=+4$: the response contains $e^{4t}$ and grows without bound. Sanity check: with $H=0$ both reduce to $G=\frac{10}{s+1}$. ✓ Given: the p. 1 structure with $G 1=2$, $G 2=\dfrac{1}{s+1}$, $G 3=\dfrac{1}{s}$, $H 1=1$, $H 2=2$. Asked: $T(s)$ and $T(0)$. $$ T=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ $$ G 1G 2G 3=\frac{2}{s(s+1)},\quad G 1G 2H 1=\frac{2}{s+1},\quad G 2G 3H 2=\frac{2}{s(s+1)} $$ $$ T=\frac{2}{s(s+1)+2s+2}=\frac{2}{s^2+3s+2}=\frac{2}{(s+1)(s+2)} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{2}{s^2+3s+2},\qquad T(0)=1 $$ Sanity check at a test point , $s=1$: $G 1=2$, $G 2=0.5$, $G 3=1$, so $T=\dfrac{1}{1+1+1}=\dfrac13$; the polynomial form gives $\dfrac{2}{1+3+2}=\dfrac13$. ✓ The DC gain $T(0)=2/2=1$: as $s\to0$ the integrator $G 3=1/s$ makes both $G 1G 2G 3$ and $G 2G 3H 2$ grow like $1/s$, so $T(0)=\lim\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{G 2G 3H 2}=\frac{G 1}{H 2}=\frac22=1$. Given: the p. 1 diagram. Asked: $T(s)$ by graphical reduction, to check the professor's algebra. The take-off point $X$ lies inside the $H 2$ loop. Move it forward past $G 3$ to $Y$. Because $Y=G 3X$, the branch needs $\frac{1}{G 3}$. Loop-product check: $H 1$ loop was $G 1G 2H 1$; now $G 1G 2G 3\cdot\frac{1}{G 3}\cdot H 1=G 1G 2H 1$. ✓ $$ \frac{G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ Forward: $F=\dfrac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2}$. Loop product: $F\cdot\dfrac{H 1}{G 3}=\dfrac{G 1G 2H 1}{1+G 2G 3H 2}$. $$ T=\frac{F}{1+F\dfrac{H 1}{G 3}}=\frac{\dfrac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2}}{\dfrac{1+G 2G 3H 2+G 1G 2H 1}{1+G 2G 3H 2}}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2} $$ the same as the professor's algebraic result on p. 2. ✓ Situation: a student moves the $X$ take-off point of the p. 1 system to $Y$ but keeps only $H 1$ in the branch: Inner loop as before, then the outer loop with feedback $H 1$ instead of $H 1/G 3$. Loop product $=\dfrac{G 1G 2G 3H 1}{1+G 2G 3H 2}$, so $$ T {\text{wrong}}=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 2G 3H 2+G 1G 2G 3H 1} $$ The $H 1$ loop product has become $G 1G 2G 3H 1$ instead of $G 1G 2H 1$ — an extra $G 3$. The branch now carries $Y=G 3X$ to $H 1$ instead of $X$. With the gains of the previous numeric example ($G 1=2$, $G 2=\frac{1}{s+1}$, $G 3=\frac1s$, $H 1=1$, $H 2=2$), multiply by $s(s+1)$: $$ T {\text{wrong}}=\frac{2}{s(s+1)+2+2}=\frac{2}{s^2+s+4},\qquad T {\text{correct}}=\frac{2}{s^2+3s+2} $$ At $s=0$: $T {\text{wrong}}(0)=0.5$ but $T {\text{correct}}(0)=1$. The compensating block $\frac{1}{G 3}$ is required; without it the result is a different system. Always ask: “What signal did this branch carry before the move? Does it still carry exactly that?” Given: the diagram below with $G 1=2$, $G 2=\dfrac1s$ and unity negative feedback. Asked: $T(s)$ and $T(0)$. Both blocks get the junction output and their outputs are added: $G=G 1+G 2=2+\dfrac1s=\dfrac{2s+1}{s}$. $$ T=\frac{G}{1+G}=\frac{\dfrac{2s+1}{s}}{1+\dfrac{2s+1}{s}}=\frac{2s+1}{s+2s+1}=\frac{2s+1}{3s+1} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{2s+1}{3s+1},\qquad T(0)=1 $$ Check at $s=1$: $G=3$, $T=3/4$; formula: $3/4$. ✓ $T(0)=1$ makes sense: the integrator $1/s$ in the forward path makes the loop product infinite at $s=0$, so $T(0)=1/H=1$. Given: $G 1=4$, $G 2=\dfrac{1}{s+2}$, $G 3=1$ in the diagram below. Asked: $T(s)$ by reduction, checked by algebra. $\Sigma 2$ sits between $G 1$ and $G 2$, inside the unity feedback loop, and receives a signal from outside the loop ($G 3R$). Rule 3 cannot be used until $\Sigma 2$ is moved. The side input $G 3R$ must now pass through $\frac{1}{G 1}$: The input of $G 1$ is now $R-Y+\dfrac{G 3}{G 1}R$. Addition does not care about order, so write it as $\Big(1+\dfrac{G 3}{G 1}\Big)R-Y$: a parallel combination (direct path $1$ plus path $\frac{G 3}{G 1}$) in front of a plain unity-feedback loop. $$ T=\Big(1+\frac{G 3}{G 1}\Big)\cdot\frac{G 1G 2}{1+G 1G 2}=\frac{(G 1+G 3)\,G 2}{1+G 1G 2} $$ With numbers: $G 1+G 3=5$, $G 1G 2=\dfrac{4}{s+2}$: $$ T=\frac{\dfrac{5}{s+2}}{1+\dfrac{4}{s+2}}=\frac{5}{s+6} $$ From the original diagram: $Y=G 2\big[G 1(R-Y)+G 3R\big]$, so $Y(1+G 1G 2)=G 2(G 1+G 3)R$, the same general formula. ✓ $$ T(s)=\frac{(G 1+G 3)G 2}{1+G 1G 2}=\frac{5}{s+6} $$ Given: the p. 4 system with $G 1=10$, $G 2=\dfrac1{s+1}$, $G 3=2$, $G 4=\dfrac1s$, $H 1=0.5$, $H 2=H 3=1$. Asked: $T(s)$, and a numeric spot-check of the formula. $$ G 1G 2G 3G 4=\frac{20}{s(s+1)},\quad G 1G 2H 1=\frac{5}{s+1},\quad G 2G 3H 2=\frac{2}{s+1},\quad G 2G 3G 4H 3=\frac{2}{s(s+1)} $$ $$ T=\frac{20}{s(s+1)+5s+2s+2}=\frac{20}{s^2+8s+2} $$ At $s=1$: $G 2=0.5$, $G 4=1$. From the algebra check, $A\,(1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3)=G 1G 2R$: $A(1+2.5+1+1)=5R$, so $A=\frac{5}{5.5}R$, and $Y=G 3G 4A=\frac{10}{5.5}R=\frac{20}{11}R$. The formula: $\frac{20}{1+8+2}=\frac{20}{11}$. ✓ $$ T(s)=\frac{20}{s^2+8s+2},\qquad T(0)=10 $$ Why spot-checks work: two rational functions that differ will almost never agree at an arbitrary test point, so agreement at one or two random values of $s$ is a fast and reliable check in an exam.

title: Edge cases
text: - Unity feedback, $H=1$: Rule 3 becomes $T=\dfrac{G}{1+G}$ (the p. 3 Rule 2 diagram is of this type). - Very large loop product: $T=\dfrac{G}{1+GH}\to\dfrac1H$ as $GH\to\infty$. The plant hardly matters; the feedback path decides. - No feedback, $H=0$: $T=G$. Setting individual $H$'s to zero is the fastest way to test a multi-loop result. - Positive feedback with $GH=1$: the denominator $1-GH$ becomes zero. For example $G=\dfrac{2}{s+1}$, $H=0.5$ positive gives $T=\dfrac{2}{s+1-1}=\dfrac{2}{s}$, a pure integrator — the output of a step grows like a ramp instead of settling. - Moving across a block with a zero: the compensating block $1/G$ swaps numerator and denominator of $G$, e.g. $G=\dfrac{s+1}{s+3}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{G}=\dfrac{s+3}{s+1}$. This is fine algebraically — the $1/G$ never appears in the final $T(s)$, because it always cancels against the $G$ it compensates (as $G 3G 4$ cancelled on p. 4). - Take-off point next to a summing junction: the rules of p. 3 move points across blocks only. Do not move a take-off point across a summing junction by these rules — the signal changes there, so the branch would carry a different signal. If you are unsure, fall back to the algebraic method.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. Read the diagram. Mark every sign at every junction, every take-off point, and list the loops with their loop products. Write the forward path product. 2. Choose the method. One or two loops, or loops that interlock in a messy way: write the equations (p. 1–2 method). Nested or easily untangled loops: reduce graphically (p. 3–4 method). 3. Reduction: combine series and parallel blocks; collapse any self-contained loop with $\frac{G}{1\pm GH}$; if no loop is self-contained, move a take-off point or summing point (with its compensating block) so that one becomes self-contained; repeat. 4. Simplify: clear nested fractions by multiplying numerator and denominator by the inner denominators. 5. Verify: (a) the loop-product check after every move; (b) set some $H$'s to zero and see that the result reduces sensibly; (c) evaluate at a test value such as $s=1$ by both methods. Moving a point without a compensating block, or putting $G$ where $\frac1G$ belongs. Cure: ask what signal the branch carried before the move and make sure it carries exactly that afterwards. Using $1+GH$ for a positive-feedback loop, or losing a “−” when writing $E=R-HY$. The denominator sign is always the opposite of the junction sign. Applying $\frac{G}{1+GH}$ to the $H 2$ loop of p. 1 while $X$ is still taken off inside it gives a wrong answer, because the $H 1$ branch would lose its signal. Move the take-off point first. Both branches carry the full signal. Only blocks change signals. Typical variations: numeric gains (substitute at the end, then clear fractions), asking only for one inner equivalent (like $G A$), asking for the diagram after a specific move (draw it and give the compensating block), asking whether two diagrams are equivalent (write both output equations, as in the p. 3 proofs).

title: Moving a summing point after a block

Practice exercises
text: A signal $X(s)$ reaches a take-off point with three outgoing branches. What signal does each branch carry? What is the output of a summing junction whose inputs are $X$ (+), $Y$ (−) and $Z$ (+)? Each branch carries the full signal $X(s)$ — a take-off point copies the signal, it does not divide it. The junction output is $X-Y+Z$, each input taken with its own sign. Check: the proofs of Rules 1–3 only work if a take-off point copies the signal (e.g. in Rule 3 the junction receives $HY$, with the full $Y$). In Rule 1 (p. 3), why does the side input $X$ pass through $\frac{1}{G 1}$ after the summing point is moved before $G 1$? Before the move, $X$ was added after $G 1$, so it reached $G 2$ unchanged. After the move it is added before $G 1$, so it gets multiplied by $G 1$. Putting $\frac{1}{G 1}$ in its path cancels that: $G 1\cdot\frac{1}{G 1}X=X$. Proof: before $Y=G 2(G 1R+X)$; after $Y=G 2G 1(R+X/G 1)=G 2(G 1R+X)$. ✓ $G(s)=\dfrac{5}{s+2}$, $H=3$, negative feedback. Find $T(s)$ and $T(0)$. $$ T=\frac{\dfrac{5}{s+2}}{1+\dfrac{15}{s+2}}=\frac{5}{s+2+15}=\frac{5}{s+17} $$ $T(0)=\frac{5}{17}\approx0.294$. Check: $s=1$: $G=5/3$, $GH=5$, $T=\frac{5/3}{6}=\frac{5}{18}$; formula $\frac{5}{18}$. ✓ Repeat the previous exercise with a “+” at the feedback input of the junction. Is the result a sensible closed-loop system? $$ T=\frac{G}{1-GH}=\frac{\dfrac{5}{s+2}}{1-\dfrac{15}{s+2}}=\frac{5}{s+2-15}=\frac{5}{s-13} $$ The pole is at $s=+13$: the response contains $e^{13t}$ and grows without limit — positive feedback with this large a loop product makes the system run away. Check: $s=1$: $T=\frac{5/3}{1-5}=-\frac{5}{12}$; formula $\frac{5}{1-13}=-\frac{5}{12}$. ✓ $G 1=\dfrac{2}{s+1}$ is in series with a parallel pair $G 2=3$ and $G 3=\dfrac1s$ (outputs added). Find the equivalent transfer function. Parallel: $G 2+G 3=3+\frac1s=\frac{3s+1}{s}$. Series with $G 1$: $$ G {eq}=\frac{2}{s+1}\cdot\frac{3s+1}{s}=\frac{2(3s+1)}{s(s+1)}=\frac{6s+2}{s^2+s} $$ Check: $s=1$: $G 1=1$, parallel $=4$, product $4$; formula $\frac{8}{2}=4$. ✓ $G(s)=\dfrac{4}{s(s+2)}$ with unity negative feedback. Find $T(s)$. $$ T=\frac{G}{1+G}=\frac{\dfrac{4}{s(s+2)}}{1+\dfrac{4}{s(s+2)}}=\frac{4}{s(s+2)+4}=\frac{4}{s^2+2s+4} $$ Check: $T(0)=1$, as expected for unity feedback with an integrator ($1/s$) in $G$. At $s=1$: $G=4/3$, $T=\frac{4/3}{7/3}=\frac47$; formula $\frac{4}{7}$. ✓ In the p. 1 system remove the $H 2$ branch. Find $T(s)$ both by Rule 3 and from the professor's general result. Rule 3: without $H 2$, the $H 1$ loop ($G 1$, $G 2$ forward, $H 1$ back) is self-contained: its equivalent is $\frac{G 1G 2}{1+G 1G 2H 1}$, followed in series by $G 3$: $$ T=\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1} $$ General result with $H 2=0$: $\frac{G 1G 2G 3}{1+G 1G 2H 1+0}$ — identical. ✓ p. 1 system with $G 1=10$, $G 2=\dfrac1{s+1}$, $G 3=\dfrac1{s+2}$, $H 1=H 2=1$. Find $T(s)$ and $T(0)$. Multiply numerator and denominator by $(s+1)(s+2)$. $G 1G 2G 3=\frac{10}{(s+1)(s+2)}$, $G 1G 2H 1=\frac{10}{s+1}$, $G 2G 3H 2=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}$. Multiply by $(s+1)(s+2)$: $$ T=\frac{10}{(s+1)(s+2)+10(s+2)+1}=\frac{10}{s^2+3s+2+10s+20+1}=\frac{10}{s^2+13s+23} $$ $T(0)=\frac{10}{23}\approx0.435$. Check directly at $s=0$: $G 1=10$, $G 2=1$, $G 3=0.5$: $T=\frac{5}{1+10+0.5}=\frac{5}{11.5}=\frac{10}{23}$. ✓ A take-off point sits before a block $G$ and feeds a branch $B$. Prove that moving it to after $G$ requires the block $\frac1G$ in the branch. Where did the professor use this? Let $Z$ be the signal before $G$. Originally the branch carries $Z$. After the move the take-off point carries $GZ$; for the branch to still carry $Z$ it needs a block $K$ with $K\cdot GZ=Z$, so $K=\frac1G$. Nothing else in the diagram changes, so the output equations are identical. The professor used it on p. 4, moving the $H 1$ take-off point past $G 3$ and $G 4$ (series, $G 3G 4$), hence the block $\frac{1}{G 3G 4}$. In the diagram $R\to\Sigma\to G\to Y$, a side input $X$ enters $\Sigma$ with +. Move the summing point to after $G$ and give the compensating block. Prove the equivalence. Before: $Y=G(R+X)=GR+GX$. After: the junction adds the side input to $GR$, so the side input must arrive as $GX$: the compensating block is $G$. Then $Y=GR+GX$. ✓ (This is Rule 1 run backwards: going ahead of a block needs $\frac1G$, going after a block needs $G$.) In the p. 4 example, the professor moved the $H 1$ take-off point past both $G 3$ and $G 4$. What would go wrong if it were moved only past $G 3$ (to point B)? At B, the $H 2$ loop would become self-contained and $G A$ could still be computed. But B lies inside the $H 3$ loop ($\Sigma 2\to G 2\to G 3\to B\to G 4\to Y\to H 3$). The next step — collapsing the $H 3$ loop into $G B$ — would then be blocked by the take-off point at B, and another move (past $G 4$, block $\frac1{G 4}$) would be needed anyway. Moving it straight to $Y$ places it outside every inner loop, so the remaining reductions are plain Rule 3 steps. (Moving to B gives branch block $\frac1{G 3}$; then moving on past $G 4$ gives $\frac{1}{G 3}\cdot\frac{1}{G 4}=\frac{1}{G 3G 4}$ — the same final picture.) In the p. 4 system let all $G i=1$ and all $H i=1$. Find $T$ from the final formula, then check by the algebraic equations. $$ T=\frac{1}{1+1+1+1}=\frac14 $$ Algebra: $A(1+G 1G 2H 1+G 2G 3H 2+G 2G 3G 4H 3)=G 1G 2R$ gives $4A=R$, $A=R/4$; $Y=G 3G 4A=R/4$. ✓ p. 4 system with $G 1=K$, $G 2=\dfrac{1}{s+1}$, $G 3=1$, $G 4=\dfrac{1}{s+2}$, $H 1=H 2=H 3=1$. Find $T(s)$ in terms of $K$, then for $K=5$. Forward path $\frac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}$. Loop products: $G 1G 2H 1=\frac{K}{s+1}$, $G 2G 3H 2=\frac{1}{s+1}$, $G 2G 3G 4H 3=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}$. Multiply by $(s+1)(s+2)$: $$ T=\frac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)+K(s+2)+(s+2)+1} $$ Expand: $(s+1)(s+2)=s^2+3s+2$; $K(s+2)=Ks+2K$; $(s+2)+1=s+3$. Sum: $s^2+(4+K)s+(5+2K)$. $$ T=\frac{K}{s^2+(4+K)s+5+2K},\qquad K=5:\ T=\frac{5}{s^2+9s+15} $$ Check at $s=0$, $K=5$: $G 2=1$, $G 4=0.5$: $T=\frac{2.5}{1+5+1+0.5}=\frac{2.5}{7.5}=\frac13$; formula $\frac{5}{15}=\frac13$. ✓ A student applies Rule 1 to the first p. 3 diagram but connects $X$ directly to the moved summing point (no $\frac1{G 1}$ block). Write the output of the student's diagram and say by how much the $X$-contribution is wrong. Student: $Y=G 2G 1(R+X)=G 1G 2R+G 1G 2X$. Correct: $Y=G 1G 2R+G 2X$. The $R$ part is right, but the $X$ contribution is multiplied by an extra factor $G 1$. The error disappears only if $G 1=1$. The missing $\frac{1}{G 1}$ is exactly what removes this factor. $G=\dfrac{K}{s+1}$, $H=0.5$, negative feedback. Find $T(0)$ for $K=10$ and $K=1000$, and the limit as $K\to\infty$. Explain. $T=\frac{K}{s+1+0.5K}$, so $T(0)=\frac{K}{1+0.5K}$. $K=10$: $\frac{10}{6}\approx1.667$. $K=1000$: $\frac{1000}{501}\approx1.996$. As $K\to\infty$, $T(0)\to\frac{1}{0.5}=2=\frac1H$. With a huge loop product the closed loop no longer depends on $G$: $T\approx\frac{G}{GH}=\frac1H$. $G=\dfrac{2}{s+1}$, $H=0.5$, positive feedback. Find $T(s)$ and describe the step response. $$ T=\frac{G}{1-GH}=\frac{\dfrac{2}{s+1}}{1-\dfrac{1}{s+1}}=\frac{2}{s+1-1}=\frac{2}{s} $$ An integrator. For a unit step $R=\frac1s$: $Y=\frac{2}{s^2}$, so $y(t)=2t$ — a ramp that never settles. The loop product at $s=0$ is exactly 1, so $1-GH=0$ there. In the feed-forward diagram of the additional examples take $G 1=2$, $G 2=\dfrac{1}{s+3}$, $G 3=2$. Find $T(s)$ and verify it with the signal equations. General result (from the example): $T=\dfrac{(G 1+G 3)G 2}{1+G 1G 2}=\dfrac{\frac{4}{s+3}}{1+\frac{2}{s+3}}=\dfrac{4}{s+5}$. Verification: $Y=G 2[G 1(R-Y)+G 3R]$: $(s+3)Y=2R-2Y+2R$, so $(s+5)Y=4R$ and $T=\frac{4}{s+5}$. ✓

title: What is this about?
text: A control engineer can only control what they can predict . Before we ask "how fast does this system respond?" or "does it oscillate?", we need a mathematical model of the physical thing — a transfer function, or at least a differential equation. This module shows how to get that model for electrical circuits , the most common building blocks of sensors, filters, amplifiers and motor drives. Start with something concrete. You close a switch and a battery starts charging a capacitor through a resistor (think of the flash of an old camera, or the "power-on" delay of a device).
