Questions you might ask: - How long until the capacitor is "full"? - What does the voltage curve look like while it charges? - If I double the resistor, what changes? The professor's answer to all of these is one sentence on page 1 : Laplace dönüşümü ilkelerini elektrik devre elemanlarının türevsel eşitliklerine uyguladığımızda, her elemanı temsil eden bir s-bölgesi gösterimi elde ederiz. Bilinen elektrik devre analizi yöntemlerini Laplace gösterimi ifadelerine uyguladığımızda Laplace uzayı çözümünü ve zaman bölgesi çözümünü bulabiliriz. In English: when we apply the Laplace transform to the differential equations of the circuit elements, every element gets an s-domain representation ( ). Then the ordinary circuit-analysis methods we already know (Ohm's law, KVL, KCL, voltage divider…) work on these s-domain expressions , and give us the and, after an inverse transform, the . Why is that such a big deal? Capacitors and inductors are described by derivatives and integrals , so a circuit containing them gives a differential equation, which is tedious to solve. The Laplace transform turns derivatives into multiplication by $s$ ([Module 03]( /m/03)), so every element becomes a kind of "resistor whose value depends on $s$" — an impedance . Circuit analysis then becomes plain algebra. A resistor converts current into voltage instantly: $v=Ri$. A capacitor and an inductor are energy stores — they have memory. A capacitor's voltage depends on all the charge that has flowed into it so far; an inductor's current depends on all the voltage that has been applied to it so far. That memory is what makes circuits have time responses (charging curves, oscillations) instead of instant answers. The Laplace transform packs that memory into the factor $s$ (or $1/s$) and into initial-value terms like $v(0)$ and $i(0)$. After this module you can: - write the time-domain law, the integral form and the Laplace (s-domain) form of a resistor, capacitor and inductor, including initial-condition terms; - explain $Z R=R$, $Z C=\frac{1}{sC}$ and $Z L=sL$, and draw s-domain element models; - model a circuit two ways : via its differential equation (I. yol) or directly with impedances and the voltage divider (II. yol); - find the step response of an RC circuit with partial fractions, and recognise it as the (ZSR); - derive the transfer function of a series RLC circuit, $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}$, and say what $R$, $L$, $C$ do to it.

title: From circuit to transfer function: the chain
text: Every problem in this module follows the same chain. Keep it in mind — each section below fills in one link. 1. Physical circuit — sources, resistors, capacitors, inductors and how they are connected. 2. Element laws — $v=Ri$, $i=C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$, $v=L\,\frac{di}{dt}$. 3. KVL / KCL — the sum of voltages around a loop is zero; the sum of currents into a node is zero. 4. Differential equation — combining 2 and 3 gives an ODE relating output to input (e.g. $V s=RC\,\frac{dV c}{dt}+V c$, derived in [Module 02]( /m/02) ). 5. Laplace transform — the ODE becomes an algebraic equation in $s$. 6. s-domain model / transfer function — solve for the output: $V c(s)$, or the ratio output/input $H(s)$. 7. Time response — partial fractions + inverse Laplace give $v c(t)$. The professor's examples show both routes: page 4 goes through the ODE (steps 2→7), page 5 ("II. yol") jumps from the circuit straight to step 6 by transforming each element first, and page 6 uses the second route to get a transfer function.

title: Passive sign convention
text: All element drawings in the notes use the same convention : the current arrow enters the element at the terminal marked + , and the voltage $v(t)$ is "+ on the left, − on the right". This is the . Under it, $v=Ri$ has a plus sign and power $v\,i 0$ means the element absorbs energy. If you reverse the current arrow relative to the voltage, every element law gets a minus sign — so always draw the arrow and the $\pm$ marks before you write an equation.

title: Resistor
text: — page 1 . The time-domain law is Ohm's law: $$ v(t)=R\,i(t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=\frac{v(t)}{i(t)} $$ - $v(t)$ — voltage across the resistor (V), + where the current enters; - $i(t)$ — current through it (A); - $R$ — resistance (Ω), a constant. The professor notes: "Herhangi bir türevsel ya da gecikme operatörü olmadığı için" — since there is no derivative or delay operator in this law, the Laplace transform changes nothing about its form. By linearity, $\L\{R\,i(t)\}=R\,\L\{i(t)\}=R\,I(s)$: $$ V(s)=R\,I(s)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=\frac{V(s)}{I(s)} $$ So the ratio $V(s)/I(s)$ — the impedance ( ) — of a resistor is simply $$ Z R=R . $$ Physically: a resistor has no memory. Its voltage right now depends only on its current right now. It dissipates energy as heat but stores none, so it never causes a delay or a "curve" in a response by itself.

title: Capacitor
text: — page 2 . The notes use both Turkish names: sığaç (the Turkish-derived word, from sığa = capacitance) and kondansatör (from French condensateur ).

title: Capacitor law in the time domain
Capacitor law in the time domain
text: $$ i(t)=C\,\frac{dv(t)}{dt} $$ - $C$ — capacitance (F, farad); practical values are µF ($10^{-6}$ F) or nF; - $v(t)$ — voltage across the plates; $i(t)$ — current into the + plate. Where it comes from. Two plates separated by an insulator store charge $q$ proportional to voltage: $q=C\,v$. Current is the rate at which charge arrives, $i=\frac{dq}{dt}$, so $i=C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$. Physical meaning. The capacitor stores energy in its electric field ($\tfrac12 Cv^2$). Current flows only while the voltage is changing . A constant voltage means zero current — at DC, after everything settles, a capacitor behaves like an open circuit . Why the voltage cannot jump. If $v$ jumped instantly from one value to another, $\frac{dv}{dt}$ would be infinite, so the current would be infinite. Real sources cannot supply that. Hence the capacitor voltage is continuous : its value just after switching equals its value just before. This is why the voltage at $t=0$, $v(0)$, is such an important number.

title: Integral form and the initial voltage
Integral form and the initial voltage
text: Integrate both sides of $i=C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$ from $0$ to $t$: $$ \int 0^t i(\tau)\,d\tau = C\,[v(t)-v(0)] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v(t)=\frac{1}{C}\int 0^t i(t)\,dt + v(0) $$ $v(0)$ is the voltage already on the capacitor at $t=0$ — the charge left over from the past. The notes write $\int 0^t i(t)\,dt$, using $t$ both as the upper limit and as the integration variable. That is common informal notation; strictly it is $\int 0^t i(\tau)\,d\tau$ with a dummy variable $\tau$. The meaning is identical. Reading the integral form: today's voltage = initial voltage + (accumulated charge)/C . The capacitor "remembers" every bit of current that ever flowed into it, and $v(0)$ summarises all of the history before $t=0$.

title: Laplace transform of the capacitor law
Laplace transform of the capacitor law
text: We need two properties from [Module 03]( /m/03) : - Derivative property: $\L\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\}=sF(s)-f(0)$. - Integral property: $\L\left\{\int 0^t f(t)\,dt\right\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}$. - And the transform of a constant: $\L\{K\}=\frac{K}{s}$ (a constant for $t\ge 0$ is $K\,u(t)$). From the derivative form. Transform $i(t)=C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$: $$ I(s)=C\,[\,sV(s)-v(0)\,]=sC\,V(s)-C\,v(0) $$ From the integral form. Transform $v(t)=\frac1C\int 0^t i\,dt+v(0)$ term by term: $$ V(s)=\frac{1}{C}\cdot\frac{I(s)}{s}+\frac{v(0)}{s}=\frac{1}{sC}\,I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s} $$ The two are the same equation : divide the first by $sC$ and rearrange, $V(s)=\frac{I(s)+C\,v(0)}{sC}=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}$. ✓ $$ I(s)=sC\,V(s)-C\,v(0)\qquad;\qquad V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}\,I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s} $$ If $v(0)=0$ ( "v(0)=0 ise" ), the extra term vanishes and $V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}\,I(s)$.

title: Capacitor impedance
text: With zero initial voltage, the ratio of voltage to current in the s-domain is $$ \frac{V(s)}{I(s)}=Z C=\frac{1}{sC} $$ Every symbol: $s$ is the Laplace variable (unit 1/s), $C$ in farads, so $\frac{1}{sC}$ has units of ohms — it really is a "resistance that depends on $s$". Impedance is defined with zero initial conditions : it describes the element itself, not its stored past. The past is handled separately by the $v(0)$ term. The capacitor impedance is $\frac{1}{sC}$. Writing $Z C=sC$ (that is the admittance , $I/V$) is the single most common error in this topic. Memory aid: a capacitor integrates current, and integration ↔ division by $s$.

title: s-domain models of a charged capacitor
s-domain models of a charged capacitor
text: The notes give the s-domain equations with the $v(0)$ term but do not draw what that term "looks like" in a circuit. Drawing it is very useful, because then the whole s-domain circuit can be solved with ordinary circuit rules. Each equation can be read as a little circuit: Series form — read $V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}$ as a sum of two voltages: the voltage across an impedance $\frac{1}{sC}$, plus the voltage of a source $\frac{v(0)}{s}$ (a step of height $v(0)$) whose + is on the same side as the + of $V(s)$. Parallel form — read $I(s)=sC\,V(s)-C\,v(0)$ as KCL: the terminal current splits into the impedance current $\frac{V(s)}{1/(sC)}=sC\,V(s)$ and a source current. For the sum to equal $sCV(s)-Cv(0)$, the source must carry $C\,v(0)$ in the opposite direction to $I(s)$, i.e. pointing toward the + terminal. Both models are equivalent (a voltage source in series with an impedance ↔ a current source in parallel with it: $\frac{v(0)/s}{1/(sC)}=C\,v(0)$). Use the series form in loop (KVL) problems, the parallel form in node (KCL) problems. The initial condition simply becomes an extra source in the s-domain circuit.

title: Inductor
text: — page 3 .

title: Inductor law in the time domain
Inductor law in the time domain
text: $$ v(t)=L\,\frac{di(t)}{dt} $$ - $L$ — inductance (H, henry); practical values are mH or µH. Where it comes from. Current in a coil creates a magnetic flux linkage $\lambda=L\,i$. By Faraday's law, a changing flux induces a voltage $v=\frac{d\lambda}{dt}=L\,\frac{di}{dt}$. Physical meaning. The inductor stores energy in its magnetic field ($\tfrac12 L i^2$). It produces voltage only while the current is changing ; with a constant current, $v=0$ — at DC, an inductor behaves like a short circuit (a plain wire). Why the current cannot jump. An instant jump in $i$ needs $\frac{di}{dt}=\infty$, i.e. an infinite voltage. So inductor current is continuous . (This is why breaking the circuit of a coil — a relay, an ignition coil — causes a large voltage spike: the inductor "fights" the sudden change.) The capacitor and the inductor are mirror images ( duals ): swap $v\leftrightarrow i$ and $C\leftrightarrow L$ and one law becomes the other.

title: Integral form and the initial current
Integral form and the initial current
text: Integrate $v=L\,\frac{di}{dt}$ from $0$ to $t$: $$ i(t)=\frac{1}{L}\int 0^t v(t)\,dt+i(0) $$ $i(0)$ is the current already flowing in the inductor at $t=0$.

title: Laplace transform of the inductor law
Laplace transform of the inductor law
text: Exactly as for the capacitor. Derivative property on $v=L\,\frac{di}{dt}$: $$ V(s)=L\,[\,sI(s)-i(0)\,]=sL\,I(s)-L\,i(0) $$ Integral property on the integral form: $$ I(s)=\frac{1}{L}\cdot\frac{V(s)}{s}+\frac{i(0)}{s}=\frac{1}{sL}\,V(s)+\frac{i(0)}{s} $$ Check they agree: divide the first by $sL$, $I(s)=\frac{V(s)+L\,i(0)}{sL}=\frac{V(s)}{sL}+\frac{i(0)}{s}$. ✓ $$ V(s)=sL\,I(s)-L\,i(0)\qquad;\qquad I(s)=\frac{1}{sL}\,V(s)+\frac{i(0)}{s} $$ If $i(0)=0$ ( "i(0)=0 olursa" ): $I(s)=\frac{1}{sL}\,V(s)$.

title: Inductor impedance
text: $$ \frac{V(s)}{I(s)}=sL\;\;(=Z L) $$ The notes write the ratio as $sL$ without a symbol; we will call it $Z L$ by analogy with $Z C$ on page 2. Units: $s$ (1/s) × $L$ (H = Ω·s) = Ω. ✓

title: s-domain models of an inductor with initial current
s-domain models of an inductor with initial current
text: Series form — $V(s)=sL\,I(s)-L\,i(0)$: voltage across impedance $sL$, minus a constant $L\,i(0)$. A minus means the source's + faces the − terminal of $V(s)$. Note that this source is $L\,i(0)$, not divided by $s$ — in the time domain it is an impulse $L\,i(0)\,\delta(t)$. Parallel form — $I(s)=\frac{V(s)}{sL}+\frac{i(0)}{s}$: the impedance current plus a step current source $\frac{i(0)}{s}$ flowing in the same direction as $I(s)$ (the inductor keeps pushing its initial current). Derivative form → the initial term has a minus sign: $I=sCV-Cv(0)$, $V=sLI-Li(0)$ (it comes from $sF(s)-f(0)$). Integral form → the initial term has a plus sign and a $1/s$: $V=\frac{I}{sC}+\frac{v(0)}{s}$, $I=\frac{V}{sL}+\frac{i(0)}{s}$ (a constant transforms to constant$/s$). If you remember where each form comes from, you can never get the sign wrong.

title: Element summary and impedance
text: Element Time-domain law Integral form s-domain law Impedance $V/I$ (zero IC) --- --- --- --- --- Resistor (direnç) $v=Ri$ — $V=RI$ $Z R=R$ Capacitor (sığaç) $i=C\frac{dv}{dt}$ $v=\frac1C\int 0^t i\,dt+v(0)$ $I=sCV-Cv(0)$, $V=\frac{1}{sC}I+\frac{v(0)}{s}$ $Z C=\frac{1}{sC}$ Inductor (endüktans) $v=L\frac{di}{dt}$ $i=\frac1L\int 0^t v\,dt+i(0)$ $V=sLI-Li(0)$, $I=\frac{1}{sL}V+\frac{i(0)}{s}$ $Z L=sL$ Once each element has an impedance, impedances combine exactly like resistances : in series they add, $Z=Z 1+Z 2+\dots$; and a voltage divider across $Z 2$ in a series string gives $V 2=V\,\frac{Z 2}{Z 1+Z 2+\dots}$. The professor says this explicitly on page 5: "Bu işlem sırasında empedans gösterimleri direnç gibi işlem görecektir" — during this operation the impedance expressions are treated like resistances .

title: Impedances at DC and at high frequency
Impedances at DC and at high frequency
text: A quick sanity tool. Think of $s$ as "how fast things change": - $s\to 0$ (DC, steady state, very slow change): $Z C=\frac{1}{sC}\to\infty$ (capacitor = open circuit ), $Z L=sL\to 0$ (inductor = short circuit ). - $s\to\infty$ (the very first instant, very fast change): $Z C\to 0$ (an uncharged capacitor looks like a short ), $Z L\to\infty$ (an inductor with no initial current looks like an open ). These limits match the physics above (DC → no capacitor current, no inductor voltage) and are a fast way to check a transfer function: set $s=0$ and see if the DC answer makes sense.

title: Charged capacitor fed by a constant current
Element-level example
text: Given: $C=1\ \text{mF}$, initial voltage $v(0)=2\ \text{V}$, current $i(t)=3\ \text{mA}$ for $t\ge 0$ (i.e. $3\,u(t)$ mA). Asked: $v(t)$. Method: use the integral-form s-domain law, because we know $I(s)$ and want $V(s)$. $I(s)=\L\{0.003\,u(t)\}=\dfrac{0.003}{s}$. $$ V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}=\frac{1}{s\cdot 0.001}\cdot\frac{0.003}{s}+\frac{2}{s}=\frac{3}{s^2}+\frac{2}{s} $$ $\Li\{1/s\}=1$ and $\Li\{1/s^2\}=t$ (ramp), so $v(t)=2+3t$ V for $t\ge 0$. $v(t)=2+3t$ V — the voltage starts at 2 V and rises linearly at 3 V/s. Check: at $t=0$, $v=2$ V ✓ (initial value kept). Time law: $\frac{dv}{dt}=3$ V/s and $\frac{i}{C}=\frac{0.003}{0.001}=3$ V/s ✓. A constant current pours charge in at a constant rate, so a straight line is exactly what physics predicts.

title: RC step response via the differential equation
section: RC step response via the ODE

title: RC step response via the ODE
text: Page 4 — the professor's first example ( Örnek ). The series RC loop: source $V s$, resistor $R$, capacitor $C$; the output is the capacitor voltage $V c$. The same loop current $i(t)$ flows clockwise through all three elements. The notes say: "Aynı devrenin daha önce bulduğumuz diferansiyel denklem çözümü üzerinden gidelim" — let's proceed via the differential equation of this circuit that we found earlier ([Module 02]( /m/02) ). Given: series RC circuit, $V c(0)=0$, input $V s=1\,u(t)$ (unit step). Asked: $V c(t)$. Method (I. yol): ODE → Laplace → partial fractions → inverse Laplace. Capacitor: $i=C\,\frac{dV c}{dt}$. Resistor: $v R=R\,i=RC\,\frac{dV c}{dt}$. KVL around the loop: $V s=v R+V c$, so $$ V s=R\,C\,\frac{dV c}{dt}+V c $$ Derivative property with $V c(0)=0$: $\L\{\frac{dV c}{dt}\}=sV c(s)-V c(0)=sV c(s)$. The input: $\L\{u(t)\}=\frac1s$. So $$ \frac{1}{s}=RC\,s\,V c(s)+V c(s) $$ Factor out $V c(s)$: $V c(s)(RCs+1)=\frac1s$, so $$ V c(s)=\frac{1}{s}\cdot\frac{1}{RCs+1}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{RCs+1} $$ Identity used (cover-up rule): for a simple factor, multiply both sides by that factor and set $s$ to its root. $A$: multiply by $s$, set $s=0$: $A=\left.\dfrac{1}{RCs+1}\right {s=0}=\dfrac{1}{0+1}=1$. $B$: multiply by $(RCs+1)$, set $s=-\frac{1}{RC}$: $B=\left.\dfrac{1}{s}\right {s=-1/RC}=\dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{-1}{RC}\right)}=-RC$. $$ V c(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{RC}{RCs+1}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+\frac{1}{RC}} $$ (divide numerator and denominator of the second term by $RC$). $\Li\{\frac1s\}=1$, $\Li\{\frac{1}{s+a}\}=e^{-at}$ with $a=\frac{1}{RC}$. $$ V c(t)=1-e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\qquad (t\ge 0) $$ "bulunur" — is found. (Strictly $V c(t)=(1-e^{-t/RC})\,u(t)$; the notes write capital $V c(t)$ for the time function.) Checks. Recombine: $\frac1s-\frac{RC}{RCs+1}=\frac{RCs+1-RCs}{s(RCs+1)}=\frac{1}{s(RCs+1)}$ ✓. At $t=0$: $1-1=0=V c(0)$ ✓ (voltage cannot jump). As $t\to\infty$: $V c\to 1=V s$ ✓ (capacitor is an open circuit at DC, no current, no drop on $R$). Final value theorem: $\lim {s\to0}s\,V c(s)=\lim {s\to 0}\frac{1}{RCs+1}=1$ ✓.

title: Zero-state response
text: "Bu çözüm, elektrik devre analizinde karşılaştığımız sıfır durum tepkesidir (ZSR: Zero State Response)" — the response of a circuit to an input when all its energy stores start empty (every capacitor voltage and inductor current is zero at $t=0$). "State" means the stored energy — here $V c(0)$. "Zero state" = $V c(0)=0$. That is exactly why the derivative property gave just $sV c(s)$, with no extra term. If the capacitor had started charged, the $v(0)$ terms from page 2 would add a second part to the answer (see [RC circuit with an initially charged capacitor]( /m/05/rc-circuit-with-an-initially-charged-capacitor)). Note also: with zero state, the ratio output/input is $\frac{V c(s)}{V s(s)}=\frac{1}{RCs+1}$ — the transfer function of this circuit. Transfer functions are always defined under zero initial conditions, which is why they and the ZSR go together.

title: The RC charging curve
text: The answer $V c(t)=1-e^{-t/RC}$ is the classic charging curve. The product $\tau=RC$ is the (unit: Ω·F = seconds). Plotted against $t/RC$, every RC circuit gives the same curve: How to read it and sketch it by hand in an exam : - Axes: horizontal time (in multiples of $RC$), vertical capacitor voltage. - Start: $V c(0)=0$ — the curve starts at zero (capacitor voltage can't jump). - Initial slope: $\frac{dV c}{dt}\big 0=\frac{1}{RC}$. Draw a straight line from the origin to the point $(RC,\,1)$ — the curve starts tangent to it. Physically, at $t=0$ the empty capacitor acts like a short, so the full $V s$ is across $R$ and $i(0)=\frac{V s}{R}$; the charging rate is $\frac{i(0)}{C}=\frac{V s}{RC}$. - Key points: at $t=RC$: 63.2% ($1-e^{-1}$); $2RC$: 86.5%; $3RC$: 95.0%; $4RC$: 98.2%; $5RC$: 99.3%. - End: horizontal asymptote at $V s=1$. Engineers say "fully charged after about $4$–$5\,RC$". - Parameters: larger $R$ (less current) or larger $C$ (more charge needed) → larger $RC$ → slower curve. The shape never changes , only the time scale. Try it: double $R$ and watch $\tau$ double; then halve $C$ and get back the original curve — only the product $RC$ matters. Changing $V s$ only scales the curve vertically (the system is linear: input $V s\,u(t)$ gives $V s(1-e^{-t/RC})$).

title: RC step response with impedances (II. yol)
section: Second way: impedances and voltage divider

title: Second way: impedances and voltage divider
text: Page 5 — "II. yol: Aynı devreyi tüm elemanların Laplace ifadesini alarak analiz edelim" — let's analyse the same circuit by taking the Laplace expression of every element. Each element is replaced by its s-domain form: the unit step source becomes $\frac1s$, $R$ stays $R$, and the (initially uncharged) capacitor becomes the impedance $\frac{1}{sC}$. Given: the same circuit, $V c(0)=0$, unit-step input. Asked: $V c(s)$ and $v(t)$. Method: "Gerilim bölücü kuralını $V c$ çıkışı için de işletelim" — apply the to the output $V c$, treating impedances like resistances. $R$ and $\frac{1}{sC}$ are in series; the share of the source voltage across $\frac{1}{sC}$ is its impedance over the total: $$ V c=\frac{1}{s}\left(\frac{\frac{1}{sC}}{R+\frac{1}{sC}}\right) $$ Write the denominator over a common denominator: $R+\frac{1}{sC}=\frac{sRC+1}{sC}$. Then the two $sC$'s cancel: $$ V c=\frac{1}{s}\left(\frac{\frac{1}{\cancel{sC}}}{\frac{sRC+1}{\cancel{sC}}}\right)=\frac{1}{s}\cdot\frac{1}{sRC+1} $$ "Bu noktadan sonra bir önceki çözümün son işlem sonuçlarını kullanabiliriz" — from here on, the partial fractions are identical to page 4: $$ V c=\frac{1}{s}\cdot\frac{1}{sRC+1}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+\frac{1}{RC}} $$ $$ v(t)=1-e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} $$ "Her iki yoldan da aynı çözüme ulaştık. Burada ikinci çözümde diferansiyel eşitlik kullanmadan salt devre analizi ve Laplace dönüşümü kurallarını işletmek yeterli oldu." — We reached the same solution both ways; in the second we never wrote a differential equation — circuit analysis plus Laplace rules were enough.

title: Comparing the two ways
text: I. yol — ODE first II. yol — impedances first --- --- --- Steps element laws + KVL → ODE → $\L$ → algebra element → impedance; circuit rules directly in $s$ Initial conditions appear automatically through $sF(s)-f(0)$ must be added as extra sources (s-domain models above) Effort for big circuits grows quickly (higher-order ODEs, substitutions) stays algebra: series/parallel, divider, KVL/KCL Good when… the ODE is given, or asked for, in the question you want a transfer function or the circuit has several elements When to prefer which. If the exam gives you a differential equation, or asks "write the differential equation of the circuit", use I. yol. If it asks for a transfer function $V o(s)/V i(s)$ or the response of a multi-element circuit, II. yol is faster and less error-prone — that is exactly what the professor does on page 6. Both must give the same answer; doing a small problem both ways is an excellent self-check.

title: Series RLC transfer function
text: Page 6 — the second Örnek : find $\dfrac{V o(s)}{V i(s)}=?$ for a series RLC circuit with the output across the capacitor. Given: series $R$, $L$, $C$ driven by $V i$, output $V o$ across $C$, zero initial conditions (needed for a transfer function). Asked: $H(s)=\frac{V o(s)}{V i(s)}$. Method: II. yol. Replace $L$ by $Ls$ and $C$ by $\frac{1}{Cs}$, then use the voltage divider — "Gerilim bölücü kuralını işletelim" . $$ V o(s)=V i(s)\,\frac{\frac{1}{Cs}}{R+Ls+\frac{1}{Cs}} $$ Divide by $V i(s)$ and bring the denominator over the common denominator $Cs$: $R+Ls+\frac{1}{Cs}=\frac{RCs+LCs^2+1}{Cs}$. So $$ \frac{V o(s)}{V i(s)}=\frac{\frac{1}{\cancel{Cs}}}{\frac{RCs+LCs^2+1}{\cancel{Cs}}} $$ After cancelling $Cs$, the numerator is $1$ and the denominator is $RCs+LCs^2+1$; written in descending powers of $s$ it is $LCs^2+RCs+1$. $$ H(s)=\frac{V o(s)}{V i(s)}=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1} $$ "olarak bulunur" — is found. Checks. Units: $LC$ has units s², $RC$ has units s, so $LCs^2$, $RCs$ and $1$ are all dimensionless ✓. DC: $H(0)=1$ — at DC the inductor is a short and the capacitor an open, so no current flows and $V o=V i$ ✓. Remove the inductor ($L=0$): $H=\frac{1}{RCs+1}$, the RC result of pages 4–5 ✓. The same circuit by I. yol would need: $i=C\frac{dV o}{dt}$, $v R=RC\frac{dV o}{dt}$, $v L=L\frac{di}{dt}=LC\frac{d^2V o}{dt^2}$, and KVL $V i=LC\,\ddot V o+RC\,\dot V o+V o$. Transforming with zero initial conditions gives $V i(s)=(LCs^2+RCs+1)V o(s)$ — the same $H(s)$. Notice how the ODE coefficients are exactly the denominator coefficients ; II. yol simply skips writing the ODE.

title: What the denominator coefficients do
text: $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}$ has a second-order denominator: the circuit has two independent energy stores ($L$ and $C$), so it has two poles — the roots of $LCs^2+RCs+1=0$: $$ s {1,2}=\frac{-RC\pm\sqrt{(RC)^2-4LC}}{2LC} $$ (quadratic formula $\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ with $a=LC$, $b=RC$, $c=1$). The sign of the discriminant $(RC)^2-4LC$ decides the character of the response: - $(RC)^2 4LC$ — two different real negative poles: the output rises to 1 without oscillating (like two RC stages). - $(RC)^2=4LC$ — a repeated real pole: the fastest rise without overshoot. - $(RC)^2<4LC$ — complex-conjugate poles: the output overshoots and oscillates before settling. Energy sloshes between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field; the resistor burns a bit of it each cycle. - $R=0$ — poles on the imaginary axis: nothing burns energy, the oscillation never dies. So $R$ (through $RC$) controls damping, while $L$ and $C$ (through $LC$) set the natural speed of the energy exchange. The detailed analysis of second-order systems — damping ratio, natural frequency, overshoot, settling time — is the subject of [Module 07]( /m/07); here it is enough to see that the circuit model produces such a system. The slider values are deliberately "toy" values (ohms, henries, farads) so that the time axis is in seconds; real circuits with mH and µF are thousands of times faster but behave identically (see the numerical example below). Try: $L=C=1$ and slide $R$ from 0 to 4 — you pass through all four cases above, with the repeated pole at $R=2$ (where $(RC)^2=4LC$).

title: RC circuit with the output across R
Output across the resistor
text: Given: series loop $V s$ – $C$ – $R$, output $v R$ across $R$, zero initial conditions. Asked: $H(s)=\frac{V R(s)}{V s(s)}$ and the unit-step response. Method: II. yol — voltage divider, now with $R$ on the output side. $$ \frac{V R(s)}{V s(s)}=\frac{R}{R+\frac{1}{sC}} $$ Multiply numerator and denominator by $sC$: $$ H(s)=\frac{RCs}{RCs+1} $$ $V R(s)=\frac1s\cdot\frac{RCs}{RCs+1}=\frac{RC}{RCs+1}=\frac{1}{s+\frac{1}{RC}}$ — the $s$ cancels, no partial fractions needed. $H(s)=\dfrac{RCs}{RCs+1}$, and $v R(t)=e^{-t/RC}$ for a unit step. Interpretation. At the first instant the empty capacitor is a short, so the whole step appears across $R$: $v R(0^+)=1$. As $C$ charges, the current dies away and so does $v R$. At DC ($s=0$) $H(0)=0$: a capacitor in series blocks DC — this circuit passes only changes ("high-pass"). Check: $v R+v C=e^{-t/RC}+(1-e^{-t/RC})=1=V s$ ✓ (KVL). Also $\frac{RCs}{RCs+1}+\frac{1}{RCs+1}=1$ ✓. Note the jump: $v R$ can jump (from 0 to 1 at $t=0$), because it is a resistor voltage; $v C$ cannot.

title: RL circuit
text: Given: $V s=10\,u(t)$ V, $R=20\ \Omega$, $L=0.5$ H, $i(0)=0$. Asked: $i(t)$, its time constant, and $v L(t)$. Method: II. yol — total series impedance, then Ohm's law in $s$. Source $\frac{10}{s}$; impedances $R=20$ and $sL=0.5s$ in series: $Z(s)=0.5s+20$. $$ I(s)=\frac{V s(s)}{Z(s)}=\frac{10}{s(0.5s+20)}=\frac{20}{s(s+40)} $$ (multiply top and bottom by 2). $\frac{20}{s(s+40)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+40}$. $A=\left.\frac{20}{s+40}\right {s=0}=0.5$; $B=\left.\frac{20}{s}\right {s=-40}=-0.5$. $i(t)=0.5\left(1-e^{-40t}\right)$ A. Then $v L=L\frac{di}{dt}=0.5\cdot 0.5\cdot 40\,e^{-40t}=10\,e^{-40t}$ V. $i(t)=0.5(1-e^{-40t})$ A, $\tau=\frac{L}{R}=\frac{0.5}{20}=25$ ms, $v L(t)=10e^{-40t}$ V. Interpretation and checks. $i(0)=0$ ✓ (inductor current can't jump). Final value $0.5$ A $=\frac{V s}{R}$ ✓ (inductor is a short at DC). At $t=0^+$ the inductor takes the whole 10 V (it acts as an open circuit at the first instant) ✓. The RL time constant is $L/R$ — not $RL$: a bigger $L$ resists change more (slower), a bigger $R$ makes it faster. Transfer function from $V s$ to $i$: $\frac{1}{Ls+R}$.

title: RC circuit with an initially charged capacitor
RC charging from a nonzero initial voltage
section: RC circuit with an initially charged capacitor

title: RC circuit with an initially charged capacitor
text: The notes' capacitor equation $V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}$ lets us go one step beyond the zero-state case. Given: series RC (as on page 4), $R=10\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C=100\ \mu\text{F}$, $V s=10\,u(t)$ V, capacitor initially at $v(0)=V 0=4$ V. Asked: $v c(t)$. Method: do it both ways, as the professor did for the zero-state case. $\tau=RC=10^4\cdot 10^{-4}=1$ s, so $RC=1$ in the formulas below. ODE: $RC\frac{dv c}{dt}+v c=V s$. Transform with the full derivative property $\L\{\dot v c\}=sV c(s)-v c(0)$: $$ RC\,[sV c(s)-V 0]+V c(s)=\frac{V s}{s} \;\Longrightarrow\; V c(s)(RCs+1)=\frac{V s}{s}+RC\,V 0 $$ $$ V c(s)=\underbrace{\frac{V s}{s(RCs+1)}} {\text{zero-state part}}+\underbrace{\frac{RC\,V 0}{RCs+1}} {\text{initial-condition part}} $$ KVL around the loop of the figure: $\frac{V s}{s}=R\,I+\frac{1}{sC}I+\frac{V 0}{s}$, so $I(s)=\frac{(V s-V 0)/s}{R+\frac{1}{sC}}=\frac{C(V s-V 0)}{RCs+1}$. Then $$ V c(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{V 0}{s}=\frac{V s-V 0}{s(RCs+1)}+\frac{V 0}{s} $$ Same function (check below). With $RC=1$: zero-state part $\frac{10}{s(s+1)}=\frac{10}{s}-\frac{10}{s+1}\to 10(1-e^{-t})$; initial-condition part $\frac{4}{s+1}\to 4e^{-t}$. $v c(t)=10(1-e^{-t})+4e^{-t}=10-6e^{-t}$ V. $v c(t)=10-6\,e^{-t}$ V $\;=\;\underbrace{10(1-e^{-t})} {\text{ZSR}}+\underbrace{4e^{-t}} {\text{from }v(0)}$. Checks. $v c(0)=10-6=4$ V ✓. $v c(\infty)=10$ V ✓. The two routes agree: II. yol gives $(V s-V 0)(1-e^{-t})+V 0=6(1-e^{-t})+4=10-6e^{-t}$ ✓. At $t=1$ s: $10-6e^{-1}=7.79$ V. Interpretation. The response splits into the zero-state response (input acting on an empty capacitor — page 4's answer scaled by 10) plus a part produced only by the stored initial voltage, which decays with the same $\tau$. (Circuit-analysis books call that second part the zero-input response ; the notes only name the ZSR.) The capacitor only has to "travel" from 4 V to 10 V, so the transient amplitude is 6 V, not 10 V.

title: Numerical RC circuit with real component values
Numerical series RLC: coefficients and pole type
Numerical RC and RLC
text: Given: $R=4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C=10\ \mu\text{F}$, step $V s=5$ V, $v c(0)=0$. Asked: $\tau$, $V c(s)$, $v c(\tau)$, the initial current, and the time to reach 4.5 V. $\tau=RC=4.7\times10^{3}\ \Omega\cdot 10\times10^{-6}\ \text{F}=4.7\times10^{-2}\ \text{s}=47$ ms. $V c(s)=\frac{5}{s}\cdot\frac{1}{0.047s+1}$, so $v c(t)=5(1-e^{-t/0.047})$ V. $v c(\tau)=5(1-e^{-1})=5\cdot0.6321=3.16$ V. Initial current $i(0^+)=\frac{V s}{R}=\frac{5}{4700}=1.064$ mA. $4.5=5(1-e^{-t/\tau})\Rightarrow e^{-t/\tau}=0.1\Rightarrow t=\tau\ln 10=0.047\cdot2.3026=0.1082$ s. $\tau=47$ ms; $v c(\tau)=3.16$ V; $i(0^+)=1.064$ mA; 4.5 V (90%) is reached at $t\approx108$ ms. Sanity check: 90% should come between $2\tau$ (86.5%) and $3\tau$ (95%): $2\tau=94$ ms, $3\tau=141$ ms, and 108 ms is in between ✓. Units: kΩ × µF = $10^3\cdot10^{-6}=10^{-3}$, i.e. kΩ·µF = ms — a handy shortcut. Given: page-6 circuit with $R=100\ \Omega$, $L=10$ mH, $C=1\ \mu$F. Asked: $H(s)$ with numbers, the poles, and whether the step response oscillates. Repeat for $R=300\ \Omega$. $LC=10\times10^{-3}\cdot1\times10^{-6}=10^{-8}\ \text{s}^2$; $RC=100\cdot10^{-6}=10^{-4}$ s. $$ H(s)=\frac{1}{10^{-8}s^2+10^{-4}s+1} $$ $(RC)^2-4LC=10^{-8}-4\cdot10^{-8}=-3\times10^{-8}<0$ → complex poles: $s {1,2}=\frac{-10^{-4}\pm j\sqrt{3\times10^{-8}}}{2\times10^{-8}}=-5000\pm j\,8660$ rad/s. $RC=3\times10^{-4}$, $(RC)^2-4LC=9\times10^{-8}-4\times10^{-8}=5\times10^{-8} 0$ → real poles: $s {1,2}=\frac{-3\times10^{-4}\pm\sqrt{5\times10^{-8}}}{2\times10^{-8}}=\frac{-3\times10^{-4}\pm2.236\times10^{-4}}{2\times10^{-8}}$, i.e. $s 1=-3820$, $s 2=-26180$ rad/s. $R=100\ \Omega$: $H(s)=\frac{1}{10^{-8}s^2+10^{-4}s+1}$, poles $-5000\pm j8660$ → decaying oscillation (overshoot). $R=300\ \Omega$: $H(s)=\frac{1}{10^{-8}s^2+3\times10^{-4}s+1}$, poles $-3820$ and $-26180$ → no oscillation. The boundary is $(RC)^2=4LC$, i.e. $R=2\sqrt{L/C}=200\ \Omega$. Checks. Product of roots must equal $c/a=1/LC=10^{8}$: $5000^2+8660^2\approx 2.5\times10^7+7.5\times10^7=10^8$ ✓; $3820\cdot26180\approx10^8$ ✓. Sum of roots $=-b/a=-RC/LC=-R/L$: $-3820-26180=-30000=-300/0.01$ ✓. The oscillation frequency $8660$ rad/s ≈ 1.4 kHz — real circuits are fast.

title: Find the three mistakes in a student solution
Common mistakes example
text: Task: unit-step response of the page-4 RC circuit with $R=1\ \text{M}\Omega$, $C=1\ \mu$F (so $RC=1$ s), $v c(0)=2$ V. Student's solution: "$Z C=sC$, so $V c(s)=\frac{sC}{R+sC}$. With the initial condition, $V c(s)=\frac{sC}{R+sC}-\frac{2}{s}$…" $Z C=\frac{1}{sC}$, not $sC$. With the wrong impedance the "transfer function" $\frac{sC}{R+sC}$ would give $H(0)=0$ — a capacitor would pass no DC voltage to itself, which is physically absurd. Correct: $\frac{1/(sC)}{R+1/(sC)}=\frac{1}{RCs+1}$. $\frac{1}{RCs+1}$ is the transfer function , not the output. For a step the output is $H(s)\cdot\frac{1}{s}$. Inverting $\frac{1}{s+1}$ alone gives $e^{-t}$ — the impulse response — which starts at 1 and falls, the opposite of charging. From the series capacitor model the initial term enters as $+\frac{v(0)}{s}$ inside the capacitor voltage, and the loop analysis (previous example) gives $V c(s)=\frac{V s-v(0)}{s(RCs+1)}+\frac{v(0)}{s}$. Writing $-\frac{2}{s}$ would start the curve at $-2$ V. $V c(s)=\frac{1-2}{s(s+1)}+\frac{2}{s}=-\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{2}{s}=\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s+1}$. $v c(t)=1+e^{-t}$ V: the capacitor starts at 2 V and discharges toward the 1 V source. Check: $v c(0)=2$ ✓, $v c(\infty)=1$ ✓. If the initial voltage is above the source, the curve must fall — a quick physical sanity test.

title: Edge cases
text: - $v(0)=V s$ (capacitor already at the source voltage). From the previous examples, $V c(s)=\frac{V s-V 0}{s(RCs+1)}+\frac{V 0}{s}=\frac{V s}{s}$: no transient at all, $v c(t)=V s$. Nothing to charge, no current flows. - $R\to 0$ in the RC circuit. $\tau=RC\to 0$ and $V c(s)\to\frac1s$: the capacitor would charge instantly. That needs an infinite current pulse, which is why "voltage can't jump" assumes some resistance in the loop. Real circuits always have some. - $C\to\infty$ or $R\to\infty$. $\tau\to\infty$: the capacitor barely charges in any finite time. $R\to\infty$ is an open loop — no current at all. - $L=0$ in the RLC circuit. $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}\to\frac{1}{RCs+1}$: the second-order model collapses to the first-order RC model of pages 4–5. - $R=0$ in the RLC circuit. $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+1}$, poles $s=\pm\frac{j}{\sqrt{LC}}$ on the imaginary axis: the step response $1-\cos\frac{t}{\sqrt{LC}}$ oscillates forever between 0 and 2 (see the exercises). A lossless LC circuit just exchanges energy. - Output across C vs across R vs across L. The same series loop gives three different transfer functions with the same denominator $LCs^2+RCs+1$; only the numerator changes ($1$, $RCs$, $LCs^2$). The denominator belongs to the circuit (its energy stores and losses); the numerator depends on where you measure. The three numerators add up to the denominator — KVL in the s-domain. - Impedance with nonzero initial conditions. $V/I=\frac{1}{sC}$ only when $v(0)=0$. With a charged capacitor the ratio $V(s)/I(s)$ is not a property of the element any more; that is why the initial condition is modelled as a separate source.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. Redraw the circuit and mark the input, the output (with + and −), the current direction and the passive sign convention on each element. 2. Read the initial conditions. "Başlangıç koşulları sıfır" / $v(0)=0$, $i(0)=0$ → zero state; transfer function questions always assume this. 3. Choose the route. ODE given or asked → I. yol. Transfer function or several elements → II. yol (impedances). 4. I. yol: element laws → KVL/KCL → ODE → Laplace with the derivative property (include $-f(0)$ terms) → solve for the output. 5. II. yol: replace $R\to R$, $C\to\frac{1}{sC}$, $L\to sL$, the source by its transform ($\frac{1}{s}$ for a unit step); add initial-condition sources if needed; apply voltage divider / series sums / KVL. 6. Clear compound fractions by multiplying numerator and denominator by the inner denominator ($sC$, $Cs$…). Write the result in descending powers of $s$. 7. For a time response: multiply $H(s)$ by the input transform, then partial fractions and the Laplace table. 8. Verify: $v(0)$ matches the initial condition, final value matches DC analysis ($C$ open, $L$ short), units of coefficients ($RC$ s, $LC$ s², $L/R$ s), $L=0$ or $R$-limits reduce to known results. - $Z C=sC$ instead of $\frac{1}{sC}$ (or $Z L=\frac{1}{sL}$). - Forgetting the input's $\frac{1}{s}$: answering with the impulse response when the step response was asked. - Wrong sign or missing $1/s$ on initial terms: $-Cv(0)$ (derivative form) vs $+\frac{v(0)}{s}$ (integral form). - RL time constant written as $RL$; correct is $\frac{L}{R}$. - Dividing the source voltage over the wrong impedance (numerator must be the impedance across which the output is measured). - Forgetting $u(t)$ / "for $t\ge0$" — acceptable in the notes' style, but remember the formula is only valid after the switch. Typical exam variations: (a) the page-4/5 RC circuit with different values or a different input amplitude; (b) the page-6 RLC with the output moved to $R$ or $L$; (c) "solve it both ways and show the results agree"; (d) numeric values in kΩ, µF, mH — convert to base units first (or use kΩ·µF = ms).

title: Time to reach a given fraction
Second way with R = 1 MΩ and C = 1 µF
RLC with the output across the resistor
RLC with the output across the inductor
RL circuit with output across L
Reading RC from a measured curve
Charging from a negative initial voltage
Practice exercises
text: Using only the law $i=C\frac{dv}{dt}$, explain why the voltage of a capacitor cannot change instantaneously. What is the analogous statement for an inductor, and why? If $v$ jumped by $\Delta v$ in zero time, $\frac{dv}{dt}$ would be infinite, so $i=C\frac{dv}{dt}$ would be infinite — no real source can deliver an infinite current, so $v C$ must be continuous: $v C(0^+)=v C(0^-)$. Physically, the voltage is set by the stored charge $q=Cv$, and moving finite charge takes time. For an inductor, $v=L\frac{di}{dt}$: an instant change of current would need infinite voltage, so inductor current is continuous. Physically, current is tied to stored magnetic energy $\tfrac12 Li^2$, which cannot change in zero time. Check: in the page-4 result $V c(t)=1-e^{-t/RC}$, $V c(0)=0=V c(0^-)$ ✓; in the RL example $i(0)=0$ ✓. A capacitor has $C=0.5$ F and $v(0)=4$ V. Write (a) $V(s)$ in terms of $I(s)$, (b) $I(s)$ in terms of $V(s)$, (c) the value of the parallel-model current source. (a) $V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}=\frac{1}{0.5s}I(s)+\frac{4}{s}=\frac{2}{s}I(s)+\frac{4}{s}$. (b) $I(s)=sCV(s)-Cv(0)=0.5s\,V(s)-2$. (c) $C\,v(0)=0.5\cdot4=2$ (A·s, the transform of an impulse of charge), directed toward the + terminal. Verification: solve (b) for $V$: $V=\frac{I+2}{0.5s}=\frac{2}{s}I+\frac{4}{s}$ — same as (a) ✓. An ideal inductor $L=0.2$ H carries $i(0)=1$ A and is short-circuited at $t=0$ (so $v(t)=0$ for $t\ge0$). Using the s-domain law, find $i(t)$. Then explain what changes if the short has a resistance $R=2\ \Omega$ instead. Use $I(s)=\frac{1}{sL}V(s)+\frac{i(0)}{s}$; for the second part use the series model and KVL. Ideal short: $V(s)=0$, so $I(s)=0+\frac{i(0)}{s}=\frac{1}{s}$ → $i(t)=1$ A for all $t\ge0$. With no resistance nothing dissipates energy; the current circulates forever (this is how superconducting magnets work). With R = 2 Ω: the inductor voltage equals $-R\,i$ (the resistor's voltage across the same two nodes, with the inductor's passive convention). Series model + KVL around the loop: $sL\,I-L\,i(0)+R\,I=0\Rightarrow I(s)=\frac{L\,i(0)}{sL+R}=\frac{0.2}{0.2s+2}=\frac{1}{s+10}$ → $i(t)=e^{-10t}$ A, decaying with $\tau=L/R=0.1$ s. Check: both give $i(0)=1$ A ✓ (current can't jump); with $R$, $i(\infty)=0$ ✓ (stored energy burned in $R$). $R=2.2\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C=47\ \mu$F. Compute $\tau$ and the time after which a step-driven RC circuit is "practically fully charged" ($5\tau$). $\tau=RC=2.2\times10^3\cdot47\times10^{-6}=103.4\times10^{-3}$ s $=103.4$ ms. (Shortcut: $2.2\cdot47=103.4$, and kΩ·µF = ms.) $5\tau=517$ ms ≈ 0.52 s, when $v c$ has reached $1-e^{-5}=99.3\%$ of the final value. Check: units Ω·F = (V/A)(A·s/V) = s ✓. For the page-4 circuit, find (in terms of $\tau=RC$) the time at which $V c$ reaches 50% and 90% of $V s$. $V c=V s(1-e^{-t/\tau})=kV s\Rightarrow e^{-t/\tau}=1-k\Rightarrow t=-\tau\ln(1-k)=\tau\ln\frac{1}{1-k}$. 50%: $t=\tau\ln2=0.693\,\tau$. 90%: $t=\tau\ln10=2.303\,\tau$. Check: 50% comes before $\tau$ (63.2%) ✓; 90% lies between $2\tau$ (86.5%) and $3\tau$ (95.0%) ✓. Repeat the page-4 example with $V s=5\,u(t)$ (still $V c(0)=0$). Find $V c(s)$, the partial-fraction coefficients and $V c(t)$. ODE transform: $\frac{5}{s}=RCs\,V c+V c\Rightarrow V c(s)=\frac{5}{s(RCs+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{RCs+1}$. $A=\left.\frac{5}{RCs+1}\right {s=0}=5$. $B=\left.\frac{5}{s}\right {s=-1/RC}=-5RC$. $V c(s)=\frac{5}{s}-\frac{5RC}{RCs+1}=\frac{5}{s}-\frac{5}{s+1/RC}$ → $V c(t)=5(1-e^{-t/RC})$. Check: linearity — 5 × the unit-step answer ✓. $V c(0)=0$, $V c(\infty)=5$ ✓. Recombine: $\frac{5(RCs+1)-5RCs}{s(RCs+1)}=\frac{5}{s(RCs+1)}$ ✓. Using II. yol (impedances and the voltage divider), find $V c(s)$ and $v c(t)$ for the page-5 circuit with $R=1\ \text{M}\Omega$, $C=1\ \mu$F and a unit-step input. $RC=10^6\cdot10^{-6}=1$ s. Capacitor impedance $\frac{1}{sC}=\frac{10^6}{s}$. $V c=\frac1s\cdot\frac{10^6/s}{10^6+10^6/s}=\frac1s\cdot\frac{1}{s+1}$ (multiply top and bottom by $s/10^6$). Partial fractions: $\frac{1}{s(s+1)}=\frac1s-\frac{1}{s+1}$ → $v c(t)=1-e^{-t}$ V. Check: matches $1-e^{-t/RC}$ with $RC=1$ ✓; $v c(1\text{ s})=0.632$ V ✓. In the page-6 series RLC circuit, take the output across $R$ instead of $C$. Find $\frac{V R(s)}{V i(s)}$ and its DC value. Explain the DC value physically. Voltage divider: $\frac{V R}{V i}=\frac{R}{R+Ls+\frac{1}{Cs}}$. Multiply top and bottom by $Cs$: $$ \frac{V R(s)}{V i(s)}=\frac{RCs}{LCs^2+RCs+1} $$ DC: $s=0$ gives $0$. At DC the capacitor is an open circuit, so no current flows and there is no voltage across $R$. Check: same denominator as page 6 ✓ (same circuit); units dimensionless ✓. Find $\frac{V L(s)}{V i(s)}$ for the page-6 circuit and verify that $\frac{V R}{V i}+\frac{V L}{V i}+\frac{V o}{V i}=1$. What does this identity express? $\frac{V L}{V i}=\frac{Ls}{R+Ls+\frac{1}{Cs}}=\frac{LCs^2}{LCs^2+RCs+1}$ (multiplied by $Cs$). Sum: $\frac{RCs+LCs^2+1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}=1$ ✓. It is KVL in the s-domain : $V R+V L+V o=V i$. At high frequency ($s\to\infty$) $\frac{V L}{V i}\to1$: the inductor takes all of a sudden change (it's an "open" at the first instant). For the series RL circuit (source $V s$, $R$, $L$), find $\frac{V L(s)}{V s(s)}$ and the unit-step response $v L(t)$. Check against the RL worked example. $\frac{V L}{V s}=\frac{sL}{R+sL}$. Step: $V L(s)=\frac1s\cdot\frac{sL}{sL+R}=\frac{L}{sL+R}=\frac{1}{s+R/L}$ → $v L(t)=e^{-Rt/L}$. Check: the RL example had $V s=10$, $R/L=40$: $10e^{-40t}$ ✓ (linearity). $v L(0^+)=1$ (inductor takes the full step), $v L(\infty)=0$ (short at DC) ✓. A step of 10 V is applied to an uncharged series RC circuit with $C=1\ \mu$F. The measured capacitor voltage reaches 6.32 V at $t=2$ ms. Find $RC$ and $R$. What voltage do you expect at $t=4$ ms and $t=10$ ms? $6.32/10=0.632=1-e^{-1}$, so $t=\tau$: $RC=2$ ms. $R=\frac{2\times10^{-3}}{10^{-6}}=2000\ \Omega=2\ \text{k}\Omega$. $t=4$ ms $=2\tau$: $10(1-e^{-2})=8.65$ V. $t=10$ ms $=5\tau$: $10(1-e^{-5})=9.93$ V. Check: kΩ·µF = ms → $2\cdot1=2$ ms ✓. Series RC, $R=1\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C=1$ mF, step input $V s=6$ V, but the capacitor starts at $v(0)=-2$ V. Find $V c(s)$ using the series capacitor model, then $v c(t)$, and the time at which $v c$ crosses 0 V. $RC=10^3\cdot10^{-3}=1$ s. From the s-domain circuit: $V c(s)=\frac{V s-V 0}{s(RCs+1)}+\frac{V 0}{s}=\frac{6-(-2)}{s(s+1)}+\frac{-2}{s}=\frac{8}{s(s+1)}-\frac{2}{s}$. Partial fractions: $\frac{8}{s(s+1)}=\frac8s-\frac{8}{s+1}$. So $V c(s)=\frac{6}{s}-\frac{8}{s+1}$ → $v c(t)=6-8e^{-t}$ V. Zero crossing: $6=8e^{-t}\Rightarrow t=\ln\frac{8}{6}=0.2877$ s ≈ 288 ms. Check: $v c(0)=6-8=-2$ ✓; $v c(\infty)=6$ ✓. Split: ZSR $6(1-e^{-t})$ + initial part $-2e^{-t}$ = $6-8e^{-t}$ ✓. In the page-6 circuit set $R=0$, $L=0.1$ H, $C=10\ \mu$F. Find $H(s)$, its poles, and the unit-step response $v o(t)$. What are the maximum and minimum of $v o$? $\Li\left\{\frac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\}=\cos\omega t$. $LC=0.1\cdot10^{-5}=10^{-6}$ s², $RC=0$: $H(s)=\frac{1}{10^{-6}s^2+1}=\frac{10^6}{s^2+10^6}$. Poles $s=\pm j1000$ (on the imaginary axis). Step: $V o(s)=\frac{10^6}{s(s^2+10^6)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+D}{s^2+10^6}$. $A=\left.\frac{10^6}{s^2+10^6}\right {0}=1$. Then $10^6=(s^2+10^6)+Bs^2+Ds\Rightarrow B=-1$, $D=0$. $V o(s)=\frac1s-\frac{s}{s^2+10^6}$ → $v o(t)=1-\cos(1000t)$ V. Max 2 V (at $1000t=\pi$), min 0 V; it oscillates forever at 1000 rad/s (≈159 Hz) because nothing dissipates energy. Check: $v o(0)=0$ ✓. Recombine: $\frac{(s^2+10^6)-s^2}{s(s^2+10^6)}$ ✓. Page-6 circuit, $R=300\ \Omega$, $L=10$ mH, $C=1\ \mu$F. Write $H(s)$ with numbers, find the poles, and say whether the step response overshoots. Which value of $R$ is the boundary? $LC=10^{-8}$, $RC=3\times10^{-4}$: $H(s)=\frac{1}{10^{-8}s^2+3\times10^{-4}s+1}$. Discriminant $(3\times10^{-4})^2-4\cdot10^{-8}=5\times10^{-8} 0$ → real poles $\frac{-3\times10^{-4}\pm2.236\times10^{-4}}{2\times10^{-8}}$: $s 1\approx-3820$, $s 2\approx-26180$ rad/s. Two real negative poles → no oscillation, no overshoot. Boundary: $(RC)^2=4LC\Rightarrow R=2\sqrt{L/C}=2\sqrt{10^{-2}/10^{-6}}=2\cdot100=200\ \Omega$. Check: $s 1s 2\approx10^8=1/LC$ ✓. A student solves the page-4 circuit as: "$V c(s)=\frac{1}{RCs+1}$, so $V c(t)=\frac{1}{RC}e^{-t/RC}$." What did they compute, what was forgotten, and how can you tell from the answer alone that it is wrong for a step input? They computed the transfer function $H(s)$ and inverted it — that is the impulse response . They forgot to multiply by the step's transform $\frac{1}{s}$. Tell-tale signs: their answer starts at $\frac{1}{RC}\ne0$ at $t=0$ (the capacitor voltage would jump — impossible for a finite step input) and decays to 0 instead of rising to $V s=1$. Correct: $V c(s)=\frac{1}{s(RCs+1)}$, $V c(t)=1-e^{-t/RC}$. Using $Z C=\frac{1}{sC}$ and $Z L=sL$ at $s=0$, explain why the page-6 transfer function satisfies $H(0)=1$, and predict the final value of $v o$ for a 12 V step. At $s=0$: $Z C\to\infty$ (open), $Z L=0$ (short). With the capacitor open, no current flows, so there is no voltage across $R$ or $L$; KVL gives $V o=V i$. Hence $H(0)=\frac{1}{0+0+1}=1$. For a 12 V step, final value theorem: $\lim {s\to0}s\cdot\frac{12}{s}H(s)=12H(0)=12$ V. (a) What is the main advantage of II. yol (p. 5) over I. yol (p. 4)? (b) Give one situation where I. yol is the natural choice. (c) How must II. yol be modified if the capacitor is initially charged? (a) No differential equation is needed: each element becomes an impedance and the familiar circuit rules (series sums, voltage divider) give the s-domain answer directly by algebra — "salt devre analizi ve Laplace dönüşümü kurallarını işletmek yeterli oldu" . (b) When the question gives the ODE or asks you to derive it, or when you want the initial conditions to enter automatically through $sF(s)-f(0)$. (c) Replace the capacitor by its s-domain model with initial condition: $\frac{1}{sC}$ in series with a source $\frac{v(0)}{s}$ (or $\frac{1}{sC}$ in parallel with a current source $Cv(0)$), following $V(s)=\frac{1}{sC}I(s)+\frac{v(0)}{s}$. Derive the differential equation of the page-6 circuit (I. yol) with $V o$ as the unknown, transform it with zero initial conditions, and confirm $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}$. Loop current $i=C\frac{dV o}{dt}$ (capacitor law). Resistor: $v R=Ri=RC\frac{dV o}{dt}$. Inductor: $v L=L\frac{di}{dt}=LC\frac{d^2V o}{dt^2}$. KVL: $V i=v R+v L+V o=LC\frac{d^2V o}{dt^2}+RC\frac{dV o}{dt}+V o$. Laplace, zero ICs ($\L\{\ddot f\}=s^2F$, $\L\{\dot f\}=sF$): $V i(s)=(LCs^2+RCs+1)V o(s)$ ⟹ $H(s)=\frac{1}{LCs^2+RCs+1}$ ✓.

title: What is this about?
text: The notes open a new chapter: . Until now we built transfer functions. Now we ask the question an engineer actually cares about: if I apply this input, what will the output do over time, and how fast, and how accurately? We start with the simplest dynamic system there is: the . A concrete picture first. Close a switch that connects a battery to a resistor and an uncharged capacitor. The capacitor voltage does not jump to the battery voltage; it rises quickly at first and then more and more slowly, creeping up to the final value. Put a cup of hot tea in a room: its temperature falls fast at first, then slowly. Press the accelerator of a car: speed rises and levels off. All of these have the same shape, because each one obeys the same rule: The rate of change is proportional to how far you are from where you are going. Far from the target → change fast. Close to the target → change slowly. That rule is a first-order differential equation, and its fingerprint is the exponential $e^{-t/\tau}$. A single number, the time constant $\tau$, tells you how fast everything happens. This module answers, for a first-order system: - What does the output do for the three standard test inputs (impulse, step, ramp — defined in [Module 02]( /m/02))? - What is the meaning of $\tau$ on each graph, and how do you sketch each graph by hand? - How long until the output has "settled"? - How big is the error that remains forever (the steady-state error $e {ss}$)? - What changes when the gain is not 1 (Example 1) or when the transfer function has an $s$ in the numerator (Example 2)? After this module you can: - reduce any unity-feedback loop with a first-order $G(s)$ to the form $T(s)=\dfrac{K}{\tau s+1}$ and read off $\tau$, the DC gain $K$, and the pole $-1/\tau$; - write the impulse, step and ramp responses immediately, and sketch them with the correct tangents, key points and final values; - compute settling time ($4\tau$–$5\tau$) and the steady-state error both in the time domain and with $\lim {s\to0}s[R(s)-Y(s)]$; - use the initial and final value theorems — and recognise when they need care; - read $\tau$ and $K$ from a measured response curve. The Laplace tools used here (partial fractions, inverse transforms, the initial and final value theorems) come from [Module 03]( /m/03).

title: The block diagram
text: The notes start from this loop : - $R(s)$ — the input (reference, the value we want). - $E(s)$ — the error, $E(s)=R(s)-Y(s)$: what comes out of the summing junction $\Sigma$ with signs $+$ (from $R$) and $-$ (from $Y$). - $\dfrac{1}{\tau s}$ — the forward-path transfer function $G(s)$. $\tau$ is a positive constant measured in seconds. - $Y(s)$ — the output. It is fed straight back (no block in the feedback path, so $H(s)=1$): this is .

title: Deriving T(s) for the standard first-order loop
Deriving T(s)
text: From the diagram: the error is $E(s)=R(s)-Y(s)$, and the block gives $Y(s)=G(s)E(s)$ with $G(s)=\dfrac{1}{\tau s}$. $$ Y(s)=G(s)\big[R(s)-Y(s)\big]\;\Rightarrow\;Y(s)\big[1+G(s)\big]=G(s)R(s)\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)} $$ This is the familiar closed-loop formula for unity negative feedback. $$ T(s)=\frac{\dfrac{1}{\tau s}}{1+\dfrac{1}{\tau s}} $$ Multiply numerator and denominator by $\tau s$: $$ T(s)=\frac{1}{\tau s+1} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{1}{\tau s+1} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{1}{\tau s+1} $$ The denominator is first-order in $s$ (highest power $s^1$) — that is exactly what "first-order system" means. The notes then say: "Ters Laplace dönüşümünü alırsak sistemin birim impulse tepkesini buluruz" — "if we take the inverse Laplace transform we find the system's unit impulse response."

title: The differential equation behind it
text: Why does this loop behave like the capacitor or the cooling tea? Read the block $\dfrac{1}{\tau s}$ in the time domain: $\dfrac{1}{s}$ is integration, so the block integrates the error and multiplies it by $\dfrac{1}{\tau}$. Equivalently, the derivative of the output is proportional to the error: $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{\tau s}E(s)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\tau s\,Y(s)=E(s)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\tau\frac{dy}{dt}=e(t)=r(t)-y(t) $$ (using $\L\{\dot y\}=sY(s)$ with zero initial conditions). Rearranged: $$ \tau\frac{dy}{dt}+y(t)=r(t) $$ and its Laplace transform is $(\tau s+1)Y(s)=R(s)$, i.e. $T(s)=\dfrac{1}{\tau s+1}$ again. $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{e(t)}{\tau}$ is the whole story of this module: - Big error → output moves fast. At the start of a step, $e=1$, so the slope is $1/\tau$. - Error shrinks → output slows down. That is why the curve bends over exponentially. - The output keeps moving as long as there is any error at all. So for a constant target it can only stop when $e=0$ → zero steady-state error for a step. - To follow a ramp of slope 1 , the output needs $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=1$, which requires a constant error $e=\tau$. That is the constant lag $\tau$ we will find for the ramp. - Smaller $\tau$ → the same error produces a bigger slope → a faster system.

title: RC circuit as a first-order system
Physical twin: the RC circuit
text: The RC circuit (see [Module 05]( /m/05)) is the textbook physical first-order system: - KVL around the loop: $v s(t)=R\,i(t)+v c(t)$. - Capacitor law: $i(t)=C\dfrac{dv c}{dt}$. - Substituting: $RC\dfrac{dv c}{dt}+v c(t)=v s(t)$. This is exactly $\tau\dot y+y=r$ with $y=v c$, $r=v s$ and $\tau=RC$. In the $s$-domain: $$ \frac{V c(s)}{V s(s)}=\frac{1}{RCs+1} $$ The "error" is the voltage across the resistor, $v s-v c$; it drives the current that charges the capacitor. When the capacitor reaches $v s$, the resistor voltage — the error — is zero and charging stops. Everything said below about $\tau$ applies to this circuit with $\tau=RC$. Given: $R=1\,\text{k}\Omega$, $C=100\,\mu\text{F}$, a 5 V step is applied at $t=0$, capacitor initially uncharged. Asked: $\tau$, $v c(t)$, the voltage after one time constant, and the settling time. $\tau=RC=(1000\,\Omega)(100\times10^{-6}\,\text{F})=0.1\,\text{s}$. The input is $5\cdot u(t)$, so $V s(s)=\dfrac{5}{s}$ and, by linearity, the output is 5 times the unit step response (derived below): $$ v c(t)=5\left(1-e^{-t/0.1}\right)=5\left(1-e^{-10t}\right)\ \text{V} $$ At $t=\tau=0.1$ s: $v c=5(1-e^{-1})=5(0.632)=3.16$ V. Settling: $4\tau=0.4$ s (98.2 %), $5\tau=0.5$ s (99.3 %). $\tau=0.1$ s, $v c(t)=5(1-e^{-10t})$ V, $v c(0.1)=3.16$ V, settled after about 0.4–0.5 s. Sanity check: $v c(0)=0$ (the capacitor starts uncharged), $v c(\infty)=5$ V (a fully charged capacitor carries no current, so it has the whole source voltage). ✓

title: Where is the pole?
text: The denominator $\tau s+1$ is zero at $$ s=-\frac{1}{\tau} $$ This single real pole lies on the negative real axis. Every response of the system contains the term $e^{-t/\tau}=e^{(-1/\tau)t}$, i.e. $e^{pt}$ with $p$ the pole. Consequently: - pole farther to the left ⇒ $1/\tau$ larger ⇒ $\tau$ smaller ⇒ faster decay; - pole close to the origin ⇒ $\tau$ large ⇒ slow, sluggish system; - pole on the left half-plane ⇒ $e^{-t/\tau}\to0$ ⇒ the system is stable and the transient dies out. You can move the pole yourself in the explorer further below.

title: Unit impulse response
text: The output when the input is the unit impulse $r(t)=\delta(t)$, whose Laplace transform is $R(s)=1$ (see [Module 02]( /m/02)). Since $Y(s)=T(s)\cdot1$, the impulse response is simply the inverse Laplace transform of the transfer function.

title: Derivation
text: Write $T(s)$ in the form of a standard transform pair. Use $\Li\left\{\dfrac{1}{s+a}\right\}=e^{-at}$ after dividing numerator and denominator by $\tau$: $$ \frac{1}{\tau s+1}=\frac{1}{\tau}\cdot\frac{1}{s+\frac{1}{\tau}} $$ so $$ y(t)=\Li\left\{1\cdot\frac{1}{\tau s+1}\right\}=\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}},\qquad t\ge0 $$ $$ y(t)=\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau} $$

title: The graph and the meaning of tau
The graph and the meaning of tau
text: The notes sketch this decaying exponential, starting at $\frac{1}{\tau}$, with a dashed tangent from the starting point down to the time axis at $t=\tau$ and ticks at $\tau$, $4\tau$, $5\tau$: - Axes: time $t$ horizontally, output $y(t)$ vertically. The plot uses $\tau=1$ s so that the time axis directly reads in multiples of $\tau$. - Start: $y(0^+)=\frac{1}{\tau}$. The impulse "kicks" the system: it instantly delivers a finite amount of output, then the system relaxes. - After one time constant: $y(\tau)=\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-1}=0.368\cdot\frac{1}{\tau}$ — the response has dropped to 36.8 % of its initial value (it has lost 63.2 %). - Final value: $y\to0$. - Shape: concave up, always positive, never actually reaching zero. The professor's comment: "Görüldüğü gibi τ zaman sabitini temsil etmektedir. Sistemin sönüm süresi yaklaşık 4τ–5τ olarak alınabilir." — "As seen, $\tau$ represents the . The system's can be taken as approximately $4\tau$–$5\tau$." How much is left after $n$ time constants? $e^{-n}$ of the initial value: $t$ $\tau$ $2\tau$ $3\tau$ $4\tau$ $5\tau$ --- --- --- --- --- --- $e^{-t/\tau}$ (fraction remaining) 0.368 0.135 0.050 0.018 0.007 After $4\tau$ only 1.8 % remains, after $5\tau$ only 0.7 % — practically zero. That is why $4\tau$–$5\tau$ is the "decay time".

title: Initial slope of the impulse response
Initial slope of the impulse response
text: Differentiate (chain rule: $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-t/\tau}=-\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}$): $$ \left.\frac{dy(t)}{dt}\right {t=0}=\left.-\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\right {t=0}=-\frac{1}{\tau^{2}} $$ "Burada t=0 anında y(t) fonksiyonunun eğimi $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$ olarak bulunur" — "here the of $y(t)$ at $t=0$ is $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$." Why the tangent hits the axis exactly at $\tau$: the tangent line starts at height $\frac{1}{\tau}$ and falls with slope $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$, so the line is $\frac{1}{\tau}-\frac{t}{\tau^2}$. It is zero when $t=\tau$. In words: if the response kept falling at its initial rate, it would be gone after exactly one time constant. This gives a graphical way to find $\tau$ from a measured curve. The notes write the middle expression as $\left.\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}e^{-t/\tau}\right {t=0}$ — without the minus sign — and then the final result as $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$. The derivative of $\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}$ is $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}e^{-t/\tau}$ (the inner derivative of $-t/\tau$ is $-\frac{1}{\tau}$). The final result $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$ is correct ; only the minus sign was dropped in the intermediate step. A decaying curve must have a negative slope.

title: Steady-state error definition
text: The error that remains after the transient has died out: $$ e {ss}=\lim {t\to\infty}e(t)=\lim {t\to\infty}\big[r(t)-y(t)\big] $$ or, with the final value theorem applied to $E(s)=R(s)-Y(s)$: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\big[R(s)-Y(s)\big] $$ The $s$-domain version comes from the final value theorem $\lim {t\to\infty}f(t)=\lim {s\to0}sF(s)$ ([Module 03]( /m/03)), valid when $f(t)$ actually settles to a finite value. Its big advantage: you get $e {ss}$ without inverting the Laplace transform. (The definition of $e {ss}$ itself was introduced in [Module 02]( /m/02).) For the impulse input : Time domain — for $t 0$ the impulse is over, $r(t)=\delta(t)=0$, so $$ e {ss}=\lim {t\to\infty}\left(0-\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\right)=0 $$ $s$-domain — "ya da Laplace dönüşümü kullanarak" ("or using the Laplace transform"), with $R(s)=1$: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\frac{1}{\tau s+1}\right)=0\cdot\left(1-1\right)=0 $$ Both routes give the same result, as the notes remark ( "sonucuna aynı şekilde ulaşırız" ).

title: Unit step response
text: "Giriş fonksiyonu R(s) olarak birim basamak (1/s) fonksiyonu alınırsa, ters Laplace dönüşümü yaparak zaman bölgesi çözümünü elde ederiz." — "If the $\left(\frac{1}{s}\right)$ is taken as the input, we obtain the by inverse Laplace transform." The step is the most important test input: it models "switch on", "change the set-point", "apply a constant load".

title: Derivation of the step response
text: $$ Y(s)=R(s)T(s)=\frac{1}{s}\cdot\frac{1}{\tau s+1} $$ Partial fractions. Write $\dfrac{1}{s(\tau s+1)}=\dfrac{A}{s}+\dfrac{B}{\tau s+1}$. Cover-up: $A=\left.\dfrac{1}{\tau s+1}\right {s=0}=1$; $B=\left.\dfrac{1}{s}\right {s=-1/\tau}=-\tau$. Hence $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{\tau}{\tau s+1}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+\frac{1}{\tau}} $$ (the last step divides numerator and denominator of the second term by $\tau$). Check by recombining: $\dfrac{(\tau s+1)-\tau s}{s(\tau s+1)}=\dfrac{1}{s(\tau s+1)}$ ✓. Inverting term by term ($\Li\{1/s\}=1$, $\Li\{1/(s+a)\}=e^{-at}$): $$ y(t)=1-e^{-t/\tau},\qquad t\ge0 $$

title: The step response graph
text: The notes draw the input level $r(t)=1$ as a dashed horizontal line, the rising curve, and a dashed tangent from the origin that reaches the level 1 exactly at $t=\tau$. - Start: $y(0)=1-1=0$. The output cannot jump — the first-order system needs time. - Final value: $y(\infty)=1$ = the input. Perfect tracking eventually. - Shape: concave down: it rises fastest at the start (largest error) and then slows down. - Connection to the impulse response: the step is the integral of the impulse, so the step response is the integral of the impulse response: $\int 0^t\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-u/\tau}du=1-e^{-t/\tau}$ ✓. Equivalently the slope of the step response is the impulse response.

title: Time constant on the step curve
Time constant on the step curve
text: $$ y(\tau)=1-e^{-1}=1-0.368=0.632 $$ At $t=\tau$ the step response has covered 63.2 % of the way to its final value. This is the most common practical definition of the time constant. Initial slope : $$ \left.\frac{dy}{dt}\right {t=0}=\left.\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\right {t=0}=\frac{1}{\tau} $$ So the tangent at the origin is the line $y=\frac{t}{\tau}$, which reaches the final value 1 at $t=\tau$: if the output kept rising at its initial speed, it would arrive in exactly one time constant. In reality it has only reached 63.2 % by then. $t$ $\tau$ $2\tau$ $3\tau$ $4\tau$ $5\tau$ --- --- --- --- --- --- $y(t)=1-e^{-t/\tau}$ 0.632 0.865 0.950 0.982 0.993

title: Settling time
text: "Sistemin yerleşme süresi yaklaşık 4τ–5τ civarındadır." — "the system's is approximately $4\tau$–$5\tau$." Where do these numbers come from? Ask: when is the output within a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the final value, i.e. $e^{-t/\tau}=\varepsilon$? $$ t=\tau\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon} $$ - 2 % band ($\varepsilon=0.02$): $t=\tau\ln50=3.91\tau\approx4\tau$ → at $4\tau$ the output is at 98.2 %. - 1 % band: $t=\tau\ln100=4.61\tau$; at $5\tau$ the output is at 99.3 %. - 5 % band: $t=\tau\ln20=3.00\tau$. $$ t s\approx4\tau\ (\pm2\%)\qquad\text{to}\qquad5\tau\ (\pm1\%) $$ 1. Draw the final-value line (here $y=1$; in general $y=K$, see Example 1). 2. Mark $\tau$ on the time axis and draw the tangent from the origin to the point $(\tau,\ \text{final value})$. 3. Mark the point $(\tau,\ 0.632\times\text{final value})$. 4. Mark $4\tau$ or $5\tau$, where the curve visibly merges with the final-value line. 5. Draw a smooth, concave-down curve starting along the tangent, through the 63 % point, flattening into the final line.

title: Step steady-state error
text: With $R(s)=\frac{1}{s}$: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{\tau s+1}\cdot\frac{1}{s}\right)=\lim {s\to0}\left(1-\frac{1}{\tau s+1}\right)=1-1=0 $$ Time domain check: $e(t)=1-(1-e^{-t/\tau})=e^{-t/\tau}\to0$ ✓. The integrator in the loop keeps pushing until the error is exactly zero — as predicted by $\tau\dot y=e$.

title: Unit ramp response
text: "Giriş fonksiyonunun birim rampa (1/s²) fonksiyonu olması durumunda çıkış fonksiyonu şöyle bulunur" — "when the input is the $\left(\frac{1}{s^2}\right)$, the output is found as follows." A ramp $r(t)=t$ models a target that moves at constant speed: an antenna tracking a satellite, a reference temperature that rises steadily.

title: Partial fractions for the ramp
text: $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\tau s+1} $$ There is a repeated pole at $s=0$, so the expansion must contain both $\frac{1}{s^2}$ and $\frac{1}{s}$: $$ \frac{1}{s^{2}(\tau s+1)}=\frac{A}{s^{2}}+\frac{B}{s}+\frac{C}{\tau s+1} $$ Multiply both sides by $s^2(\tau s+1)$: $$ 1=A(\tau s+1)+Bs(\tau s+1)+Cs^{2} $$ - $s=0$: $1=A$ → $A=1$. - $s=-\frac{1}{\tau}$: $1=C\cdot\frac{1}{\tau^2}$ → $C=\tau^2$. - Coefficient of $s^2$: $0=B\tau+C$ → $B=-\frac{C}{\tau}=-\tau$. - (Check with the coefficient of $s$: $0=A\tau+B=\tau-\tau$ ✓.) $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s^{2}}-\frac{\tau}{s}+\frac{\tau^{2}}{\tau s+1} $$ For the last term, $\dfrac{\tau^2}{\tau s+1}=\dfrac{\tau}{s+\frac1\tau}$, whose inverse is $\tau e^{-t/\tau}$. With $\Li\{1/s^2\}=t$ and $\Li\{1/s\}=1$: $$ y(t)=t-\tau+\tau e^{-t/\tau},\qquad t\ge0 $$ Checks: $y(0)=0-\tau+\tau=0$ ✓. $\dot y(t)=1-e^{-t/\tau}$, so $\dot y(0)=0$ (the curve starts flat — visible in the notes' sketch) and $\dot y\to1$ (eventually it moves at the same speed as the input). Notice $\dot y$ equals the step response, and the step response is in turn the derivative of the ramp response — again because the ramp is the integral of the step.

title: The constant lag tau
text: The notes draw $r(t)$ dashed, $y(t)$ solid below it, and a small blue double arrow labelled $\tau$ between them. - Transient part: $\tau e^{-t/\tau}$ — dies out after about $4\tau$–$5\tau$. - Steady-state part: $y {ss}(t)=t-\tau$ — a line parallel to the input (same slope 1) but shifted down by $\tau$. "Görüldüğü gibi y(t) çıkışı r(t) girişini kalıcı duruma ulaştıktan sonra da τ farkı ile izlemektedir." — "the output follows the input with a difference of $\tau$ even after reaching steady state." Because both lines have slope 1, the gap can be read in two ways: the output is $\tau$ lower (vertical gap) and also $\tau$ seconds late (horizontal gap: $y {ss}(t)=r(t-\tau)$). A system with a small time constant follows a moving target closely.

title: Ramp steady-state error
text: Time domain: $$ e(t)=r(t)-y(t)=t-\left(t-\tau+\tau e^{-\frac{t}{\tau}}\right)=\tau-\tau e^{-t/\tau}\;\xrightarrow{t\to\infty}\;\tau $$ $s$-domain: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^{2}}-\frac{1}{\tau s+1}\cdot\frac{1}{s^{2}}\right)=\lim {s\to0}s\,\frac{\tau s+1-1}{s^{2}(\tau s+1)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{\tau s^2}{s^2(\tau s+1)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{\tau}{\tau s+1}=\tau $$ (The notes do the same cancellation by crossing out $s$, $+1-1$ and $s^2$.) $$ e {ss}=\tau $$ Why a constant error and not zero? From $\tau\dot y=e$: to keep up with a target moving at speed 1, the output needs $\dot y=1$, and the only way the integrator produces that speed is to be fed a constant error $e=\tau$. Zero error would mean zero speed, and the output would fall behind. So a constant lag is the price of tracking a ramp with this loop.

title: Summary of the three responses
text: Input $r(t)$ $R(s)$ Output $y(t)$ of $\frac{1}{\tau s+1}$ Start Final behaviour $e {ss}$ --- --- --- --- --- --- $\delta(t)$ $1$ $\frac{1}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}$ $\frac1\tau$, slope $-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$ $\to0$ $0$ $u(t)$ $\frac1s$ $1-e^{-t/\tau}$ $0$, slope $\frac1\tau$ $\to1$ $0$ $t$ $\frac{1}{s^2}$ $t-\tau+\tau e^{-t/\tau}$ $0$, slope $0$ $\to t-\tau$ $\tau$ Each response is the derivative of the one below it, just as each input is the derivative of the one below it. One number, $\tau$, controls all three.

title: Explore tau and K
text: The first slider changes $\tau$, the second the DC gain $K$ of the more general form $T(s)=\frac{K}{\tau s+1}$ that Example 1 introduces below (keep $K=1$ for the standard loop). Watch: - the pole at $-1/\tau$ moves left as $\tau$ shrinks, and all three curves get faster; - the tangents always hit their targets at $t=\tau$; - with $K\ne1$ the step response settles at $K$ instead of 1 (step error $1-K$), and the ramp response no longer stays parallel to the input (ramp error infinite).

title: Example 1 with DC gain below one
The gain form of a first-order TF
Example 1: closed-loop transfer function of G = 4/(s+1)
section: The gain form of a first-order TF

title: The gain form of a first-order TF
text: A real loop rarely gives exactly $\frac{1}{\tau s+1}$. Any first-order transfer function without a zero can be brought to the gain–time-constant form $$ T(s)=\frac{b}{s+a}=\frac{b/a}{\frac{1}{a}s+1}=\frac{K}{\tau s+1},\qquad K=\frac{b}{a},\ \ \tau=\frac{1}{a} $$ The trick: make the constant term of the denominator equal to 1 by dividing numerator and denominator by $a$. - $\tau=\frac1a$ is the time constant (the pole is $-a=-\frac{1}{\tau}$). - $K=T(0)$ is the (steady-state gain): what a constant input of 1 produces in steady state, since a constant corresponds to $s\to0$. Because the system is linear, multiplying $T$ by $K$ just multiplies every response by $K$: $$ y \delta(t)=\frac{K}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau},\qquad y {step}(t)=K\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),\qquad y {ramp}(t)=K\left(t-\tau+\tau e^{-t/\tau}\right) $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{K}{\tau s+1},\qquad y {step}(t)=K\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),\qquad e {ss,step}=1-K $$ Given: unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{4}{s+1}$. Asked: $T(s)$, its $\tau$ and DC gain. $$ T(s)=\frac{\dfrac{4}{s+1}}{1+\dfrac{4}{s+1}} $$ Multiply numerator and denominator by $(s+1)$: $$ T(s)=\frac{4}{(s+1)+4}=\frac{4}{s+5} $$ Divide numerator and denominator by 5: $$ T(s)=\frac{4/5}{\frac{1}{5}s+1}=\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1} $$ (the notes write this with decimal commas, $\frac{0{,}8}{0{,}2s+1}$). $K=0.8$, $\tau=0.2$ s, closed-loop pole at $s=-5$. $$ T(s)=\frac{4}{s+5}=\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1},\qquad K=0.8,\ \ \tau=0.2\ \text{s} $$ Interpretation: the plant alone, $\frac{4}{s+1}$, has time constant 1 s (pole at $-1$). Feedback moved the pole to $-5$: the closed loop is 5 times faster . The price: the DC gain is 0.8, not 1, so a step will not be tracked perfectly. Unlike the standard loop, $G=\frac{4}{s+1}$ contains no integrator (no pure $\frac1s$), so nothing forces the error to zero.

title: Example 1 step response
text: Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{0.8}{0.2s+1}$, $r(t)=u(t)$. Asked: $y(t)$, $e {ss}$, the graph. $$ Y(s)=\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1}\cdot\frac{1}{s} $$ This is $K=0.8$ times the standard step response with $\tau=0.2$: $y(t)=0.8\left(1-e^{-t/0.2}\right)$. Explicitly with partial fractions: $\frac{0.8}{s(0.2s+1)}=\frac{4}{s(s+5)}=\frac{0.8}{s}-\frac{0.8}{s+5}$ (cover-up: $\frac{4}{5}=0.8$ at $s=0$; $\frac{4}{-5}=-0.8$ at $s=-5$). $$ y(t)=0.8\left(1-e^{-5t}\right) $$ $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1}\cdot\frac{1}{s}\right)=\lim {s\to0}s\,\frac{0.2s+1-0.8}{s(0.2s+1)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{0.2s+0.2}{0.2s+1}=0.2 $$ (the notes cross out the two $s$ factors, then set $s=0$: $1-0.8=0.2$.) $y(0)=0$; $y(\tau)=y(0.2)=0.8\times0.632=0.506$; initial slope $\frac{K}{\tau}=\frac{0.8}{0.2}=4$; $y(\infty)=0.8$; settled after $5\tau=1$ s. $$ y(t)=0.8\left(1-e^{-5t}\right),\qquad y {ss}=0.8,\qquad e {ss}=0.2 $$ Sanity check: time domain $e(t)=1-0.8+0.8e^{-5t}\to0.2$ ✓. Also from the loop equation in steady state: $Y=G(0)E=4E$ and $E=1-Y$, so $Y=4(1-Y)\Rightarrow Y=0.8$, $E=0.2$ ✓. The notes' graph: dashed lines at 1 (input) and 0.8 (final value), the curve rising to 0.8, and a dotted vertical line at $t=1$ s where it has practically settled ($5\tau=5\times0.2=1$ s). The gap between 1 and 0.8 is the steady-state error. Why exactly 0.2? In general $e {ss,step}=1-T(0)=1-K$. For a unity loop with $G=\frac{b}{s+a}$: $T(0)=\frac{G(0)}{1+G(0)}$, and $G(0)=4$ here, so $T(0)=\frac{4}{5}$ and $e {ss}=\frac{1}{1+G(0)}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2$. A larger loop gain $G(0)$ would make the error smaller, but never zero without an integrator.

title: Example 1 impulse response
text: Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{4}{s+5}$, $R(s)=1$. Asked: $y(0)$, $y(\infty)$, $e {ss}$, $y(t)$. $$ Y(s)=T(s)\cdot1=\frac{4}{s+5}=\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1} $$ $$ y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}sY(s)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{4s}{s+5}=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{4}{1+5/s}=4 $$ $$ y(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sY(s)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{4s}{s+5}=\frac{0}{5}=0 $$ $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\frac{4}{s+5}\right)=0\cdot\left(1-\frac45\right)=0 $$ $K/\tau$ times the decaying exponential: $$ y(t)=0.8\cdot\frac{1}{0.2}e^{-\frac{t}{0.2}}=4e^{-5t} $$ $$ y(t)=4e^{-5t},\qquad y(0^+)=4,\qquad y(\infty)=0,\qquad e {ss}=0 $$ Sanity check: $4e^{0}=4$ matches the initial value theorem; $4e^{-\infty}=0$ matches the final value theorem. ✓ The notes' graph starts at 4 and has practically reached 0 at $t=1$ s $=5\tau$. The notes write $y(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sY(s)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\frac{4}{s+5}=0$. The second limit should be $s\to0$ (final value theorem), not $s\to\infty$. Taken literally, $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{4s}{s+5}=4$ — that is the initial value. The correct final value is $\lim {s\to0}\frac{4s}{s+5}=0$, which is what the notes conclude. Remember: $s\to\infty$ ↔ $t\to0^+$ and $s\to0$ ↔ $t\to\infty$ .

title: Initial and final value theorems
text: Example 1 is the first place the notes use both theorems ([Module 03]( /m/03)) to check a response without inverting it: $$ y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}sY(s),\qquad y(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sY(s) $$ - Initial value theorem ( ): needs $Y(s)$ strictly proper (numerator degree lower than denominator degree), otherwise $y(t)$ contains an impulse at $t=0$ and the limit diverges — see Example 2. - Final value theorem ( ): needs $y(t)$ to actually settle, i.e. all poles of $sY(s)$ in the left half-plane. If $y(t)$ grows (like a ramp response), $\lim {s\to0}sY(s)=\infty$ just tells you "it grows without bound". - The notes write $y(0)$; strictly it is $y(0^+)$, the value just after the impulse. Before $t=0$ the output is 0, so the impulse response jumps from 0 to 4 at $t=0$.

title: Example 1 ramp response
text: Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{4}{s+5}$, $R(s)=\dfrac{1}{s^2}$. Asked: $y(t)$, $y {ss}(t)$, $e {ss}$. $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s^{2}}\cdot\frac{4}{s+5}=\frac{A}{s^{2}}+\frac{B}{s}+\frac{C}{s+5} $$ Multiply by $s^2(s+5)$: $4=A(s+5)+Bs(s+5)+Cs^2$. - $s=0$: $4=5A$ → $A=0.8$. - $s=-5$: $4=25C$ → $C=0.16$. - coefficient of $s^2$: $0=B+C$ → $B=-0.16$. - check, coefficient of $s$: $0=A+5B=0.8-0.8$ ✓. $$ Y(s)=\frac{0.8}{s^{2}}+\frac{-0.16}{s}+\frac{0.16}{s+5} $$ $$ y(t)=0.8t-0.16+0.16e^{-5t} $$ Check: $y(0)=-0.16+0.16=0$ ✓. Same as $K(t-\tau+\tau e^{-t/\tau})$ with $K=0.8$, $\tau=0.2$: $0.8t-0.16+0.16e^{-5t}$ ✓. "$t 5\tau$ (1 s) olduğunda $0{,}16e^{-5t}$ terimi ihmal edilebilir" — for $t 5\tau=1$ s the exponential : $$ y {ss}(t)=0.8t-0.16 $$ $$ e {ss}(t)=t-\left(0.8t-0.16\right)=0.2t+0.16 $$ This grows without bound. $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^{2}}-\frac{4}{s^{2}(s+5)}\right)=\lim {s\to0}s\,\frac{s+5-4}{s^{2}(s+5)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+1}{s(s+5)}=\infty $$ $$ y(t)=0.8t-0.16+0.16e^{-5t},\qquad e(t)\to0.2t+0.16\to\infty $$ Why infinite? In steady state the output rises with slope 0.8 (the DC gain), while the input rises with slope 1. Two lines with different slopes drift apart: every second the output falls another 0.2 behind. Compare with the standard loop, where $K=1$ gave equal slopes and a constant gap $\tau$. A system that cannot even hold a constant (step error 0.2) has no chance of following a ramp. The notes draw $r(t)$ dashed and $y(t)$ solid with smaller slope; unlike the p. 4 sketch, the two lines diverge .

title: Example 2 with a zero at the origin
text: The block diagram of Example 2 has no $+$/$-$ signs at $\Sigma$. The solution uses $\frac{G}{1+G}$, which is the negative-feedback formula, so the loop is taken as unity negative feedback like the others.

title: Example 2: closed-loop transfer function of G = s/(s+1)
Biproper transfer functions
text: Given: unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{s}{s+1}$. Asked: $T(s)$ and a form suitable for inversion. $$ T(s)=\frac{\dfrac{s}{s+1}}{1+\dfrac{s}{s+1}}=\frac{s}{(s+1)+s}=\frac{s}{2s+1}=\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5} $$ (the last form divides numerator and denominator by 2). Write $0.5s=0.5(s+0.5)-0.25$: $$ T(s)=\frac{0.5(s+0.5)-0.25}{s+0.5}=0.5-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5} $$ Check: $\frac{0.5s+0.25-0.25}{s+0.5}=\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}$ ✓. $$ T(s)=\frac{s}{2s+1}=\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}=0.5-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5},\qquad \tau=2\ \text{s} $$ Here the numerator and denominator have the same degree (both 1). Such a transfer function is called biproper : proper (numerator degree not larger than denominator degree) but not strictly proper. Consequences: - $T(\infty)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{s}{2s+1}=0.5\ne0$: part of the input passes straight through to the output instantly (a "direct feed-through" of 0.5). At very high frequencies $G\to1$, so $T\to\frac{1}{1+1}=0.5$. - $T(0)=0$: the DC gain is zero. The $s$ in the numerator of $G$ is a zero at the origin — a differentiator — so constants are blocked completely. - The pole is still at $-0.5$, so the time constant is $\tau=\frac{1}{0.5}=2$ s (also visible from $\frac{s}{2s+1}$: $\tau s+1$ with $\tau=2$).

title: Example 2 impulse response
text: Given: $T(s)=0.5-\dfrac{0.25}{s+0.5}$, $R(s)=1$. Asked: $y(t)$, $y(0^+)$, $y(\infty)$, $e {ss}$. Use $\Li\{1\}=\delta(t)$ and $\Li\left\{\frac{1}{s+a}\right\}=e^{-at}$: $$ y(t)=\Li\left\{0.5-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5}\right\}=0.5\,\delta(t)-0.25e^{-0.5t} $$ For $t 0$ the impulse term is zero, so $y(0^+)=-0.25e^{0}=-0.25$. Via the initial value theorem applied to the strictly proper part only (see below): $$ y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\left(-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5}\right)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{-0.25s}{s}=-0.25 $$ $$ y(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}sY(s)=\lim {s\to0}s\,\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}=0 $$ $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}\right)=0\cdot(1-0)=0 $$ $$ y(t)=0.5\,\delta(t)-0.25e^{-0.5t},\qquad y(0^+)=-0.25,\qquad y(\infty)=0,\qquad e {ss}=0 $$ Interpretation: half of the impulse passes straight through (the direct feed-through 0.5). Then the output swings negative to $-0.25$ and creeps back to 0 with time constant 2 s. The notes draw the impulse as a blue upward arrow at $t=0$ (an impulse has no finite height; the arrow carries its area 0.5), and a blue curve rising from $-0.25$ towards 0. The notes' sketch puts ticks 0.5 and 1 on the time axis and shows the curve practically at 0 by $t=1$. With $\tau=2$ s the true curve is far slower: $y(1)=-0.25e^{-0.5}=-0.152$ (still 61 % of the initial value), $y(\tau)=y(2)=-0.092$, and it only settles after $4\tau$–$5\tau=8$–$10$ s. The plot above uses the true time scale. The shape in the notes is right; only the time axis is qualitative.

title: Initial value theorem with an impulse
Initial value theorem with an impulse
text: "Bu fonksiyonda görüldüğü gibi ilk değer teoremini uygulamak sorunludur. Sıfırdan hemen sonraki an için t=0⁺ fonksiyonun alacağı değer sonludur, hesaplanabilir." — "As seen in this function, applying the initial value theorem is problematic . For the instant just after zero, $t=0^+$, the value the function takes is and can be calculated." What exactly is the problem? Apply the theorem literally to the whole $Y(s)$: $$ \lim {s\to\infty}sY(s)=\lim {s\to\infty}\left(0.5s-\frac{0.25s}{s+0.5}\right)=\infty-0.25=\infty $$ The term $0.5s$ blows up. This is no accident: the constant $0.5$ in $Y(s)$ is the impulse $0.5\delta(t)$, and at $t=0$ an impulse is "infinite". The initial value theorem is derived for functions without impulses at the origin, i.e. for strictly proper $Y(s)$. The fix (what the notes do implicitly): 1. Split $Y(s)$ by long division into constant + strictly proper remainder: $Y(s)=0.5+Y r(s)$, with $Y r(s)=-\dfrac{0.25}{s+0.5}$. 2. The constant is the impulse; it acts only at $t=0$ and is gone at $t=0^+$. 3. Apply the theorem to $Y r$ only: $y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}sY r(s)=-0.25$.
