The notes' line $y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\left(0.5-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5}\right)=\left.\frac{-0.25s}{s}\right {s\to\infty}=-0.25$ silently drops the $0.5s$ term — which is exactly step 3. Equivalently, for a biproper $Y(s)$ you can use $y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\big[Y(s)-Y(\infty)\big]$. As written, $\lim {s\to\infty}s\left(0.5-\frac{0.25}{s+0.5}\right)$ diverges because of $0.5s$. The result $y(0^+)=-0.25$ is nevertheless correct for the non-impulsive part of $y(t)$ and agrees with $-0.25e^{0}$. In an exam, write the split explicitly (step 1 above) so that your working is mathematically correct. The final value theorem has no such problem: $Y(s)=\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}$ has its only pole at $-0.5$, $sY(s)\to0$ as $s\to0$, and $y(\infty)=0$ .

title: Ramp tracking with the standard loop for tau = 0.5 s
More worked examples
text: Given: a closed-loop transfer function $T(s)=\dfrac{5}{s+2}$. Asked: $\tau$, DC gain, pole, settling time, the three responses and their steady-state errors. Divide by 2 (the constant term of the denominator): $T(s)=\dfrac{2.5}{0.5s+1}$ → $K=2.5$, $\tau=0.5$ s, pole $s=-2$. - Impulse: $y=\frac{K}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}=5e^{-2t}$ (equivalently $\Li\{\frac{5}{s+2}\}$). Starts at 5, initial slope $-\frac{K}{\tau^2}=-10$. - Step: $y=2.5(1-e^{-2t})$; $y(0.5)=2.5\times0.632=1.58$; $y {ss}=2.5$. - Ramp: $y=2.5(t-0.5+0.5e^{-2t})=2.5t-1.25+1.25e^{-2t}$. $t s\approx4\tau=2$ s. Step: $e {ss}=1-K=1-2.5=-1.5$ (negative: the output overshoots the target value in steady state, it settles at 2.5 when asked for 1). Ramp: $e(t)\to t-(2.5t-1.25)=-1.5t+1.25\to-\infty$; the output runs away ahead of the input because its slope 2.5 is larger than 1. $K=2.5$, $\tau=0.5$ s, pole $-2$, $t s\approx2$ s; $e {ss,step}=-1.5$, $e {ss,ramp}=-\infty$, $e {ss,impulse}=0$. Sanity check: FVT on the step: $\lim {s\to0}s\cdot\frac{5}{s+2}\cdot\frac1s=\frac52=2.5$ ✓. IVT on the impulse: $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{5s}{s+2}=5$ ✓. A very common slip is to write "first-order step response $=1-e^{-t/\tau}$" for every first-order system. That is only true when $K=1$. For $\frac{5}{s+2}$ the final value is $2.5$, not 1. Always compute $y {ss}=T(0)$ (for a unit step) before sketching. Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{10}{2s+1}$, unit step input. Asked: $y(t)$, the values at $t=1$, 2 and 8 s, and the settling time. Already in gain form: $K=10$, $\tau=2$ s (pole $-0.5$). $$ y(t)=10\left(1-e^{-t/2}\right) $$ - $y(1)=10(1-e^{-0.5})=10(1-0.6065)=3.93$ - $y(2)=y(\tau)=10(0.632)=6.32$ - $y(8)=y(4\tau)=10(1-e^{-4})=10(0.9817)=9.82$ — inside the 2 % band $[9.8,\,10.2]$. $y(t)=10(1-e^{-t/2})$; $y(1)=3.93$, $y(2)=6.32$, $y(8)=9.82$; $t s\approx4\tau=8$ s ($5\tau=10$ s for 99.3 %). Sanity check: initial slope $K/\tau=5$; tangent $5t$ reaches 10 at $t=2=\tau$ ✓. Given: the standard loop of the notes with $G(s)=\dfrac{2}{s}$ (i.e. $\frac{1}{\tau s}$ with $\tau=0.5$). Asked: $T(s)$, the ramp response, $y(3)$, $e {ss}$. $\frac{2}{s}=\frac{1}{0.5s}$ → $\tau=0.5$ s, and $T(s)=\frac{G}{1+G}=\frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{1}{0.5s+1}$ (DC gain 1). $y(t)=t-0.5+0.5e^{-2t}$. At $t=3$ s: $y(3)=3-0.5+0.5e^{-6}=2.5012$. $e {ss}=\tau=0.5$. Check: $e(3)=3-2.5012=0.4988\approx0.5$ (already $6\tau$ after the start). $T(s)=\frac{1}{0.5s+1}$, $y(t)=t-0.5+0.5e^{-2t}$, $e {ss}=0.5$: the output lags the ramp by 0.5 (and by 0.5 s).

title: Loop G = 9/(s+1): open-loop vs closed-loop time constant
Choosing K for a required settling time
Open-loop versus closed-loop time constant
text: For a unity loop around $G(s)=\dfrac{K}{s+a}$: $$ T(s)=\frac{K}{s+a+K}=\frac{\frac{K}{a+K}}{\frac{1}{a+K}s+1},\qquad \tau {CL}=\frac{1}{a+K},\qquad K {DC}=\frac{K}{a+K},\qquad e {ss,step}=\frac{a}{a+K} $$ Given: $G(s)=\dfrac{9}{s+1}$, unity negative feedback. Asked: $\tau$ of the plant and of the closed loop, the step response and step error. $G(s)=\frac{9}{s+1}$: pole $-1$, $\tau {OL}=1$ s, DC gain $9$. $$ T(s)=\frac{9}{s+1+9}=\frac{9}{s+10}=\frac{0.9}{0.1s+1} $$ $\tau {CL}=0.1$ s, $K=0.9$. $y(t)=0.9(1-e^{-10t})$, $t s\approx4\tau {CL}=0.4$ s, $e {ss}=1-0.9=0.1$ (also $\frac{a}{a+K}=\frac{1}{10}$). $\tau {OL}=1$ s but $\tau {CL}=0.1$ s; $y(t)=0.9(1-e^{-10t})$; $e {ss}=0.1$. The common mistake: reading $\tau=1$ s from $G(s)$ and claiming the system settles in 4 s. The question almost always asks about the closed-loop response, so first compute $T(s)$, then read $\tau$ from $T(s)$. Feedback with gain 9 made the system 10 times faster and reduced the step error from "no regulation" to 0.1. Given: $G(s)=\dfrac{K}{s+2}$ in a unity negative-feedback loop. Asked: $K$ such that the closed-loop settling time ($4\tau$ criterion) is 0.5 s; the resulting step error. $4\tau {CL}=0.5$ → $\tau {CL}=0.125$ s → closed-loop pole at $-\frac{1}{0.125}=-8$. $\tau {CL}=\frac{1}{a+K}=\frac{1}{2+K}=0.125$ → $2+K=8$ → $K=6$. $T(s)=\frac{6}{s+8}=\frac{0.75}{0.125s+1}$, $e {ss}=1-0.75=0.25$. $K=6$, $T(s)=\frac{6}{s+8}$, $e {ss,step}=0.25$. Interpretation: a larger $K$ buys both speed and accuracy in this loop; with no integrator, the step error is never exactly zero.

section: Reading tau from a measured graph

title: Reading tau from a measured graph
text: Given: the measured unit step response above. The output settles at 1.6. Asked: $\tau$, $K$ and the transfer function, by two methods. The input is a unit step, the output settles at $1.6$ → $K=1.6$. $0.632\times1.6=1.011$. Draw a horizontal line at 1.011 and read where the curve crosses it: $t\approx0.75$ s. So $\tau\approx0.75$ s. The tangent at $t=0$ has slope $K/\tau$ and reaches the final value at $t=\tau$. Draw the tangent through the first samples and see where it hits $y=1.6$: at $t\approx0.75$ s. (Numerically: initial slope $\approx\frac{1.6}{0.75}=2.13$ per second.) $$ T(s)\approx\frac{1.6}{0.75s+1} $$ Which method in practice? The 63.2 % method is more reliable: drawing a tangent at the very start of a noisy measured curve is hard, and a small error in its slope shifts its intersection noticeably. Use the tangent as a cross-check. Important: 63.2 % of the final value (1.6), not of the input (1).

title: Example 2 driven by a unit step
Edge cases
text: - $\tau\to0$: $T(s)\to1$. The pole goes to $-\infty$, the step response becomes an instant jump, the ramp lag $\tau$ vanishes and the impulse response $\frac1\tau e^{-t/\tau}$ becomes an impulse itself. An ideal, infinitely fast system. - Large $\tau$: pole near the origin, sluggish response, large ramp lag. - $K\ne1$ (Example 1): the step is not tracked exactly ($e {ss}=1-K$) and the ramp error is infinite, because output and input slopes differ. $K 1$ gives negative step error and $-\infty$ ramp error. - Zero at the origin, biproper $T(s)$ (Example 2): impulse in the impulse response, a jump at $t=0^+$ in the step response, and the initial value theorem must be applied to the strictly proper part. - Impulse input: $e {ss}=0$ for every stable system, because both input and output vanish after the transient — the impulse error tells you little about accuracy; the step and ramp errors do. - FVT on a growing signal: $\lim {s\to0}s(\ldots)=\infty$ only says "unbounded". It cannot give you the steady-state function $y {ss}(t)=0.8t-0.16$ — for that you need the time-domain expression. Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{0.5s}{s+0.5}$ (Example 2), unit step input. Asked: $y(t)$, $y(0^+)$, $e {ss}$. $$ Y(s)=\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}\cdot\frac{1}{s}=\frac{0.5}{s+0.5}\;\Rightarrow\;y(t)=0.5e^{-0.5t} $$ The $s$ cancels: this $Y(s)$ is strictly proper, so there is no impulse. $y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}=0.5$. The output jumps to 0.5 at $t=0$ — the direct feed-through of half the step. $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{0.5}{s+0.5}\right)=1-0=1$. $y(t)=0.5e^{-0.5t}$, $y(0^+)=0.5$, $y(\infty)=0$, $e {ss}=1$. Interpretation: a loop with a differentiating plant ($G=\frac{s}{s+1}$, DC gain 0) cannot hold any constant output at all: the step is "forgotten" with time constant 2 s and the full step remains as error.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. Reduce the loop. If a block diagram is given, compute $T(s)=\frac{G}{1+G}$ (unity negative feedback). Simplify to a single fraction. 2. Check the type. First-order denominator? Numerator a constant → gain form $\frac{K}{\tau s+1}$. Numerator contains $s$ → biproper, do long division first (Example 2). 3. Normalise. Divide by the constant term of the denominator: $\frac{b}{s+a}=\frac{b/a}{(1/a)s+1}$. Read $\tau=\frac1a$, $K=\frac ba$, pole $-a$. 4. Write the response for the given input: $R(s)=1,\ \frac1s,\ \frac{1}{s^2}$; partial fractions; invert. Or use the ready forms $\frac K\tau e^{-t/\tau}$, $K(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, $K(t-\tau+\tau e^{-t/\tau})$. 5. Characteristic numbers: $y(\tau)=0.632K$ (step), initial slopes $\pm K/\tau$ or $-K/\tau^2$, settling time $4\tau$–$5\tau$. 6. Steady-state error: $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s[R(s)-Y(s)]$; confirm with $\lim {t\to\infty}[r(t)-y(t)]$. 7. Verify: IVT ($s\to\infty$) against $y(0^+)$, FVT ($s\to0$) against $y(\infty)$; recombine partial fractions. 8. Sketch: final-value line, tangent to $(\tau,\text{final})$, 63 % point, $4\tau$–$5\tau$ mark. For $G=\frac{4}{s+1}$ the plant has $\tau=1$ s, but the closed loop has $\tau=0.2$ s. Read $\tau$ from $T(s)$, not from $G(s)$. $\frac{4}{s+5}$ does not have $\tau=5$ or $\tau=4$. Divide by 5: $\frac{0.8}{0.2s+1}$, so $\tau=0.2$ s $=1/(\text{pole magnitude})$. Initial value: $s\to\infty$. Final value and $e {ss}$: $s\to0$. (The notes themselves slip once on p. 6.) For $K\ne1$ the step response reaches $0.632K$ at $t=\tau$, not $0.632$. Example 1: $y(0.2)=0.506$. The FVT gives a single number $\lim {t\to\infty}f(t)$ and only when that limit exists. For a ramp response $y(t)=0.8t-0.16+\ldots$ there is no finite limit; $\lim {s\to0}sY(s)=\infty$. To get the steady-state behaviour $0.2t+0.16$ of the error you must use the time-domain expression. Likewise, never apply the IVT to a $Y(s)$ that contains a constant term without removing it first. For $T(s)=\frac{K}{\tau s+1}$ with unit inputs: impulse $e {ss}=0$; step $e {ss}=1-K$; ramp $e {ss}=\tau$ if $K=1$, otherwise $\pm\infty$. For a unity loop, $K=1$ exactly when $G(s)$ contains an integrator $\frac1s$ (like $\frac{1}{\tau s}$).

Find tau with the tangent method

Practice exercises
text: A first-order system $\frac{1}{\tau s+1}$ receives a unit step. What percentage of the final value has the output reached at $t=\tau$, $2\tau$ and $3\tau$? What percentage of the initial value remains in the impulse response at the same instants? Step: $y=1-e^{-t/\tau}$ → $1-e^{-1}=63.2\,\%$, $1-e^{-2}=86.5\,\%$, $1-e^{-3}=95.0\,\%$. Impulse: $\frac{y(t)}{y(0^+)}=e^{-t/\tau}$ → $36.8\,\%$, $13.5\,\%$, $5.0\,\%$. Check: the two percentages always add up to 100 %, because the step response is $1-e^{-t/\tau}$ and the normalised impulse response is $e^{-t/\tau}$. For $y(t)=1-e^{-t/\tau}$, find the exact time (in multiples of $\tau$) when the output first reaches 98 % and 99 % of its final value. Compare with the notes' rule $4\tau$–$5\tau$. $1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.98$ → $e^{-t/\tau}=0.02$ → $t=\tau\ln50=3.91\tau$. $e^{-t/\tau}=0.01$ → $t=\tau\ln100=4.61\tau$. So "$4\tau$" is the 2 % settling time (rounded) and "$5\tau$" comfortably covers the 1 % criterion ($1-e^{-5}=99.3\,\%$). Verification: $1-e^{-3.912}=1-0.0200=0.980$ ✓. The loop of the notes has $G(s)=\frac{1}{0.5s}$. Give $T(s)$, the unit step response, the time at which $y=0.632$, and the ramp steady-state error. $\tau=0.5$ s. $T(s)=\frac{1}{0.5s+1}$. Step: $y=1-e^{-2t}$. $y=0.632$ at $t=\tau=0.5$ s (check: $1-e^{-1}=0.632$ ✓). Ramp: $e {ss}=\tau=0.5$ (check: $\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{1}{s^2(0.5s+1)}\right)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{0.5}{0.5s+1}=0.5$ ✓). For $T(s)=\frac{5}{s+2}$ find $\tau$, the DC gain, the 2 % settling time, $y {ss}$ and $e {ss}$ for a unit step. Divide numerator and denominator by 2. $T=\frac{2.5}{0.5s+1}$: $\tau=0.5$ s, $K=2.5$, $t s\approx4\tau=2$ s. Step: $y=2.5(1-e^{-2t})$, $y {ss}=2.5$, $e {ss}=1-2.5=-1.5$. Verification by FVT: $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{5}{s(s+2)}\right)=1-\frac52=-1.5$ ✓. Find the unit impulse response of $T(s)=\frac{3}{s+3}$, its value and slope at $t=0^+$, and verify $y(0^+)$ with the initial value theorem. $y(t)=\Li\{\frac{3}{s+3}\}=3e^{-3t}$. Gain form $\frac{1}{\frac13s+1}$: $K=1$, $\tau=\frac13$ s, so $y=\frac1\tau e^{-t/\tau}=3e^{-3t}$ ✓. $y(0^+)=3$. Slope: $\dot y=-9e^{-3t}$ → $-9=-\frac{1}{\tau^2}$ ✓. IVT: $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{3s}{s+3}=3$ ✓. The tangent $3-9t$ hits zero at $t=\frac13=\tau$ ✓. A unit step is applied to an unknown first-order system. The output settles at 2.0, and it passes 1.264 at $t=4$ s. Find $T(s)$. $K=2$ (final value of the unit step response). $\frac{1.264}{2}=0.632$ → that instant is $t=\tau$, so $\tau=4$ s. $$ T(s)=\frac{2}{4s+1} $$ Check: $y(4)=2(1-e^{-1})=1.264$ ✓. The measured unit step response of a first-order system starts with slope 0.5 per second and settles at 1.5. Find $\tau$, $T(s)$ and the output value at $t=\tau$. The tangent at the origin has slope $\frac{K}{\tau}$ and reaches the final value $K$ at $t=\tau$. So $\tau=\frac{K}{\text{slope}}=\frac{1.5}{0.5}=3$ s. $T(s)=\frac{1.5}{3s+1}$, $y(3)=1.5\times0.632=0.948$. Check: $\frac{d}{dt}1.5(1-e^{-t/3})\big 0=\frac{1.5}{3}=0.5$ ✓. Repeat the professor's Example 1 for $G(s)=\frac{9}{s+1}$ with unity negative feedback: $T(s)$, unit step response and $e {ss}$, unit impulse response with $y(0^+)$ and $y(\infty)$, unit ramp response and its $e {ss}$. $T=\frac{9}{s+10}=\frac{0.9}{0.1s+1}$: $K=0.9$, $\tau=0.1$ s. Step: $y=0.9(1-e^{-10t})$; $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{9}{s(s+10)}\right)=1-0.9=0.1$. Impulse: $y=\frac{0.9}{0.1}e^{-10t}=9e^{-10t}$; IVT $\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{9s}{s+10}=9$; FVT $\lim {s\to0}\frac{9s}{s+10}=0$; $e {ss}=0$. Ramp: $\frac{9}{s^2(s+10)}=\frac{A}{s^2}+\frac{B}{s}+\frac{C}{s+10}$: $A=\frac{9}{10}=0.9$, $C=\frac{9}{100}=0.09$, $B=-C=-0.09$ (check $s$-coefficient: $10B+A=-0.9+0.9=0$ ✓). $y=0.9t-0.09+0.09e^{-10t}$; $e(t)\to0.1t+0.09\to\infty$; $s$-domain: $\lim {s\to0}s\frac{s+10-9}{s^2(s+10)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+1}{s(s+10)}=\infty$ ✓. Recombination check at $s=3$: $\frac{9}{9\cdot13}=0.07692$ and $\frac{0.9}{9}-\frac{0.09}{3}+\frac{0.09}{13}=0.1-0.03+0.006923=0.07692$ ✓. As in the professor's Example 2, take $G(s)=\frac{2s}{s+1}$ with unity negative feedback. Find $T(s)$, its time constant, the unit impulse response, $y(0^+)$ (careful!) and $e {ss}$. Long division: write $T(s)$ as a constant plus a strictly proper fraction. $T=\frac{2s}{s+1+2s}=\frac{2s}{3s+1}=\frac{\frac23s}{s+\frac13}$. Time constant $\tau=3$ s (pole $-\frac13$). Long division: $\frac23s=\frac23\left(s+\frac13\right)-\frac29$, so $T(s)=\frac23-\frac{2/9}{s+1/3}$. Check at $s=3$: $\frac{6}{10}=0.6$ and $0.6667-\frac{0.2222}{3.3333}=0.6667-0.0667=0.6$ ✓. Impulse: $y(t)=\frac23\delta(t)-\frac29e^{-t/3}$. $y(0^+)$: the IVT on the whole $Y(s)$ diverges ($\frac23s\to\infty$); apply it to the strictly proper part: $\lim {s\to\infty}s\left(-\frac{2/9}{s+1/3}\right)=-\frac29\approx-0.222$ ✓ ($=-\frac29e^0$). $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\frac{2s}{3s+1}\right)=0$. Using the closed loop of Example 2, $T(s)=\frac{s}{2s+1}$, compute the unit step response, $y(0^+)$ with the IVT, and $e {ss}$. Why is the IVT unproblematic this time? $Y=\frac{s}{2s+1}\cdot\frac1s=\frac{1}{2s+1}=\frac{0.5}{s+0.5}$ → $y=0.5e^{-0.5t}$. $Y(s)$ is strictly proper (the $s$ cancelled), so there is no impulse and the IVT applies directly: $y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{0.5s}{s+0.5}=0.5$ ✓ $(=0.5e^0)$. $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{0.5}{s+0.5}\right)=1-0=1$. The system has zero DC gain, so it cannot hold a constant output; the whole step remains as error. In Example 1 the step error is a finite 0.2, but the ramp error is infinite. In the standard loop the ramp error is finite ($\tau$). Explain both facts using slopes. In steady state a first-order system with DC gain $K$ responds to a ramp with $y {ss}(t)=K(t-\tau)$, a line of slope $K$. The input has slope 1. The error is $e(t)=(1-K)t+K\tau$. - Standard loop, $K=1$: the $t$ term vanishes → constant error $K\tau=\tau$. - Example 1, $K=0.8$: $e(t)=0.2t+0.16$ grows by 0.2 every second → infinite. Check with Example 1's numbers: $(1-0.8)t+0.8\times0.2=0.2t+0.16$ ✓. Compute the unit ramp response of $T(s)=\frac{1}{2s+1}$ at $t=10$ s, and the error at that instant. How close is it to $e {ss}$? $\tau=2$: $y=t-2+2e^{-t/2}$. $y(10)=10-2+2e^{-5}=8+0.01348=8.0135$. $e(10)=10-8.0135=1.9865$. $e {ss}=\tau=2$; at $t=5\tau$ the error is within $2e^{-5}=0.0135$ (0.7 %) of it. Check: $e(t)=\tau(1-e^{-t/\tau})=2(1-e^{-5})=1.9865$ ✓. A plant $G(s)=\frac{K}{s+4}$ is placed in a unity negative-feedback loop. Find $K$ so that the unit step steady-state error is 0.2. Then give the closed-loop $\tau$, the settling time ($4\tau$) and the ramp steady-state error. $T=\frac{K}{s+4+K}$, $T(0)=\frac{K}{4+K}$, $e {ss}=1-T(0)=\frac{4}{4+K}=0.2$ → $4+K=20$ → $K=16$. $T=\frac{16}{s+20}=\frac{0.8}{0.05s+1}$: $\tau=0.05$ s, $t s\approx0.2$ s. Ramp: DC gain $0.8\ne1$ → $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{16}{s^2(s+20)}\right)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+4}{s(s+20)}=\infty$. Check: $1-0.8=0.2$ ✓. For unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\frac{1}{s+1}$, find $T(s)$ and sketch the unit step response, labelling the final value, the 63 % point, the tangent and the settling time. What is $e {ss}$ for a step and for a ramp? $T=\frac{1}{s+2}=\frac{0.5}{0.5s+1}$: $K=0.5$, $\tau=0.5$ s. Sketch: final-value line at 0.5 (input line at 1 above it); tangent from the origin with slope $\frac{K}{\tau}=1$ reaching 0.5 at $t=0.5$ s; point $(0.5,\ 0.316)$; settled by $4\tau=2$ s ($5\tau=2.5$ s). $y(t)=0.5(1-e^{-2t})$. Step $e {ss}=1-0.5=0.5$; ramp $e {ss}=\infty$ (output slope 0.5, input slope 1). Check: $0.5(1-e^{-1})=0.316$ ✓. In the series RC circuit, $R=10\,\text{k}\Omega$, $C=47\,\mu\text{F}$, and a 5 V step is applied to the uncharged circuit. Find $\tau$, $v c(1\,\text{s})$ and the settling time. $\tau=RC=10^4\times47\times10^{-6}=0.47$ s. $v c(t)=5(1-e^{-t/0.47})$. $v c(1)=5(1-e^{-2.128})=5(1-0.1191)=4.40$ V. $t s\approx4\tau=1.88$ s ($5\tau=2.35$ s). Check: $v c(0)=0$, $v c(\infty)=5$ V ✓. Describe what happens to the pole, the step response, the impulse response and the ramp error of $\frac{1}{\tau s+1}$ as $\tau\to0$. Is this physically achievable? Pole $-\frac1\tau\to-\infty$. Step response $1-e^{-t/\tau}$ → an instant jump to 1 ($t s=4\tau\to0$). Impulse response $\frac1\tau e^{-t/\tau}$: height $\frac1\tau\to\infty$, width $\sim\tau\to0$, area $\int 0^\infty\frac1\tau e^{-t/\tau}dt=1$ always → it tends to $\delta(t)$, i.e. the output copies the input. Ramp error $e {ss}=\tau\to0$. Overall $T(s)\to1$: a perfect, infinitely fast system. Physically impossible — real systems store energy (capacitors, masses, heat capacity) and need time, so $\tau 0$; in the loop of the notes, $\tau\to0$ would mean an infinitely large gain $\frac1\tau$. A student solves: "$G(s)=\frac{4}{s+1}$ in unity feedback. $\tau=1$ s, so the step response is $1-e^{-t}$, it settles in 4 s, and $y(\infty)=\lim {s\to\infty}sY(s)=1$." List every mistake and give the correct results. 1. $\tau$ was read from the open-loop $G$; the closed loop is $T=\frac{4}{s+5}$, $\tau=0.2$ s. 2. The DC gain was ignored: the response is $0.8(1-e^{-5t})$, not $1-e^{-t}$. 3. Settling time is therefore $4\tau=0.8$ s ($5\tau=1$ s), not 4 s. 4. The final value uses $s\to0$, not $s\to\infty$: $y(\infty)=\lim {s\to0}s\cdot\frac{4}{s+5}\cdot\frac1s=0.8$. Hence $e {ss}=0.2$, not 0. (Compare the professor's Example 1, p. 5–6.)

title: What is this about?
text: Push a car down at one corner and let go. Depending on how worn the shock absorbers are, the body either sinks back slowly without bouncing, returns as fast as possible without bouncing, or bobs up and down a few times before settling. Three very different behaviours — yet all three come from one equation with only two knobs: how "stiff and quick" the system is, and how much "friction" (damping) it has. That is exactly what a is. Its output obeys a differential equation with a second derivative (a mass with a spring and a damper, an RLC circuit, a motor driving a load, a position servo in a feedback loop). In the previous module the first-order system could only rise smoothly like $1-e^{-t/\tau}$. A second-order system can also overshoot and oscillate , and that is what makes it both more useful (it can be fast) and more dangerous (it can ring). In this module the professor takes the standard second-order loop and works out, for every combination of - input : unit impulse, unit step, unit ramp, and - damping case : overdamped, critically damped, underdamped, the exact time response $y(t)$ (by partial fractions and the inverse Laplace transform) and the . These nine derivations are the core of the exam. Two numbers describe everything: - $\omega n$ — the in rad/s: how fast the system wants to move (how stiff the spring is relative to the mass). - $\xi$ — the (dimensionless; English books call it the damping ratio and often write $\zeta$): how strongly the motion is braked. After this module you can: - derive $T(s)=\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2}$ from the loop and read $\omega n$, $\xi$, $\alpha$, $\omega$, $\theta$ and the roots off any second-order transfer function (also with a DC gain different from 1); - decide whether a system is overdamped, critically damped or underdamped and say what that means physically; - derive the impulse, step and ramp responses in all three cases with partial fractions (distinct, repeated and complex roots); - convert $\cos\omega t+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t$ into a single shifted sine, and know why the ramp response has phase $2\theta$; - compute steady-state errors with $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s[R(s)-Y(s)]$; - sketch every response by hand, with the right start, slope and final behaviour.

title: The standard second-order system
text: The professor starts from this loop : - $R(s)$ is the reference (input), $Y(s)$ the output, $E(s)=R(s)-Y(s)$ the error leaving the summing junction. - The forward block $G(s)=\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}$ is the "plant plus controller". The factor $\frac1s$ is an integrator (for a motor: speed integrates to position); $\frac{1}{s+2\xi\omega n}$ is a lag. - The feedback is unity (the output itself is subtracted), with a minus sign. $\omega n$ (rad/s) is the : the frequency at which the system would oscillate forever if there were no damping at all ($\xi=0$). $\xi$ is the . It measures how much the motion is braked: $\xi=0$ no braking (endless oscillation), small $\xi$ light braking (decaying oscillation), $\xi=1$ just enough braking to prevent any oscillation, $\xi 1$ heavy braking (sluggish).

title: Deriving the closed-loop transfer function
text: The notes simply state the ; here is where it comes from. Around the loop: $$ E(s)=R(s)-Y(s),\qquad Y(s)=G(s)E(s) $$ Substitute the first into the second and collect $Y(s)$: $$ Y(s)=G(s)R(s)-G(s)Y(s)\ \Longrightarrow\ Y(s)\big[1+G(s)\big]=G(s)R(s)\ \Longrightarrow\ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)} $$ Now insert $G(s)=\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}$ and multiply numerator and denominator by $s(s+2\xi\omega n)$: $$ T(s)=\frac{\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}}{1+\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}}=\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)+\omega n^2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2} $$ $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2} $$ Two things to notice: - DC gain is 1. At $s=0$: $T(0)=\omega n^2/\omega n^2=1$. A constant input is eventually reproduced exactly at the output. (This comes from the integrator $1/s$ in the loop.) - The pattern to recognise in an exam: constant term $=\omega n^2$, coefficient of $s$ $=2\xi\omega n$, coefficient of $s^2$ $=1$. If a transfer function is not normalised (leading coefficient not 1), divide through first.

title: The differential equation behind T(s)
text: Cross-multiplying $Y(s)(s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2)=\omega n^2R(s)$ and reading $s\leftrightarrow\frac{d}{dt}$ (zero initial conditions): $$ \ddot y(t)+2\xi\omega n\,\dot y(t)+\omega n^2\,y(t)=\omega n^2\,r(t) $$ This is the equation every response in this module solves. (All responses below were also checked by solving this ODE numerically.)

title: Physical intuition: mass-spring-damper and RLC
text: A mass $m$ on a spring $k$ with a damper $b$, whose spring end is moved by $r(t)$: $m\ddot y+b\dot y+ky=k\,r$. Divide by $m$: $$ \ddot y+\frac{b}{m}\dot y+\frac{k}{m}y=\frac{k}{m}r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega n^2=\frac km,\qquad 2\xi\omega n=\frac bm\ \Rightarrow\ \xi=\frac{b}{2\sqrt{km}} $$ Stiffer spring or lighter mass → higher $\omega n$ (faster). More friction → higher $\xi$ (less bounce). The car-suspension story from the introduction is exactly this. The same equation appears in electric circuits (the RLC circuits of [Module 05]( /m/05)): KVL around the loop with $i=C\dot v o$: $v i=Ri+L\dot i+v o=RC\dot v o+LC\ddot v o+v o$, so $$ \ddot v o+\frac RL\dot v o+\frac1{LC}v o=\frac1{LC}v i\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\omega n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad \xi=\frac R2\sqrt{\frac CL} $$ The resistor is the damper: $R=0$ gives an undamped LC oscillator, a large $R$ gives a sluggish, non-oscillating response.

title: Roots of the characteristic equation
text: The behaviour is decided by the roots (poles) of the denominator $s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2=0$ — the . Quadratic formula with $a=1$, $b=2\xi\omega n$, $c=\omega n^2$: $$ s {1,2}=\frac{-2\xi\omega n\pm\sqrt{4\xi^2\omega n^2-4\omega n^2}}{2}=-\xi\omega n\pm\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1} $$ $$ s {1,2}=-\xi\omega n\pm\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1} $$ Everything hinges on the sign of $\xi^2-1$ under the square root.

title: Three damping cases
text: The system is treated in three different ways depending on the damping factor : Case Turkish Condition Roots Typical motion --- --- --- --- --- Overdamped aşırı sönümlü $\xi 1$ real and distinct (gerçek ve ayrık): $-p 1,\,-p 2$ slow, no overshoot Critically damped kritik sönümlü $\xi=1$ real and repeated (gerçek ve katlı): $-\omega n,\,-\omega n$ fastest without overshoot Underdamped düşük sönümlü $\xi<1$ complex conjugate (karmaşık ve eşlenik): $-\alpha\pm j\omega$ decaying oscillation

title: Overdamped case
text: If $\xi 1$ then $\xi^2-1 0$, the square root is real, and the roots are real and distinct . The professor names them $s 1=-p 1$, $s 2=-p 2$ with $$ p 1=\xi\omega n-\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1},\qquad p 2=\xi\omega n+\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1} $$ Both $p 1$ and $p 2$ are positive (because $\sqrt{\xi^2-1}<\xi$), so both roots lie on the negative real axis; $p 1$ is the smaller one — the slow root that dominates the response. Two handy facts (Vieta's formulas for the quadratic) used again and again below: $$ p 1p 2=\omega n^2,\qquad p 1+p 2=2\xi\omega n,\qquad p 2-p 1=2\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1} $$

title: Critically damped case
text: If $\xi=1$ the square root vanishes and the roots are real and repeated : $s {1,2}=-\omega n$. The denominator is a perfect square: $s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2=(s+\omega n)^2$.

title: Underdamped case
text: If $\xi<1$ then $\xi^2-1<0$; write $\sqrt{\xi^2-1}=j\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$. The roots are complex conjugate : $$ s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega=-\xi\omega n\pm j\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2},\qquad \alpha=\xi\omega n,\quad \omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2} $$ $\alpha$ is the decay rate (real part), $\omega$ the frequency at which the response actually oscillates (the damped frequency; the professor writes plain $\omega$, many books write $\omega d$). The notes say "$\xi<1$". The formulas really need $0<\xi<1$: at $\xi=0$ the roots sit on the imaginary axis (pure oscillation, covered as a limit in [Edge cases]( /m/07/undamped-limit)), and $\xi<0$ would put them in the right half-plane (unstable). In this course $\xi$ is a damping, so it is non-negative.

title: Geometry of the complex roots
text: The underdamped root $-\alpha+j\omega$ has distance from the origin $$ \sqrt{\alpha^2+\omega^2}=\sqrt{\xi^2\omega n^2+\omega n^2(1-\xi^2)}=\omega n $$ so the poles lie on a circle of radius $\omega n$. The angle $\theta$ between the ray to the pole and the negative real axis satisfies $$ \cos\theta=\frac{\alpha}{\omega n}=\xi,\qquad \sin\theta=\frac{\omega}{\omega n}=\sqrt{1-\xi^2},\qquad \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi} $$ This is the same $\theta$ the professor introduces on p. 9 for the step response. In polar form the roots are $-\alpha\pm j\omega=-\omega n e^{\mp j\theta}$, a fact we will use to see where the phase $2\theta$ in the ramp response comes from. Moving along the circle (fixed $\omega n$) from the real axis towards the imaginary axis lowers $\xi=\cos\theta$: the poles move right (slower decay $\alpha$) and up (faster oscillation $\omega$). At $\theta=90^\circ$ ($\xi=0$) there is no decay at all. At $\theta=0$ ($\xi=1$) the two poles meet on the real axis — critical damping — and for $\xi 1$ they split along the real axis, one towards the origin ($-p 1$, slow) and one away ($-p 2$, fast).

title: Example 1: type and parameters of the system
Example 1: identifying the parameters
text: Given: unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{2}{s^2+2s+2}$. Asked: the type (damping case) and the parameters of the system ( ). Method: the type is a property of the closed loop , so first find $T(s)$, then match its denominator with $s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2$. $$ T(s)=\frac{G}{1+G}=\frac{\dfrac{2}{s^2+2s+2}}{1+\dfrac{2}{s^2+2s+2}}=\frac{2}{s^2+2s+2+2}=\frac{2}{s^2+2s+4} $$ (Multiply top and bottom by $s^2+2s+2$.) $$ \omega n^2=4\Rightarrow\omega n=2\ \text{rad/s},\qquad 2\xi\omega n=2\Rightarrow\xi=\frac{2}{2\cdot2}=0.5 $$ (The notes write 0,5 with a decimal comma.) $$ \alpha=\xi\omega n=0.5\cdot2=1,\qquad \omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=2\sqrt{0.75}=\sqrt3=1.732 $$ $$ s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega=-1\pm j1.732 $$ $\xi=0.5<1$ → complex-conjugate roots → underdamped (düşük sönümlü). The notes leave this word implicit. $T(s)=\dfrac{2}{s^2+2s+4}$, $\omega n=2$ rad/s, $\xi=0.5$, $\alpha=1$, $\omega=1.732$ rad/s, $s {1,2}=-1\pm j1.732$: an underdamped system. ($\theta=\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{0.75}/0.5)=60^\circ$.) Sanity check: $(s+1)^2+3=s^2+2s+4$ ✓. Also $ s 1 =\sqrt{1+3}=2=\omega n$ ✓. $T(s)=\dfrac{2}{s^2+2s+4}=0.5\cdot\dfrac{4}{s^2+2s+4}$. The numerator is 2, not $\omega n^2=4$, so this closed loop has DC gain $T(0)=0.5$: it is the standard form times 0.5 . The notes do not mention it, but it matters as soon as you compute responses: every response of this system is 0.5 times the standard one, and the step settles at 0.5, not 1. The reason is that $G(s)$ here has no integrator (no factor $1/s$). Example 2 handles exactly this situation.

title: Partial fraction toolkit
text: Every response below is found the same way: $Y(s)=T(s)R(s)$, split into , and invert term by term with the ([Module 03]( /m/03)). The professor uses three coefficient-finding rules ( ):

title: Distinct real roots
text: For a simple factor $(s+p)$ in the denominator: $$ \frac{K}{s+p}\quad\text{with}\quad K=\lim {s\to-p}\big[(s+p)Y(s)\big]\qquad\xrightarrow{\ \Li\ }\qquad Ke^{-pt} $$ Multiply by the factor, cancel, then substitute the root ("cover-up" rule).

title: Repeated roots
text: For a double factor $(s+p)^2$ there are two terms: $$ \frac{K a}{(s+p)^2}+\frac{K b}{s+p},\qquad K a=\lim {s\to-p}\big[(s+p)^2Y(s)\big],\quad K b=\lim {s\to-p}\frac{d}{ds}\big[(s+p)^2Y(s)\big] $$ and $\Li\left\{\dfrac{1}{(s+p)^2}\right\}=te^{-pt}$. The same rule applies to $s^2$ (a double root at $s=0$, $p=0$): $\dfrac{K 1}{s^2}+\dfrac{K 2}{s}$ with $K 1=\lim s^2Y$, $K 2=\lim \frac{d}{ds}[s^2Y]$, and $\Li\{1/s^2\}=t$. Why the derivative? If $(s+p)^2Y(s)=K a+K b(s+p)+(s+p)^2(\dots)$, then at $s=-p$ the value gives $K a$ and the first derivative gives $K b$.

title: Complex-conjugate roots (K and K star)
text: The professor writes $p 1=\alpha+j\omega$, $p 2=\alpha-j\omega$, so $(s+p 1)(s+p 2)=(s+\alpha)^2+\omega^2$ and the roots are $-p 1=-\alpha-j\omega$, $-p 2=-\alpha+j\omega$. Because $Y(s)$ has real coefficients, the two coefficients are complex conjugates: $$ \frac{K}{s+\alpha+j\omega}+\frac{K^ }{s+\alpha-j\omega},\qquad K=\lim {s\to-\alpha-j\omega}\big[(s+\alpha+j\omega)Y(s)\big] $$ Inverting gives $Ke^{-(\alpha+j\omega)t}+K^ e^{-(\alpha-j\omega)t}$. The two terms are conjugates, and $z+z^ =2\,\mathrm{Re}\,z$, so with $K=a+jb$: $$ Ke^{-(\alpha+j\omega)t}+K^ e^{-(\alpha-j\omega)t}=2e^{-\alpha t}\,\mathrm{Re}\{(a+jb)(\cos\omega t-j\sin\omega t)\}=2e^{-\alpha t}\big(a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t\big) $$ $$ \frac{K}{s+\alpha+j\omega}+\frac{K^ }{s+\alpha-j\omega}\ \xrightarrow{\ \Li\ }\ 2e^{-\alpha t}\big(a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t\big),\qquad K=a+jb $$ You only ever compute one complex coefficient; its conjugate partner comes for free. The professor does the same thing directly with Euler's formula $\sin x=\dfrac{e^{jx}-e^{-jx}}{2j}$ (p. 6) — both routes give the same result.

title: Unit impulse response
text: : $r(t)=\delta(t)$, $R(s)=1$, so $Y(s)=T(s)$. That is why the professor writes the transfer function directly as $Y(s)$.

title: Impulse: overdamped
text: With real distinct roots : $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+p 1)(s+p 2)}=\frac{K 1}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 2}{s+p 2} $$ The notes leave $K 1,K 2$ unevaluated; with the cover-up rule: $$ K 1=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s+p 2}\right {s=-p 1}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2-p 1},\qquad K 2=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s+p 1}\right {s=-p 2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 1-p 2}=-\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2-p 1} $$ Inverse Laplace ( , the notes write lower-case $k 1,k 2$ — same coefficients): $$ y(t)=k 1e^{-p 1t}+k 2e^{-p 2t}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2-p 1}\left(e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t}\right)=\frac{\omega n}{2\sqrt{\xi^2-1}}\left(e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t}\right) $$ (using $p 2-p 1=2\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1}$). Since $p 1 e^{-p 2t}$ for $t 0$: the response is positive , starts at 0, rises to a single hump and decays — no oscillation, no zero crossing. The slow exponential $e^{-p 1t}$ governs the long tail.

title: Impulse: critically damped
text: With the repeated root $s {1,2}=-\omega n$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+\omega n)^2}\quad\xrightarrow{\ \Li\{1/(s+p)^2\}=te^{-pt}\ }\quad y(t)=\omega n^2\,t\,e^{-\omega nt} $$ No partial fractions are even needed: it is already a single table entry. The hump peaks where $\frac{d}{dt}(te^{-\omega nt})=e^{-\omega nt}(1-\omega nt)=0$, i.e. at $t=1/\omega n$, with height $\omega n/e$. The notes write "$s {1,2}=\omega n$" for the repeated root. A minus sign is missing: the root is $s {1,2}=-\omega n$ (as correctly written on pp. 2, 8 and 12). The formula $Y(s)=\omega n^2/(s+\omega n)^2$ on the same page is right, and $s+\omega n=0$ gives $s=-\omega n$.

title: Impulse: underdamped
text: Complex roots $s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega$; with $p 1=\alpha+j\omega$, $p 2=\alpha-j\omega$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+p 1)(s+p 2)}=\frac{K}{s+p 1}+\frac{K^ }{s+p 2} $$ Cover-up at $s=-p 1=-\alpha-j\omega$ (the other factor $s+p 2=s+\alpha-j\omega$ becomes $-2j\omega$ there): $$ K=\lim {s\to-\alpha-j\omega}\big[(s+\alpha+j\omega)Y(s)\big]=\frac{\omega n^2}{-\alpha-j\omega+\alpha-j\omega}=\frac{-\omega n^2}{2j\omega} $$ $$ K^ =\lim {s\to-\alpha+j\omega}\big[(s+\alpha-j\omega)Y(s)\big]=\frac{\omega n^2}{-\alpha+j\omega+\alpha+j\omega}=\frac{\omega n^2}{2j\omega} $$ Inverse Laplace, then factor out $e^{-\alpha t}$ and use Euler's identity $\sin x=\frac{e^{jx}-e^{-jx}}{2j}$ : $$ y(t)=\frac{-\omega n^2}{2j\omega}e^{-(\alpha+j\omega)t}+\frac{\omega n^2}{2j\omega}e^{-(\alpha-j\omega)t}=\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\underbrace{\left(\frac{e^{j\omega t}-e^{-j\omega t}}{2j}\right)} {\sin\omega t}=\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t $$ Finally $\omega n^2/\omega=\omega n^2/(\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2})=\omega n/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$: $$ y(t)=\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\,e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t $$ Check with the conjugate-pair rule: $K=\frac{-\omega n^2}{2j\omega}=j\frac{\omega n^2}{2\omega}$, so $a=0$, $b=\frac{\omega n^2}{2\omega}$ and $2e^{-\alpha t}(b\sin\omega t)=\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t$ ✓. Physical meaning: a sine at the damped frequency $\omega$ inside an exponentially shrinking envelope $\pm\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}$. The zero crossings are at $\omega t=k\pi$, i.e. every $\pi/\omega$ seconds.

title: Impulse response family
text: The notes show the impulse response for $\xi=0.25$, $1$ and $2$ (no $\omega n$ given; here $\omega n=1$, so the time axis is in units of $1/\omega n$ and for another $\omega n$ you rescale $t$ by $1/\omega n$ and $y$ by $\omega n$). Exact functions plotted: - $\xi=0.25$: $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.9375}}e^{-0.25t}\sin(0.968t)$ — tall first peak, then a negative lobe, a smaller positive one…: a decaying oscillation about 0. - $\xi=1$: $y=te^{-t}$ — one hump, peak $1/e=0.368$ at $t=1$, no zero crossing. - $\xi=2$: $y=\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}\left(e^{-0.268t}-e^{-3.732t}\right)$ — the lowest, flattest hump and the slowest tail. "As seen, increasing the damping factor reduces the system oscillation" ( ). How to sketch by hand: every curve starts at $y(0)=0$ with initial slope $y'(0^+)=\omega n^2$ (the same for all $\xi$ — the impulse "kicks" the velocity). Underdamped: draw the envelope $\pm\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}$, cross zero every $\pi/\omega$. Critical: one hump at $t=1/\omega n$, height $\omega n/e$. Overdamped: lower, wider hump with a long tail. All tend to 0.

title: Steady-state error for the impulse
text: The steady-state error is the final value of $e(t)=r(t)-y(t)$; by the final value theorem : $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\big[R(s)-Y(s)\big]=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2}\right)=0\cdot(1-1)=0 $$ The impulse is over at $t=0^+$ and the output dies out, so the error is zero. In several $e {ss}$ and $Y(s)$ expressions the notes write the denominator as $s^2+2\xi\omega n+\omega n^2$ — the $s$ in the middle term is missing. The correct denominator is always $s^2+2\xi\omega n\,s+\omega n^2$. The slip does not change any limit computed at $s=0$ (the middle term vanishes there anyway), so all of the professor's results stand. On p. 8 the formula for $K 1$ also still shows $\xi$ although $\xi=1$ in that section — again harmless at $s=0$.

title: Unit step response
text: : $r(t)=1$ for $t\ge0$, $R(s)=\frac1s$ : $$ Y(s)=\frac1s\cdot\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2} $$ The extra $\frac1s$ adds one more partial fraction, $\frac{K 1}{s}$, which becomes the constant final value.

title: Step: overdamped
text: All roots real and distinct ($0,\,-p 1,\,-p 2$): $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+p 1)(s+p 2)}=\frac{K 1}{s}+\frac{K 2}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 3}{s+p 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y(t)=K 1+K 2e^{-p 1t}+K 3e^{-p 2t} $$ The notes stop here. The coefficients by the cover-up rule, simplified with $p 1p 2=\omega n^2$: $$ K 1=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+p 1)(s+p 2)}\right {s=0}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 1p 2}=1 $$ $$ K 2=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+p 2)}\right {s=-p 1}=\frac{\omega n^2}{-p 1(p 2-p 1)}=-\frac{p 2}{p 2-p 1},\qquad K 3=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+p 1)}\right {s=-p 2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{-p 2(p 1-p 2)}=\frac{p 1}{p 2-p 1} $$ $$ y(t)=1-\frac{p 2\,e^{-p 1t}-p 1\,e^{-p 2t}}{p 2-p 1},\qquad p 2-p 1=2\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1} $$ Checks. $y(0)=1-\frac{p 2-p 1}{p 2-p 1}=0$ ✓. $y(\infty)=1$ ✓. Differentiate: $\dot y=\frac{p 1p 2}{p 2-p 1}(e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t})=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2-p 1}(e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t})$ — exactly the overdamped impulse response, as it must be (the step is the integral of the impulse). Since $\dot y 0$ for all $t 0$, the overdamped step rises monotonically and never overshoots.

title: Step: critically damped
text: Repeated root $s {1,2}=-\omega n$; the professor sets $p=\omega n$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2}\cdot\frac1s=\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+\omega n)^2}\cdot\frac1s=\frac{K 1}{s}+\frac{K 2}{s+p}+\frac{K 3}{(s+p)^2} $$ Coefficients (the notes compute them in the order $K 1$, $K 3$, $K 2$ — the derivative coefficient needs the same bracket as $K 3$): $$ K 1=\lim {s\to0}\big[sY(s)\big]=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\omega n s+\omega n^2}\right {s=0}=1 $$ $$ K 3=\lim {s\to-p}\big[(s+\omega n)^2Y(s)\big]=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s}\right {s=-\omega n}=-\omega n $$ $$ K 2=\lim {s\to-p}\frac{d}{ds}\big[(s+\omega n)^2Y(s)\big]=\lim {s\to-p}\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{\omega n^2}{s}\right)=\left.\frac{-\omega n^2}{s^2}\right {s=-\omega n}=-1 $$ Inverse Laplace ($\frac1s\to1$, $\frac{1}{s+p}\to e^{-pt}$, $\frac{1}{(s+p)^2}\to te^{-pt}$): $$ y(t)=1-e^{-\omega nt}-\omega nt\,e^{-\omega nt} $$ Checks. $y(0)=1-1-0=0$ ✓, $y(\infty)=1$ ✓, $\dot y=\omega ne^{-\omega nt}-\omega ne^{-\omega nt}+\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}=\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}$ = the critical impulse response ✓. Recombining: $\frac1s-\frac{1}{s+\omega n}-\frac{\omega n}{(s+\omega n)^2}=\frac{(s+\omega n)^2-s(s+\omega n)-\omega ns}{s(s+\omega n)^2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+\omega n)^2}$ ✓.

title: Step: underdamped
text: Complex roots $s {1,2}=-\alpha\pm j\omega$, $p 1=\alpha+j\omega$, $p 2=\alpha-j\omega$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{K 1}{s}+\frac{K 2}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 2^ }{s+p 2} $$ The notes say "applying the coefficient-finding methods given earlier" and jump to the result. Here are the missing steps. $K 1$: $K 1=\left.\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}\right {s=0}=1$. $K 2$: cover up $(s+p 1)$ and substitute $s=-\alpha-j\omega$. The remaining factors are $s$ and $s+p 2=s+\alpha-j\omega$, which equals $-2j\omega$ at that point: $$ K 2=\frac{\omega n^2}{(-\alpha-j\omega)(-2j\omega)}=\frac{\omega n^2}{2j\alpha\omega+2j^2\omega^2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{-2\omega(\omega-j\alpha)} $$ Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $(\omega+j\alpha)$ and use $\omega^2+\alpha^2=\omega n^2$: $$ K 2=-\frac{\omega n^2(\omega+j\alpha)}{2\omega(\omega^2+\alpha^2)}=-\frac{\omega+j\alpha}{2\omega}=-\frac12-j\frac{\alpha}{2\omega} $$ Invert with the conjugate-pair rule ($a=-\frac12$, $b=-\frac{\alpha}{2\omega}$): $$ y(t)=1+2e^{-\alpha t}\left(-\frac12\cos\omega t-\frac{\alpha}{2\omega}\sin\omega t\right)=1-e^{-\alpha t}\left(\cos\omega t+\frac{\alpha}{\omega}\sin\omega t\right) $$ and $\dfrac{\alpha}{\omega}=\dfrac{\xi\omega n}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\dfrac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$: $$ y(t)=1-e^{-\alpha t}\left[\cos\omega t+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t\right] $$ Checks. $y(0)=1-[1+0]=0$ ✓; $y(\infty)=1$ ✓.

title: Amplitude-phase form of the step response
Amplitude-phase form of the step response
text: The professor then "combines the sinusoidal terms" ( ) . The identity behind it: $$ A\cos x+B\sin x=R\sin(x+\varphi),\qquad R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2},\quad \sin\varphi=\frac AR,\quad\cos\varphi=\frac BR $$ (Proof: expand $R\sin(x+\varphi)=R\sin\varphi\cos x+R\cos\varphi\sin x$ and compare coefficients.) Here $A=1$, $B=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$: $$ R=\sqrt{1+\frac{\xi^2}{1-\xi^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}},\qquad \sin\varphi=\frac{1}{R}=\sqrt{1-\xi^2},\qquad\cos\varphi=\frac BR=\xi $$ So $\varphi$ is exactly the pole angle $\theta$ ($\cos\theta=\xi$) and $\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}$: $$ y(t)=1-\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin(\omega t+\theta),\qquad \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi} $$ At $t=0$: $\frac{\sin\theta}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=1$, so $y(0)=0$ ✓. For $0<\xi<1$, $\theta$ lies between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, so the calculator's $\tan^{-1}$ gives the right angle directly. In $\sin(\omega t+\theta)$, $\omega t$ is in radians . Either use $\theta$ in radians ($\theta[\text{rad}]=\theta[^\circ]\cdot\pi/180$) or convert $\omega t$ to degrees. Mixing them (e.g. $\sin(4.58\cdot0.5+66.42)$ with the calculator in radian mode) gives garbage. What the formula says physically: the output oscillates around the final value 1 at the damped frequency $\omega$, inside the envelope $1\pm\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$. A smaller $\xi$ gives a slower decay $\alpha=\xi\omega n$ and a larger overshoot. Because $\dot y$ equals the impulse response $\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t$, the step's peaks and valleys are where $\sin\omega t=0$: $t=\pi/\omega,\ 2\pi/\omega,\dots$ At the first peak $t=\pi/\omega$, $\cos\omega t=-1$, $\sin\omega t=0$, so $y {\max}=1+e^{-\alpha\pi/\omega}$.

title: Step response family
text: The notes' figure: step responses for $\xi=2,\ 1,\ 0.25$ with the final value shown dashed. Exact functions ($\omega n=1$): - $\xi=0.25$: $y=1-1.033\,e^{-0.25t}\sin(0.968t+75.5^\circ)$ — large overshoot (peak $1+e^{-0.25\pi/0.968}=1.44$ at $t=3.24$), then a decaying ripple around 1. - $\xi=1$: $y=1-e^{-t}-te^{-t}$ — monotonic, the fastest curve without overshoot. - $\xi=2$: $y=1-1.077e^{-0.268t}+0.077e^{-3.732t}$ — monotonic and slow; still clearly below 1 at $t=10$. "The figure shows the time-domain responses of three different types of system with damping factors $\xi=2,1,0.25$." How to sketch by hand: draw the dashed final value $1$. Start every curve at $(0,0)$ with a horizontal tangent . Underdamped: first peak at $t=\pi/\omega$ with height $1+e^{-\alpha\pi/\omega}$, then valleys/peaks every $\pi/\omega$ closing in on 1. Critical: S-shaped rise, about $0.59$ at $t=2/\omega n$ and $0.96$ at $t=5/\omega n$. Overdamped: lower S-curve dominated by the slow exponential $e^{-p 1t}$.

title: Why every step response starts flat
Why every step response starts flat
text: In the hand sketch the $\xi=1$ and $\xi=2$ curves leave the origin with a visible non-zero slope. The true step response of a second-order system has zero initial slope for every $\xi$ . Two ways to see it: 1. Derivative = impulse response. $\dot y {\text{step}}(t)=y {\text{impulse}}(t)$, and all three impulse responses start at $0$ ($\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}$, $\sin\omega t$, $e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t}$ all vanish at $t=0$). So $\dot y(0^+)=0$. 2. Initial value theorem applied to $\dot y$: $\L\{\dot y\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)=T(s)$, hence $$ \dot y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\cdot\big[sY(s)\big]=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{s\,\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}=0 $$ Applying the theorem once more gives $\ddot y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\big[s^2Y(s)\big]=\omega n^2$, so near $t=0$ every step response looks like $\frac{\omega n^2t^2}{2}$ (dashed curve above). Physically: a step force cannot instantly give a mass a velocity, only an acceleration. The professor's ordering of the curves (0.25 fastest, then 1, then 2) is correct; only the starting slope of the sketch is off.

title: Steady-state error for the step
text: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\big[R(s)-Y(s)\big]=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}\cdot\frac1s\right)=\lim {s\to0}\left(1-\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}\right)=1-1=0 $$ The standard second-order system follows a step with zero steady-state error in all three damping cases — because its DC gain is 1 (its loop contains an integrator). If the closed loop has DC gain $K\ne1$, then $e {ss}=1-K$ (Example 2 gives 0.2).

title: Unit ramp response
text: : $r(t)=t$, $R(s)=\frac{1}{s^2}$ : $$ Y(s)=\frac{1}{s^2}\cdot\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2} $$ Now $s=0$ is a double root, so there are two terms $\frac{K 1}{s^2}+\frac{K 2}{s}$, and $K 2$ needs the derivative rule. These two terms are the same in all three cases: $$ K 1=\lim {s\to0}\big[s^2Y(s)\big]=\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega n^2}=1,\qquad K 2=\lim {s\to0}\frac{d}{ds}\left[\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}\right]=\left.\frac{-\omega n^2(2s+2\xi\omega n)}{(s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2)^2}\right {s=0}=\frac{-2\xi\omega n^3}{\omega n^4}=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n} $$ So every ramp response contains $t-\dfrac{2\xi}{\omega n}$: after the transient, the output is a line of slope 1 that lags the input by $\dfrac{2\xi}{\omega n}$.

title: Ramp: overdamped
text: $$ Y(s)=\frac{K 1}{s^2}+\frac{K 2}{s}+\frac{K 3}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 4}{s+p 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y(t)=K 1t+K 2+K 3e^{-p 1t}+K 4e^{-p 2t} $$ The notes leave the coefficients unevaluated. $K 1=1$, $K 2=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ (above), and by cover-up with $p 1p 2=\omega n^2$: $$ K 3=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2(s+p 2)}\right {s=-p 1}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 1^2(p 2-p 1)}=\frac{p 2}{p 1(p 2-p 1)},\qquad K 4=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2(s+p 1)}\right {s=-p 2}=\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2^2(p 1-p 2)}=-\frac{p 1}{p 2(p 2-p 1)} $$ $$ y(t)=t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac{1}{p 2-p 1}\left(\frac{p 2}{p 1}e^{-p 1t}-\frac{p 1}{p 2}e^{-p 2t}\right) $$ Check $y(0)=0$: $\frac{1}{p 2-p 1}\left(\frac{p 2}{p 1}-\frac{p 1}{p 2}\right)=\frac{p 2^2-p 1^2}{p 1p 2(p 2-p 1)}=\frac{p 1+p 2}{p 1p 2}=\frac{2\xi\omega n}{\omega n^2}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$, which cancels $-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ ✓.

title: Ramp: critically damped
text: With $p=\omega n$, repeated roots $s {1,2}=-\omega n$: $$ Y(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{(s+\omega n)^2}\cdot\frac{1}{s^2}=\frac{K 1}{s^2}+\frac{K 2}{s}+\frac{K 3}{(s+p)^2}+\frac{K 4}{s+p} $$ Two double roots, so two derivative coefficients: $$ K 1=\lim {s\to0}\big[s^2Y(s)\big]=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2}\right {s=0}=1 $$ $$ K 2=\lim {s\to0}\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2}\right)=\left.\frac{-\omega n^2(2s+2\omega n)}{(s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2)^2}\right {s=0}=\frac{-2\omega n^3}{\omega n^4}=-\frac{2}{\omega n} $$ $$ K 3=\lim {s\to-\omega n}\big[(s+\omega n)^2Y(s)\big]=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2}\right {s=-\omega n}=1 $$ $$ K 4=\lim {s\to-\omega n}\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2}\right)=\left.\frac{-2s\,\omega n^2}{s^4}\right {s=-\omega n}=\left.\frac{-2\omega n^2}{s^3}\right {s=-\omega n}=\frac{2}{\omega n} $$ (The notes write the derivative in quotient-rule form $-2s\omega n^2/s^4$; it simplifies to $-2\omega n^2/s^3$.) $$ y(t)=t-\frac{2}{\omega n}+t\,e^{-\omega nt}+\frac{2}{\omega n}e^{-\omega nt} $$ Checks. $y(0)=-\frac2{\omega n}+\frac2{\omega n}=0$ ✓. $\dot y=1-\omega nte^{-\omega nt}+e^{-\omega nt}-2e^{-\omega nt}=1-e^{-\omega nt}-\omega nte^{-\omega nt}$ — the critical step response ✓ (the ramp is the integral of the step). With $\xi=1$, $\frac{2}{\omega n}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ ✓. In $K 2$ the notes write the squared denominator as $(s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n)^2$; the last term must be $\omega n^2$: $(s^2+2\omega ns+\omega n^2)^2$. With the correct denominator the value at $s=0$ is $\omega n^4$ and $K 2=-2\omega n^3/\omega n^4=-2/\omega n$, exactly the professor's result.

title: Ramp: underdamped
text: $$ Y(s)=\frac{K 1}{s^2}+\frac{K 2}{s}+\frac{K 3}{s+p 1}+\frac{K 3^ }{s+p 2},\qquad p 1=\alpha+j\omega,\ p 2=\alpha-j\omega $$ $K 1=1$, $K 2=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ as for every case. For $K 3$ the polar form of the root is the cleanest route. From the [geometry of the roots]( /m/07/geometry-of-the-complex-roots), $-\alpha-j\omega=-\omega n(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=-\omega ne^{j\theta}$, so $s^2=\omega n^2e^{j2\theta}$ at that root, and $s+p 2=-2j\omega$ there: $$ K 3=\left.\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2(s+\alpha-j\omega)}\right {s=-\alpha-j\omega}=\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega n^2e^{j2\theta}\,(-2j\omega)}=\frac{e^{-j2\theta}}{-2j\omega}=\frac{j\,e^{-j2\theta}}{2\omega}=\frac{\sin2\theta+j\cos2\theta}{2\omega} $$ (using $\frac{1}{-j}=j$ and $je^{-j2\theta}=j\cos2\theta+\sin2\theta$). Conjugate-pair rule with $a=\frac{\sin2\theta}{2\omega}$, $b=\frac{\cos2\theta}{2\omega}$: $$ 2e^{-\alpha t}\left(\frac{\sin2\theta}{2\omega}\cos\omega t+\frac{\cos2\theta}{2\omega}\sin\omega t\right)=\frac1\omega e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta) $$ (sine addition formula $\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$). $$ y(t)=t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac{1}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta),\qquad \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi} $$ The notes define $\theta$ on p. 14 exactly as in the step response. The notes give $y(t)=t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac1\omega e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+\theta)$. With $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}$ (as defined on p. 14) the phase must be $2\theta$. The quickest test is $y(0)=0$ (the output cannot jump): - with $2\theta$: $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\xi\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$, so $y(0)=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac{2\xi\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=0$ ✓; - with $\theta$: $y(0)=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{1-2\xi}{\omega n}$, which is non-zero unless $\xi=0.5$ ✗. A numerical solution of the ODE confirms the $2\theta$ version (see [Example 2]( /m/07/ramp-response-of-example-2), where the phase becomes $132.84^\circ$ instead of $66.42^\circ$). The amplitude $\frac{1}{\omega}$ and the offset $-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ in the notes are correct.

title: Why the phase is 2 theta
text: There is a pattern across the three inputs. Each extra $\frac1s$ in $R(s)$ multiplies the complex coefficient by $\frac1s$ evaluated at the pole, $\frac{1}{-\omega ne^{j\theta}}$ — i.e. it rotates the phase by $\theta$ (and divides the size by $\omega n$): Input $R(s)$ Oscillating part of $y(t)$ --- --- --- impulse $1$ $\dfrac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t)$ — phase $0$ step $\dfrac1s$ $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+\theta)$ — phase $\theta$ ramp $\dfrac{1}{s^2}$ $+\dfrac{1}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta)$ — phase $2\theta$ The same thing seen in the time domain: the ramp response is the integral of the step response. Differentiating $e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+\varphi)$ gives $e^{-\alpha t}(\omega\cos(\cdot)-\alpha\sin(\cdot))=\omega ne^{-\alpha t}\big(\sin\theta\cos(\cdot)-\cos\theta\sin(\cdot)\big)=-\omega ne^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+\varphi-\theta)$. So $$ \frac{d}{dt}\left[-\frac{1}{\omega n}e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta)\right]=e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+\theta) $$ and integrating the step response from 0 to $t$: $$ \int 0^t\left[1-\frac{e^{-\alpha\tau}\sin(\omega\tau+\theta)}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\right]d\tau=t-\frac{\sin2\theta-e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta)}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac1\omega e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta) $$ (using $\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=\omega$ and $\frac{\sin2\theta}{\omega}=\frac{2\xi\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$). Each integration adds $\theta$ to the phase: impulse $0$ → step $\theta$ → ramp $2\theta$.

title: Ramp response family
text: The notes' figure: the dashed ramp $r(t)$ and the outputs for $\xi=2,1,0.25$, all starting at the origin with zero slope and ending as straight lines parallel to $r(t)$. Exact functions ($\omega n=1$): - $\xi=0.25$: $y=t-0.5+1.033e^{-0.25t}\sin(0.968t+151.0^\circ)$ — closest to the ramp, with a visible wobble. - $\xi=1$: $y=t-2+te^{-t}+2e^{-t}$. - $\xi=2$: $y=t-4+0.289\,(13.93e^{-0.268t}-0.0718e^{-3.732t})$ — the largest lag. How to sketch by hand: draw $r(t)=t$ dashed and the asymptote $t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ parallel to it. The output starts at the origin tangent to the $t$-axis ($y\approx\omega n^2t^3/6$), bends up and joins the asymptote; for small $\xi$ it overshoots the asymptote slightly and wobbles around it with period $2\pi/\omega$.

title: Steady-state error for the ramp
text: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}\cdot\frac{1}{s^2}\right)=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s^2+2\xi\omega ns}{s(s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2)}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+2\xi\omega n}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n} $$ $$ e {ss,\text{ramp}}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n} $$ This is the constant gap between $r(t)=t$ and the asymptote $t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$ — it agrees with the time-domain result. More damping → more lag; a faster system (larger $\omega n$) → less lag. That is why the $\xi=2$ line in the figure lies furthest below $r(t)$. impulse $e {ss}=0$ · step $e {ss}=0$ · ramp $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n$. These hold for $T(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}$, i.e. for the loop of p. 1 with its integrator. For any other loop, compute $\lim {s\to0}s[R-Y]$ again (Example 2 gives 0, 0.2, ∞).

title: Interactive explorer
text: Slide $\xi$ and $\omega n$. The s-plane, the case name, the formulas in use, the read-outs and all three responses update together. Things to try: (1) start at $\xi=0.4$ and raise it to 1 — the poles slide along the circle of radius $\omega n$ onto the real axis and the overshoot disappears; (2) go above 1 — the poles split along the real axis, and the step becomes sluggish; (3) set $\xi=0$ — the poles sit on the $j\omega$ axis and the oscillation never dies; (4) double $\omega n$ at fixed $\xi$ — the shapes stay the same, the time axis shrinks by 2 and the ramp lag halves.

title: Example 2: impulse, step and ramp responses

title: Example 2: a complete problem
text: Given: unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+5}$. Asked: the (and, as the notes go on to do, the steady-state error for each). Method: closed loop → write $T(s)$ as (DC gain) × (standard form) → read $\omega n,\xi$ → use the underdamped formulas multiplied by the DC gain → $e {ss}$ from the final value theorem. $$ T(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+5}}{1+\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+5}}=\frac{20}{s^2+4s+25}=\frac{0.8\cdot(5)^2}{s^2+2\cdot0.4\cdot5\,s+(5)^2} $$ Matching: $\omega n^2=25\Rightarrow\omega n=5$; $2\xi\omega n=4\Rightarrow\xi=0.4$; numerator $20=0.8\cdot25$, so the DC gain is $T(0)=20/25=0.8$. $\xi<1$: underdamped (düşük sönümlü). $$ s {1,2}=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-100}}{2}=-2\pm j\frac{\sqrt{84}}{2}=-2\pm j4.58 $$ so $\alpha=\xi\omega n=2$, $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=5\sqrt{0.84}=4.583$ rad/s, $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{0.84}}{0.4}=66.42^\circ=1.159$ rad. Every response is $0.8\times$ the standard one. $$ y(t)=0.8\cdot\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t=0.8\cdot\frac{5}{\sqrt{0.84}}e^{-2t}\sin4.58t=4.364\,e^{-2t}\sin4.58t $$ Direct check: $\frac{20}{(s+2)^2+21}\to\frac{20}{\sqrt{21}}e^{-2t}\sin\sqrt{21}t$ and $20/\sqrt{21}=4.364$ ✓. Steady-state error : $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(1-\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+25}\right)=0$. $Y(s)=\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+25}\cdot\dfrac1s$ : $$ y(t)=0.8\left[1-e^{-2t}\left(\cos4.58t+\frac{0.4}{\sqrt{0.84}}\sin4.58t\right)\right]=0.8\left[1-e^{-2t}\left(\cos4.58t+0.436\sin4.58t\right)\right] $$ Equivalent amplitude-phase form: $y(t)=0.8-0.873\,e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+66.42^\circ)$ (since $0.8/\sqrt{0.84}=0.873$). Steady-state error (the $s$ factors cancel, as struck through in the notes): $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{20}{s^2+4s+25}\cdot\frac1s\right)=\left.\frac{s^2+4s+25-20}{s^2+4s+25}\right {s=0}=\frac{5}{25}=0.2 $$ $Y(s)=\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+25}\cdot\dfrac{1}{s^2}$ . With the corrected phase $2\theta=132.84^\circ$ : $$ y(t)=0.8\left(t-\frac{2\cdot0.4}{5}+\frac{1}{4.58}e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+2\theta)\right)=0.8t-0.128+0.1746\,e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+132.84^\circ) $$ ($0.8\cdot0.16=0.128$, $0.8/4.583=0.1746$.) Check: $y(0)=-0.128+0.1746\sin132.84^\circ=-0.128+0.128=0$ ✓. Steady-state error: $$ e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{20}{s^2+4s+25}\cdot\frac{1}{s^2}\right)=\left.\frac{s^2+4s+25-20}{s(s^2+4s+25)}\right {s\to0}=\frac{5}{0}=\infty $$ $\omega n=5$, $\xi=0.4$, DC gain $0.8$, roots $-2\pm j4.58$ (underdamped). - Impulse: $y(t)=4.364\,e^{-2t}\sin4.58t$, $e {ss}=0$. - Step: $y(t)=0.8\left[1-e^{-2t}(\cos4.58t+0.436\sin4.58t)\right]$, $e {ss}=0.2$. - Ramp: $y(t)=0.8t-0.128+0.1746\,e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+132.84^\circ)$, $e {ss}=\infty$. Interpretation. The impulse response is a damped sine dying out in about $4/\alpha=2$ s. The step response peaks at $t=\pi/\omega=0.686$ s with $y=0.8(1+e^{-2\pi/4.583})=0.8\cdot1.254=1.003$ — right at the level 1 the professor marks in his sketch — and settles at 0.8, leaving an error of 0.2. For the ramp the output grows with slope 0.8 while the input grows with slope 1, so the gap $t-y\approx0.2t+0.128$ grows forever.

title: Impulse response of Example 2
text: The first peak is where $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-2t}\sin\omega t)=0$, i.e. $\tan\omega t=\omega/\alpha=\tan\theta$, so $t=\theta/\omega=1.159/4.583=0.253$ s, $y=2.41$. Then a small negative lobe and a tiny ripple, as in the sketch .

title: Step response of Example 2
text: As in the notes' sketch : dashed lines at 1 and 0.8, the curve peaks at about 1 and settles at 0.8.

title: Ramp response of Example 2
text: The sketch on p. 17 shows exactly this: $y(t)$ wobbles briefly, then grows as a line of smaller slope (0.8) than $r(t)$, so the two lines diverge — $e {ss}=\infty$. The notes write $y(t)=0.8t-0.128+0.174\,e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+66.42^\circ)$, inheriting the phase slip of p. 13. Correct: $y(t)=0.8t-0.128+0.1746\,e^{-2t}\sin(4.58t+132.84^\circ)$. The plot above compares both with a numerical solution of $\ddot y+4\dot y+25y=20t$ (zero initial conditions): the ODE gives $y(0.1)=0.00299$, $y(0.5)=0.2081$, $y(1)=0.6857$; the $132.84^\circ$ form reproduces these exactly, while the $66.42^\circ$ form gives $0.0948$, $0.2525$, $0.6598$ and even $y(0)=0.032\ne0$. Also, $0.8/4.583=0.1746$ rounds to $0.175$ (the notes truncate it to 0,174). The values $0.128$ and $\theta=66.42^\circ$ themselves are computed correctly. $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n$ was derived for the loop of p. 1, whose forward path $\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}$ contains an integrator . In Example 2 the forward path $\frac{20}{s^2+4s+5}$ has none (it is "type 0"), so the closed loop's DC gain is 0.8, not 1: it cannot even hold a constant (step error 0.2), let alone follow a ramp (error ∞). Always compute $e {ss}$ from $\lim {s\to0}s[R(s)-Y(s)]$ for the actual system instead of blindly reusing $2\xi/\omega n$.

title: Overdamped system with xi = 1.25 and omega_n = 4
Underdamped system with xi = 0.6 and omega_n = 5
Reading parameters when the DC gain is not 1
From the open-loop G(s) to T(s) and the ramp error
Additional worked examples
text: Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{16}{s^2+10s+16}$. Asked: case, roots, impulse/step/ramp responses, ramp $e {ss}$. $\omega n^2=16\Rightarrow\omega n=4$; $2\xi\omega n=10\Rightarrow\xi=1.25 1$: overdamped. $\sqrt{\xi^2-1}=\sqrt{0.5625}=0.75$, so $p {1,2}=\xi\omega n\mp\omega n\cdot0.75=5\mp3$: $p 1=2$, $p 2=8$. Indeed $s^2+10s+16=(s+2)(s+8)$, $p 1p 2=16=\omega n^2$ ✓. $K 1=\left.\frac{16}{s+8}\right {s=-2}=\frac{16}{6}=\frac83$, $K 2=\left.\frac{16}{s+2}\right {s=-8}=-\frac83$: $$ y(t)=\frac83\left(e^{-2t}-e^{-8t}\right) $$ $Y=\frac{16}{s(s+2)(s+8)}$: $K 1=\frac{16}{16}=1$, $K 2=\frac{16}{(-2)(6)}=-\frac43$, $K 3=\frac{16}{(-8)(-6)}=\frac13$: $$ y(t)=1-\frac43e^{-2t}+\frac13e^{-8t} $$ Formula check: $\frac{p 2}{p 2-p 1}=\frac86=\frac43$, $\frac{p 1}{p 2-p 1}=\frac26=\frac13$ ✓; $y(0)=1-\frac43+\frac13=0$ ✓. $Y=\frac{16}{s^2(s+2)(s+8)}$: $K 1=1$, $K 2=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=-\frac{2.5}{4}=-0.625$ (directly: $\frac{d}{ds}\frac{16}{s^2+10s+16}\big 0=-\frac{16\cdot10}{256}=-0.625$ ✓), $K 3=\frac{16}{(-2)^2(6)}=\frac23$, $K 4=\frac{16}{(-8)^2(-6)}=-\frac1{24}$: $$ y(t)=t-0.625+\frac23e^{-2t}-\frac1{24}e^{-8t} $$ $y(0)=-0.625+0.6667-0.0417=0$ ✓. Overdamped, roots $-2$, $-8$. Impulse $\frac83(e^{-2t}-e^{-8t})$; step $1-\frac43e^{-2t}+\frac13e^{-8t}$; ramp $t-0.625+\frac23e^{-2t}-\frac1{24}e^{-8t}$; $e {ss,\text{ramp}}=0.625$. The slow root $-2$ dominates: by $t=1$ s the $e^{-8t}$ term is already $0.0003$, while $e^{-2t}=0.135$. Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{9}{s^2+6s+9}$. Asked: all three responses. $\omega n=3$, $2\xi\cdot3=6\Rightarrow\xi=1$: critically damped, $T=\frac{9}{(s+3)^2}$, double root $-3$. $y(t)=9te^{-3t}$, peak at $t=1/3$ s of height $3/e=1.10$. $Y=\frac{9}{s(s+3)^2}$: $K 1=1$; $K 3=\left.\frac9s\right {-3}=-3$; $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\frac9s\right {-3}=\left.-\frac{9}{s^2}\right {-3}=-1$: $$ y(t)=1-e^{-3t}-3te^{-3t} $$ $Y=\frac{9}{s^2(s+3)^2}$: $K 1=1$; $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\frac{9}{(s+3)^2}\right 0=\left.\frac{-18}{(s+3)^3}\right 0=-\frac23$; $K 3=\left.\frac{9}{s^2}\right {-3}=1$; $K 4=\left.\frac{-18}{s^3}\right {-3}=\frac{2}{3}$: $$ y(t)=t-\frac23+te^{-3t}+\frac23e^{-3t} $$ Impulse $9te^{-3t}$; step $1-e^{-3t}-3te^{-3t}$; ramp $t-\frac23+te^{-3t}+\frac23e^{-3t}$; $e {ss}$: 0, 0, $\frac23$ (= $2\xi/\omega n$ with $\xi=1$). Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{25}{s^2+6s+25}$. Asked: all three responses, computing the complex coefficients explicitly (to see the $2\theta$ appear with numbers). $\omega n=5$, $\xi=6/10=0.6$, $\alpha=3$, $\omega=5\sqrt{0.64}=4$, roots $-3\pm j4$. $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{0.8}{0.6}=53.13^\circ$. $y(t)=\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t=\frac{5}{0.8}e^{-3t}\sin4t=6.25\,e^{-3t}\sin4t$. $K 1=1$. At $s=-3-j4$: $s+3-j4=-8j$, and $$ K 2=\frac{25}{(-3-j4)(-8j)}=\frac{25}{24j+32j^2}=\frac{25}{-32+24j}=\frac{25(-32-24j)}{32^2+24^2}=\frac{-32-24j}{64}=-0.5-0.375j $$ Conjugate-pair rule: $2e^{-3t}(-0.5\cos4t-0.375\sin4t)$, so $$ y(t)=1-e^{-3t}(\cos4t+0.75\sin4t)=1-1.25\,e^{-3t}\sin(4t+53.13^\circ) $$ ($\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=0.75$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=1.25$ ✓.) $K 1=1$, $K 2=-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=-0.24$. At $s=-3-j4$: $s^2=9+24j-16=-7+24j$, so $$ K 3=\frac{25}{(-7+24j)(-8j)}=\frac{25}{192+56j}=\frac{25(192-56j)}{192^2+56^2}=\frac{192-56j}{1600}=0.12-0.035j $$ The pair gives $2e^{-3t}(0.12\cos4t-0.035\sin4t)=e^{-3t}(0.24\cos4t-0.07\sin4t)$. Amplitude $\sqrt{0.24^2+0.07^2}=0.25=\frac1\omega$ ✓. Phase: $\sin\varphi=\frac{0.24}{0.25}=0.96$, $\cos\varphi=\frac{-0.07}{0.25}=-0.28$ — a second-quadrant angle, $\varphi=106.26^\circ=2\cdot53.13^\circ=2\theta$ ✓. $$ y(t)=t-0.24+0.25\,e^{-3t}\sin(4t+106.26^\circ) $$ Impulse $6.25e^{-3t}\sin4t$; step $1-1.25e^{-3t}\sin(4t+53.13^\circ)$; ramp $t-0.24+0.25e^{-3t}\sin(4t+106.26^\circ)$; $e {ss}$: 0, 0, 0.24. The phase came out as $106.26^\circ$, not $53.13^\circ$, straight from the arithmetic: the numbers themselves confirm the $2\theta$ correction. Note also that $\cos\varphi<0$: a plain $\tan^{-1}(0.96/-0.28)$ on a calculator would give $-73.74^\circ$ — always check the quadrant from the signs of sine and cosine. Given: $T(s)=\dfrac{18}{s^2+3s+9}$. Asked: $\omega n$, $\xi$, DC gain, step response and its steady-state error. The denominator fixes $\omega n^2=9$, $\omega n=3$, $2\xi\omega n=3\Rightarrow\xi=0.5$. Write the numerator as gain × $\omega n^2$: $18=2\cdot9$, so $T=2\cdot\frac{9}{s^2+3s+9}$, DC gain $K=T(0)=2$. Do not use the numerator to find $\omega n$ — $\omega n$ always comes from the constant term of the denominator. $\alpha=1.5$, $\omega=3\sqrt{0.75}=2.598$, $\theta=60^\circ$, $\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=0.577$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=1.155$: $$ y(t)=2\left[1-e^{-1.5t}(\cos2.598t+0.577\sin2.598t)\right]=2-2.309\,e^{-1.5t}\sin(2.598t+60^\circ) $$ $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s\left(\frac1s-\frac{18}{s(s^2+3s+9)}\right)=1-\frac{18}{9}=-1$. The output settles at 2 while the reference is 1: the error is negative (output above reference). $\omega n=3$, $\xi=0.5$, $K=2$; $y(t)=2-2.309e^{-1.5t}\sin(2.598t+60^\circ)$; $e {ss}=-1$. Sanity check: $y(0)=2-2.309\sin60^\circ=2-2.000=0$ ✓. Given: unity negative feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{16}{s(s+4)}$. Asked: $T(s)$, $\omega n$, $\xi$, the ramp response and its steady-state error. $T=\dfrac{G}{1+G}=\dfrac{16}{s(s+4)+16}=\dfrac{16}{s^2+4s+16}$. This is exactly the standard form (numerator $=\omega n^2$): $\omega n=4$, $2\xi\cdot4=4\Rightarrow\xi=0.5$. Compare with the p. 1 loop: $\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}=\frac{16}{s(s+4)}$ ✓. In general $G=\frac{K}{s(s+a)}$ gives $\omega n=\sqrt K$, $\xi=\frac{a}{2\sqrt K}$. $\alpha=2$, $\omega=4\sqrt{0.75}=3.464$, $\theta=60^\circ$, $2\theta=120^\circ$, $\frac1\omega=0.2887$, $\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=0.25$: $$ y(t)=t-0.25+0.2887\,e^{-2t}\sin(3.464t+120^\circ) $$ $y(0)=-0.25+0.2887\cdot0.866=0$ ✓. $T(s)=\frac{16}{s^2+4s+16}$, $\omega n=4$, $\xi=0.5$; $y(t)=t-0.25+0.2887e^{-2t}\sin(3.464t+120^\circ)$; $e {ss,\text{ramp}}=0.25$. Because this loop contains the integrator, the step error is 0 and the ramp error is finite — unlike Example 2. Using the system $G(s)=\frac{20}{s^2+4s+5}$ with unity feedback, here is what four typical slips produce, evaluated at $t=0.5$ s for the ramp (true value from the ODE: $y(0.5)=0.2081$). The roots of $s^2+4s+5$ are $-2\pm j1$, which would suggest $\omega n=\sqrt5=2.236$ and $\xi=\frac{4}{2\sqrt5}=0.894$. Wrong system! The response is governed by the closed-loop denominator $s^2+4s+25$: $\omega n=5$, $\xi=0.4$. The feedback changed the poles. Writing $y(t)=1-e^{-2t}(\cos4.58t+0.436\sin4.58t)$ (standard form) predicts a final value 1 and $e {ss}=0$. The true final value is 0.8 and $e {ss}=0.2$. Always factor the numerator as $K\omega n^2$. $0.8\cdot0.5-0.128+0.1746e^{-1}\sin(2.291\,\text{rad}+66.42^\circ)$: with $66.42^\circ=1.159$ rad, $\sin(3.450)=-0.304$, giving $y(0.5)=0.272-0.0195=0.2525$ instead of $0.2081$. Quick detector: $y(0)=0.032\ne0$. Correct: $4.583\cdot0.5=2.291$ rad, $2\theta=132.84^\circ=2.318$ rad, $\sin(4.610)=-0.9949$, so $y(0.5)=0.272+0.1746\cdot0.3679\cdot(-0.9949)=0.272-0.0639=0.2081$ ✓. If instead you type $\sin(2.291+132.84)$ in radian mode you get $\sin(135.13\,\text{rad})=-0.043$ and $y(0.5)=0.269$ — wrong. Only closed-loop poles + DC gain 0.8 + phase $2\theta$ + consistent units give $y(0.5)=0.2081$, matching the ODE.

title: Undamped limit
text: With $\xi=0$: $\alpha=0$, $\omega=\omega n$, $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{0}=90^\circ$, roots $\pm j\omega n$ on the imaginary axis. The underdamped formulas (valid as a limit) give $$ \text{impulse: }y=\omega n\sin\omega nt,\qquad\text{step: }y=1-\sin(\omega nt+90^\circ)=1-\cos\omega nt,\qquad\text{ramp: }y=t-0+\frac{1}{\omega n}\sin(\omega nt+180^\circ)=t-\frac{\sin\omega nt}{\omega n} $$ The oscillation never decays (an ideal LC circuit, a frictionless spring): the step response swings between 0 and 2 forever, and "steady state" does not exist — the final value theorem does not apply because $Y(s)$ has poles on the imaginary axis. Here $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n=0$ would be wrong to quote: the ramp error $\frac{\sin\omega nt}{\omega n}$ oscillates forever.

title: Approaching critical damping
text: As $\xi\to1^-$: $\omega\to0$, $\alpha\to\omega n$. Since $\frac{\sin\omega t}{\omega}\to t$ for $\omega\to0$, $$ \frac{\omega n^2}{\omega}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t\ \longrightarrow\ \omega n^2te^{-\omega nt} $$ — the underdamped impulse response turns smoothly into the critical one. Likewise $\cos\omega t\to1$ and $\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t=\xi\omega n\frac{\sin\omega t}{\omega}\to\omega nt$, so the step tends to $1-e^{-\omega nt}(1+\omega nt)$ ✓. From above ($\xi\to1^+$), $p 1,p 2\to\omega n$ and $\frac{e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t}}{p 2-p 1}\to te^{-\omega nt}$ (a derivative quotient). The formulas change shape at $\xi=1$ only because the partial-fraction structure changes (two different roots → one repeated root); the physical response itself changes continuously. That is why the critical case needs the derivative formula.

title: Non-unity DC gain and non-standard loops
Non-unity DC gain and non-standard loops
text: If $T(s)=\dfrac{b}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}$ with $b\ne\omega n^2$, write $T=K\cdot\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}$ with $K=b/\omega n^2$ and multiply every response by $K$ (Examples 1 and 2). The steady-state errors change: step $e {ss}=1-K$, ramp $e {ss}=\infty$ unless $K=1$.

title: Summary of results
text: Standard form $T(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}$; $p {1,2}=\xi\omega n\mp\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1}$; $\alpha=\xi\omega n$; $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$; $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}$. Overdamped $\xi 1$ Critical $\xi=1$ Underdamped $0<\xi<1$ $e {ss}$ --- --- --- --- --- Impulse $\frac{\omega n^2}{p 2-p 1}(e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t})$ $\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}$ $\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t$ $0$ Step $1-\frac{p 2e^{-p 1t}-p 1e^{-p 2t}}{p 2-p 1}$ $1-e^{-\omega nt}-\omega nte^{-\omega nt}$ $1-\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin(\omega t+\theta)$ $0$ Ramp $t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac{1}{p 2-p 1}\left(\frac{p 2}{p 1}e^{-p 1t}-\frac{p 1}{p 2}e^{-p 2t}\right)$ $t-\frac2{\omega n}+te^{-\omega nt}+\frac2{\omega n}e^{-\omega nt}$ $t-\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}+\frac1\omega e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\omega t+2\theta)$ $\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}$

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. Get the closed loop. If a loop is drawn, $T=\frac{G}{1+GH}$ (unity: $\frac{G}{1+G}$). Clear fractions so the denominator is $s^2+as+b$ (divide by the leading coefficient if needed). 2. Read the parameters. $\omega n=\sqrt b$, $\xi=\frac{a}{2\omega n}$, DC gain $K=\frac{\text{numerator}}{\omega n^2}$. 3. Classify. $\xi 1$ aşırı sönümlü, $\xi=1$ kritik sönümlü, $\xi<1$ düşük sönümlü. Compute the roots ($p 1,p 2$ or $\alpha,\omega,\theta$). 4. Form $Y(s)=T(s)R(s)$ with $R=1$, $\frac1s$ or $\frac1{s^2}$. 5. Partial fractions: cover-up for simple roots, derivative rule for repeated roots (and for $\frac1{s^2}$), one complex coefficient $K$ for the conjugate pair. 6. Invert and simplify; for complex roots use the conjugate-pair rule, then (if asked) the amplitude-phase form — step phase $\theta$, ramp phase $2\theta$. 7. Multiply by $K$ if the DC gain is not 1. 8. Verify: $y(0)=0$ for step and ramp; $\dot y(0)=0$ for the step; $y(\infty)$ from the final value theorem; derivative of step = impulse. 9. Steady-state error: $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}s[R(s)-Y(s)]$ for the actual system. - Taking $\omega n$, $\xi$ from the open-loop $G(s)$ instead of the closed-loop $T(s)$. - Forgetting the DC gain factor (Example 2's 0.8). - Writing $\theta$ instead of $2\theta$ in the underdamped ramp response (the notes do this too). - Mixing degrees and radians inside $\sin(\omega t+\theta)$. - Writing the critical root as $+\omega n$ (sign slip, as on p. 5) — poles of a stable system have negative real parts. - Forgetting the derivative term for a repeated root or for the double pole at $s=0$ of a ramp input. - Quoting $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n$ for a loop without an integrator. - Sketching a step response that leaves the origin with a slope. "Türünü ve parametrelerini bulunuz" → steps 1–3 only. "Birim impulse / basamak / rampa cevaplarını bulunuz" → steps 1–8 for each input. "Kalıcı durum hatası" → step 9. If the numbers are "nice" (e.g. roots $-3\pm j4$), computing $K$ numerically, as in the $\xi=0.6$ example, is often faster and less error-prone than plugging into the general formulas.
