Practice exercises
text: For $T(s)=\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}$, give the Turkish and English names of the three cases, the condition on $\xi$, the type of roots, and what the step response looks like in each. From $s {1,2}=-\xi\omega n\pm\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1}$: - $\xi 1$: aşırı sönümlü (overdamped): real, distinct roots $-p 1,-p 2$; slow monotonic rise, no overshoot. - $\xi=1$: kritik sönümlü (critically damped): real repeated root $-\omega n$; fastest rise without overshoot. - $0<\xi<1$: düşük sönümlü (underdamped): complex-conjugate roots $-\alpha\pm j\omega$; overshoot and decaying oscillation around 1. Check: the sign of $\xi^2-1$ decides whether the square root is real, zero or imaginary. A unity negative feedback loop has $G(s)=\dfrac{36}{s(s+6)}$. Find $T(s)$, $\omega n$, $\xi$, the roots and the type. $T=\frac{36}{s(s+6)+36}=\frac{36}{s^2+6s+36}$. $\omega n=6$, $2\xi\cdot6=6\Rightarrow\xi=0.5$: underdamped. $\alpha=3$, $\omega=6\sqrt{0.75}=5.196$, roots $-3\pm j5.196$. Check: $(s+3)^2+27=s^2+6s+36$ ✓; $ s 1 =\sqrt{9+27}=6=\omega n$ ✓. Since it matches $\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}$, the step error is 0 and the ramp error $2\xi/\omega n=1/6$. Find the unit step response of $T(s)=\dfrac{9}{s^2+10s+9}$. Factor the denominator; check $\xi 1$ first. $\omega n=3$, $\xi=\frac{10}{6}=1.667 1$: overdamped. $s^2+10s+9=(s+1)(s+9)$, so $p 1=1$, $p 2=9$ (check: $\xi\omega n\mp\omega n\sqrt{\xi^2-1}=5\mp3\cdot\frac43=5\mp4$ ✓). $Y=\frac{9}{s(s+1)(s+9)}$: $K 1=\frac99=1$, $K 2=\frac{9}{(-1)(8)}=-\frac98$, $K 3=\frac{9}{(-9)(-8)}=\frac18$. $$ y(t)=1-\frac98e^{-t}+\frac18e^{-9t} $$ Verification: $y(0)=1-1.125+0.125=0$ ✓; $\dot y(0)=\frac98-\frac98=0$ ✓; $y(\infty)=1$ ✓. For the same $T(s)=\dfrac{9}{s^2+10s+9}$, find the unit impulse response and the time of its peak. $K 1=\frac{9}{-1+9}=\frac98$, $K 2=-\frac98$: $y(t)=\frac98(e^{-t}-e^{-9t})$ (this is the derivative of the previous step response ✓). Peak: $\dot y=\frac98(-e^{-t}+9e^{-9t})=0\Rightarrow e^{8t}=9\Rightarrow t=\frac{\ln9}{8}=0.275$ s, $y=\frac98(0.760-0.084)=0.760$. For $T(s)=\dfrac{16}{(s+4)^2}$ find the unit step and unit ramp responses and the ramp steady-state error. $\omega n=4$, $\xi=1$. Using the critical formulas (derived with $K 1=1$, $K 3=-\omega n$, $K 2=-1$ for the step and $K 1=1$, $K 2=-2/\omega n$, $K 3=1$, $K 4=2/\omega n$ for the ramp): $$ y {\text{step}}=1-e^{-4t}-4te^{-4t},\qquad y {\text{ramp}}=t-0.5+te^{-4t}+0.5e^{-4t} $$ $e {ss,\text{ramp}}=\frac{2}{\omega n}=0.5$. Verification: $y {\text{ramp}}(0)=-0.5+0.5=0$ ✓, $\frac{d}{dt}y {\text{ramp}}=1+e^{-4t}-4te^{-4t}-2e^{-4t}=y {\text{step}}$ ✓. $\xi=0.6$, $\omega n=10$ rad/s. Write $T(s)$, the unit impulse response, and the unit step response in both forms. $T=\frac{100}{s^2+12s+100}$. $\alpha=6$, $\omega=10\cdot0.8=8$, $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{0.8}{0.6}=53.13^\circ$. Impulse: $\frac{10}{0.8}e^{-6t}\sin8t=12.5e^{-6t}\sin8t$. Step: $y=1-e^{-6t}(\cos8t+0.75\sin8t)=1-1.25e^{-6t}\sin(8t+53.13^\circ)$. Check $y(0)$: $1-1.25\cdot0.8=0$ ✓. For Example 1 ($T=\frac{2}{s^2+2s+4}$, p. 3), find the unit impulse and unit step responses and the step steady-state error. The DC gain is $2/4=0.5$. $T=0.5\cdot\frac{4}{s^2+2s+4}$, $\omega n=2$, $\xi=0.5$, $\alpha=1$, $\omega=\sqrt3$, $\theta=60^\circ$. Impulse: $0.5\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{0.75}}e^{-t}\sin\sqrt3t=1.155e^{-t}\sin1.732t$ (direct: $\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+3}\to\frac{2}{\sqrt3}e^{-t}\sin\sqrt3t$ ✓). Step: $y=0.5\left[1-e^{-t}\left(\cos\sqrt3t+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\sin\sqrt3t\right)\right]=0.5-0.577e^{-t}\sin(1.732t+60^\circ)$. $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}\left(1-\frac{2}{s^2+2s+4}\right)=1-0.5=0.5$. Check $y(0)=0.5-0.577\cdot0.866=0$ ✓. For Example 2, $y(t)=4.364e^{-2t}\sin4.58t$. Find when the impulse response reaches its first maximum and its value. Show that in general this happens at $t=\theta/\omega$. $\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t\right)=e^{-\alpha t}(\omega\cos\omega t-\alpha\sin\omega t)=0\Rightarrow\tan\omega t=\frac\omega\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}=\tan\theta$, so the first maximum is at $\omega t=\theta$, $t=\theta/\omega$. Example 2: $\theta=1.159$ rad, $t=1.159/4.583=0.253$ s, $y=4.364\,e^{-0.506}\sin(1.159)=4.364\cdot0.603\cdot0.917=2.41$. Three unit step responses with the same $\omega n$ are shown: curve A overshoots to about 1.44, curve B rises monotonically and reaches 0.96 at $\omega nt=5$, curve C rises monotonically but is still at about 0.7 at $\omega nt=5$. Assign $\xi=0.25,\ 1,\ 2$ and explain. A: $\xi=0.25$ (only underdamped systems overshoot; $1+e^{-\pi\cdot0.25/0.968}=1.44$). B: $\xi=1$ ($1-6e^{-5}=0.96$). C: $\xi=2$ ($1-1.077e^{-0.268\cdot5}+0.077e^{-18.7}=0.72$). More damping → slower, no overshoot — compare the figure on p. 10. Let $\xi=0$, $\omega n=2$. Using the underdamped formulas as a limit, find the impulse, step and ramp responses. Does the system have a steady-state error for the step? $\alpha=0$, $\omega=2$, $\theta=90^\circ$. Impulse: $\frac{2}{1}\sin2t=2\sin2t$. Step: $1-\sin(2t+90^\circ)=1-\cos2t$. Ramp: $t-0+\frac12\sin(2t+180^\circ)=t-\frac12\sin2t$. Check by Laplace: $\frac{4}{s(s^2+4)}=\frac1s-\frac{s}{s^2+4}\to1-\cos2t$ ✓. The step response oscillates between 0 and 2 forever: no steady state exists; the final value theorem cannot be used because the poles $\pm j2$ are on the imaginary axis. Explain, in two different ways, why every unit step response of the standard second-order system has $\dot y(0^+)=0$, and why the sketch on p. 10 needs correcting. (1) $\dot y {\text{step}}=y {\text{impulse}}$, and all impulse responses start at 0 ($\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}$, $e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t$, $e^{-p 1t}-e^{-p 2t}$ vanish at $t=0$). (2) IVT: $\dot y(0^+)=\lim {s\to\infty}s\cdot sY(s)=\lim {s\to\infty}\frac{s\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega ns+\omega n^2}=0$. Physically a force step changes acceleration, not velocity, instantly. The sketch draws the $\xi=1$ and $\xi=2$ curves leaving the origin with a slope; they should start tangent to the $t$-axis. Unity feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{25}{s(s+5)}$. Find the steady-state error to a unit ramp. $T=\frac{25}{s^2+5s+25}$: $\omega n=5$, $\xi=0.5$. $e {ss}=\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2$. Check from the definition: $e {ss}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{1-T}{s}=\lim {s\to0}\frac{s+5}{s^2+5s+25}=\frac{5}{25}=0.2$ ✓. A system of the standard form must have $\omega n=10$ rad/s and a ramp steady-state error of 0.1. Find $\xi$, the case, and the open-loop $G(s)$ of the p. 1 loop. $\frac{2\xi}{10}=0.1\Rightarrow\xi=0.5$: underdamped. $G=\frac{\omega n^2}{s(s+2\xi\omega n)}=\frac{100}{s(s+10)}$, $T=\frac{100}{s^2+10s+100}$. Check: $e {ss}=\lim\frac{s+10}{s^2+10s+100}=0.1$ ✓. Write the unit ramp response for $\xi=0.5$, $\omega n=2$ and verify $y(0)=0$. $\alpha=1$, $\omega=\sqrt3=1.732$, $\theta=60^\circ$, $2\theta=120^\circ$, $\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=0.5$: $$ y(t)=t-0.5+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3t+120^\circ) $$ $y(0)=-0.5+0.5774\cdot0.866=-0.5+0.5=0$ ✓. A student writes the ramp response for $\xi=0.6$, $\omega n=5$ as $y=t-0.24+0.25e^{-3t}\sin(4t+53.13^\circ)$. Show that it is wrong without solving anything, and correct it. For which single value of $\xi$ would the student's version accidentally satisfy $y(0)=0$? $y(0)=-0.24+0.25\cdot\sin53.13^\circ=-0.24+0.2=-0.04\ne0$ — impossible, the output must start at 0. Correct: $\sin(4t+106.26^\circ)$, giving $-0.24+0.25\cdot0.96=0$ ✓. In general the $\theta$ version gives $y(0)=\frac{1-2\xi}{\omega n}$, which is 0 only for $\xi=0.5$ — the one case where the slip goes unnoticed. The closed-loop poles of a standard second-order system are $-3\pm j4$. Find $\omega n$, $\xi$, $\theta$ and $T(s)$. $\omega n= {-3+j4} =5$, $\xi=\cos\theta=\frac{\alpha}{\omega n}=\frac35=0.6$, $\theta=53.13^\circ$. $T=\frac{25}{(s+3)^2+16}=\frac{25}{s^2+6s+25}$. Find $y(t)$ for $Y(s)=\dfrac{4}{s(s+2)^2}$ using the professor's coefficient formulas. $Y=\frac{K 1}{s}+\frac{K 2}{s+2}+\frac{K 3}{(s+2)^2}$. $K 1=\frac{4}{4}=1$; $K 3=\left.\frac4s\right {-2}=-2$; $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\frac4s\right {-2}=\left.-\frac4{s^2}\right {-2}=-1$. $y(t)=1-e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t}$ — the critical step response with $\omega n=2$. Recombine: $\frac{(s+2)^2-s(s+2)-2s}{s(s+2)^2}=\frac{4}{s(s+2)^2}$ ✓. Unity feedback around $G(s)=\dfrac{10}{s^2+6s+6}$. Find $T(s)$, $\omega n$, $\xi$, DC gain, the unit step response, and the steady-state errors for step and ramp inputs. $T=\frac{10}{s^2+6s+16}$: $\omega n=4$, $\xi=\frac{6}{8}=0.75$ (underdamped), $K=\frac{10}{16}=0.625$. $\alpha=3$, $\omega=4\sqrt{1-0.5625}=2.646=\sqrt7$, $\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=1.134$. $$ y(t)=0.625\left[1-e^{-3t}(\cos2.646t+1.134\sin2.646t)\right] $$ $e {ss,\text{step}}=1-0.625=0.375$. Ramp: $\lim {s\to0}\frac{1-T(s)}{s}=\frac{0.375}{0}=\infty$. (No integrator in $G$, as in Example 2.) Find the unit ramp response of $T(s)=\dfrac{9}{s^2+10s+9}$ and check it against $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n$. $p 1=1$, $p 2=9$, $\xi=5/3$, $\omega n=3$. $Y=\frac{9}{s^2(s+1)(s+9)}$: $K 1=1$; $K 2=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\frac{9}{s^2+10s+9}\right 0=-\frac{90}{81}=-\frac{10}{9}$; $K 3=\frac{9}{(1)(8)}=\frac98$; $K 4=\frac{9}{(81)(-8)}=-\frac1{72}$. $$ y(t)=t-\frac{10}{9}+\frac98e^{-t}-\frac1{72}e^{-9t} $$ $y(0)=-1.1111+1.125-0.0139=0$ ✓. $\frac{2\xi}{\omega n}=\frac{10/3}{3}=\frac{10}{9}$ ✓. For the standard system, what happens to the ramp steady-state error if (a) $\xi$ is doubled, (b) $\omega n$ is doubled? Relate this to the p. 14 figure. $e {ss}=2\xi/\omega n$: (a) doubles, (b) halves. In the p. 14 figure ($\omega n$ fixed) the $\xi=2$ line lies furthest below $r(t)$ and $\xi=0.25$ closest. Trade-off: low $\xi$ gives small ramp lag but large oscillation. A unit step applied to a standard second-order system gives $y(t)=1-e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t}$. Find $\xi$, $\omega n$, $T(s)$ and the impulse response. The form $1-e^{-\omega nt}-\omega nte^{-\omega nt}$ is the critically damped step: $\xi=1$, $\omega n=2$, $T=\frac{4}{(s+2)^2}$. Impulse = derivative: $\dot y=2e^{-2t}-2e^{-2t}+4te^{-2t}=4te^{-2t}=\omega n^2te^{-\omega nt}$ ✓. A system's unit impulse response is $y(t)=10e^{-3t}\sin4t$. Find $\omega n$, $\xi$, its DC gain and $T(s)$. $\alpha=3$, $\omega=4\Rightarrow\omega n=\sqrt{9+16}=5$, $\xi=3/5=0.6$. The standard impulse amplitude is $\frac{\omega n^2}{\omega}=\frac{25}{4}=6.25$, so the DC gain is $K=\frac{10}{6.25}=1.6$ and $T=1.6\cdot\frac{25}{s^2+6s+25}=\frac{40}{s^2+6s+25}$. Check: $\L\{10e^{-3t}\sin4t\}=\frac{10\cdot4}{(s+3)^2+16}=\frac{40}{s^2+6s+25}$ ✓. Using the fact that the derivative of the step response is the impulse response, find the time and the value of the first peak of the step response of Example 2, and compare with the professor's sketch. $\dot y=4.364e^{-2t}\sin4.583t=0$ first at $4.583t=\pi$, $t=0.686$ s. There $\cos=-1$, $\sin=0$: $y=0.8[1-e^{-2\cdot0.686}(-1)]=0.8(1+e^{-1.371})=0.8(1+0.254)=1.003$. The sketch on p. 16 shows the peak touching the dashed line at 1 — consistent.

title: Mathematical definition of the control criteria
What is this about?
text: Real systems are rarely exactly first or second order. A DC motor driving a load through a gearbox, a room heated by a radiator whose water must warm up first, an aircraft pitch loop with an actuator — when you write the transfer function honestly, the denominator has three, four or more roots. Solving those exactly is possible (partial fractions, exactly as before), but an engineer wants something faster: a way to look at the poles and immediately predict how the response will look — how fast it rises, how much it overshoots, how long it takes to settle. This module gives you exactly that, in two halves: 1. (pp. 1–4). In a every pole contributes its own exponential term with its own . Poles far to the left die out almost immediately; the poles closest to the $j\omega$ axis decay slowest and therefore dominate what you see. So a complicated system often behaves like a simple first- or second-order one. We also see what a zero does to the response. 2. (pp. 5–10). In [Module 02]( /m/02) you met rise time, peak time, overshoot and settling time as words on a sketch. In [Module 07]( /m/07) you derived the underdamped second-order step response. Here we combine the two: we derive formulas that compute $t r$, $t p$, $m$ and $t s$ directly from $\xi$ and $\omega n$. Think of a step response as a choir: each pole sings one exponential "voice". A pole at $s=-10$ sings loudly for a tenth of a second and then falls silent; a pole at $s=-1$ keeps singing for several seconds. If you record the choir after the first half second, you essentially only hear the slow voice. That slow voice is the dominant pole . If the dominant poles are a complex pair, the "song" is the familiar damped oscillation of a second-order system — and then the formulas of the second half of this module tell you its rise time, peak, overshoot and settling time without plotting anything. After this module you can: - split a higher-order step response into one term per pole, give each term its time constant $\tau=1/\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert$, and judge stability from the sign of the real parts; - identify the dominant poles and decide whether a second-order approximation is trustworthy; - explain (and compute) why a zero close to the dominant poles increases overshoot and speeds up the rise; - derive and use $t r=\dfrac{\pi-\cos^{-1}\xi}{\omega}$, $t p=\dfrac{\pi}{\omega}$, $m=e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$, $t s=\dfrac{4}{\xi\omega n}$ (2 %) or $\dfrac{3}{\xi\omega n}$ (5 %); - solve the professor's type of exam problem: given a unity-feedback loop, find all transient parameters and sketch the response — and also run the formulas backwards (from specifications to $\xi,\omega n$).

title: Higher-order systems
text: The page title is Yüksek Dereceden Kontrol Sistemleri — higher-order control systems. The professor's key statement: A system whose transfer function has many denominator roots (poles) — payda kökü yani kutup sayısı fazladır . When it is split into , each fraction is solved with the first- and second-order methods you already know, and the sum of these independent solutions gives the general solution ( bağımsız çözümlerin toplamı genel çözümü verir ). So nothing new is needed to solve a higher-order system. For a step input $R(s)=1/s$ and distinct poles $p 1,\dots,p n$: $$ Y(s)=T(s)\,\frac1s=\frac{A 0}{s}+\frac{A 1}{s-p 1}+\frac{A 2}{s-p 2}+\dots+\frac{A n}{s-p n} $$ and with $\Li\left\{\dfrac{1}{s-p}\right\}=e^{pt}$: $$ y(t)=\underbrace{A 0} {\text{steady state}}+\underbrace{A 1e^{p 1t}+A 2e^{p 2t}+\dots+A ne^{p nt}} {\text{one transient term per pole}} $$ A complex-conjugate pair $p=-\alpha\pm j\omega$ gives one combined term $e^{-\alpha t}(B\cos\omega t+C\sin\omega t)$ — the second-order solution of [Module 07]( /m/07).

title: Each pole has its own time constant
Each pole has its own time constant
text: A real pole at $s=p=-a$ (with $a 0$) produces the term $A\,e^{-at}=A\,e^{-t/\tau}$ with $$ \tau=\frac1a=\frac{1}{\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert}. $$ For a complex pair $-\alpha\pm j\omega$ the oscillation is wrapped in the envelope $e^{-\alpha t}$, so the time constant of the pair is $\tau=1/\alpha$, again $1/\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert$. The imaginary part sets how fast it oscillates ; only the real part sets how fast it dies out . The professor's three observations : Pole location Time constant What its term does --- --- --- Real part far left (towards $-\infty$) small $\tau$ dies out quickly ( daha çabuk sönümlenir ) Real part negative but close to $0$ large $\tau$ dies out slowly, long decay time ( sönüm süresi uzun ) Real part positive — ($e^{+at}$ grows) unstable output ( kararsız çıkış ) The notes say about poles whose real part is near 0: "zaman sabiti düşük olacağından sönüm süresi uzun olacaktır" ("since the time constant is low , the decay time is long"). This is a slip: a pole near the origin has a large time constant, $\tau=1/\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert$ (e.g. $p=-0.1$ gives $\tau=10$ s). The sentence should read "zaman sabiti yüksek olacağından sönüm süresi uzun olacaktır" . The conclusion (long decay) is correct.

title: Stability from the sign of the real part
Stability from the sign of the real part
text: Each term behaves like $e^{(\operatorname{Re}p)\,t}$ in magnitude: - $\operatorname{Re}p<0$: the term decays to zero — it is a transient . - $\operatorname{Re}p 0$: the term grows without bound — the output is unstable, however small its coefficient $A$ is. - $\operatorname{Re}p=0$ (on the $j\omega$ axis): the term neither grows nor decays (a constant or a sustained oscillation). So the whole system is stable only if every pole is in the left half-plane. One bad pole is enough to ruin everything, because a growing exponential eventually beats every decaying one.

title: Dominant poles
text: Bu durumda, genel çözümde sağ tarafta kalan kutuptan gelen bileşenin etkisi daha baskın olacaktır — the component coming from the pole furthest to the right (closest to the $j\omega$ axis, among the stable poles) is the most dominant in the general solution. The pole (or complex pair) of a stable system that lies closest to the imaginary axis. Its term has the largest time constant, so after the fast terms have died out, the response is essentially that term alone. $T(s)=\dfrac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\dfrac{10}{(s+10)(s+1)}$. Find the unit step response, the term contributed by each pole and its time constant, and compare the two terms at $t=0.5$ s. The denominator roots are $s 1=-1$ and $s 2=-10$. Both are negative → stable. $$ Y(s)=\frac{10}{s(s+1)(s+10)}=\frac{A 0}{s}+\frac{A 1}{s+1}+\frac{A 2}{s+10} $$ Cover-up rule (multiply by the factor and set $s$ to its root): $$ A 0=\left.\frac{10}{(s+1)(s+10)}\right {s=0}=\frac{10}{10}=1,\qquad A 1=\left.\frac{10}{s(s+10)}\right {s=-1}=\frac{10}{(-1)(9)}=-\frac{10}{9}, $$ $$ A 2=\left.\frac{10}{s(s+1)}\right {s=-10}=\frac{10}{(-10)(-9)}=\frac{1}{9}. $$ $$ y(t)=1-\frac{10}{9}e^{-t}+\frac19e^{-10t} $$ Check: $y(0)=1-\frac{10}{9}+\frac19=0$ ✓ (a step into a strictly proper system starts at zero); $y(\infty)=1=T(0)$ ✓ (final value theorem). From $s 1=-1$: $-\frac{10}{9}e^{-t}$, time constant $\tau 1=1$ s. From $s 2=-10$: $\frac19e^{-10t}$, time constant $\tau 2=0.1$ s. $e^{-0.5}=0.6065$ while $e^{-10\cdot0.5}=e^{-5}=0.00674$. Including the coefficients: $\frac{10}{9}(0.6065)=0.6739$ versus $\frac19(0.00674)=0.00075$. The slow term is about 900 times bigger. Half a second after the step, the far pole has practically vanished. $y(t)=1-\frac{10}{9}e^{-t}+\frac19e^{-10t}$. The pole $s 1=-1$ ($\tau=1$) is dominant; the term of $s 2=-10$ ($\tau=0.1$) decays ten times faster and starts with a coefficient ten times smaller, so the system behaves essentially like $\dfrac{1}{s+1}$. Two small slips on page 2: - The notes write "$e^{10t}=0{,}00674$". The minus sign is missing: the value $0.00674$ is $e^{-10t}$ at $t=0.5$, i.e. $e^{-5}$. ($e^{+5}$ would be $148.4$.) - The notes say "zaman sabiti yüksek olan $s 2$ kökü" ("the root $s 2$ with the high time constant"). But $s 2=-10$ has the small time constant $\tau 2=0.1$, as the notes themselves state two lines earlier. The intended meaning is "the root $s 2$ with the large magnitude" (or "with the small time constant"): its term decays fast and contributes little to the total response. How to read the second graph: the thick curve is the exact $y(t)$. The pink dashed curve keeps only the dominant term ($1-\frac{10}{9}e^{-t}$): it is wrong only during the first ~0.3 s (it even starts at $-0.11$, because we threw away the $+\frac19$ that made $y(0)=0$), and after that it lies on top of the exact curve — at $t=0.5$ the two differ by $0.00075$. The blue dashed curve is the reduced model $\frac{1}{s+1}$ obtained by deleting the far pole and keeping the DC gain ($\frac{10}{(s+10)(s+1)}\approx\frac{10}{10(s+1)}$); it reaches the right final value and has the right shape, but runs slightly ahead (maximum error $0.077$), because the deleted pole really did add a small delay of about $\tau 2=0.1$ s. Both are "dominant-pole approximations"; the second is the one you use to predict specifications.

title: Why far poles have small coefficients
Why far poles have small coefficients
text: The professor adds a second reason why far poles matter little: when computing the partial-fraction numerator coefficients for far-away roots, the absolute value of the denominator turns out large, so the coefficient is small — especially when the denominator degree is high. Look at the cover-up computation of $A 2$ above: we evaluate the other factors at $s=-10$, getting $(-10)(-9)=90$, a big number in the denominator, so $A 2=10/90$ is small. For the near pole we evaluate at $s=-1$, getting $(-1)(9)=-9$, a smaller number, so $\lvert A 1\rvert=10/9$ is large. In general, for $Y(s)=\dfrac{K}{s\prod(s-p i)}$: $$ A k=\frac{K}{p k\prod {i\neq k}(p k-p i)} $$ A far pole $p k$ is far from every other pole and from the origin, so each factor in the denominator is large; the more poles there are, the more large factors multiply together. A far pole is therefore doubly weak: small coefficient and fast decay . A fast pole is like a very quick follower: it reaches its own little equilibrium almost instantly, so the slow part of the system "sees" it as a plain gain. That is exactly why replacing $\frac{10}{s+10}$ by its DC value $1$ gives a good model.

title: How to decide whether a pole is dominant
Third-order system with a far pole
section: How to decide whether a pole is dominant

title: When the extra pole is not far enough
section: How to decide whether a pole is dominant

title: How to decide whether a pole is dominant
text: The notes give the principle (closest to the $j\omega$ axis dominates) and the numerical illustration $e^{-0.5}$ versus $e^{-5}$ — a pole ten times further left has a term that is $e^{-4.5}\approx1/90$ as large after half a time constant of the slow pole, and also a smaller coefficient. A practical rule of thumb used by engineers, consistent with that comparison: If the other poles have real parts at least about 5 times further from the $j\omega$ axis than the dominant pole(s), and there is no zero near the dominant poles, the response can be predicted from the dominant poles alone (keeping the correct DC gain). With a ratio of 5, when the dominant term has fallen to $e^{-1}$, the far term has fallen to $e^{-5}\approx0.007$ of its initial value. The closer the ratio is to 1, the worse the approximation. Try it — the interactive below keeps the second-order system of pages 3–4, $\frac{25}{s^2+6s+25}$ (poles $-3\pm j4$, $\xi=0.6$, $\omega n=5$), and adds a real pole at $s=-p$ with the DC gain kept at 1. Watch the full response approach the dashed second-order curve as $p$ grows, and watch the far pole's coefficient shrink. $T(s)=\dfrac{400}{(s+20)(s^2+4s+20)}$. Is a second-order approximation justified? If so, predict $\%m$, $t p$ and $t s$ (2 %). $s^2+4s+20=0\Rightarrow s=-2\pm j4$; the third pole is $s=-20$. DC gain $T(0)=\frac{400}{20\cdot20}=1$. Real parts: $-2$ (pair) and $-20$. Ratio $20/2=10\ge5$ → the pair $-2\pm j4$ is dominant. Coefficient of the far pole in the step response (cover-up): $$ A=\left.\frac{400}{s(s^2+4s+20)}\right {s=-20}=\frac{400}{(-20)(400-80+20)}=\frac{400}{-6800}=-0.0588 $$ Small, and it decays with $\tau=0.05$ s. Keep the DC gain: $T(s)\approx\dfrac{20}{s^2+4s+20}$. Then $\omega n^2=20\Rightarrow\omega n=4.472$, $2\xi\omega n=4\Rightarrow\xi=\frac{2}{4.472}=0.4472$, $\alpha=2$, $\omega=4$. $$ \%m=100\,e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=100\,e^{-0.4472\pi/0.8944}=100\,e^{-\pi/2}=20.79\,\% $$ $t p=\pi/\omega=\pi/4=0.785$ s, $t s=4/(\xi\omega n)=4/2=2$ s. Dominant pair $-2\pm j4$; predicted $\%m\approx20.8\,\%$, $t p\approx0.79$ s, $t s\approx2$ s. (A numerical evaluation of the exact third-order response gives $\%m=20.2\,\%$, $t p=0.84$ s, $t s=1.92$ s — the approximation is good; the far pole just adds a small delay.) $T(s)=\dfrac{60}{(s+3)(s^2+4s+20)}$, again DC gain $\frac{60}{3\cdot20}=1$, pair $-2\pm j4$, but now the real pole is at $-3$. Ratio of real parts $3/2=1.5$ — far below 5. The real pole's step-response coefficient: $$ A=\left.\frac{60}{s(s^2+4s+20)}\right {s=-3}=\frac{60}{(-3)(9-12+20)}=\frac{60}{-51}=-1.176 $$ This is not small — it is as large as the steady-state value itself. The second-order formulas would predict $20.8\,\%$ overshoot at $t p=0.785$ s, but the true response overshoots only about $4.1\,\%$, at $t\approx1.19$ s. The slow real pole drags the whole response down: the approximation is not valid. Lesson: "closest to the $j\omega$ axis" tells you which poles dominate, but you also need enough separation for the other poles to be negligible.

title: Effect of a system zero
text: Sistem Sıfırının Etkisi — the effect of the system zero. Poles decide which exponentials appear; zeros (roots of the numerator) decide how much of each appears. The professor shows this with one second-order system and two zero positions.

title: A zero at -25 and at -5 added to 25/(s^2+6s+25)
The three step responses
text: $T(s)=\dfrac{25}{s^2+6s+25}$: $\omega n^2=25\Rightarrow\omega n=5$, $2\xi\omega n=6\Rightarrow\xi=0.6$, poles $s=-3\pm j4$. Compare its unit step response with the responses after adding a zero at $s=-25$ and at $s=-5$, the latter "without affecting the steady-state gain" ( kalıcı durum kazancını etkilemeyecek şekilde ). $$ Y(s)=\frac{25}{s^2+6s+25}\cdot\frac1s=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{s^2+6s+25} $$ $A=\left.\frac{25}{s^2+6s+25}\right {s=0}=1$. Multiply out: $25=(s^2+6s+25)+(Bs+C)s$. Comparing $s^2$: $0=1+B\Rightarrow B=-1$. Comparing $s$: $0=6+C\Rightarrow C=-6$. Complete the square, $s^2+6s+25=(s+3)^2+4^2$: $$ Y(s)=\frac1s-\frac{s+6}{(s+3)^2+4^2}=\frac1s-\frac{(s+3)}{(s+3)^2+4^2}-\frac34\cdot\frac{4}{(s+3)^2+4^2} $$ Using $\Li\left\{\frac{s+a}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}\right\}=e^{-at}\cos\omega t$ and $\Li\left\{\frac{\omega}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}\right\}=e^{-at}\sin\omega t$: $$ y(t)=1-0.75\,e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t $$ This is the general formula $1-e^{-\alpha t}\left[\cos\omega t+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t\right]$ with $\alpha=3$, $\omega=4$, $\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75$. $T 1(s)=\dfrac{s+25}{s^2+6s+25}$ (DC gain $25/25=1$). $Y 1=\dfrac{s+25}{s(s^2+6s+25)}$, $A=1$, and $s+25=(s^2+6s+25)+(Bs+C)s$ gives $B=-1$, $6+C=1\Rightarrow C=-5$: $$ Y 1(s)=\frac1s-\frac{(s+3)+2}{(s+3)^2+4^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad y 1(t)=1-0.5\,e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t $$ $T 2(s)=\dfrac{5(s+5)}{s^2+6s+25}$; the factor 5 makes $T 2(0)=\frac{25}{25}=1$. $5s+25=(s^2+6s+25)+(Bs+C)s$ gives $B=-1$, $6+C=5\Rightarrow C=-1$: $$ Y 2(s)=\frac1s-\frac{(s+3)-2}{(s+3)^2+4^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad y 2(t)=1+0.5\,e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t $$ All three start at $y(0)=1-0-1=0$ and end at $1$ ✓. Peak values (numerically): $y$: $1.095$ at $0.785$ s ($9.48\,\%$); $y 1$: $1.097$ at $0.740$ s ($9.70\,\%$); $y 2$: $1.195$ at $0.509$ s ($19.4\,\%$). $y(t)=1-0.75e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t$, $y 1(t)=1-0.5e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t$, $y 2(t)=1+0.5e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t$. The far zero ($-25$) changes almost nothing; the zero at $-5$, close to the dominant poles ($\lvert-3\pm j4\rvert=5$), nearly doubles the overshoot and makes the response much faster. The notes give $y(t)=1-\mathbf{0{,}6}\,e^{-3t}\sin(4t)-e^{-3t}\cos(4t)$. The correct coefficient is $0.75$: - From the partial fractions above: $\frac{s+6}{(s+3)^2+16}$ splits as $(s+3)+3$, and $3=\frac34\cdot4$, so the sine coefficient is $\frac34$. - From the general formula: the coefficient is $\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75$. The value $0.6$ is $\xi$ itself — most likely the $\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$ was forgotten. - Independent check: a step response of a system with no zeros must start with zero slope ($\dot y(0)=\lim s\cdot sY(s)=\lim\frac{25s}{s^2+6s+25}\cdot\frac{s}{s}\to0$). Differentiating $1-c\,e^{-3t}\sin4t-e^{-3t}\cos4t$ at $t=0$ gives $-4c+3$, which is zero only for $c=0.75$. - Consistency with the notes' own $y 1$: below we show $y 1=y+\frac{1}{25}\dot y$; that gives $-0.75+0.25=-0.5$, exactly the $0.5$ the notes have for $y 1$. With $0.6$ it would not work. The graph reproduces the professor's figure with the exact functions. All three curves start at the origin and settle at 1. $y 2$ (zero at $-5$) rises first and has the highest peak; $y 1$ (zero at $-25$) is barely distinguishable from $y$; $y$ (no zero) is the slowest with the smallest overshoot. The professor's conclusion: a zero far from the dominant poles has a small, negligible effect; as zeros approach the dominant poles their effect on the response becomes larger ( baskın kutuplara yaklaştıkça sıfırların sistem cevabı üzerindeki etkisi daha yüksek olmaktadır ).

title: Why a nearby zero increases overshoot
Zero at -10 with the same poles
section: Why a nearby zero increases overshoot

title: Why a nearby zero increases overshoot
text: Write the zero so that the DC gain stays 1: $T z(s)=\dfrac{s+z}{z}\,T(s)$, zero at $s=-z$. Then $$ T z(s)=T(s)+\frac1z\,s\,T(s)\quad\Rightarrow\quad Y z(s)=Y(s)+\frac1z\,sY(s). $$ Multiplying by $s$ in the Laplace domain is differentiation in time (because $y(0)=0$, $\L\{\dot y\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)$). Therefore $$ y z(t)=y(t)+\frac1z\,\frac{dy}{dt}. $$ For our system $\dot y(t)$ is the impulse response $\Li\left\{\frac{25}{(s+3)^2+4^2}\right\}=\frac{25}{4}e^{-3t}\sin4t=6.25\,e^{-3t}\sin4t$. So - $z=25$: $y 1=y+0.25\,e^{-3t}\sin4t$ → coefficient $-0.75+0.25=-0.5$ ✓; - $z=5$: $y 2=y+1.25\,e^{-3t}\sin4t$ → coefficient $-0.75+1.25=+0.5$ ✓. Physical meaning: a zero adds a bit of the derivative of the response to the response. While $y$ is rising, $\dot y 0$, so the added term pushes the output up → faster rise and higher peak . The size of the push is $1/z$: a far zero (large $z$) adds almost nothing, a zero near the poles adds a lot. (A zero closer than the poles' natural frequency, like $z=5=\omega n$ here, already doubles the overshoot.) $T(s)=\dfrac{2.5(s+10)}{s^2+6s+25}$ (DC gain $\frac{25}{25}=1$). Find $y(t)$ and compare its overshoot with the zero-free system. $z=10$: $y z=y+\frac{1}{10}\cdot6.25e^{-3t}\sin4t$, so the sine coefficient is $-0.75+0.625=-0.125$: $$ y z(t)=1-e^{-3t}\cos4t-0.125\,e^{-3t}\sin4t $$ $2.5s+25=(s^2+6s+25)+(Bs+C)s$: $B=-1$, $6+C=2.5\Rightarrow C=-3.5$. Remainder $-\frac{s+3.5}{(s+3)^2+16}=-\frac{(s+3)+0.5}{(s+3)^2+16}$, and $0.5=0.125\cdot4$ ✓. $y z(t)=1-e^{-3t}\cos4t-0.125e^{-3t}\sin4t$. Numerically the peak is $1.113$ at $t=0.656$ s ($11.3\,\%$), versus $9.48\,\%$ at $0.785$ s without the zero: between the far-zero case ($-25$) and the near-zero case ($-5$), as expected.

title: Mathematical definition of the control criteria
text: İkinci dereceden düşük sönümlü bir sistemin cevabı genel sistem tepkesine ait tüm kriterlerin gösterimini barındırmaktadır — the response of a second-order underdamped ( düşük sönümlü ) system displays all the criteria of a general system response. That is why we derive the criteria on it — and thanks to the dominant-pole idea, these formulas also predict higher-order systems with a dominant complex pair.

title: The underdamped response
text: From [Module 07]( /m/07), for $T(s)=\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2}$ with $0<\xi<1$ and a unit step: $$ y(t)=1-e^{-\alpha t}\left[\cos\omega t+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t\right],\qquad \alpha=\xi\omega n,\quad \omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2} $$ - $\xi$ — damping ratio; $\omega n$ — natural frequency (rad/s); - $\alpha=\xi\omega n$ — decay rate = minus the real part of the poles; $1/\alpha$ is the time constant of the envelope; - $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$ — damped frequency = imaginary part of the poles $s=-\alpha\pm j\omega$; - $\theta$ — the angle between the pole ray and the negative real axis: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\alpha}{\omega n}=\xi$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\omega}{\alpha}=\dfrac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}$. A compact form that we will use to check every result: since $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$ and $\cos\theta=\xi$, $$ \cos\omega t+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t=\frac{\sin\theta\cos\omega t+\cos\theta\sin\omega t}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{\sin(\omega t+\theta)}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}} $$ (identity $\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B$), so $$ y(t)=1-\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin(\omega t+\theta). $$ The professor's general graph: the curve starts at 0 with zero slope, crosses the final value $y {ss}=1$ at $t r$, peaks at $t p$ (the blue arrow $m$ is the overshoot above 1), dips below 1, rises again with a smaller second overshoot and stays inside a tolerance band from $t s$ onwards. The graph above is the exact response for $\xi=0.4$, $\omega n=1$ with the ±2 % band shaded. Kriterlere ilişkin matematiksel tanımları sırasıyla inceleyelim — let us go through the criteria one by one.

title: Rise time
text: $t r$: the time at which the underdamped response first reaches its final value, $y(t r)=1$ (0→100 % rise time). Derivation . Set $y(t r)=1$: $$ 1-e^{-\alpha t r}\left[\cos\omega t r+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t r\right]=1 \;\Rightarrow\; e^{-\alpha t r}\left[\cos\omega t r+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t r\right]=0. $$ An exponential is never zero ($e^{-\alpha t r}\neq0$), so the bracket must vanish: $$ \cos\omega t r+\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin\omega t r=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\sin\omega t r}{\cos\omega t r}=\tan\omega t r=-\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}=-\frac{\omega}{\alpha} $$ (the last step: multiply numerator and denominator by $\omega n$). Hence $$ t r=\frac1\omega\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{\omega}{\alpha}\right). $$ Choosing the right branch — the important subtlety. $\tan$ repeats every $\pi$, so $\tan\omega t r=-\omega/\alpha$ has infinitely many solutions. Which one is the rise time? - For $0<\omega t<\pi/2$ both $\cos$ and $\sin$ are positive, so the bracket is positive and cannot be zero. - The bracket can vanish only where $\cos\omega t r<0$ and $\sin\omega t r 0$: the second quadrant , $\pi/2<\omega t r<\pi$. That is the first crossing. - A calculator's $\tan^{-1}$ returns values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$; for the negative argument $-\omega/\alpha$ it returns $-\theta$, a negative angle — giving a negative "time". Adding $\pi$ (the period of $\tan$) moves it into the second quadrant: $$ \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{\omega}{\alpha}\right)=\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega}{\alpha}\right)=\pi-\cos^{-1}\xi, $$ because $\tan^{-1}(\omega/\alpha)=\theta$ and $\cos\theta=\xi$. Geometrically, $\pi-\theta$ is the angle of the pole $-\alpha+j\omega$ measured from the positive real axis — the notes call it the angle of the conjugate root ( eşlenik diğer kökün açısı ) . $$ t r=\frac{\pi-\cos^{-1}\xi}{\omega}=\frac{\pi-\theta}{\omega}\qquad(\theta\ \text{in radians}) $$ Cross-check with the compact form: $y=1$ ⇔ $\sin(\omega t+\theta)=0$ ⇔ $\omega t+\theta=\pi$ (first time after $t=0$, since $\omega t+\theta$ starts at $\theta\in(0,\pi/2)$) ⇔ $t r=(\pi-\theta)/\omega$ ✓. What it tells you: a larger $\omega$ (poles higher up) means a faster rise; a smaller $\xi$ means a larger $\theta$ and therefore a smaller numerator $\pi-\theta$, so lightly damped systems rise faster — and pay for it with overshoot.

title: Peak time
text: $t p$: the time of the first (largest) maximum of $y(t)$. Derivation . At a maximum the derivative is zero ( türevini sıfıra eşitlemeliyiz ). Differentiate with the product rule, $\frac{d}{dt}\left[e^{-\alpha t}f(t)\right]=e^{-\alpha t}\left(f'(t)-\alpha f(t)\right)$, with $k=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$ and $f=\cos\omega t+k\sin\omega t$: $$ \frac{dy}{dt}=e^{-\alpha t}\left(\alpha\cos\omega t+\omega\sin\omega t+k\alpha\sin\omega t-k\omega\cos\omega t\right) $$ Set it to zero at $t=t p$. Now use $k\omega=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\,\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=\xi\omega n=\alpha$, i.e. $\alpha=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\omega$: the two cosine terms cancel ($\alpha\cos-\alpha\cos=0$). The sine terms combine: $$ \omega+k\alpha=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}+\frac{\xi^2\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{\omega n\left[(1-\xi^2)+\xi^2\right]}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}} $$ so $$ \frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{\omega n}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\,e^{-\alpha t}\sin\omega t=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\sin\omega t p=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\omega t p=0,\pi,2\pi,3\pi,\dots $$ $\omega t=0$ is the flat start (not a peak); the first value after 0 is $\pi$: $$ t p=\frac{\pi}{\omega}=\frac{\pi}{\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}} $$ The derivative is written with the factor $e^{\alpha t p}$. It should be $e^{-\alpha t p}$ (the exponential in $y$ is $e^{-\alpha t}$). The bracket is correct and the result is unaffected, because either exponential is non-zero and drops out when the expression is set to zero. Also, the relation written as "$\alpha=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\omega$" has an extra stroke in the handwriting; it is an equality, as shown above. Two useful facts hidden in this derivation: - $\dot y(t)$ is the impulse response of $T(s)$ (because $\L\{\dot y\}=sY(s)=T(s)$). The step response peaks exactly where the impulse response crosses zero. - Odd multiples $\omega t=\pi,3\pi,\dots$ are maxima, even multiples $2\pi,4\pi,\dots$ are minima: the oscillation's half-period is exactly $\pi/\omega$.

title: Maximum overshoot
text: The overshoot is computed as a ratio ( oransal olarak hesaplanır ) relative to the final value: $$ m=\frac{y(t p)-y(\infty)}{y(\infty)}\qquad\text{or}\qquad \%m=\frac{y(t p)-y(\infty)}{y(\infty)}\times100. $$ Derivation . Substitute $\omega t p=\pi$ into $y(t)$: $\cos\pi=-1$, $\sin\pi=0$: $$ y(t p)=1-e^{-\alpha t p}\left[-1+0\right]=1+e^{-\xi\omega n(\pi/\omega)}. $$ With $y(\infty)=1$: $$ m=\frac{y(t p)-1}{1}=e^{-\xi\omega n\pi/\omega},\qquad\text{and since}\ \frac{\omega n}{\omega}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}: $$ $$ m=e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}},\qquad \%m=100\,e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}} $$ The notes write $y(t p)=1-e^{-\xi\omega n(\pi/\omega)}$. The sign must be plus : at $\omega t p=\pi$ the bracket equals $\cos\pi=-1$, and $1-e^{-\alpha t p}\cdot(-1)=1+e^{-\alpha t p}$. A peak is above the final value, so it must be $1+$ something positive. The next line of the notes, $m=+e^{-\xi\omega n(\pi/\omega)}$, is only consistent with the plus sign — the final formula for $m$ is correct. What it tells you: $m$ depends only on $\xi$ — not on $\omega n$. Speeding a system up (larger $\omega n$) with the same damping leaves the overshoot unchanged. Some values: $\xi=0.2\to52.7\,\%$, $\xi=0.4\to25.4\,\%$, $\xi=0.6\to9.48\,\%$, $\xi=0.7\to4.6\,\%$, $\xi=0.8\to1.5\,\%$. If the system has DC gain $K\neq1$ ($T(s)=K\frac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2}$), the whole response is multiplied by $K$, so $y(\infty)=K$ and $y(t p)=K(1+m)$ — the ratio $m$ is the same.

title: Settling time
text: $t s$: the time after which the response stays within a tolerance band ( tolerans aralığı ) around its final value. The notes take $t s\approx4\tau$ (sometimes $5\tau$) for a 2 % band, and $3\tau$ for a 5 % band, where $\tau=1/(\xi\omega n)$. Where it comes from. From the compact form, the deviation from the final value is $$ y(t)-1=-\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\sin(\omega t+\theta),\qquad \lvert y(t)-1\rvert\le\frac{e^{-\xi\omega n t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}. $$ The oscillation lives inside the envelope $1\pm\frac{e^{-\xi\omega n t}}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$, a first-order decay with time constant $\tau=\frac{1}{\xi\omega n}=\frac1\alpha$ — the time constant of the real part of the poles, exactly as in the first section. The notes' rule uses the simplified envelope $e^{-\xi\omega n t}$ (dropping $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$): - 2 % band: $e^{-\xi\omega n t s}=0.02\Rightarrow\xi\omega n t s=\ln50=3.91\approx4$; - 5 % band: $e^{-\xi\omega n t s}=0.05\Rightarrow\xi\omega n t s=\ln20=3.00\approx3$. $$ t s=4\tau=\frac{4}{\xi\omega n}\ \ (\pm2\,\%),\qquad t s=3\tau=\frac{3}{\xi\omega n}\ \ (\pm5\,\%) $$ $t s=4/(\xi\omega n)$ is an estimate based on the envelope, not the exact last crossing of the band. The true curve touches the envelope only at isolated instants, so it can enter the band for good a bit earlier (or, for larger $\xi$ where $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$ matters, slightly later). For the worked example below the formula gives $0.667$ s while the exact curve settles in the 2 % band at $0.594$ s. Exams use the formula.

title: Interactive criteria explorer
text: Move $\xi$ and $\omega n$ and watch the formulas act on the curve. Things to try: keep $\xi=0.6$ and change $\omega n$ — $m$ stays at $9.48\,\%$ while all times scale as $1/\omega n$. Keep $\omega n$ fixed and lower $\xi$ — the pole ray swings towards the $j\omega$ axis ($\theta$ grows), overshoot grows, rise gets faster, settling gets slower. Switch the band between 2 % and 5 %.

title: Summary of the criteria
text: Criterion Turkish Formula Depends on --- --- --- --- Rise time Yükselme süresi $t r=\dfrac{\pi-\cos^{-1}\xi}{\omega}$ $\xi$ and $\omega$ Peak time Tepe zamanı $t p=\dfrac{\pi}{\omega}$ imaginary part $\omega$ only Max. overshoot Maksimum aşma $m=e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$ $\xi$ only Settling time Yerleşme süresi $t s=\dfrac{4}{\xi\omega n}$ (2 %), $\dfrac{3}{\xi\omega n}$ (5 %) real part $\alpha$ only Reading it with the s-plane: poles higher (larger $\omega$) → shorter $t p$, $t r$; poles further left (larger $\alpha$) → shorter $t s$; ray closer to the real axis (smaller $\theta$, larger $\xi$) → smaller overshoot.

title: Transient parameters of G = 70/(s^2+12s+30) with unity feedback
Worked example: unity feedback
text: Şekildeki sistemin birim basamak tepkesinin geçici durum parametrelerini bulunuz — find the transient-state parameters ( geçici durum parametreleri ) of the unit step response of the system in the figure. Unity negative feedback: $T(s)=\dfrac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}$. Multiply numerator and denominator by $s^2+12s+30$: $$ T(s)=\frac{70}{s^2+12s+30+70}=\frac{70}{s^2+12s+100} $$ $$ T(s)=0.7\,\frac{(10)^2}{s^2+2\cdot10\cdot0.6\,s+(10)^2} $$ $\omega n^2=100\Rightarrow\omega n=10$ rad/s; $2\xi\omega n=12\Rightarrow\xi=\frac{12}{20}=0.6$; DC gain $K=\frac{70}{100}=0.7$. Since $0<\xi<1$ the response is underdamped and the formulas apply. $s^2+12s+100=0\Rightarrow s {1,2}=\frac{-12\pm\sqrt{144-400}}{2}=-6\pm j8$. So the decay rate is $\alpha=\xi\omega n=6$ and $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=10\cdot0.8=8$ rad/s. $$ \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}{\xi}=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-0.36}}{0.6}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{0.8}{0.6}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac43\right)=53.13^\circ=0.9273\ \text{rad} $$ (equivalently $\theta=\cos^{-1}0.6$). $$ t p=\frac{\pi}{\omega}=\frac{3.1416}{8}=0.3927\ \text{s}\approx0.39\ \text{s} $$ $$ \%m=100\,e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}=100\,e^{-0.6\pi/0.8}=100\,e^{-3\pi/4}=100\cdot0.09478=9.48 $$ (the notes write 9.47 — truncated rather than rounded). The final value is not 1 but the DC gain: $y(\infty)=T(0)=0.7$. So $$ y(t p)=y(\infty)(1+m)=0.7+0.7\cdot\frac{9.478}{100}=0.7663 $$ $$ t r=\frac{\pi-\cos^{-1}(0.6)}{8}=\frac{3.1416-0.9273}{8}=\frac{2.2143}{8}=0.2768\ \text{s} $$ (notes: 0.276 s). Note the angle is used in radians . $$ t s=\frac{4}{\xi\omega n}=\frac{4}{0.6\cdot10}=\frac23=0.667\ \text{s}\quad(\pm2\,\%);\qquad\frac{3}{6}=0.5\ \text{s}\quad(\pm5\,\%) $$ $$ y(t)=0.7\left[1-e^{-6t}\left(\cos8t+0.75\sin8t\right)\right] $$ $y(0)=0.7(1-1)=0$ ✓; $y(\infty)=0.7=T(0)$ ✓; $y(0.3927)=0.7(1+e^{-6\cdot0.3927})=0.7(1+0.0948)=0.766$ ✓; $y(0.2768)=0.7$ ✓ (checked numerically). The steady-state error for a unit step is $1-0.7=0.3$ (see [Module 02]( /m/02)). $T(s)=\dfrac{70}{s^2+12s+100}$, poles $-6\pm j8$, $\xi=0.6$, $\omega n=10$, $\theta=53.13^\circ$; $t r=0.277$ s, $t p=0.393$ s, $\%m=9.48$, $y(t p)=0.766$, $y(\infty)=0.7$, $t s=0.667$ s (2 %). - "$\alpha=-6$" : here the notes give the real part of the root , $-6$. In the response formula $y=1-e^{-\alpha t}[\dots]$ used on pp. 5–8, $\alpha=\xi\omega n=+6$ is the positive decay rate. Use $\alpha=6$ in $e^{-\alpha t}$; plugging $-6$ would make the exponential grow. The later computations in the notes do not use $\alpha$, so the results are unaffected. - "$\sqrt{1-3{,}6}$" : should be $\sqrt{1-0{,}36}=\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=0.8$ ($\xi^2=0.36$). The following value $\tan^{-1}(4/3)$ is correct. - "$e^{-\xi\pi\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$" : the division bar is missing — the exponent is $-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=-0.6\pi/0.8=-3\pi/4$, which is what the notes then use. The professor's graph with the exact function: levels $0.7$ (final value) and $0.766$ (peak), time axis to $0.8$ s. The curve crosses $0.7$ at $t r=0.277$ s, peaks at $t p=0.393$ s, dips very slightly (minimum $0.7(1-m^2)=0.6937$ at $2t p=0.785$ s) and is inside the shaded ±2 % band from about $0.59$ s; the formula's $t s=0.667$ s is marked. One difference from the hand sketch: the true curve starts with zero slope (a second-order system with no zero cannot jump in velocity), whereas the sketch starts steeply. Draw the final-value line at $K$ (here 0.7) and a second line at $K(1+m)$. Mark $t r$ on the time axis and let the curve start flat at the origin and cross $K$ there. Put the peak at $(t p,\,K(1+m))$. The next extremum is a dip at $2t p$ of depth $Km^2$ below $K$ — usually tiny. Then mark $t s$ and let the curve flatten onto $K$.

text: $T(s)=\dfrac{16}{s^2+4s+16}$: $\omega n=4$ rad/s, $2\xi\omega n=4\Rightarrow\xi=0.5$. Find $t r$, $t p$, $\%m$, $t s$. $\alpha=\xi\omega n=2$, $\omega=4\sqrt{1-0.25}=4\cdot0.8660=3.4641$ rad/s, $\theta=\cos^{-1}0.5=60^\circ=\pi/3=1.0472$ rad. Poles $-2\pm j3.464$. $t r=\dfrac{\pi-\pi/3}{3.4641}=\dfrac{2.0944}{3.4641}=0.605$ s; $t p=\dfrac{\pi}{3.4641}=0.907$ s; $\%m=100\,e^{-0.5\pi/0.8660}=100\,e^{-1.8138}=16.3$; $t s=\dfrac{4}{2}=2$ s (2 %), $\dfrac32=1.5$ s (5 %). $t r=0.605$ s, $t p=0.907$ s, $\%m=16.3\,\%$, $t s=2$ s (2 %) / $1.5$ s (5 %). Sanity: $t r A designer wants $\%m=10$ and $t s=2$ s (2 % band). Find $\xi$, $\omega n$, the pole locations and the corresponding $T(s)$ with unit DC gain. $m=e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\Rightarrow\ln m=-\dfrac{\xi\pi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$. Square: $(\ln m)^2(1-\xi^2)=\xi^2\pi^2$, so $(\ln m)^2=\xi^2\left(\pi^2+(\ln m)^2\right)$ and $$ \xi=\frac{-\ln m}{\sqrt{\pi^2+(\ln m)^2}} $$ (positive root, since $\ln m<0$). With $m=0.1$: $\ln0.1=-2.3026$, $(\ln m)^2=5.3019$, $\pi^2=9.8696$: $$ \xi=\frac{2.3026}{\sqrt{15.1715}}=\frac{2.3026}{3.8951}=0.591 $$ $t s=\dfrac{4}{\xi\omega n}=2\Rightarrow\xi\omega n=\alpha=2$, so $\omega n=\dfrac{2}{0.591}=3.383$ rad/s and $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=3.383\cdot0.8066=2.729$ rad/s. $\omega n^2=11.45$, $2\xi\omega n=4$: $T(s)=\dfrac{11.45}{s^2+4s+11.45}$, poles $-2\pm j2.729$. $\xi=0.591$, $\omega n=3.38$ rad/s, poles $-2\pm j2.73$. Check: $100e^{-0.591\pi/0.8066}=10.0\,\%$ ✓, $4/(0.591\cdot3.383)=2.00$ s ✓. Unity feedback with $G(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+8)}$. Find $K$ so that $\xi=0.6$, then the criteria. $T(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+8)+K}=\dfrac{K}{s^2+8s+K}$, so $\omega n^2=K$ and $2\xi\omega n=8$. $\omega n=\dfrac{8}{2\cdot0.6}=6.667$ rad/s, $K=\omega n^2=44.44$. Then $\alpha=4$, $\omega=6.667\cdot0.8=5.333$ rad/s. $\%m=9.48$ (only $\xi$ matters); $t p=\pi/5.333=0.589$ s; $t r=(\pi-0.9273)/5.333=0.415$ s; $t s=4/4=1$ s. $K=44.4$; $\%m=9.48\,\%$, $t r=0.415$ s, $t p=0.589$ s, $t s=1$ s. DC gain $T(0)=K/K=1$, so here $y(t p)=1.095$. Same system as pp. 9–10: $\xi=0.6$, $\omega n=10$, $\omega=8$, $\theta=53.13^\circ$, DC gain 0.7. Here are four tempting wrong answers and why they are wrong. $t r=\dfrac{180-53.13}{8}=15.86$ "s" — nonsense, 50 times longer than the true response takes. The formula comes from $\omega t r=\pi-\theta$, an angle in radians because $\omega$ is in rad/s. Correct: $(3.1416-0.9273)/8=0.277$ s. $t p=\pi/10=0.314$ s — too early. The oscillation runs at the damped frequency $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=8$. Correct: $\pi/8=0.393$ s. $y(t p)=1+0.0948=1.095$ — but the output settles at $0.7$, not 1. Correct: $y(t p)=0.7(1.0948)=0.766$. $y(t p)=0.7(1+9.48)=7.34$ — the 9.48 is a percentage. Use $m=0.0948$ in formulas and multiply by 100 only for $\%m$. Correct values: $t r=0.277$ s, $t p=0.393$ s, $y(t p)=0.766$, $\%m=9.48$. Quick checks that catch these: $t r

title: Edge cases
text: - $\xi\to0$ (undamped): $\alpha\to0$, $m\to e^0=1$ (100 % overshoot, the response swings between 0 and 2), $t s=4/(\xi\omega n)\to\infty$ (never settles), $\theta\to90^\circ$ and $t r\to\frac{\pi/2}{\omega n}$, $t p\to\pi/\omega n$. Poles on the $j\omega$ axis. - $\xi\to1$ (critical damping): $\omega\to0$, so $t p=\pi/\omega\to\infty$ and $t r\to\infty$ (the formulas lose meaning — the response no longer crosses its final value), and $m\to e^{-\infty}=0$. The formulas of this module are only for $0<\xi<1$ . For $\xi\ge1$ there is no overshoot and no peak. - Negative real part becomes positive: if any pole has $\operatorname{Re}p 0$, the "criteria" do not exist — the output diverges. - Poles not well separated: the dominant-pole approximation fails (see [How to decide whether a pole is dominant]( /m/08/how-to-decide-whether-a-pole-is-dominant) and the example "When the extra pole is not far enough"). - Zero near the dominant poles: the second-order formulas underestimate overshoot and overestimate rise time; use $y z=y+\frac1z\dot y$ or the full partial-fraction solution. - DC gain ≠ 1: $t r$ is defined by reaching the final value $K$, $m$ is relative to $K$; $\xi$, $\omega n$ and all times are unchanged by $K$.

title: How to solve exam problems
text: 1. If a block diagram is given, find the closed-loop $T(s)$ (unity feedback: $T=\frac{G}{1+G}$). 2. Write the denominator as $s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2$ → read $\omega n$ and $\xi$. Check $0<\xi<1$. 3. DC gain $K=T(0)$ = final value for a unit step. 4. Compute $\alpha=\xi\omega n$, $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$, poles $-\alpha\pm j\omega$, $\theta=\cos^{-1}\xi$ (in radians for $t r$). 5. $t r=(\pi-\theta)/\omega$, $t p=\pi/\omega$, $\%m=100e^{-\xi\pi/\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}$, $y(t p)=K(1+m)$, $t s=4/\alpha$ (2 %) or $3/\alpha$ (5 %). 6. Sketch: final line at $K$, peak at $(t p,K(1+m))$, flat start, $t r$, $t s$ marked. 7. Verify: $t r 1. Find all poles; any with $\operatorname{Re}p 0$ → unstable, stop. 2. Pick the pole(s) closest to the $j\omega$ axis: the dominant ones. Time constant of each: $\tau=1/\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert$. 3. Check separation (rule of thumb ≥ 5×) and that no zero lies near the dominant poles. 4. Reduced model: keep the dominant poles, keep the DC gain $T(0)$. 5. Apply the second-order formulas to the reduced model. If asked for the exact response, do partial fractions and show that the far-pole coefficient is small. 1. From $\%m$: $\xi=\dfrac{-\ln m}{\sqrt{\pi^2+\ln^2m}}$ (with $m$ as a fraction). 2. From $t s$: $\xi\omega n=4/t s$ (or $3/t s$); from $t p$: $\omega=\pi/t p$; then $\omega n$. 3. Poles $-\xi\omega n\pm j\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$; $T(s)=\dfrac{\omega n^2}{s^2+2\xi\omega n s+\omega n^2}$. $\cos^{-1}\xi$ must be in radians next to $\pi$. Set your calculator to RAD, or convert: $53.13^\circ=0.9273$ rad. $\tan^{-1}(-\omega/\alpha)$ on a calculator gives a negative angle and a negative time. The rise time is on the branch $(\pi/2,\pi)$: add $\pi$, or simply use $t r=(\pi-\cos^{-1}\xi)/\omega$. $t p$ and $t r$ use the damped frequency $\omega=\omega n\sqrt{1-\xi^2}$; $t s$ uses $\xi\omega n$. Only $m$ is free of frequencies. If the numerator is not $\omega n^2$, the final value is $K=T(0)$. Overshoot is relative: $y(t p)=K(1+m)$, not $1+m$. $\%m=9.48$ means $m=0.0948$. Formulas like $y(t p)=K(1+m)$ and the inversion $\xi=-\ln m/\sqrt{\pi^2+\ln^2m}$ need the fraction. Far from the $j\omega$ axis = small time constant = fast. Close to the axis = large time constant = slow = dominant. (The notes' wording slips on pp. 1–2 invert this; the mathematics doesn't.)

text: A stable system has poles at $-2$, $-15$ and $-1\pm j3$. Which pole(s) are dominant, and what is the time constant of each? Time constants $\tau=1/\lvert\operatorname{Re}p\rvert$: pole $-2$: $0.5$ s; pole $-15$: $0.067$ s; pair $-1\pm j3$: $1$ s. The pair $-1\pm j3$ is closest to the $j\omega$ axis (real part $-1$), has the largest time constant and is dominant . Note that the imaginary part (3) does not matter for dominance — only the real part does. Check of separation: the next pole ($-2$) is only 2× further left, so a pure second-order approximation would be rough. Find the unit step response of $T(s)=\dfrac{6}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}$ and evaluate each term at $t=1$ s. Is the far pole's contribution small here? Cover-up rule for each of the four fractions of $\frac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}$. $A 0=\frac{6}{1\cdot2\cdot3}=1$; $A 1=\frac{6}{(-1)(1)(2)}=-3$; $A 2=\frac{6}{(-2)(-1)(1)}=3$; $A 3=\frac{6}{(-3)(-2)(-1)}=-1$. $$ y(t)=1-3e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}-e^{-3t} $$ Check: $y(0)=1-3+3-1=0$ ✓, $y(\infty)=1=T(0)$ ✓. At $t=1$: $-3e^{-1}=-1.104$, $3e^{-2}=0.406$, $-e^{-3}=-0.050$; $y(1)=0.253$. The far pole ($-3$) has coefficient $-1$, not small, because the poles are close together (the denominators $p k\prod(p k-p i)$ are not large). Its term is still the smallest at $t=1$ ($0.05$), but the pole $-2$ term ($0.41$) is far from negligible. No single pole dominates strongly — dominance needs separation . For $y(t)=1-\frac{10}{9}e^{-t}+\frac19e^{-10t}$ (p. 2), compute both transient terms at $t=1$ s and their ratio. $\frac{10}{9}e^{-1}=1.111\cdot0.3679=0.4088$; $\frac19e^{-10}=0.1111\cdot4.54\cdot10^{-5}=5.04\cdot10^{-6}$. Ratio $\approx81\,000$ (at $t=0.5$ s it was about 900). The ratio is $10\,e^{9t}$: it grows exponentially — the far pole becomes irrelevant ever faster. $y(1)=1-0.4088+0.000005=0.5912$. When the extrema occur is set by the oscillating factor: $\dot y\propto\sin\omega t$ vanishes at $\omega t=\pi$, so $t p=\pi/\omega$ — the imaginary part of the poles. The notes say: "Reel kısmı 0'a yakın negatif kutupların zaman sabiti düşük olacağından sönüm süresi uzun olacaktır." What is wrong, and what is the correct statement in terms of $\tau$? For a pole with real part $-a$, $\tau=1/a$. A real part close to 0 means small $a$, hence a large time constant ("yüksek"), and a long decay — e.g. $-0.2$ gives $\tau=5$ s, $t s\approx20$ s. The conclusion "decay time is long" is right; the reason should read "zaman sabiti yüksek olacağından".
